descs.en: A blind date. He arrived in a three-piece suit. She came straight from a crash site with dirt on her face. He tried to manage her. She laughed at him.

synopsis.title: Synopsis
synopsis.content:
Ren Hao fixes problems for big companies: kidnappings, scandals, the things that never make the news. He's loud, direct and used to being obeyed, and he says I love you to everyone, including the woman who runs the dumpling shop.

Xu Song-Zhu rebuilds what happened from the wreckage. Flight recorders, scorched memory boards, the last minutes of strangers. His sister sets them up at a French restaurant with candles. He orders her water and tells her to wash her face. She laughs, and tells him he's awfully bossy for a man who's known her an hour.

He loves her out loud from the first week. She can't say it back. And then a passenger jet goes into the sea with a hundred and eighty people on board, on his client's airline, and the woman he loves is the one who has to listen to how it ended.

Opposites · Loud hero · She can't say it · He has to learn to ask · Complete in 40 chapters, plus ten side stories

authorNote.title: Author Note
authorNote.content:
This one is loud and quick and joyful, and then, when it has to be, very quiet. Her job is listening to people's last words, and the book doesn't look away from what that costs her, or from the families who wait for them.

He tries to love her the way he protects clients, with drivers and schedules and a full fridge. She needs room, and the time to find three words she's been afraid of since she was nineteen. Watching a man like that learn to ask first, and a woman like that learn to say it, is the whole of it.

contentWarn.title: Content Warning
contentWarn.content:
21+ · For adult readers.

Loud, funny and romantic, with air accident investigation shown plainly. It includes:

• Love scenes on the page throughout

• A parent's death in an air crash, and grief years later

• Air crashes: wreckage and bodies on the water, recovery, identification, and the families who wait

• Cockpit and cabin recordings of the last moments of a flight

• A funeral, and a child who has lost a parent

• Workplace betrayal, and a relationship placed under public scrutiny

• Controlling behaviour within a loving relationship: tracking, arranging, moving in without asking, and the work of unlearning it

chapters.title: Three-Piece Suit, Flight Suit
chapters.desc: Isla sets her brother up on a blind date. Ren Hao (27) arrives in a three-piece suit with a typed agenda; Xu Song-Zhu (25, crash investigator) arrives from a light-aircraft site with fuel on her boots. He tells her to wash her face. At the taxi rank she kisses him to shut him up.
chapters.epigraph: “Did you just tell me to go and wash my face?”
chapters.content:
On Friday the thirteenth of June, 2025, Ren Hao arrived at the French restaurant at five to seven with a typed agenda in his inside pocket, because his sister had said “dinner, me and a friend, you’re paying,” and he disliked walking into a room without knowing what it was for.

1. Isla: the inspector. Behave (see 22 May).
2. Her friend: air accident investigation. Ask what that involves.
3. Mum’s birthday. Joint present this year, she promised.
4. Wine (ask first).

He was twenty-seven. He ran a risk consultancy on three floors of a tower in the business district, and he had sat across tables from men who kept armed guards in their kitchens. His sister, two years younger and still in possession of a laptop charger he’d lent her in 2019, remained the only person alive who could make him feel he’d lost an argument before it started.

Isla sat down opposite him in a green dress, already reading the menu. “She’s coming from a crash site. She’ll be late. Don’t be difficult about it.”

“I’m never difficult.”

“You brought a list.”

He took his hand away from his jacket. “It’s short.”

At ten past seven Isla rang the friend’s duty phone. At twenty past she rang her mobile and put it on speaker, low, under the candles.

“Where are you?”

“Leaving.” A woman’s voice, bright and quick, with wind behind it.

“Please don’t tell me you’re still at the crash site.”

“I’m not at the crash site. I’m in the car park of the crash site.”

“That’s the same place!”

The woman laughed, and rang off, and Ren Hao watched his sister put the phone away with an expression he’d known since she was four, which meant that something was going exactly to plan.

✦ ✦ ✦

Xu Song-Zhu had aviation fuel on her boots.

She also had a streak of dried mud along her left cheekbone that she didn’t know about, a tear at the knee of a dark blue flight suit worn with the top half tied round her waist, and a bruise coming up above her wrist where a wing strut had caught it. She’d spent six hours in a soybean field forty minutes north of the city beside a four-seater that had lost power on climb-out and been put down by its pilot, quite beautifully, between two rows of irrigation pipe. The pilot was alive, with a broken ankle and two cracked ribs, and he’d cried when she told him the nose gear had done exactly what it was designed to do.

She stopped beside the table at twenty to eight and looked at Ren Hao the way someone might look at an interesting component.

He stood. Isla said, “Song-Zhu, my brother. Hao, Song-Zhu,” with enormous innocence, and Song-Zhu shook his hand with mud still under her thumbnail and sat down in the chair he’d pulled out, and he saw her notice that he waited until she’d settled before he sat.

“Very French,” she said, of the candles.

“It’s a French restaurant.”

“I can tell. The water glasses are judging me.”

“I’ve ordered you still water. And I told the kitchen about the coriander,” he said.

She looked at Isla. “You told him about the coriander?”

“It was the only thing I told him,” said Isla, which was a lie, as Ren Hao would work out in a little under twenty minutes.

✦ ✦ ✦

The first course was a chilled leek and potato soup sent out with the chef’s compliments. Ren Hao tasted it, put his spoon down and lifted one finger to the waiter.

“I’m sorry. This has gone cold.”

The waiter looked at the soup, and then, for help, at Song-Zhu.

“It’s meant to be cold. It’s vichyssoise. That’s the entire point of it,” said Song-Zhu.

“Take mine away anyway,” said Ren Hao, with dignity, and Song-Zhu put her face in her napkin. Before the waiter could reach it, she pulled his bowl across to her side and ate it herself.

Isla’s phone buzzed. She read it, and sighed beautifully, and stood up.

“Work. The consulate. I’m so sorry. You two eat.” She kissed her brother’s cheek and squeezed Song-Zhu’s shoulder and was gone between the tables before he’d finished getting up.

He sat down again slowly. He looked at the empty chair. Then at the woman across from him, who was eating his soup and watching him with great interest.

“I’ve just understood something,” he said.

“That this is a date?”

“That my sister left at five past eight.”

She glanced at his jacket. “She told me in March. She said if she told you, you’d bring a list. You brought a list anyway.”

“It was for a family dinner.”

“Read it to me.”

“No.”

“Then I’ll guess. One: Isla’s inspector. Two: ask the friend what she does.”

He took the page out, unfolded it, uncapped his pen, and drew a neat line through item one. She laughed out loud, a real laugh with her whole body in it, so that two people at the next table turned round.

“You actually crossed it off.”

“She’s not here. It can’t be discussed.”

“Oh, I like you. That’s going to be a problem,” she said.

✦ ✦ ✦

By the main course he’d learned that she disliked people who talked loudly in restaurants, loved convenience-store coffee with something close to religion, and had once slept nine hours across four chairs in an airport in a country she refused to name. She’d learned that he ran a corporate risk firm, that his parents taught at a university in Vancouver, and that he was fond of schedules.

“They prevent unnecessary complications,” he said.

“Not every complication is unnecessary.”

He decided not to argue, and asked instead what she did at a crash.

The brightness went somewhere quieter. She turned her glass on the cloth. “Today I walked the ground. Where it touched first, where it slid, where it stopped. Fuel from both tanks into a clean jar, held up to the light. Then a farmer told me it was upside down, which it wasn’t, and a fireman told me it was on fire, which it wasn’t either. People are bad at the last ten seconds. Fear rewrites them. On other days there’s a recorder, and I listen to that instead. People think we’re there to find someone to blame. We’re not even allowed to. We’re there to find out what happened, so it doesn’t happen again.”

“Do you ever get used to it?”

“No. If I ever get used to it, I should stop.”

He held her gaze, and nodded once, the way he’d nod at something he meant to remember word for word.

She nodded at the folded page by his bread plate. “What’s item three?”

“My mother’s birthday. Isla promised a joint present. She’s promised a joint present every year since she was fourteen.”

“What does your mother like?”

“Crosswords. In English, because she says it keeps her honest. Newspapers she disagrees with. Being right.”

“Then get her a book of crosswords with one mistake in it, and a red pen. She’ll be happy for a month,” said Song-Zhu.

He considered this with the face of a man reviewing a proposal from a department he hadn’t known existed. Then he uncapped his pen and wrote, under item three, crosswords (one error), red pen, and she watched him do it and managed not to laugh, which cost her something.

“You’re not crossing that one off.”

“No. That one’s good.”

Then he looked at her cheek.

“There’s something on your face. Left side.”

She rubbed the right. Then her forehead.

“You’re making it worse. There’s a washroom by the bar. You might want to wash your face,” he said, entirely seriously.

Song-Zhu went still.

“Ren Hao.”

“Yes.”

“Did you just tell me to go and wash my face?”

“I’m suggesting that—”

“In a French restaurant.”

She laughed so loudly the waiter dropped a spoon. It wasn’t a restaurant laugh. It came up from somewhere under her ribs, and she put her hand over her mouth to stop it and couldn’t.

“You’ve ordered my water, and told the kitchen what I don’t eat, and made a list, and sent back the soup, and now you’re sending me to wash my face. You’re awfully bossy for a man who’s known me an hour,” she managed.

She leaned in across the candle, close enough that he could smell fuel and grass and something like oranges under it.

“Is this how you talk to terrorists, or are you just nervous around girls?”

For the first time that evening he was caught entirely off guard. She saw it land. And against what was clearly his own will, his mouth moved: a small, startled smile.

“Neither. And I don’t talk to terrorists. I talk to their accountants.”

Before dessert he went to the washroom himself and came back with a wet linen napkin and held it out without a word. She looked at it. Then she took it, and wiped her cheek, and he said, “Left,” and she gave him a look of pure murder and did the left.

✦ ✦ ✦

At twenty to ten they were on the pavement, arguing about a car.

“I can get a taxi myself.”

“I know you can. It’s already booked.”

“Ren Hao. I’m twenty-five.”

“I never suggested otherwise.”

“Then stop looking at me like I’m about to walk into the traffic.”

He wasn’t rude. He wasn’t arrogant the way men in that kind of suit usually were. He just seemed to have an almost medical need to make sure everything round him was working. The waistcoat buttoned all the way down. The cuffs exactly where cuffs were meant to be. A man who’d send a calendar invitation before asking someone to dinner. She found it unbearably funny.

A black car pulled into the rank. He opened the rear door.

She didn’t get in. She looked up at him, which was a fair way up.

“Do you think I’m difficult?”

He considered it much too seriously. “I think you’re unpredictable.”

“That’s a diplomatic answer.”

“It’s an accurate one.”

Her eyes went, for half a second, to his mouth.

“One more thing. You’ve been talking too much,” she said.

She took a fistful of his waistcoat and pulled him down and kissed him.

Hard, with no polite little pause to see whether he minded. One moment Ren Hao was standing by a car door with his phone in his hand, wondering whether he could ask her to message him when she got in. The next, she had him by the waistcoat at a taxi rank in the business district. His free hand hovered near her waist, waiting for permission. Then he put it there. His other hand came up to her face, and his thumb found her cheek, carefully, on the side where the mud had been, and he kissed her back. Her fist tightened. She tasted of the chocolate from dessert, and when she bit his lower lip, lightly, he made a sound he’d never made in a public place in his adult life.

When she let go she was smiling. His tie had gone sideways. One waistcoat button had come undone and he hadn’t felt it go.

“Think of it as a review. Not bad. Room for improvement,” she said.

“Where?”

“Stop telling women to wash their faces.”

He laughed, short and genuinely surprised, the first unguarded sound she’d had from him all night. She liked it more than she’d meant to.

She got in. Just before the door closed she leaned back out.

“Oh, and Hao? Don’t make a list about me.”

The car pulled away. He stood on the pavement with his phone open on the taxi app, watching her move away from him at forty kilometres an hour, and touched his lower lip. Then he did up the button, and stood there a while longer anyway.

✦ ✦ ✦

At eleven he rang his sister.

“WHY. DO YOU THINK I NEED HELP FINDING SOMEONE?” he said.

Isla had clearly been waiting by the phone. “Because you do. Did you tell her to wash her face?”

He said nothing.

“Oh, Hao.”

“It was a reasonable observation.”

“Good night, Hao. Be nice to her,” said Isla, and rang off laughing.

✦ ✦ ✦

Just before midnight Song-Zhu sat cross-legged on her bed with her hair wet, eating instant noodles out of the pan.

Isla (Matchmaker): ALIVE??

Song-Zhu: Unfortunately.

Isla (Matchmaker): He rang me at eleven. At full volume. What did you DO

Song-Zhu: He told me to wash my face.

Isla (Matchmaker): HAHAHAHAHA I KNEW HE WOULD

Isla (Matchmaker): And?

She thought about the moment at the taxi rank when his hand had hovered and then decided.

Song-Zhu: I kissed him.

Three dots appeared. Disappeared. Appeared again.

Isla (Matchmaker): YOU WHAT

Song-Zhu: Taxi rank. Good night, Isla.

She dropped the phone on the duvet and found she was smiling at the wall.

✦ ✦ ✦

At fourteen minutes past midnight, across the city, Ren Hao sat at his desk with his waistcoat on the bed and his tie somewhere in the bathroom, and wrote an email. Isla had sent the address in March, with a photograph of the two of them at a dumpling place and the message you would like her, she would hate you, try anyway. He read the draft three times.

To: Xu Song-Zhu
Subject: Dinner, Friday 13 June: minutes
Present: Ren Hao, Xu Song-Zhu. Isla Ren (until 8.05; to be discussed with Isla).
1. Item one withdrawn.
2. Soup. Ms. Xu correct. Noted for the record.
3. Washroom. Withdrawn, with apologies.
4. Review (taxi rank). Received. Room for improvement accepted.
5. Any other business: I would like another opportunity.
Ren Hao

He sent it before he could improve it. It was possibly the most ridiculous thing he’d ever written, and he didn’t regret a word.

chapters.title: Follow-Up
chapters.desc: She answers his midnight minutes with a voice note from a field. A twin turboprop on its back, two people on board; she pulls the recorder from the tail. He turns up at the hangar fence with lunch for twelve.
chapters.epigraph: “She’s not my friend. She’s a menace.”
chapters.content:
Just after eight on Saturday morning a voice note arrived from a number Ren Hao didn’t have.

He was in his office at the top of his three floors, alone except for the cleaners, halfway through an exposure report on a shipping client with a habit of sailing where it shouldn’t. He knew who it was before he opened it. Nobody else he knew would answer a midnight email with a voice note.

Forty-three seconds. A low mechanical roar, a clank, somebody far off shouting about a trolley, and then her.

“Good morning, Mr. Ren. Before you start: yes, I’ve eaten breakfast. Yes, I’ve washed my face. Both sides. I took your advice about personal hygiene extremely seriously.”

A pause in which he could hear her smiling.

“Is it rude to answer an email with a voice note? Because you sent me minutes, Hao. With numbered items.”

He looked at the email in his sent folder. In daylight it looked like something a lawyer would send.

“Anyway. I’m at an airfield up north. We’ve got a twin down in a field past the perimeter.”

Her voice didn’t drop or go dramatic. It went smaller, the way a voice does when someone steps into a narrower room.

“Two on board. Neither of them made it. I’m waiting for the photographer before anyone touches anything. There’s something I want in the tail.”

An engine running up somewhere.

“Item five. Any other business. Next time I’m choosing the restaurant. I’ll tell you when I’ve got an evening. Try not to schedule me, Hao. Bye.”

He played it a third time. Not for the accident; he’d heard enough to know two deaths in a field weren’t an anecdote to her. For the last line.

He saved the number, typed her name, and after some thought added something in brackets, and left it. Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots)

Joyce, his assistant, who didn’t believe in weekends for anybody else, rang at half past. “The board call’s moved from ten to eleven. Finance wants to know if you’re coming to lunch.”

“Cancel mine. Send my apologies.”

“Shall I book you somewhere else?”

He looked at the phone in his other hand. “No. I’ll sort out lunch myself.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At a quarter to nine Xu Song-Zhu stood in wet grass two hundred metres short of a runway, looking at what was left of a twin turboprop.

It had come in low on a charter from the coast, a businessman and his pilot, clipped the top of a line of trees short of the threshold and cartwheeled. The left wing had folded back along the fuselage at an angle that made the whole aircraft look put away. The nose was buried to the windscreen. The bodies had gone at dawn, after she’d seen them, after the photographer had, after everything had been written down in the order it was found.

“Photographs complete?”

Dexter, two years senior and in possession of a clipboard for every occasion, ticked a box. “All done. Overview, ground marks, both wings, engines, cabin.”

“Anything moved before we got here?”

“Fire crew cut the right cabin door to reach the passenger.”

“Write that on its own line, with the time they gave you. I don’t want anyone in six months thinking the door came off on impact.”

They walked to the tail along the plank path the police had laid. On a type this size the cockpit voice recorder sat in the tail cone behind an access panel: an orange box the size of a shoebox, FLIGHT RECORDER DO NOT OPEN stencilled on its side in two languages, because the one thing that was never black about a black box was the box.

She crouched and didn’t touch it. Photographs first: panel closed, panel open, the unit in its tray, the connectors, the plate close enough to read the serial. Then measurements. Then her hands.

People talked about recorders like oracles. They weren’t. A recorder couldn’t tell you what anyone had meant, or what had broken, or what two men had been thinking while the trees came up. What it gave you was sound: voices, switches, alarms, the engines, the wind on the airframe, the note a propeller makes when it starts to go wrong. And sound, laid beside the wreck and the logs and the radar and the weather and the farmer with his hands, could tell you a great deal.

She lifted it out, heavier than it looked, and held it in both hands a second the way she always did. Not superstition, she’d have said. There were two people’s last minutes in it, and it seemed rude to just put it in a bag.

“Seal.”

She signed across the seal and Dexter signed under her and wrote the time. “Chain of custody. It stays with me until the lab has it. If a journalist asks, the recorders have been recovered and will be examined in due course.”

“Recorders, plural? It hasn’t got a data recorder.”

She stood, and her knees cracked. “They don’t need to know that today. And if you’re about to ask about my date, I’ll put you in the bag with it.”

“Who said anything about a date?”

“Who told you?”

“Your friend Isla rang the duty phone at ten past seven last night to ask if you’d left the site yet.”

“She’s not my friend. She’s a menace.” She peeled off a glove. There was a new email.

Good morning, Song-Zhu.
I’m sorry about the two people on board. I hope the work goes safely.
Understood on dinner. I’ll leave the arrangements to you, as requested.
One question: do you prefer Song-Zhu, or Zhu?

She smiled at the screen in a way that made Dexter look at her and then carefully look away.

Song-Zhu: Song-Zhu. Zhu sounds like you’re calling me in for a disciplinary.

Song-Zhu: Don’t worry. I’m hard to discipline.

✦ ✦ ✦

Before ten he messaged to ask whether she’d had lunch. A minute later she sent a photograph of an empty paper coffee cup on the bonnet of a car.

Ren Hao: Is that meant to be an answer?

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): 👍

He rang a restaurant he trusted and asked how many people normally worked an air accident site on a Saturday. They said they had no idea. He said, then make it twelve.

Which was how, just before noon, he came to be standing at a chain-link fence on the edge of a small airfield in a pale blue shirt with the sleeves rolled to the elbow, beside a delivery van and a great many paper bags.

“You sure this is the place, sir?” said the driver.

“Yes.”

“You work here?”

“No.”

The driver looked at the bags, and at him, and at the fence. “Right.”

Beyond the fence was a flying club: a squat hangar with its doors half open, a windsock, small aircraft tied down on the grass, and at the far end of the runway a white tent and blue tape in a field. In front of the hangar, at a long table, people in dark overalls bent over laptops. He saw her straight away, flight suit zipped to the collar this time, clipboard on her hip, moving quickly, the way someone moves who has somewhere else to be before she’s finished being here.

He rang her.

“It’s eleven fifty-three,” she said.

“Good nearly afternoon. Are you busy?”

She looked at the sealed bag on the table that had two men’s voices in it. “Not at all. I’m on holiday.”

“That’s unfortunate. I’m outside. By the gate with the sign about dogs.”

She turned round slowly. Across fifty metres of tarmac and grass stood a man in a pale blue shirt beside a van.

“Ren Hao. How much lunch?”

A pause. “Twelve.”

She shut her eyes. “You bought lunch for twelve people without asking me.”

“It seemed simpler.”

She laughed, out loud, and Dexter looked up from his photographs.

“That’s a very expensive way of finding out whether I’m hungry.”

“Are you?”

She’d last eaten at five that morning, in a petrol station. “Yes.”

“Good. Come and get it.”

She ended the call. “Who was that?” said Dexter.

She looked at the fence. “A problem.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She came through the gate and stopped three metres short of him and looked at the bags, and at him, and at the bags.

“On a Saturday. In that shirt.”

He held one bag out on its own. “To bring lunch to whoever’s working with you. That one’s yours.”

Rice, chicken and greens. Cut fruit. Water. And tucked flat between them, a small packet of wet wipes.

She held it up between two fingers. “Are you implying something?”

His eyes went, with enormous restraint, to her cheek.

Her hand flew up. “Is there something on my face?”

“Not at the moment.”

“You’re still thinking about last night.”

“I remember it very clearly.”

She shook the packet at him, laughing and trying not to. Polished shoes on a grass verge. Sleeves rolled the same number of turns on each arm. Not a crease anywhere.

“You look like you’re on your way to a board meeting.”

“I’ve eaten in stranger places than a hangar.”

“Name one.”

“A building site in the rain, under a tarpaulin, with a client whose foreman had just been kidnapped.”

“All right. That one’s better.”

Then, more seriously, because he’d been looking past her at the tent and the tape: “I’m sorry about this morning. The two of them.”

He wasn’t being polite. He’d heard the voice note and understood what was in it, and he was saying so once, plainly, and then he’d leave it alone.

She nodded, and because that was easier than answering, looked at the bags. “Do you always feed people when you’re nervous?”

“Only when I’m trying to make a good impression.”

“That’s dangerous. I might start expecting it.”

“That wouldn’t be a problem.”

There was no hesitation in it at all. He set it down between them like a box of rice, and she looked away first.

“Inside, before you feed the entire aviation industry,” she said.

✦ ✦ ✦

The hangar was loud. Someone was running a compressor at the far end, a radio on a shelf played a song from ten years ago, and a small offended-looking man in a club jacket was making tea in a corner like it was his sacred duty.

Song-Zhu put her bag on the table. “Everyone, apparently we’re having lunch. This is Ren Hao. He’s an overenthusiastic delivery service.”

Dexter looked from him to her and smiled slowly.

“Don’t,” said Song-Zhu.

“I haven’t said a word.”

“Your face has.”

There were nine of them, counting the tea man, and Ren Hao took the three spare boxes out to the two police officers at the tape and the crane driver without making anything of it. He met Mabel Wong, the investigator-in-charge, small and grey-haired with reading glasses on a cord, who shook his hand and looked at him three seconds longer than was comfortable. He met two engineers from the authority and the club’s chief instructor, who’d known the dead pilot twenty years and wasn’t eating much.

Song-Zhu watched him over her rice. He didn’t treat the hangar as beneath him. He didn’t flinch at the compressor or ask why everything was dirty. When the chief instructor began, haltingly, to talk about the pilot, who’d learned to fly here at seventeen and once landed a glider in a car park, Ren Hao put his box down and gave the man his whole attention and said nothing until he’d finished.

“Your boyfriend’s generous,” Dexter murmured.

She choked on her water. “He’s not my boyfriend.”

“Yet.”

Across the table Ren Hao looked up at exactly the wrong moment, while she was still glaring, and their eyes met.

✦ ✦ ✦

Later he noticed that she hadn’t touched her own lunch. She was at the far end of the table with a technician, pointing at a run of photographs, the chopsticks lying side by side on the lid.

He waited one minute. Then another. Then he went round.

“Your lunch.”

She looked at it like it had appeared from nowhere. Then she smiled, slow. “You’re doing it again. Managing me.”

“Reminding you.”

She ate a piece of chicken, pointedly, looking at him. “See? Eating. You’re easy to please.”

“Not where you’re concerned.”

Her chopsticks stopped halfway. Dexter became deeply interested in a photograph of a wingtip. Mabel Wong turned a page in a manual she’d certainly already read.

Song-Zhu pointed the chopsticks at his chest. “You’re dangerous.”

“So I’ve been told.”

✦ ✦ ✦

By half past one he’d stayed much longer than he’d meant to. He’d learned in an hour and a half that her working days had no shape, that investigators spent most of their lives waiting for other people to finish things, and that she drank coffee when she was tired and forgot water even with the bottle in her hand. She was more serious at work than at dinner. Not cold; focused. When a technician got a number wrong in the log she corrected it so lightly the man barely noticed he’d been corrected. He liked watching her do it more than was sensible.

She caught him at the hangar door. “You’re going? It’s practically still morning.”

“Would you like me to stay?”

She thought about it honestly, and he liked that too. Then she looked out at the tent. “I’ve got to go back to work.”

“I know.”

“You’re not going to ask when I’m free next?”

“You said you wanted to choose. I’ll wait.”

“Can you actually wait? How long for?”

“That is a difficult question,” he said.

He held out a card. Thick white stock, his name in plain black letters, Managing Director, nothing else.

“I’ve already got your number.”

“That’s my mobile. This is the office.”

“Do you have a different phone number for every department of your life?”

“Not every department.”

“That’s worse!” But she slipped it into the chest pocket of her flight suit behind her phone. Then she reached up and straightened his collar.

It was already straight. They both knew it. Her fingers stayed at the edge of it a little longer than they needed to, against his neck, and he stood still and let them.

“Try not to miss me too much,” she said.

He didn’t have to think. “I already do.”

Her smile faltered, only for a second, and he saw it, and liked having seen it more than he could have explained.

“Go. Bye, Hao,” she said.

She stood in the hangar door and watched him walk back to the gate: polished shoes on wet grass, posture annoyingly perfect. A man who’d spent his Saturday feeding nine strangers at an accident site because a woman had sent him a voice note.

Oh, she thought. This is going to be interesting.

✦ ✦ ✦

Mr. Yau, who’d driven for the firm six years and noticed everything and said almost nothing, glanced at him in the mirror on the airfield road. “Was lunch all right, sir?”

Ren Hao thought about the fuel and wet grass, and the wet wipes, and her fingers at his collar. “Yes.”

His phone buzzed.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): The team says thank you. The tea man says you can come back.

Ren Hao: Did you finish yours?

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Yes, Dad.

He laughed, alone in the back of the car, and Mr. Yau’s eyes flicked to the mirror and away.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Dexter says you should come again. I told him you’re not a canteen.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): But you can come again.

Ren Hao: When?

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Hao.

Ren Hao: Sorry. Take your time.

A minute later she sent a photograph with no caption: an evidence bag with an orange box inside, sealed, signed twice across the seal, a label in her handwriting, lying on a steel table under a strip light.

He understood she hadn’t sent it to show off. She’d sent it the way you’d tell someone this is where I am, and this is what I carry.

Ren Hao: Be careful.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Always.

The fields gave way to the ring road and the ring road to the city. Three reports were waiting for him, two calls, and a meeting already moved twice. He sat in the back of his own car thinking about a woman who’d told him not to schedule her, and for once didn’t mind having something in his life he couldn’t plan.

chapters.title: What She Listens To
chapters.desc: Noodles behind the cargo terminal. He asks what she does; she tells him she listens to the last thirty minutes of strangers. A pilot’s words she won’t repeat. In the car park she kisses him against his car.
chapters.epigraph: “Everything sounds completely normal. Right up until it doesn’t.”
chapters.content:
Ren Hao had started to recognise the sound of his phone when it was her, which was embarrassing, and he knew it. He got messages all day from clients, partners, his sister and a great many people who wanted to tell him things that could have been an email. Now, whenever the screen lit, some small part of him hoped for a badly lit photograph with a one-word caption.

It was Thursday the nineteenth of June. He was in the back of the car outside a client’s building after a meeting that had run forty minutes over, and Mr. Yau was waiting to be told where to go.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Dinner.

A plastic tray holding something that had once been rice, something that had once been vegetables, and something brown.

Ren Hao: Did you cook that?

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): I bought it. From a machine. The machine cooked it. Badly.

Ren Hao: Can you cook?

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Eggs. Also instant noodles, which taste different every time depending on the water. It’s a skill.

He laughed, and in the mirror Mr. Yau’s eyes moved to him and away.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Are you free tonight?

Ren Hao: I can be.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): You sound like a man who has to rearrange a government to have dinner. Come and get me. I’m choosing. And don’t wear a suit, or I’ll feel underdressed and have to be rude to you about it.

She sent an address. He looked down at his charcoal trousers and his tie.

“Home first, please. Then somewhere else,” he told Mr. Yau.

✦ ✦ ✦

The address was a gate in a long grey fence on the far side of the airport, in the part the public never saw: the operational compound, where the aviation authority kept its engineers, its stores and, in a low brick building with no sign at all, its accident investigators. There was a barrier, a security hut, and a guard who looked at Ren Hao’s car and then his clipboard with the face of a man deciding whether to be impressed.

He waited outside the barrier in a navy polo shirt and black trousers. He’d left his watch at home, which had felt, on the way out of the door, like going out without his trousers.

She came through the side gate just before eight in a grey T-shirt and a dark jacket, staff lanyard round her neck and a takeaway coffee in one hand, though it was evening. She stopped, looked him slowly up and down, and smiled.

“Well. You look normal.”

“Is that a compliment?”

“From me it’s practically a proposal.”

Close to, he could see she was tired: something underneath crash-site tired, sitting behind her eyes. He opened his mouth.

“Have you eaten?” he said.

She stared at him, and then laughed. “Oh my God. Is that the first thing you’re going to say to me every time?”

“Probably.”

“Hello, Mr. Ren’s driver,” she said, past him, to the car.

“Good evening, miss,” said Mr. Yau, to the barrier.

“There’s a noodle place behind the cargo terminal. The pilots go there. The soup’s scalding and the tables are sticky and you’ll hate it,” she told Ren Hao.

“I won’t hate it.”

“Then I’ll be very disappointed,” said Song-Zhu, and got in.

✦ ✦ ✦

The noodle place had six tables and a television showing a football match nobody was watching. The soup came in bowls the size of hubcaps, and the man at the counter knew her name, didn’t know his and wasn’t interested in finding out. Ren Hao ate everything and said nothing about the tables, and she watched him not saying anything about the tables with enormous enjoyment.

She had a great many stories, and most of them started halfway through and needed three questions before he understood them. He didn’t mind. He liked how she used her hands, and how her eyebrows went up before she’d said why something was funny, and how she abandoned one story halfway because she’d remembered a better one.

She was telling him about a colleague who’d locked himself out of a secure room with his own lunch inside when she caught him looking.

“Your serious face,” she said.

“This is my face.”

“That’s unfortunate for you.”

He laughed, and put his chopsticks down. “Can I ask you something? I know what your job’s called. I’d like to know what it is.”

She put hers down too.

She held up a second finger. “Most aircraft carry two recorders. Neither of them’s black. They’re orange, so you can find them in a field or at the bottom of the sea. The flight data recorder is numbers: height, speed, heading, what the engines and the controls were doing, thousands of things many times a second. And the cockpit voice recorder. That’s the one people want to know about, because it’s people. A microphone in each pilot’s headset, one for the jump seat, and one in the ceiling that hears the whole cockpit. Everything they say to each other and on the radio. Every switch, every warning, every noise the aeroplane makes. The old ones kept the last thirty minutes on a loop. Newer ones keep two hours. But the part I live in, nearly always, is the end.”

He’d gone still.

“We download it in the lab, and then somebody has to listen. There’s a room for it. Soundproofed, no windows. Four lines of waveform on a screen, the data recorder’s timeline underneath, a pair of very good headphones, and you play it. Again and again. A second at a time, sometimes. You match the voices to the numbers. Then a group of us sits down and makes a transcript, and argues about every word.”

“And you listen first.”

“Mostly. It’s good, being alone in there. I talk to myself.”

“What about?”

“The words. I read the transcript back out loud, so I can hear when one’s wrong.”

She turned her glass on the sticky table.

“Do you want to know the hard part? People think it’s hearing somebody die. Sometimes it is. But that isn’t usually the bit that stays. It’s the ordinary things. One pilot asking the other if he’s checked something. Somebody saying the weather’s better than forecast. Somebody laughing. Somebody saying they’ll be home tomorrow and they’ll bring something back.”

She looked at her hands.

“Everything sounds completely normal. Right up until it doesn’t.”

The football went on silently above them.

“You’re listening to the last thirty minutes of strangers’ lives,” he said.

Her fingers stopped on the glass.

“Sometimes less. Sometimes more,” she said.

He didn’t ask the next question. He filled her glass from the metal jug, and she watched him do it, and then looked away to the window.

✦ ✦ ✦

While the man at the counter was taking their bowls she said, “There was a pilot. A long time ago. A freighter, a night flight. They’d had trouble for nearly forty minutes and didn’t know what it was. At first it’s all procedure: checklists, readings, calls. They’re doing everything right. And then there’s a point where one of them stops talking about the aircraft and says something about his family. Something ordinary. He asks the other one to tell his wife something.”

He waited.

“I’m not going to tell you what he said.”

“You don’t have to.”

She gave a small laugh with nothing in it. “It’s not mine. It belongs to his wife. I can’t tell you what I had for lunch on Monday. But I could draw you exactly how his voice went on that word. I know where it sits on the waveform.”

His jaw had tightened, and she saw it.

“Don’t do that face. The one that says you want to fix it.”

“I wasn’t going to.”

“You’re thinking about it.”

“Perhaps,” he said.

He was used to difficult conversations. His whole business was people in situations they couldn’t control: men who’d lost companies overnight, families with a ransom figure in a phone call at three in the morning. He understood fear. This was something else. She sat in a room with no windows and listened to the moment people stopped having a future, and then went home and ate noodles out of the pan and sent him photographs of bad dinners.

“How long have you been doing it?”

“Nearly three years. Straight from university.”

“Does anyone ever ask how you are?”

She blinked. It was such a simple question, and she found she had nothing ready for it. “At work. Mabel does.”

“And outside work?”

“Not really.”

Something moved in his face. It wasn’t pity, which she’d have hated, and he seemed to know that. It looked more like a man who’d just found a whole room in her life he hadn’t known was there, and was standing in its doorway.

She reached across and stole the last piece of pickled radish from his saucer. “Your eyebrows are sad.”

“I don’t think you need me to tell you how to feel about your work. But if you ever want to talk about it, I’ll listen. Even at three in the morning,” he said.

“That’s a dangerous promise. I might actually ring.”

“I hope you do.”

✦ ✦ ✦

It was nearly eleven when they came out. He’d sent Mr. Yau home at nine and said he’d drive her himself, in the car the firm kept for exactly that kind of evening, which she found extremely funny. The car park behind the cargo terminal was almost empty under the yellow lights, and somewhere beyond the fence a freighter was running its engines up for the night.

She walked ahead, swinging her bag by its strap, and turned round by his car with the brightness gone out of her face.

“Did I make you uncomfortable? Talking about the room?”

“No. Why?”

She looked down at her trainers. “Because I don’t usually tell people. Some go quiet. Some get curious in a way I don’t like, like I’ve got something juicy in my bag. And some tell me how brave I am, which I hate. I’m not brave every day. Some days I’m just tired. I like my job. I like that once in a while someone changes a procedure because of what I heard, and nobody has to hear it again. But I don’t want to spend my whole life being the girl who listens to people die.”

He took her hand. “You’re the woman who argues with me about water and thinks twelve people can be fed out of one bad decision, and you’re very good at your job. I listened to you talk about it. You care about getting it right even when getting it right is the worst part. I don’t need to understand all of it to respect it.”

She stepped into him without warning, and he caught her before he knew he’d moved. She put her face against his chest. His shirt smelled of soap and something woody, and under her ear his heart went steady and slow, which was absurdly comforting for a sound.

“You’re very warm. That wasn’t a compliment,” she said into his shirt.

“I’ll take it anyway.”

When she lifted her head he was looking down at her with an expression she hadn’t seen on him yet, quieter than the amused one and the patient one, underneath both. She took a handful of the front of his polo shirt and kissed him.

It wasn’t like the taxi rank. There was no joke on the end of it. She’d spent an evening telling someone about the room with no windows, which she never did, and he hadn’t tried to make it smaller, or brave, or make it go away. He’d just held on. So she kissed him because she wanted to.

For about three seconds he kissed her back with enormous restraint. Then she pulled him closer and the restraint went. He turned them both until her back was against the cold side of the car, one hand flat on the roof beside her head, the other spread low on her back, and kissed her slowly and thoroughly and not at all like a man in a polo shirt being normal. The freighter beyond the fence went to full power and the noise came across the car park like weather, and she laughed into his mouth.

He lifted his head. “You’re going to crease my shirt.”

“Are you serious?” She pulled him back down by the collar.

He laughed into the kiss, and this time there was nothing careful in it. When he drew back an inch she chased his mouth, and he liked that so much he did it again on purpose to make her do it again.

He brushed her hair off her face and his thumb stopped on her cheekbone. “You’re beautiful.”

No joke on it. She hadn’t asked, and he hadn’t waited to be asked.

“You’re getting better at this,” she said.

“You’re making it hard to say good night.”

“Good,” said Song-Zhu.

✦ ✦ ✦

He drove her home. She sat with one leg folded under her and watched the streets go by, and for once didn’t talk. At a red light she said, “Why did you come to dinner on Friday? Isla says you didn’t know.”

“I thought it was dinner with my sister. She said she was bringing a friend from work who needed feeding. That should have warned me.”

“And when she left?”

“I thought, she’s set me up, and I’m going to ring her at eleven and shout.”

He watched the light.

“And then you ate my soup, and I thought, I’ll ring her at eleven and shout, and I’ll thank her.”

She laughed. A few streets later, looking straight ahead: “What did you think, when you first saw me? Honestly.”

“That you’d had a very hard day.”

“That’s not what I meant!”

“I liked you. With the mud, and the boots. When you laughed at me, I was sure,” he said.

She looked at him in the passing streetlight and smiled out of the window the rest of the way home.

✦ ✦ ✦

He walked her up to the third floor, along a corridor with a flickering light and a pot plant someone had given up on. She stood with her keys in her hand.

“You’re the one who’s good at arranging things,” she said.

“I thought you didn’t want to be scheduled.”

“Improvise.”

He laughed, low, put his hand on her waist and kissed her, and kept it there afterwards like he’d forgotten it.

She unlocked the door and turned back. “Better. Hao? Thank you for listening.”

“Any time,” said Ren Hao, and waited in the corridor until he heard the lock turn.

✦ ✦ ✦

Hao (Three-Piece): Home.

Song-Zhu: I liked tonight. Even though I talked about work all night.

Hao (Three-Piece): Most of all because you did.

Song-Zhu: You’re not scared of me? I listen to dead people for a living.

Hao (Three-Piece): I run a company for people having the worst day of their lives. I don’t think either of us needs to be frightened of the other.

She read that twice before she answered.

Song-Zhu: Why me, then? You don’t do this for everybody.

He sat in the dark in the firm’s car outside his own building with the engine off and thought about a woman who’d come to a French restaurant in boots that smelled of fuel and kissed him at a taxi rank to shut him up, who could talk about death with a composure that frightened him and then laugh at a badly cooked egg.

Hao (Three-Piece): Because I like you.

Song-Zhu: I like you too. Don’t let it go to your head.

Song-Zhu: Next time I’m choosing again. And I want dessert. And you kiss me before I go in.

Hao (Three-Piece): I don’t think that will be a problem.

There were recordings Xu Song-Zhu would remember for the rest of her life, because remembering them was part of the job. That night, lying in the dark with the phone on the pillow, she found herself remembering other things: the warmth of him through a polo shirt, and the way he’d asked whether anyone outside work ever asked how she was, and then waited for the answer.

chapters.title: His Firm
chapters.desc: She visits his firm: three floors, a receptionist’s birthday, a kidnap negotiation live on a screen. After hours, explicit, against the glass on the thirty-second floor.
chapters.epigraph: “Tonight you’re just Hao.”
chapters.content:
On Friday the fourth of July Xu Song-Zhu discovered that Ren Hao was a great deal more frightening at work.

His territory turned out to be three floors of a glass tower in the business district with its own lifts. She had a lieu day after a week of nights on the twin from the airfield, and on Tuesday she’d said on the phone, you’ve seen where I work, now I want to see yours, and he’d said Friday so fast she suspected he’d been waiting. She’d imagined an office. She hadn’t imagined an atrium.

Hao (Three-Piece): You’re here?

Song-Zhu: There’s a very tall building in front of me. Might be yours. Your receptionist is looking at me.

Her phone rang. “Don’t move. I’m coming down myself.”

“I’m not a fugitive, Hao. Why do you sound like you’re running an extraction?”

“Wait there,” he said, and she could hear him smiling.

The receptionist was about sixty, with silver hair in a neat bun, a coral cardigan that took real courage and a name plate that said Ruby. When Song-Zhu gave her name, Ruby typed, and something came into her face that looked like delight held down hard by professionalism. “Miss Xu. Please do take a seat.”

He came across the lobby from the lifts in a charcoal three-piece suit, every hair in place, looking like a man who could make everyone in the building nervous by asking the time. When he saw her the seriousness went somewhere else and the smile came instead, and before she’d finished standing up he’d pulled her into a hug, both arms, in the middle of his own lobby.

“Missed you.”

“We saw each other on Monday.”

“Four days,” said Ren Hao.

Then he turned to the desk. “Ruby. Happy birthday.”

He went round the end of the desk and hugged her too, lifting her an inch off the floor so her reading glasses swung on their chain. “There’s a cake in the fourth-floor kitchen and nobody touches it until you’ve had the first slice. Joyce has orders.”

“Thank you, Mr. Ren,” said Ruby, pink to the hairline.

A man with a stack of folders came past, and Song-Zhu watched Ren Hao’s face reorganise itself into something cool and level for a “Morning, Raymond.”

Raymond walked on quite fast. Ren Hao took her hand.

“Come on.”

“You hold hands with people at work?”

“You aren’t people,” he said, and heard it.

She squeezed his fingers. “Lead on, boss.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The client floor was glass meeting rooms, open-plan desks, phones ringing and a printer somewhere at the back making a noise like a goose in pain. Everyone who passed him said good morning, and every one of them stood a little straighter as they said it.

On the floor above, Joyce met them at the lift, early thirties, tablet under one arm and phone at her ear. Beside her desk, sitting upright on a small tartan cushion, was a white dog about the size of a loaf of bread. The dog stood up. Its tail went so fast its whole back end moved.

Ren Hao crouched down in the three-piece suit and the dog put both front paws on his knee.

“Hello, sweetheart. Have you been the best girl on the floor? I love you. Yes, I do. You’re the only one in this building who never gives me any problems.”

Song-Zhu looked at Joyce. Joyce looked at her. Then both of them looked down at the managing director crouched on the carpet in a suit worth more than Song-Zhu’s car, entirely unbothered. So that was how it worked. The staff got brief instructions, the clients got chosen words, the receptionist got a hug and a cake, and a small white dog on a tartan cushion got declarations of love.

He stood, brushing white hair off his trouser leg with all the dignity available. “This is Joyce’s dog. Momo.”

Song-Zhu crouched, and Momo came to her at once and leaned her whole weight against Song-Zhu’s shin. “Does she know you love her?”

“Yes.”

“Good. Wouldn’t want her getting the wrong idea.”

Joyce, finally, gave up and smiled.

✦ ✦ ✦

The top floor was quieter: smaller offices, a room of screens he called operations, and two secure meeting rooms with keypads on the doors. One door was propped open, and inside a whole wall was a screen. A map with three pins in a country she knew from the shape of its coast. A list of names, half of them initials. A timeline down one side, every entry timed. And in one corner a call window with no picture, only a waveform moving.

A man in a headset was speaking low. “Ask her to repeat the question exactly as it was put. Word for word.”

Ren Hao stood beside her. “Kidnap for ransom. A client’s regional manager, taken on Tuesday between two sites. We’re advising the family and his company. We’re not police and we don’t talk to the people who have him. The family chose his brother-in-law to do that. We sit behind him.”

She read the timeline. Call 3, 14.52. Demand restated. Communicator held position. Call 4, 21.10. Proof-of-life request sent.

“Proof of life?”

“Questions only he can answer. His first dog’s name. What he ate on his wedding day. The answers came back last night, right first time. He’s alive.”

She recognised the shape of it, though not the subject: every contact logged, every change written down the moment it happened, before anyone could remember it differently.

“You have people out there?”

“Local partners. We’ve used them since our first year. A separate team sits with the family. They don’t need to watch this.”

An analyst turned round: another message to the family’s phone, a different number. Ren Hao was across the room in three steps. “Nothing goes to the family until it’s verified. Log the number and the time, preserve the message exactly as received. If it’s a second group trying to cash in, I want to know before they do.”

There was nothing in his voice now of the man who’d hugged Ruby, or the man on the carpet with the dog. His questions were short and exact. He let everyone finish what they were saying. When he gave an instruction nobody had to ask what he meant. He wasn’t loud. He didn’t need to be.

When he came back she said, “You’re good at that. Being in charge of something terrible.”

“Thank you. The family liaison wants me on the next call. Wait in my office? There’s coffee. And don’t wander into any rooms with keypads,” he said.

“Do I look like someone who wanders into restricted areas?”

He gave her a long, frank look. “Yes.”

✦ ✦ ✦

His office was big without being decorated: a desk facing the window, a meeting table, a low leather sofa, shelves of reports and a few books with broken spines he’d clearly read. The outer wall was glass from floor to ceiling, and the city lay below in the morning haze, the harbour flat and grey at the edge of everything.

On the desk was one photograph: Ren Hao at about eighteen with his arm round a much smaller girl in a school blazer, both squinting into sunlight. She picked it up.

“You’re snooping,” he said from the doorway. He’d loosened his tie.

“Isla?”

“The day I left for university.”

“You’re very fond of her.”

“It’s the only answer you’re getting,” he said, and took the photograph out of her hands and put it back exactly where it had been, at exactly the same angle, while she bit the inside of her cheek.

“You’re going to hate me here. I make a lot of jokes, and I don’t respect authority.”

He put his arms round her by the window and said “Missed you” into her hair again, like he’d been saving it.

✦ ✦ ✦

By seven that evening she’d learned that his office was best at dusk, when the lights came on in the tower opposite floor by floor like somebody filling in a form, and that Joyce’s dog liked her better than him.

The regional manager had been released at ten past four, alive, thinner, at a petrol station on a road with a number for a name. The brother-in-law had rung the operations room afterwards and cried down the phone for three minutes, and nobody in the room had said a word. Ren Hao had shaken every person’s hand, shut his own door for a quarter of an hour, and then sent everyone home.

Now the floor was empty and the lights over the desks had gone to their evening setting. He stood at his desk with a document. She sat on the edge of his meeting table swinging one foot.

“You said ten minutes twenty minutes ago.”

“I was interrupted.”

“By who?”

He looked at her over the top of the page, and put it down.

She slid off the table and stopped in front of him. “Your office is very private. Do you ever bring anyone in here? Apart from clients.”

“Staff.”

“Ren Hao. You’re being difficult on purpose,” she said, and took hold of his waistcoat in one fist the way she had at the taxi rank.

He looked down at her hand. “Careful. You’ll undo it.”

Six small horn buttons, done up all the way. She looked back up at him. “Maybe I want to.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The first kiss was hers. She pulled him down by the waistcoat before he could say anything sensible, and he made a sound into her mouth and kissed her back slowly, like a man with every intention of taking his time.

She disagreed. She tugged with both hands, and something gave with a small sharp tick and went skittering across the floor.

He lifted his head. “That was a button off a waistcoat made for me in a shop with no sign on the door.”

“Then you’d better take it off before I find the rest of them.”

He laughed against her mouth, low and helpless, and she felt it all down her body. When she reached for his jacket he caught her wrists. “Let me.”

He stepped back half a pace. Jacket over the back of the sofa. Then the waistcoat, the five buttons left, one at a time, watching her face, and she watched his hands and forgot to be funny. The tie. The cufflinks, side by side on the desk. He came back to her in his shirtsleeves with his collar open and the city behind him gone dark blue and full of lights, and she realised she was holding her breath.

“You’re staring.”

“Appreciating. Enormously.”

He put both hands on her face and kissed her again, and this time it wasn’t slow at all. He walked her back three steps, four, until her shoulders met the window. The glass was cold through her blouse and she gasped, and he stopped at once.

“Don’t you dare stop,” she said.

He undid her blouse with the whole city behind her, one button and then the next, slow enough that it was plainly on purpose, and put his mouth to her throat, then her collarbone, and she spread her palms flat on the glass because she had to hold on to something.

“Can anyone see?”

“Thirty-second floor. Tinted glass. They’d need a helicopter. Do you want to know what I’m going to do first?” he said against her skin, in a voice she’d never heard from him in any restaurant.

“Tell me.”

So he told her, the way he’d given instructions in the room with the screen: exactly, in order, with nothing left out. What he’d take off her, and in which order. Where he’d put his mouth, and for how long. What he’d do when she started to shake, and what after that. He said what he meant, a foot from her face with his hands on her waist, and every word went through her like current.

Then he did all of it, in that order. He drew her trousers down and she stepped out of them and her shoes together, and he knelt on his own office carpet and kissed the inside of her knee, and higher, and higher, until she was saying his name at the ceiling with her head back against the glass. When she tried to pull him up too soon he held her hips to the window and said, “Not yet. I told you what comes next,” and she laughed and swore at him and then couldn’t do either. She came with her hands flat on the cold glass and the whole lit city at her back, and he held her up through it, and afterwards stayed with his forehead against her stomach, breathing as hard as she was.

When he stood she pulled at his shirt with fingers that weren’t working, gave up on the tiny buttons and dragged it over his head. His belt. The rest. She put her hand on him and his eyes closed.

“Now, Hao.”

He turned her gently to face the city, her palms on the window, and kissed the back of her neck, his hand spread low on her stomach to hold her against him. He took her so slowly she thought she’d lose her mind, telling her each thing half a second before his body did it, so she knew exactly what was coming and still couldn’t bear it when it came. In the tower opposite a cleaner was hoovering an empty floor, small and far away and lit, and Song-Zhu watched her through the haze of her own breath and didn’t care.

“Tell me if it’s too much,” he said against her ear.

“It’s not enough.”

He laughed, a breath against her neck, and gave her more, and when she said his name in a voice that broke in the middle he stopped talking altogether. He came with his face in her shoulder and one hand flat on the glass over hers, their fingers laced, and the sound he made was so unlike anything she’d heard from him in a lobby or a room full of screens that she kept it, and took it home, and thought about it for a week.

✦ ✦ ✦

Afterwards they lay on the sofa, which was too short for him, with his jacket over them both. He’d drawn the blinds halfway at some point, so the bottom of the window showed the two of them reflected, a tangle on dark leather, and the top showed the towers and the sky.

“Your staff would be devastated. They think you’re terrifying,” she said into his chest.

“Perhaps I am.”

She lifted her head. “Not with me.”

“No. Not with you,” said Ren Hao, and something in the way he said it made her smile go and something softer come instead.

“Was that all right? The glass,” he asked.

“It was so far beyond all right that I’d like it in writing.”

“Tell me if I ever do something you don’t want. Even in the middle.”

“I’ll tell you. I’ll probably shout it,” said Song-Zhu, and he nodded like a term had been agreed.

✦ ✦ ✦

By half past eight she was on his sofa in her blouse, buttoned wrong, hair destroyed and lipstick nowhere at all, watching him try to rescue his shirt in the mirror by the door. The shirt was creased from collar to hem. His hair was doing something it had clearly never been allowed to do before. She laughed until he turned round.

There was still a button under his desk somewhere. She got down on her hands and knees and found it in under a minute, under the radiator, and held it up between finger and thumb like a recovered component. “Here. Logged. Chain of custody.”

He took it and looked at it, and at her kneeling on his floor with her blouse buttoned wrong, and put it in his trouser pocket with great care, the way she’d held the recorder in the field.

“Dinner. Somewhere you don’t have to be Mr. Ren. With noodles,” she said.

In the lift she leaned against the wall with her hand in his. “Do you actually love your job?”

He watched the numbers going down. “Most of the time. Sometimes because of the terrible parts. People only ring us when something’s already gone wrong. We can’t always stop it. Sometimes the most we can do is make the damage smaller.”

“You sound like me. Don’t try to fix me,” she said.

The lobby was empty, Ruby’s desk dark, a slice of birthday cake on a plate under a napkin at the corner of it, clearly left for somebody. As they crossed the atrium he said, “I do reserve the right to buy you lunch.”

She laughed so loudly the security guard looked up. “No more wet wipes.”

“We’ll see,” said Ren Hao.

✦ ✦ ✦

At a noodle shop with plastic stools by the ferry pier, his phone buzzed.

Joyce (and Momo): Mr. Ren, Momo is sitting outside your office again. She isn’t waiting for you. She’s waiting for Miss Xu.

He turned the screen round. Song-Zhu gasped with delight, and went on eating his noodles, because she’d finished her own.

“She loves me. She hates Raymond,” she said.

“She loves everybody.”

Song-Zhu leaned across and kissed his cheek with broth on her mouth. “You’re not half as frightening as everyone thinks.”

“That’s a shame. I quite like being frightening,” he said, and caught her hand across the table.

She kissed his knuckles first. “You can be frightening on Monday. Tonight you’re just Hao.” He lifted her hand and put his mouth to her knuckles, and for the rest of the evening that was exactly who he was.

chapters.title: Hooked
chapters.desc: He can’t stop. His driver follows her taxi for nine nights. She notices the plate, does the biscuit test, and laughs, which is worse. He fires Mr. Yau; she makes him rehire him with a raise.
chapters.epigraph: “Well. You do. But I like you anyway.”
chapters.content:
By the middle of July Ren Hao had a problem, and he understood it perfectly: its cause, its symptoms and roughly what a cure would look like. He had no intention of taking one. Xu Song-Zhu could vanish for fourteen hours, send him thirty seconds of engine noise with one cheerful sentence on the end, and improve his entire day.

Early on Monday a photograph arrived: a paper cup of coffee balanced on the wing of an aircraft, the sun coming up behind it.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Breakfast.

Ren Hao: That’s coffee. Coffee isn’t breakfast.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): You sound like my mother.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): There’s a cat here. His name is Chairman. He’s supervising. He gets fish, and unlike some people he doesn’t ask me if I’ve eaten every twenty minutes.

The cat was small and extremely ginger and sat beside a red toolbox with the face of someone who’d been sent the wrong file.

Ren Hao: Is there fish for you?

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): I hate you.

Across his breakfast table Joyce, who’d come round with the week’s papers because he had a seven o’clock call, read his diary aloud, got three answers in a row that were all “Good,” and gathered up the papers and left him to it.

✦ ✦ ✦

The first hangar had been an accident. The second was an excuse. By the third, even Mr. Yau had stopped asking.

Ren Hao told himself he was visiting a client: a maintenance contractor whose risk assessment his firm had finished in June, and which wasn’t expecting a visit from the managing director on a Tuesday afternoon, or ever. Neither was Song-Zhu. She stood by the engine of a cargo aircraft on a stand with a clipboard under her arm, listening to a technician explain something about a bearing, a thumbprint of grease on her cheekbone.

He’d been in the middle of an argument with a senior partner when he decided to leave the office. He’d promised himself ten minutes. She looked up, saw him and smiled, and the argument stopped existing.

“What are you doing here?”

“Working. Nearby.”

“How nearby?”

“Near enough.”

The technician looked between the two of them. “Your boyfriend?”

Song-Zhu’s eyebrows went up. Ren Hao said nothing whatsoever.

“He’s a visitor,” she told the technician.

“Right. Visitor,” said the technician, and left them to it.

She came over with the clipboard against her chest. “If you keep turning up at my work, people will think you’ve got a hobby.”

“I have. You.”

She reached up and wiped a smear of grease off his sleeve that she’d put there with her own thumb a second earlier. “That’s not a hobby, that’s a symptom. Now you’re dirty. Now you belong here. Coffee? The machine makes something that’s legally coffee.”

When she reached back for his hand without looking, he took it without thinking at all.

Twice more that week he found reasons to be in buildings she was in. Once he sat beside her for twenty minutes while she frowned at a long document full of times, tapping her pen on her thumb, murmuring each sentence under her breath before she typed it. When a colleague disagreed with her about a timing she let him finish, and then she was right. She didn’t need to be the loudest person in a room. She only needed to be correct.

“You’ll get bored,” she said, when she closed the file and found him still there.

“I doubt it.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Mr. Yau had driven for the firm six years. He was dependable and quiet and good at knowing what Ren Hao wanted before Ren Hao had finished deciding to want it. He also noticed things, and wrote them down in a small black notebook in the glovebox, a habit from an earlier job he didn’t talk about.

On Monday he noticed the long way back from a client, past the airport compound. On Tuesday, a dinner cancelled seven minutes after a voice note. On Wednesday, forty-five minutes outside a hangar.

On Thursday, late, Mr. Ren rang him at home and asked him to follow a taxi.

Mr. Yau, who was in his slippers, put down his tea. “Sir?”

“She’s leaving the compound now. Her phone’s nearly flat. I’d like to know she gets home.”

There was a pause long enough to have a whole opinion in it. “Understood, sir.”

Ren Hao had his reasons and they were good ones. Her hours had no shape. She’d mentioned, as a joke, a taxi breaking down on the expressway at one in the morning and the driver suggesting she walk. He knew the figures on what happened to women alone in cars at night in every city his firm worked in, because knowing them was his job. He’d imagined a dozen small things going wrong, and without quite deciding to, he’d arranged for one of them not to.

He didn’t consider it surveillance. He considered it a precaution. That distinction, he was going to discover, existed entirely inside his own head.

Mr. Yau (Wheels): Miss Xu has arrived home safely, sir.

Ren Hao: Home?

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Alive. Battery 2%. Night x

He told himself he’d stop after two or three nights. Then there was another late shift, and another, and it became the end of his day: the last emails, a message from Mr. Yau, a message to her. He learned to read her moods from her punctuation. A full stop meant tired. An exclamation mark meant amused. Three question marks meant he’d said something stupid. No punctuation at all meant she was eating.

He’d got good at reading her. He hadn’t yet got good at understanding her.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the ninth night she rang him just before midnight, as he was taking his watch off.

“Hello, Mr. Ren. Are you busy? Do you know a Mr. Yau?” Her voice was suspiciously cheerful.

He went completely still. One second. Two. “Yes.”

“Lovely man,” said Song-Zhu.

He said nothing at all, and she laughed: not angry, not even especially offended. Profoundly delighted. Which was much worse.

“He’s very professional. He hasn’t said a word to me all week. He just keeps being there. I noticed on Tuesday: a grey saloon, no company badge, two cars back on the expressway. Then Wednesday, same car. So I wrote the plate in my notebook, because I’m a professional, and tonight I tested my theory. I asked the taxi to go round by the old fish market, which nobody ever goes round by, and there he was. Then I went into a convenience store and bought biscuits and came out the other door onto the other street, and he was waiting on the corner opposite. He’d worked it out. He’s good, Hao. So I knocked on his window and asked if he’d like a biscuit.”

Ren Hao made a sound he hadn’t made since he was fourteen.

“He said no thank you, miss. Then I asked for his card, and he gave it to me, because I think he’d decided it wasn’t worth lying, and I said I’d sort it out with his boss. And now I’m sorting it out with his boss.”

“Did he frighten you?”

She was still smiling; he could hear it. There was something under it now. “Hao. Why?”

He didn’t have an answer ready, which didn’t happen to him. He could have said her hours were impossible, that he knew what the world was like for a woman alone in a taxi at one in the morning. All true. None of it answered what she’d asked.

“I wanted to know you got home safely.”

“You could have asked me.”

“I do ask. And you tell me.”

She let out a breath that wasn’t a laugh. “Then why the driver? I’m not a confidential package, Ren Hao.”

He looked at the floor. “I know.”

And then, to his astonishment, she laughed again. “Oh my God. You actually put a tail on me.”

“Please don’t call it that. It was an arrangement.”

She could barely breathe. “An arrangement. You had me followed home for nine nights and you want to call it an arrangement.”

He lay back on the bed and looked at the ceiling. He’d faced hostile boards and talked a frightened man off a seventeenth-floor ledge. He’d never in his life been as thoroughly beaten as by one woman laughing at him down the phone.

“I’ll stop it. I’ll tell him tomorrow.”

“Not tomorrow. Tomorrow’s Saturday. The poor man’s followed my taxi for nine nights on his own time. Let him have a lie-in. He didn’t ask to be your romantic security detail. Listen. I like that you care. But you have to let me decide what I need. If I want picking up, I’ll ask. I’m not going to get into the wrong car to prove a point. I’m twenty-five and I take apart aeroplanes. And tell Mr. Yau thank you. He got me home, didn’t he?” Her voice came down out of the laughter.

“Song-Zhu—”

“Good night, handsome,” she said, and rang off.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Saturday morning Mr. Yau sat in Ren Hao’s office at eight o’clock exactly, in a pressed jacket, with his notebook in his inside pocket.

Ren Hao folded his hands on the desk. “I owe you an apology. I asked you to follow Miss Xu’s taxi. It was outside your job and it was wrong of me, and the responsibility’s mine. She knows.”

“Ah. Yes, sir. She does.”

Ren Hao opened a drawer and took out a single sheet of paper. “I think it’s best if you leave the firm. Not because of your work, which has been flawless for six years. Because I put you somewhere you should never have been put, and I don’t want you carrying my private decisions round in your glovebox. A full year’s salary and the best reference I’ve ever written.”

For the first time that morning Mr. Yau looked alarmed. “With respect, sir, I don’t think that’s necessary.”

Ren Hao picked up his pen to sign, and his phone rang.

“Good morning. Have you sacked Mr. Yau?”

He shut his eyes. “How do you know that?”

“I rang him to ask how he was. I had his card. He said you’d asked him in for a conversation, and he sounded like a man walking to the gallows.”

“I put him in an impossible position.”

“So you’re sacking him for your mistake. You made a stupid decision. You’re allowed to apologise for it without somebody else losing his job. That’s not taking responsibility, Hao, that’s moving it onto him and calling it generous.” Her voice was clear.

Through the glass Mr. Yau stood in the corridor, straight, reading a fire-safety notice.

“Keep him. And give him a pay rise,” said Song-Zhu.

“You don’t negotiate my payroll.”

“I’d be excellent at it. You’ve already decided, haven’t you?”

He looked at the sheet of paper. “Have a good day, Song-Zhu.”

“You too, darling.”

He tore the sheet in half, then in half again, and called Mr. Yau back in. “Your job’s unchanged. The additional arrangement ends here, for good. Your salary goes up from next month, because you did your job well and then did something that wasn’t your job better than I did. And if Miss Xu rings you again, you may answer.”

At the door Mr. Yau stopped, and said with great care, “She’s a very nice young woman, sir. She bought me biscuits.”

Ren Hao laughed out loud. “Get out, Mr. Yau.”

Mr. Yau, smiling slightly, got out.

✦ ✦ ✦

She rang that evening while he was still at his desk. “Did you keep him? With a rise? And did you apologise properly, not one of your board apologies?”

“Properly. Yes to all three.”

“Then I’ve got a real question. Why didn’t you just tell me you were worried?”

Outside, the evening traffic moved in long slow ropes of light. Beside the photograph of him and Isla there was a new one now. Joyce had found it on the firm’s social account from a client dinner, printed it and put it there without a word: Song-Zhu at a restaurant table laughing at something out of frame, and him beside her, not laughing, looking at her. He hadn’t known anyone had taken it.

“I thought if I made sure you were safe, I wouldn’t have to bother you with it.”

“You don’t bother me when you worry, Hao. Well. You do. But I like you anyway. I’d rather you told me than arranged me. Do you understand the difference?”

He thought about it properly. “I’m starting to.”

She was quiet a second. “Good. And if you want someone to pick me up, you ask me. I’ll probably say no. Sometimes I’ll say yes, and then it’ll be because I wanted it. I miss you too, you know.”

He stopped moving. She’d said it the way she’d have told him the weather, with no idea what it did to him.

“When can I see you?”

“Tomorrow. The noodle place by the ferry pier. And you’re not allowed to send a car.”

He closed the report he hadn’t finished.

“You’re stopping work?” she said, hearing it.

“Because I miss you.”

A small, pleased laugh. “Was that so hard?”

“Extremely,” said Ren Hao.

✦ ✦ ✦

He came on Sunday by taxi. She was already at a table by the window in a pale blue shirt with the sleeves rolled, and when he bent to kiss her cheek she said, “No driver? Nobody behind a lamp post?”

“Nobody.”

She took a small paper bag from under her chair and put it on the table. Inside was a packet of biscuits: same brand, same flavour, same convenience store.

“For your driver. He gave his to the security guard at your building. I checked,” she said sweetly.

He laughed so loudly the man at the next table dropped his chopsticks, and reached across and took her hand, and she let him. They talked about her week and his meetings and a hangar coffee machine that had finally died with dignity, and she stole his pickles. Somewhere between the noodles and dessert he understood something. He’d spent nine nights making sure he knew where she was, and the thing he wanted was simpler and much harder: for her to tell him, because she wanted to.

“You’re doing that face. The one where you’ve just decided something,” she said.

He lifted her hand and kissed her knuckles. “I’m going to keep missing you. Out loud.”

“That’s your big decision? Very impressive,” she said, and leaned across the table and kissed him, quick and warm and on purpose, and went back to her noodles.

He was, he realised, entirely and helplessly hooked. And she knew it, and was having a wonderful time.

chapters.title: The Schedule
chapters.desc: He makes her a colour-coded week. She burns it in the sink. The fight ends against the sink and then on her sofa, explicit, laughing, over the laundry he doesn’t mention.
chapters.epigraph: “Because I don’t want you to run my life.”
chapters.content:
Ren Hao had made a mistake, and it was a beautiful one: colour-coded, professionally formatted, printed on heavy cream paper, three pages in a navy folder with a clear plastic cover.

He’d spent three evenings on it. It allowed for her working hours, as far as anyone could know them; her briefings; site visits that came without warning; her journey to the compound; her eating habits, which frankly needed intervention; and the fact that she forgot to sleep when a case got interesting. He’d even left blank spaces. He thought the blank spaces were generous.

On Saturday the ninth of August he arrived at her flat at half past ten with the folder under one arm and a bag of groceries in the other. She opened the door barefoot, hair clipped up in a way that had clearly happened by accident, in an enormous T-shirt with a faded cartoon rabbit on the front.

“What’s in the folder, Hao? Is it legal? Is it about me?”

“Yes to both.”

She considered him the way she might consider a known hazard at the door of a building, and stood aside. “Come in. I already regret this.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Her flat was small: a sofa that had seen things, a kitchen along one wall, one bedroom, a narrow balcony facing the back of the next building, where someone kept a great many orchids. Books in stacks by the sofa, not on shelves. Three mugs on the coffee table in three stages of abandonment. A laundry basket in the hall, overflowing, and beside it a heap of clean clothes that hadn’t made it into anything, and one sock lying on its own in the doorway like a casualty.

Ren Hao noticed all of it and said nothing at all.

“Make your own coffee. I’m the host. Hosts delegate,” she said.

While he worked out which of her cupboards held mugs and which held only lids, she sat on the arm of the sofa and opened the folder.

XU SONG-ZHU · WEEKLY ROUTINE (DRAFT)

Monday in pale blue. Tuesday in green. Wednesday in a soft yellow. Blocks for meals, work, travel, rest, exercise, and one every day in careful lilac, labelled personal time. At the bottom of the third page, in a beautifully aligned box with a hairline border:

Flexible adjustments may be made in line with operational requirements.

He came out with two mugs. “Your schedule. A draft. Your hours are irregular and you forget to eat, so I built in room to change it.”

She put her finger on a block. “Why is there a lunch box on Tuesday?”

“Because you should eat lunch on Tuesday.”

“Am I a person or a department? Why have I got opening hours?”

He sat beside her. He pointed at a long empty box at the end of Saturday. “That pink one’s your lighter day. Usually. And that’s for us. I thought we could keep Saturday evenings.”

She looked at the box, and shut the folder gently, and stood up.

She took the long-nosed lighter from the kitchen drawer, the one for the hob, which hadn’t sparked on its own since spring. She slid the pages out of their sleeve. She ran the tap a little, so the sink was wet.

He stood up. “Song-Zhu. Wait.”
