She held the corner of Monday over the sink and clicked the lighter. A small blue flame caught the cream paper and turned orange and began, neatly, to climb. She dropped all three pages in together, and they flared and curled. Tuesday went brown and Wednesday went black and the lilac boxes marked personal time went up in a little rush of light, and she turned the tap on full, and it was over in a hiss and a smell of smoke and wet ash.

“Flexible adjustments,” she said.

He shut his eyes. “Oh my God.”

Above the kitchen door the smoke alarm, which had never once gone off for her cooking, chose this moment to discover its purpose. It shrieked. Song-Zhu put her hands over her ears and laughed. Ren Hao looked at the alarm, and at her, and took off his jacket, and stood on one of her dining chairs in his shirtsleeves and polished shoes, fanning the ceiling with the empty navy folder while she held the chair steady and told him he was doing it wrong.

“I’ve had training in crisis management,” he said from up there.

“It isn’t a crisis. It’s toast-level smoke.”

It stopped. In the silence the orchid neighbour’s radio came on across the gap between the buildings, playing something cheerful. He climbed down, and folded the empty folder in half, and put it on the counter beside the sink like a flag lowered at sunset.

✦ ✦ ✦

He wasn’t angry. That was the first thing she noticed. He stood in her kitchen looking at the black remains of three evenings, mainly bewildered, like a man who’d pressed a button and watched the lift go sideways.

“Don’t look like I’ve drowned your firstborn. You made me a timetable.”

“I was trying to help. Why did you set it on fire?”

She leaned back against the counter. “Because I don’t want you to run my life.”

“I wasn’t trying to run your life.”

He meant it. That was the whole trouble. He cared so much that he sometimes forgot there was a difference between looking after someone and organising them.

She folded her arms. “I know you want me to eat and sleep and not spend sixteen hours in a room listening to other people’s worst moments. But I don’t want to be one more project on your desk.”

He looked at the ash settled round the plughole. “You’re not a project.”

“Then don’t give me opening hours.”

He let out a breath. “I don’t think I can win an argument with someone who sets fire to the evidence.”

She burst out laughing, and he lost the fight with his face. She pulled him across the kitchen by the hand and put her arms round his waist, and he held her.

“I did leave you a blank evening. Saturday. Completely blank,” he said into her hair.

“Oh, you’re unbelievable,” she said, and shoved his chest, and he caught her hand, and that was when the argument turned into something else.

✦ ✦ ✦

She was still laughing, and he was looking at her with that patient, helpless expression that always made her want to kiss him until he forgot whatever sensible thing he was about to say. She took hold of his shirt with her wet hand.

“You’re planning something,” he said.

She kissed him. He answered at once, and she leaned back against the edge of the sink and pulled him with her. It still had a little of the fight in it. She could feel it in how he held her, a fraction harder than usual, a half-second’s pause before he kissed her again, like he was deciding whether he’d been told off.

“I can burn the folder too,” she said against his mouth.

He laughed and kissed her again, smiling this time. Her hands went up his chest and left damp prints on his shirt, and when she touched his face her fingers smelled of smoke. He kissed her palm. She kissed his jaw, and the corner of his mouth, and he spread his hand at the small of her back and pulled her off the sink and against him, and she bit his lower lip, and he stopped asking questions.

He tried to get them both to the sofa without letting go and his foot caught the laundry basket. He looked at the basket, and at the heap of clean clothes that came up to his shin, and at her. She waited with great interest to see what he’d say. He said nothing. He picked her up.

She shrieked and grabbed his shoulders. “Hao! Put me down!”

“Why?”

He settled her higher, her legs round his waist, and stepped over the whole heap, the shirts and the towels and the escaped sock, without looking down, like a man crossing a stream he’d crossed every day of his life.

“You’re very good at obstacles,” she said into his neck.

He put her down on the sofa, which complained, and stood over her breathing harder than he’d have admitted, his hair out of place and her wet handprints on his shirt. She pushed a piece of hair off his forehead.

“You’re handsome. Even when you’re carrying me over the laundry.”

“Most of all then,” said Ren Hao, and kissed her.

✦ ✦ ✦

The sofa wasn’t built for two people to forget the world on. One cushion kept sliding. She complained about it twice, and the second time he threw it across the room without looking where it went.

She was laughing when she pulled his shirt over his head. She was still laughing when he got the rabbit T-shirt off her and put his mouth on her breast, and then she wasn’t. Her hands went into his hair. He kissed his way down her stomach and she lifted her hips so he could drag her shorts down, and he knelt on her floor and pulled her to the edge of the cushions by her thighs, not gently, and she gasped his name with a laugh at the back of it and then no laugh at all. She’d told him she wanted it rough and he’d listened. She held the back of the sofa with one hand and his hair with the other and came with her heel digging into his shoulder and her head thrown back against a cushion halfway to the floor.

Then she sat up, flushed, hair everywhere, pushed him back by the shoulders until he was the one on the sofa, and climbed into his lap.

“My turn.”

“Is that on the schedule?”

“The schedule’s in the sink,” she said, and undid his belt.

He lifted his hips to let her pull his trousers down, and she took him in her hand and watched his face change, and sank down onto him slowly, all the way, until he swore under his breath in a language she hadn’t known he spoke.

She rode him on her terrible sofa in the middle of a Saturday morning with the sun coming through the balcony door and the orchids next door going pink in it. She set the pace: slow until he begged her with his hands on her hips, then fast until he couldn’t speak. The sofa knocked against the wall and they both laughed, breathless, and then neither of them could spare the air to laugh. He held her by the waist and looked up at her like something he’d been told about and never expected to see. When she came again she leaned down and put her forehead to his and said his name into his mouth, and he followed with his arms locked round her back and his face in her neck.

“Your neighbours,” he said eventually, into her shoulder.

“Eighty-three and seventy-nine and both deaf since 2019. I’m a professional investigator.”

He laughed until she nearly slid off him.

✦ ✦ ✦

By late afternoon she lay with her head on his chest under a blanket she didn’t remember fetching. His shirt was somewhere. The sun had crossed the floor and was lying on the laundry heap, which he still hadn’t mentioned. She traced a line on his palm with one finger.

“Are you still upset about the schedule?”

He held up one hand like a man taking an oath. “I’ll burn the next one myself.”

They lay in a silence that was comfortable and only a little sticky. Then he said, “Would you tell me when you know you’re working late? I don’t want to arrange anything, or have anyone pick you up. I just don’t want to be sitting there waiting for a message and inventing reasons it hasn’t come.”

She lifted her head. “I can do that. I’ll forget sometimes. And sometimes I won’t know till the last minute myself.”

“Then tell me then. And tell me when you’re free, so I can ask to see you.”

She reached up and kissed him properly. “That’s much better than a lilac box.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He found his watch under the coffee table and his shirt behind the sofa. His tie, apparently, was in the bedroom, though he couldn’t remember either of them going in there. He stood in the evening light and saw the laundry heap again in all its glory.

He looked at it. He looked at her. She raised one eyebrow and waited. He turned his back on it.

“Good decision!” said Song-Zhu.

“Can I order us something? You haven’t had anything since breakfast,” he said.

“Something messy. Something you couldn’t possibly put in a colour-coded food plan.”

They ate on her sofa out of the cartons: noodles, a spicy aubergine that went everywhere, and dumplings with chives and prawn. She had one leg tucked under her. He tried hard to keep the aubergine off his trousers, and after watching him struggle she handed him a napkin.

“I liked the blank Saturday. Next time don’t give it a colour. And don’t call it personal time, it sounds like a dentist. Just ask me,” she said.

“Then can I make one suggestion? Dinner, once a week. You choose the night, every week, when you know your week.”

She thought about it. “That’s not a schedule. That’s a date. Approved.”

She leaned back against him.

A while later she said, “I’ve kept the ash, by the way. In a jar.”

“Why?”

“In case you wanted it back.”

He put his mouth to her hair. “Keep it. As evidence that I should never make you a timetable again.”

She laughed into his shoulder, and for once Ren Hao let a whole evening happen without organising a minute of it.

chapters.title: His Sister Likes Her Too Much
chapters.desc: Isla and Song-Zhu, two glasses of wine and every secret of his childhood. The ten minutes at nine. A kiss in the corridor; Isla shouts.
chapters.epigraph: “You’re different with her.”
chapters.content:
Ren Hao made one mistake when he invited Song-Zhu to dinner with his sister. He assumed Isla would behave.

It wasn’t a reasonable assumption. Isla could get information out of anyone. She was charming when she wanted to be and disarmingly sweet when she didn’t, and incapable of leaving a subject alone once it interested her. It was why the consulate sent her to sit with families on the worst night of their lives, and why he’d never once in twenty-five years won an argument with her at a dinner table. She’d known Song-Zhu nine months, since a cold night in November and half a cereal bar in a stairwell. She’d never yet known her as the woman her brother was seeing.

The messages began before six on Saturday.

Isla (Matchmaker): What does she drink? Red or white? I’m asking you. As a test.

Ren Hao: Then I don’t know.

Isla (Matchmaker): Terrible boyfriend.

Ren Hao: I’m not her boyfriend.

Isla (Matchmaker): That’s not what I asked. Does she like flowers?

Ren Hao: Ask Ruby. She’s been redirecting them from my desk to hers every Monday since June. And she’s coming for dinner. Please don’t interrogate her.

Isla (Matchmaker): A family dinner. I’m welcoming her into the family

Ren Hao: I regret introducing the two of you.

Isla (Matchmaker): I introduced YOU. Know your place

✦ ✦ ✦

He opened the door before Song-Zhu could ring. Plain black dress, light cardigan, small gold earrings, hair loose, and a bottle of wine held against her chest like a shield. He bent and kissed her, longer than a greeting at a front door strictly required.

“Peace offering. For your sister. I hear she’s dangerous. You texted me behave three times this morning.”

“Because I know you.”

She kicked her shoes off onto the rack, where his own stood in a straight line, looked at the straight line and then at him, and visibly decided not to say anything.

“Song-Zhu!”

Isla came out of the kitchen in a cream blouse with a wooden spoon in her hand and threw both arms round her, spoon and all.

“Finally. Finally. In his flat. With his shoes all lined up.”

She held her at arm’s length and turned to her brother.

“Why didn’t you tell me she looked like this when she’s not covered in fuel?”

“You’ve had lunch with her eleven times. You introduced us.”

“In a stairwell, and a dumpling shop, and once in a hospital car park. Never in earrings,” said Isla, and took Song-Zhu by the hand and led her away down the hall, and Ren Hao stood holding the wine with the strong feeling that he was about to become irrelevant in his own flat.

✦ ✦ ✦

Dinner was meant to be simple. He’d ordered from a place Isla liked and laid it out in dishes with serving spoons, because he wasn’t a man who could put a takeaway carton on a table with a guest at it. Song-Zhu looked at the serving spoons, and then at him, and bit her lip.

For twenty minutes it went exactly as planned. Isla asked about work, and asked the right questions: how long a recorder took to download when it had been in seawater; whether the families heard before the press; whether it got easier.

“Some of it does. You learn how to do the work. The rest you learn to carry,” said Song-Zhu.

Isla nodded and didn’t ask for more. She of all people knew where those conversations went. She asked instead what Song-Zhu did when she wasn’t working.

“Sleep. Sometimes I eat.”

“You’re my kind of person,” said Isla.

“She also likes making trouble,” said Ren Hao, across the table.

“Hers. I’m on her side. I’ve been on her side since November and you’ve only been on it since June,” said Isla, and poured another glass of wine, and that was where it began to go wrong for him.

✦ ✦ ✦

It started with school.

Song-Zhu gestured at him with her glass. “Was he always like this? Looks like he was born in a tie.”

Isla’s eyes lit up like a runway. Ren Hao put his fork down. “Don’t.”

“He packed his school bag every night. Books in timetable order. Pencils sharpened to the same length. If I borrowed anything and didn’t put it back, he’d come and stand in my bedroom doorway at eleven at night and ask where his ruler was. He made lists for our parents of things in the house that needed mending. With priorities. And once, when I was eight and he was ten, he decided I wasn’t using my time efficiently. So he made me a timetable,” said Isla.

Song-Zhu stopped laughing. Slowly, with enormous ceremony, she turned her head and looked at him. Then she put both hands flat on the table and laughed until there were tears in her eyes, and Isla, who had no idea why it was quite this funny, laughed too, because Song-Zhu was.

“You made your eight-year-old sister a timetable.”

“She kept forgetting her homework. She asked me to help.”

“Was it colour-coded?” said Song-Zhu sweetly.

He looked at her for so long that Isla glanced between the two of them, narrowed her eyes, and filed something away.

“It might have been.”

Song-Zhu put her face in her napkin. Two women, two glasses of wine, one target: he’d been outnumbered in his own home for less than an hour.

Then the cake. At thirteen he’d tried to bake one for their mother, weighed everything on the kitchen scales, written the oven temperature on a sticky note, and produced something completely flat.

“It was meant to be a dense cake.”

“It was a biscuit with ambitions,” said Isla.

Song-Zhu bent forward over the table, helpless. “Have you got more? Please.”

“You too?” he said.

“I’m getting to know you.”

“You’re getting to know my childhood.”

“Same thing,” she said, and he didn’t argue, because he could see that for her it was.

Isla turned her glass slowly by the stem. “There’s the time he cried.”

He went still.

Isla smiled at her plate. “The first maths competition he lost. He was thirteen and he’d prepared for months. He thought if he worked hard enough he couldn’t lose, and he came second by half a mark, and went into his room and wouldn’t come out. I was eleven. I didn’t know what to say. So I sat on the floor outside his door with my back against it until he came out. About three hours. I read a whole book. He was annoying. But he was mine.”

Under the table Song-Zhu found his hand. She wasn’t teasing him now. He turned his hand over and squeezed her fingers once, hard, and didn’t let go straight away.

And then Isla ruined it. “He also had a truly terrible haircut.”

“Show me,” said Song-Zhu instantly, and Isla was already reaching for her phone.

✦ ✦ ✦

When he came back from refilling the water jug they were on the sofa with their heads together, Song-Zhu with a hand over her mouth. On the screen was a boy of about fifteen with hair much too long and school trousers belted somewhere round his ribs, holding up a certificate with the grave face of a man receiving a state honour.

“What is that?”

“Oh, Hao. Your hair.”

“He came first in the whole school, the year after the maths thing. He never came second again in his life,” said Isla.

“Of course you did. You were born holding a spreadsheet,” said Song-Zhu.

Isla laughed so much she slid sideways off the cushion, and he took the phone out of her hand while she was helpless and sat down on Song-Zhu’s other side.

“Can I have the photograph?” Song-Zhu leaned against his arm.

“No.”

“I’ve sent it to her,” said Isla from the floor.

✦ ✦ ✦

By nine the table had fallen into chaos. Isla had taken her cardigan off. Song-Zhu sat on the floor against Isla’s knees. Ren Hao stood in the kitchen doorway with two plates, having tried for the fifth time to clear the table and been stopped for the fifth time by a new story: the afternoon in Vancouver when he’d locked himself out at fourteen and got into the house through the cat flap as far as his shoulders.

He’d never seen his sister like this with anyone he’d been seeing. Isla was sociable by nature and kind for a living, but careful about who she let in. She didn’t tell people about the cat flap. She didn’t open the small private country that had only ever had the two of them in it, a long way from their parents’ house, in a city neither of them had been born in. And here she was, opening it. Something warm settled in his chest, and beside it a strong suspicion that the two of them together were going to be impossible to manage.

Isla tipped her head back against the sofa. “Do you know what I like about him? He always turns up. If I ring him, he answers. When I had exams at school he’d wait outside my classroom pretending he was just walking past, with a snack. Every time.”

“You were my sister,” he said, holding the plates.

There was a little silence, and then Isla said, as if it followed, “Wei Long’s like that. Differently. But like that.”

Song-Zhu sat up. “The inspector.”

Isla’s whole face went soft in a way her brother hadn’t quite got used to. “Did I ever tell you about the ten minutes? On the mornings I’ve got business at the station I go up to his floor at nine and sit on the corner of his desk. And he stops. Whatever he’s doing. He puts the pen down and looks at me, for ten minutes. Sometimes we hardly say anything. The whole squad room waits. Then I get off the desk and he picks up his pen.”

“Why do you love it?”

“Because in those ten minutes he doesn’t want anything from me. He isn’t fixing anything. He just stops, and he’s there.”

Song-Zhu looked up at the kitchen doorway. “I want one.”

“You want to sit on my desk at nine?” said Ren Hao.

She pointed at him. “You’d book it. You’d make a spreadsheet. I want you to stop. When I ring you at nine, whatever you’re doing, whoever you’re with. Ten minutes.”

He looked at her, sitting on his floor with his sister’s knee at her shoulder, asking for the one thing he’d never given anybody in his working life.

“All right.”

Isla gave her brother a long, slow, unmistakable look, and smiled into her wine.

✦ ✦ ✦

Song-Zhu had a briefing at eight. When she went to find her shoes, they’d been moved in her absence onto the rack, into line.

At the door Isla held on to her. “I’m really glad it’s you. And I’m keeping her. Whatever you do,” she told her brother.

“Do I get a say in this?”

“No,” said both of them.

He walked her down the dim hall towards the front door with her hand in his.

“Thank you for letting me meet her like this. As this,” she said.

He tucked a strand of hair behind her ear. “I wanted you to.”

“Your childhood was adorable. You’re still making timetables, and I’m never going to let it go,” she said, and pulled him down by his shirt and kissed him.

He caught her round the waist. She smiled against his mouth and he kissed her again, harder, his hand going into the hair at the back of her head, and she held the front of his shirt in both fists, and for a few seconds the hall went away—

“OH! YOU TWO! THE DOOR IS RIGHT THERE!”

Isla stood at the end of the hall with a tea towel, looking at Song-Zhu’s hand still twisted in his shirt. She pointed the tea towel at her brother like a weapon. “Sorry. I thought you’d left. Behave.”

“She’s my girlfriend,” said Ren Hao.

The words came out on their own. He hadn’t known they were coming until they were already in the hall.

Song-Zhu turned and looked up at him. Her cheeks had gone pink. She looked at the floor and smiled at it.

Isla made a small delighted noise, like a kettle. “Well! That’s wonderful! Good night, girlfriend!”

“Tell her I’ll text her, and that I want the haircut in better resolution,” said Song-Zhu in the doorway, and laughed all the way down to the lift.

✦ ✦ ✦

When he came back Isla was on the sofa with a glass of water, and there was no teasing in her face at all.

“You really like her.”

“Yes.”

“You’re different with her. Less like you’re about to chair a meeting. Happier.”

He thought about it. Song-Zhu wasn’t easy. She was stubborn and unpredictable and capable of setting fire to three pages of careful planning in her kitchen sink. But being with her was easy in a way he hadn’t expected. He didn’t have to perform. He could be the man who made his sister a timetable at ten, and she’d laugh at him for it and hold his hand under the table.

Isla got up and hugged him. “Next time I’m inviting her without you.”

“She’ll spend the whole evening laughing at me.”

“Exactly,” said Isla, and went to get her coat.

✦ ✦ ✦

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Home. Your sister’s sent me the haircut. And the cake.

Ren Hao: I’m changing my number.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Don’t. I like this one. Are we actually boyfriend and girlfriend now, or did you say it to get rid of her?

He remembered the hall, and how the words had come out before he’d thought them. He hadn’t planned it. It had just been true, and his mouth had known before he did.

Ren Hao: Would you like to be?

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): I thought I already was. Good night, boyfriend.

A minute later Isla rang. “Did you tell her? That you love her?”

He didn’t say anything.

“Oh, you haven’t.”

“Good night, Isla,” he said, and rang off.

He hadn’t said it. He’d felt it for weeks, at a hangar fence and in a car park and on a terrible sofa. He said I love you to his sister and his receptionist and a dog on a tartan cushion without thinking about it at all. This one he wanted to say when it was ready, in a moment that belonged only to the two of them, not shouted down a hall at a woman with a tea towel.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): One more thing. Ten minutes at nine. I’m ringing you on Monday. Be ready. No schedule. Just you.

Ren Hao: Just me.

chapters.title: A Typhoon at the Airport
chapters.desc: A typhoon closes the airport. He brings a camp bed, a suit carrier and soup. A go-around in the storm. Explicit: the camp bed collapses.
chapters.epigraph: “You brought a bed to an airport. In a typhoon.”
chapters.content:
On Tuesday the second of September, a little after four, Ren Hao received a photograph of a unhappy sky: nearly all grey, a bruise of darker cloud piled over the airport perimeter, and in one corner a wet wing under rain coming in sideways.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Getting ugly. Duty investigator for the storm. I’m here till it’s gone.

He was in a meeting about restructuring his own crisis-response team, which wasn’t the same as having one.

Ren Hao: Are you going home?

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Hao. I’m working.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Departures stopped. They’re reviewing arrivals. And you’re doing the thing where you pretend not to worry while secretly preparing to take over the weather.

Ren Hao: I don’t have that authority.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Good. Stay humble.

✦ ✦ ✦

At six the airport suspended all flights. The typhoon had come further west than forecast, and faster. The wind was past the limits for either runway, the rain was taking the visibility with it, and the warning across the city had gone to its second-highest level.

A voice note: footsteps, a phone ringing, the hum of a building full of computers. “Well, handsome. Looks like I’m sleeping here.”

He rang her. “Where are you?”

“Investigators’ office, by the cargo apron. It’s a concrete building built to survive things hitting it. There’s a sofa.”

“Is it a comfortable sofa?”

She laughed at his silence. “I’ll live, Hao.”

“I’m bringing you something.”

“It’s a typhoon. The airport’s shut and the roads will be awful.”

“I’ll manage.”

She was quiet, and then he heard her smile. “Bring soup. The kind that tastes like you’d like me to survive the night. And don’t bring a whole office. One person. One boyfriend. One soup.”

He smiled at the window, where rain was hitting the glass of the thirty-second floor in handfuls. “One boyfriend?”

“Don’t get excited.”

“Already done,” said Ren Hao.

✦ ✦ ✦

By half past seven he’d packed for a small expedition. A thermal container of soup from the place with the good broth by his office. Rice, water, cut fruit. A phone charger and a full battery. A towel. Dry clothes for her, a soft cotton shirt and loose trousers bought on the way in her size, which he knew from the label on her cardigan. Socks. All of it in a suit carrier, which was what made Mr. Yau look at him in the basement car park.

“Are you staying the night, sir?”

“No. She may need something dry.”

Then Ren Hao went back into the storeroom by the lifts and came out with a folding camp bed in a canvas bag, which the firm kept for operations nights and which nobody, to anybody’s knowledge, had ever unfolded.

Mr. Yau looked at the camp bed. “Sir. Do they allow beds?”

It was a fair question. “I’ll ask.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The airport was chaos. Mr. Yau got them round to the cargo side by a route Ren Hao hadn’t known existed, through a gate where a guard with water running off his hood looked at the camp bed on the back seat and then waved them on, with the air of a man who’d seen stranger things in a typhoon but couldn’t think of one.

Song-Zhu came down to the door of the low brick building, hair pinned anyhow, a pen behind one ear, tired. When she saw him in the rain with his arms full her face changed, not much, but enough. Then she saw the long canvas bag with the handle.

“Hao. What’s that?”

“A camp bed.”

She looked at him for several seconds in the doorway with the wind trying to get in round her, and began to laugh. “You brought a bed to an airport. In a typhoon.”

“To the investigators’ office, technically. And clothes.”

Her laughter went somewhere else. “You brought me clothes.”

“Your office has a sofa. Not a wardrobe.”

She stepped forward into the noise of the rain and put both arms round his waist and held on, her cheek against his wet shirt, while the rain beat on the glass canopy over the door.

“Come on, before security decides you’re opening a hotel,” she said.

✦ ✦ ✦

The investigators’ office hadn’t been designed for sleeping. It was desks crowded with files, monitors on arms, a wall of photographs and charts from open cases, and a kettle with a sign that said DESCALE ME, I BEG YOU. Four people at desks with headsets round their necks looked up when Ren Hao came in carrying a camp bed, and as one looked down again.

“Duty team. Ignore them. They’re very good at it,” said Song-Zhu.

Her room for the night was a box at the end of the corridor: a desk, a filing cabinet, a radio handset crackling, a screen showing the approach radar, and a sofa bought to discourage anyone from sleeping on it. On the screen a handful of labelled blips crawled round the edges of the storm like insects round a lamp.

He unfolded the camp bed. It had a great many joints.

“You’re losing,” she said.

The leg clicked. She pressed one hand flat on the canvas and the whole thing wobbled end to end like a nervous animal. She sat on it, and it gave a sharp metallic crack, and they both stared at it, and she stood up again slowly.

“Let’s not push it.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She ate the soup at the desk out of a ceramic bowl he’d brought because he couldn’t give anyone soup in a carton. She’d changed into the dry clothes, and found the socks at the bottom of the carrier, new, still on their cardboard.

“You bought me socks. You’re getting good at this. Being useful without being asked.”

“I’ve always been useful.”

She pointed the spoon at him. “Don’t spoil it.”

For a while there was only the rain and the tower on the radio, talking to the last few aircraft holding out over the sea. She was tired enough that she’d stopped being bright for him. Every so often she pinched the bridge of her nose and went back to the soup. He wanted to ask whether someone else could do this. He wanted to tell her to sleep. Instead he pulled the other chair up beside her.

She nodded at the screen. “We’ve had diversions all evening. One freighter’s been holding forty minutes to see if there’s a gap. If anything goes wrong on that runway tonight, I start the clock: who to ring, what to keep, what to stop anyone touching. Mostly it means sitting here all night while nothing goes wrong, and being very glad.”

Before she went to check in with the duty team she held out her hand. “Give me your phone.”

She did something to it and something to hers, and gave it back with a map of the airport on the screen and a small blue dot on the cargo side.

“Location. The compound’s three kilometres across and nothing’s signposted. If you go out to the car and get lost, I’m not sending a search party in this. It’s a typhoon. It’s practical.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Towards ten the room changed. The lights stayed too bright and the rain kept coming, but something went through the building, and she felt it before anyone said anything. On the radio the tower’s voice went flatter and quicker. On the screen a single blip coming in from the sea on the line of the runway was much closer to the edge of everything.

Song-Zhu stood up. He stepped back out of her way without being asked.

“The freighter. He’s on finals. The wind’s changing over the threshold.”

A pilot’s voice, calm, much too calm. Wind shear, going around.

The blip stopped coming down. Beside it a data block flicked: height, ground speed, still sinking for a second, a second more, even with the engines at full power, the air going out from under him. Her hands were braced on the edge of the desk. She didn’t blink. The tower said something, and the pilot said something back.

Then the number went up. Slowly, then less slowly. The blip lifted off the line of the runway and went out over the sea, climbing.

Climbing, runway heading. Request diversion.

She breathed out, and the whole building seemed to breathe out with her. She picked up the handset, and her voice was absolutely steady. “Duty investigator. I want the tower recording from the start of his approach preserved. Radar data, same window. Wind readings from both ends of the runway at one-second intervals. And somebody ring his company now, before he lands at the alternate, and ask them to pull the voice recorder breaker at the gate, so the last two hours don’t get recorded over. Confirmation in writing.”

She stayed at the screen. He stayed behind her and didn’t ask if she was all right, not yet. He’d never seen her like this: no mischief at all, only attention, so total that the rest of the room fell away from her like water off a wing.

When her shoulders came down he picked up the bowl. “Soup?”

She turned, looked at him like she’d forgotten he was there, and smiled. She held the bowl in both hands without eating, just for the warmth, and he put his hand on her back between her shoulder blades and took it away again.

✦ ✦ ✦

Before midnight it was over, as far as anything was over. The freighter had landed two hundred kilometres up the coast on a dry runway without a scratch. Its company had pulled the breaker and sent a scanned form to prove it. Tomorrow someone would decide whether it had been a serious incident or a pilot doing his job very well in a typhoon, and she thought it was the second.

When she came back he’d moved the camp bed under the window with the towel folded on it and the battery plugged in beside it.

“You’re staying?”

“Did you think I’d leave you here? I brought my laptop.”

“Of course you did. In the suit carrier. Next to my socks,” she said.

He drew her in and kissed her cheek and her temple, and then her mouth, slow and warm, and she put her arms up round his neck.

“Stay with me,” she said against him.

✦ ✦ ✦

After midnight the building went as quiet as a building in a typhoon could. The rain had moved round to the other side of the building, a long low roar like the sea. She’d locked the door. He’d changed into the clean shirt from the carrier.

She pulled him down beside her and the camp bed creaked like a ship. “Don’t laugh. You’re laughing inside.”

She kissed him, and it went deep almost at once. Her fingers went into his hair. He kissed her jaw, the place under her ear she liked, back to her mouth. This wasn’t his flat with its lined-up shoes or hers with its laundry but a small room at the edge of an airport with the radio murmuring and a storm coming in off the sea and four exhausted colleagues thirty metres away, surrounded by her work. She wanted him in the middle of it. He wanted to be what she came back to.

“You’re still wearing trousers. You’re at my work now. It’s a strong suggestion,” she said.

He laughed against her mouth and did as he was told.

She pulled the borrowed shirt over her head. He looked at her in the light from the radar screen and put his mouth on her collarbone and then lower, until she arched against him and her breath went ragged. She pushed him onto his back on the canvas and the frame complained and she ignored it. She unbuttoned his clean shirt one button at a time, looking at him, and kissed her way down his chest, and at his belt she looked up and he’d stopped breathing the way she had at the screen.

She took him into her mouth, and he said her name to the ceiling of the duty investigator’s rest room in a voice with nothing professional left in it, and put a hand over his own mouth because of the corridor. She laughed round him and he nearly died. She was slow and wicked and thorough and stopped every time he got close, on purpose, and looked up at him, and waited, until he took his hand away and said please out loud.

Then she climbed up him and took him inside her, and they both went still.

“Look at me,” she said.

She rode him slowly on a camp bed in a typhoon, the rain roaring on the far wall and the radar sweeping blue light across her skin every four seconds, and he watched her face in that light like he was trying to learn it. He sat up so he could hold her properly and put his mouth on her throat. The rhythm went from slow to something else. He said her name into her shoulder and she said his into his hair, because of the corridor, and it got harder to be quiet, and harder, and she was close, she was right there—

The camp bed collapsed.

There was no warning worth mentioning. One moment he was holding her with an arm round her back and the other braced on the canvas. The next, a metal leg folded neatly underneath them like a knee, the frame lurched, and the two of them went down sideways in a tangle of aluminium and canvas onto the carpet tiles. Not loud, but spectacularly undignified: a clatter, a soft thump, and silence.

She was on top of him, staring into his face from three centimetres away with her hair hanging round them both. Then she buried her face in his neck and laughed until it shook her whole body, and his.

“Are you hurt?” he said into her hair.

One leg of the bed had folded in on itself. Another stuck out into the room at an angle that shouldn’t have been possible. He shut his eyes. “I brought a defective bed.”

“You brought a defective bed to my work.”

“Everything all right, Song-Zhu?” someone called from down the corridor.

“Filing cabinet,” she called back, so steadily and professionally that he had to put his face in her shoulder.

There was a small crease between his eyebrows, the one he always got when he couldn’t understand how a thing had gone wrong. She smoothed it with her thumb. “Good. Because I’m not finished.”

She kissed him there on the floor and moved against him, and he was still inside her, and they both remembered at the same moment. He laughed against her mouth and rolled them off the wreckage onto the carpet, his hand behind her head, and finished what they’d started: slowly at first, laughing, foreheads together, and then not slowly and not laughing, the floor hard under her back and her heels locked behind his thighs. She came biting down on his shoulder so as not to make a sound, and he followed with his face in her hair and a sound he couldn’t stop, and a long way off somebody turned the radio up.

✦ ✦ ✦

Later they lay on the towel and the blanket on the carpet tiles. The camp bed lay against the wall like something that had been shot.

She put her cheek back on his chest and traced a line along his ribs. “The whole city stopped today. Nobody could fly. Thousands of people asleep on terminal floors. And we couldn’t stop, because the one time we stop is the one time something happens. When he went round I knew it was right. You could hear it in his voice. But when you’re watching the numbers you still feel every one. You’re waiting for the one that doesn’t go up.”

He held on.

“Do you get that? At work? The second where you don’t know what comes next?”

“Often. You decide with what you’ve got, accept what you haven’t, and keep going.”

“That’s very you. Next time just bring soup. And a blanket. No furniture. And no lists,” she said, nearly asleep, and was asleep before he’d answered.

✦ ✦ ✦

She woke at a quarter to seven to the sound of the duty key in the lock. He was still asleep on the floor with one arm folded under his head, his shirt wrinkled and his hair a disaster, and without its composure his face looked about nineteen. She looked at the camp bed lying against the wall with its legs in the air and began to laugh without making a sound.

He opened one eye, followed her finger, and shut it again.

The door opened. Dexter came in with a mug of coffee, on his way to the radio charger in the filing cabinet, and stopped dead at the two of them on the floor under a blanket, and at the camp bed, and at the two of them again.

“Good morning,” said Song-Zhu pleasantly, from the floor.

“Morning,” said Dexter, and took out the charger, and walked out, and shut the door without a single question.

“He’ll tell everyone by eight. Mabel will put it in the duty log. Oh-six-forty-two. Camp bed: total loss,” said Song-Zhu.

He put his arm over his eyes. She leaned down and kissed his cheek and held out her hand to pull him up off the floor.

He’d brought soup, and dry clothes, and a blanket, and somewhere for her to sleep. The weather had seen to the rest.

chapters.title: The Loudest Man She Knows
chapters.desc: He says I love you in a restaurant, at volume. Half the room applauds. She can’t say it back. She kisses him instead.
chapters.epigraph: “I didn’t say it to get an answer.”
chapters.content:
Ren Hao had never been any good at keeping things to himself. He said what he meant. He told people when they’d done well and when they’d disappointed him and when they were about to make a terrible mistake, in that order, often in the same meeting. He said good morning to the security guards by name. He rang his sister to remind her to take an umbrella when she was already standing under one.

And he’d recently acquired a girlfriend, which he appeared to find tremendously enjoyable. For a fortnight he’d rung Song-Zhu at lunch. He’d sent her photographs of things that reminded him of her, including an aggressively ugly ceramic duck in a shop window on Harbour Road with the caption you. He kissed her hello wherever they were, and used the word girlfriend to Joyce, to Mr. Yau, to a waiter, and once to a man from a utility company who’d rung about his meter.

She was still getting used to it. Not to him: to being loved that openly, in daylight, in front of people.

On Friday she rang him at lunch to ask whether he was free on Saturday, and heard him say, away from the phone, “One moment, my girlfriend’s on the line,” to somebody with a clipboard.

“Who’s that?”

“A man from the utility company. He’s come about the meter. He can’t find it.”

“It’s in the cupboard by your front door, behind the umbrellas. I saw it when I was looking for a coat hook.”

She heard him repeat this, word for word, with “My girlfriend says” in front of it, and then a pause, and a cupboard door, and a man’s voice saying something grateful.

“He’s found it. He says thank you. He also says you must be very observant,” said Ren Hao.

“I’m a professional investigator. You didn’t have to tell him I was your girlfriend.”

“He asked who was on the phone.”

“You could have said a friend.”

“That wouldn’t have been accurate,” he said, so reasonably that she put her forehead down on her desk in the investigators’ office and laughed into a file, and Dexter, across the room, asked whether she needed a doctor.

When she could breathe she said, “Saturday. Somewhere with fish. You choose. I’m too tired to choose.”

“I already know where.”

“Of course you do.”

She found out that Saturday exactly how openly she was going to be loved.

✦ ✦ ✦

The restaurant was in the business district, dark wood and soft light and enough space between the tables for private conversation, chosen because she’d once mentioned wanting to try their fish. She arrived twelve minutes late. He kissed her hello and said absolutely nothing about it. Progress.

“You’ve been reading the same page of the menu for four minutes,” he said.

“It says the fish costs about the same as my car.”

She chose steamed fish with ginger and a dish of greens. He chose beef, and asked for an extra plate so they could share, and she found she liked watching him ask for it more than she’d expected.

He told her about a new analyst who’d misunderstood a reporting line, and an argument between two of his department heads that had somehow become his fault. She told him the freighter from the typhoon had been signed off in under a week as a textbook go-around, and that a colleague had sent a photograph of his lunch to the all-staff group by mistake: a sad boiled egg, alone on a plate, captioned the usual suspect.

He laughed properly, the laugh that made his eyes go narrow and his shoulders come down. He had a face that could make a whole boardroom reconsider its choices, and when he laughed like that he looked younger. More like the boy Isla had described, who made lists for his parents and baked a cake that came out as a biscuit.

✦ ✦ ✦

They shared the beef and argued about the best part of the fish. At one point he reached across and wiped a spot of sauce from the corner of her mouth with his thumb.

“I could have done that.”

“I wanted to.”

He took her hand across the table, his thumb moving over her knuckles, and she looked down at their hands lying on the white cloth between the plates. There were people all round them. He didn’t make a show of it. He just saw no reason to hide it. She was still learning what to do with that. Sometimes being cared for so openly made her feel she’d walked into a room without knowing the rules.

He saw her face change and waited.

“You’ve got your knowing face on,” she said.

“You don’t like the greens as much as you said. You’ve moved them all to my side of the plate.”

“Because you’re bigger. You need more greens. It’s scientific.”

He shook his head, smiling, and the smile went somewhere quieter. “I like having dinner with you.”

“Because you steal my greens.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Dessert came after nine. She’d chosen something with chocolate and cream. He’d ordered a small fruit tart because he didn’t want anything too sweet, and was eating half of hers.

She was scrolling through her photographs for a vending machine at the cargo terminal that sold, as far as anyone could tell, only boiled eggs and umbrellas. He wasn’t looking at the phone. He was looking at her: at her hair fallen forward over one shoulder, the crease between her eyebrows as she tried to enlarge the picture, the way she was already laughing before she’d got to why it was funny.

He’d known for a while that he was in trouble. He’d liked her from the first evening. He’d liked her more at the taxi rank. Then she’d brought chaos into a life he’d arranged carefully, and he’d started looking forward to every interruption. He liked her first thing in the morning and when she was so tired she was cross. He liked her terrible flat and her terrible jokes. He liked that she could make him feel ridiculous and completely himself in the same five minutes.

“Song-Zhu.”

She looked up from the phone.

“I love you,” said Ren Hao.

She blinked.

“I really love you,” he said, apparently unaware that the room around them had gone a little quieter. His face was open and warm and unguarded, the way it never was at work, the way she’d only ever seen it in the dark.

And then, because he was Ren Hao, he said it again, in the voice he used to stop a boardroom. “I love you.”

A waiter carrying a tray of glasses stopped in the middle of the floor. A woman by the window put her glass down slowly.

“Hao. Your voice.”

He looked puzzled for one second, and then looked round. A man in a grey suit lifted his glass to them. A woman near the door began to clap. Somebody joined her, and then half the restaurant was applauding: the waiter with the tray, the couple at the next table, an elderly man in the corner who clearly had no idea what was going on and was clapping anyway out of solidarity.

Song-Zhu wanted the floor to open.

Ren Hao lifted one hand in a small awkward acknowledgement, like a man thanked for holding a door. “Thank you.”

“Don’t encourage them,” she hissed.

He turned back to her with an enormous smile. “Sorry.”

He didn’t look sorry in the slightest. A minute later the waiter who’d stopped with the tray brought two small glasses of dessert wine on the house, set them down without a word, and went away beaming.

✦ ✦ ✦

She’d imagined him saying it. She’d wondered whether it would be at his flat on a quiet evening, or in the middle of an argument, or over the washing-up. She’d practised saying it back once, alone in her bathroom with her toothbrush in her mouth, and it had sounded perfectly simple.

Now he was sitting in front of her looking at her like he’d just put something precious into her hands, and she couldn’t.

She loved him. She knew that much. She loved how he listened, and remembered small things, and could be serious without being cold. She loved that he’d carried a camp bed into an airport in a typhoon. She loved that he’d never once made her feel strange about the parts of her life that were hard to explain. But saying it out loud felt like opening a door and finding no way to shut it again. Her whole working life had taught her that ordinary things changed in an instant, and here was a man loving her as if nothing about tomorrow were uncertain, out loud, to applause.

His smile went softer. “Are you all right?”

“I’m sorry. I can’t say it,” she whispered.

His thumb moved over the back of her hand. “That’s all right.”

“It isn’t that I don’t—”

He lifted their hands and kissed her knuckles, and when he spoke there was no disappointment in it anywhere. “I know. You don’t have to say anything because I did. I didn’t say it to get an answer.”

Her eyes stung, stupidly.

“I said it because I love you. That’s all it was for,” he said, lower now.

That made it worse, because he hadn’t hurt her. He’d given her room to be frightened without making her feel guilty for it.

She stood up. He looked up at her, startled, and got to his feet as she came round the table, and before he could ask anything she took the front of his shirt in both hands and kissed him. It wasn’t careful or polite. She kissed him trying to put everything she couldn’t say into the small space between their mouths. For one second he was completely taken by surprise. Then his arms came round her and he kissed her back, and somebody in the room made a delighted noise, and she didn’t care at all.

When she pulled away she rested her forehead on his. His eyes were bright.

“I’ll take that. That’s a yes. I’m taking it as a yes,” he said.

She laughed, and her eyes were wet, and he brushed his thumb under one of them.

“I’m not crying.”

“You’re a terrible liar,” said Ren Hao, and put his mouth to her hair.

✦ ✦ ✦

Outside the night was cool and the traffic on the main road went past steadily, entirely unconcerned that her boyfriend had just declared his love to a room full of strangers and been applauded for it.

“You said it so loudly. Half the restaurant clapped.”

“That was kind of them. The man in the corner was clapping for the wrong table, I think.”

“He was clapping for love in general.”

“Then he had the right table,” said Ren Hao.

She stopped under a streetlight and put her arms round his waist. “I wasn’t expecting it. Or the applause. You’re not upset? That I didn’t say it?”

“I’d rather hear it when you want to say it than because you’re worried I’ll be disappointed if you don’t. I’m not disappointed. I’m in love with you on a pavement. It’s a very good evening.”

Her throat went tight again. She put her cheek against his chest and he put his chin on her hair.

“And for the record, I liked the kiss,” he said.

She lifted her face and he kissed her again, quieter this time, no audience, just a Saturday night and a taxi going past slowly with its window down and the driver whistling.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the car he drove with one hand on the wheel and the other on the console near hers. After a while she reached over and laced her fingers through his.

“I don’t think I’ve ever been loved like this. Not like it’s something you have to hide, or earn by being useful. You just say it.”

“I don’t see a reason not to.”

“That’s the frightening part,” she said to the window.

At a red light he lifted her hand to his mouth. “I don’t want you ever to have to wonder whether I love you.”

At her building she turned under the awning and caught his wrist before he could say good night. “I love being with you.”

It came out carefully, each word checked.

“I just need a bit of time.”

“Take as long as you like. I’m not going anywhere,” said Ren Hao.

✦ ✦ ✦

His phone lit on the passenger seat before he was home.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): I didn’t say it because I’m scared.

He pulled in at the side of the road.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Not of you. Of how much it matters.

Ren Hao: You don’t have to explain anything else tonight.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): You really are very loud. Especially when you love someone.

Ren Hao: Good night. I love you.

He put the phone down, and picked it up again.

Ren Hao: Sorry. Once more for luck. I love you.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): HAHAHAHA

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Keep saying it. Good night, Hao.

He sat at the side of the road with the hazard lights ticking and laughed to himself, alone, like an idiot, while a delivery rider went past and looked in at him. He wasn’t going to stop saying it. He didn’t need to hear it back and he didn’t expect her to catch up by any particular date. He’d spent too much of his life believing affection was something to be measured and managed and kept in its place. She’d asked him to keep saying it, so he would, loudly if necessary, and he’d wait. He was good at waiting, when something mattered.

chapters.title: Not Yet
chapters.desc: Why she can’t: her father, a cargo pilot, and fifty seconds of his recorder at nineteen. He sits with her all night on the kitchen floor.
chapters.epigraph: “I wanted to say it back. When you said it. I wanted to so much.”
chapters.content:
On Sunday evening Ren Hao’s phone lit on the dining table beside a dinner he hadn’t touched.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Are you busy? Can I come round?

Ren Hao: Of course. What’s wrong?

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): I don’t want to go out. I don’t want to eat either. Can you just be there?

He shut the laptop.

Ren Hao: Yes. I’ll be here.

✦ ✦ ✦

He heard the lift, and her footsteps in the corridor slower than usual, and opened the door before she knocked. She stood with her hands pushed into her jacket pockets. Under the tiredness of a long shift, which he knew by now, something was held much too tightly behind her eyes.

He didn’t ask what had happened. He stood aside.

She put her bag down by the sofa and didn’t take her jacket off. She didn’t say anything about the shoes lined up in the hall or tell him off for the untouched plate. She stood in the middle of his living room.

“Would you like a hug?” he said.

Her mouth trembled, and she nodded. At first she stood still against him with her arms at her sides. Then her hands came round his waist and she pressed her face into his chest, and he felt her breathing change: not crying, not yet, only trying hard not to.

He took her to the sofa. She sat at one end and then moved along until she was against him, and he put his arm round her, and for several minutes neither of them spoke.

“I think I owe you an explanation. For last night,” she said.

“You don’t owe me anything.”

She looked at the window, where the city was dark and full of other people’s lights. “I want to tell you. I’ve never told anyone this. My father was a pilot.”

She said it the way she’d have given an aircraft’s registration.

Her fingers found a loose thread on her sleeve and worked at it. “A cargo pilot. Freighters, mostly nights. Sometimes three days away, sometimes a week. When I was small I thought it was the best job in the world. He brought me things from airports. Postcards. Terrible little toys. Once a snow globe from somewhere with a name I couldn’t say. I dropped it two days later on the kitchen tiles, and he said he’d get me another one. He didn’t. He died when I was nineteen.”

His hand stopped moving on her shoulder.

“His aircraft went down. At night.”

She didn’t say where, or give him a date, or describe the weather or who’d been waiting at the other end. She was walking slowly up to something she’d spent six years walking round.

The smile went. “I was already doing engineering. Aerospace, second year. Not because of this. I liked aircraft. He used to explain the flaps to me when I was little, and why the wings bend. Afterwards I read every final report on every freighter accident in the last twenty years, in the university library, at night. I thought if I understood enough I’d understand why he wasn’t coming home.”

Her voice caught.

“And then I heard him.”

✦ ✦ ✦

It wasn’t meant to happen, and she told him that first, as if it mattered that he understood. Cockpit recordings were protected. Every investigator learned that on their first day: the voice recorder belonged to the investigation, and nobody else ever heard it. Not the airline, not the police, not the press, not the families. The words that mattered went into the report as a transcript, as few as possible, and the rest stayed in the room for good.

“There was a family briefing five months after, in the country where he came down. My mother sat through two hours of slides. At the end she asked the investigator-in-charge, an older man with very tired eyes, whether her husband had been afraid. Just that. Was he afraid. He looked at her a long time, and at me beside her with a notebook full of questions, and said he couldn’t answer that. Then he asked us to wait. He came back forty minutes later with a laptop and a form, and we both signed it, promising never to repeat or record or describe what we heard. And he played us fifty seconds.”

Ren Hao had gone completely still.

She looked down. “He told us it was the only time in thirty-one years he’d done it. He said he’d probably lose his job if anyone found out. He didn’t. He retired two years later, and sent me a card when I qualified. It was his secret too. Not just mine.”

“What did you hear?”

“Him. His voice, the other pilot, the radio, the ordinary sounds in a cockpit. I knew his voice better than anyone’s in the world. I could tell when he was tired. I could tell when he was drinking coffee.”

A small broken laugh.

“He sounded completely normal. That’s what I couldn’t stand. Ordinary calls, everything he was meant to do. The same voice that told me to put a coat on when it was cold.”

A tear ran down her cheek.

“And I kept waiting.”

He took her hand. “For what?”

“I don’t know. For him to say something that would explain it. To sound frightened, so I’d understand. To say my name. But he didn’t. He was just there, and then the investigator stopped it. Fifty seconds, and it wasn’t even the end. I’ve never known what came after.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Ren Hao had sat with executives who’d lost everything and families who’d had the worst phone call of their lives. He knew how to sit through a silence. Watching her try to say this made him feel entirely helpless.

She spent her days with other people’s last recordings. She knew how to preserve them, analyse them, separate what could be known from what couldn’t. And once she’d been nineteen with a notebook, beside her mother, listening to her father’s voice in a room where he’d never hear hers again.

“Was your mother all right? Afterwards?”

“No. We didn’t talk about it. Not on the plane home, not ever. I didn’t want to make her hear it again through me.”

Her voice dropped.

“And I didn’t want anyone to think I was strange for wanting to hear it. Because I’d asked. The first question in my notebook was Can we hear the recorder. They said no, and I was angry. Part of me thought that if I could hear him, I could have him a bit longer.”

“You’re not required to be rational about losing your father. You were nineteen. You wanted to hear someone you loved. There’s nothing strange about that. Not one thing,” said Ren Hao.

Her face crumpled, and he drew her in, and this time she cried.

It wasn’t dramatic. The tears came and kept coming: six years of grief held down, finally given somewhere to go. He didn’t tell her to stop. He didn’t tell her it would be all right, because he didn’t know that, and he didn’t tell her what her father would have thought of her, because he hadn’t known her father and wasn’t going to turn her pain into a sentence that made him feel better. He held on.

When she pulled back she wiped her face with both hands and gave him a small embarrassed smile. “Your shirt.”

There was a wet patch on his shoulder the size of a hand. “It’s a shirt. I have others. Many others.”

She laughed, weakly, and then again with less pain in it, and he pushed her hair back off her face and brought her a glass of water.

She rubbed her eyes. “I wanted to say it back. When you said it. I wanted to so much. But I thought about the laptop. For years I believed that if I loved someone enough I could somehow keep them, and I couldn’t. I couldn’t even understand what happened. And when you said it I was so happy, Hao. And more frightened than I’ve been since I was nineteen. I don’t want to spend every day waiting for the phone to ring at four in the morning.”

“You don’t have to.”

“I know that in my head. My head’s very good at knowing things. The rest of me is stupid.”

He lifted her hand and kissed it. “The rest of you is grieving. Those aren’t the same thing.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Near midnight she said she wanted more water, and then that she wanted to sit somewhere else, and he followed her into the kitchen without asking why. She lowered herself to the floor with her back against the cupboard under the counter. He sat down beside her.

“Your trousers,” she said.

“They wash.”

They listened to the flat: the fridge humming, a car somewhere below, the kitchen clock moving on.

“I’ve never told anyone about the laptop. Not my friends, not Mabel, not Isla. Everyone knows my father died. It’s on my file. Half of them think it’s why I took the job. But nobody knows I heard him. You’re the only person in the world apart from my mother and a retired man in another country.”

He didn’t ask why she’d chosen him. He didn’t want her to feel she owed him a reason for the trust.

“Don’t tell anyone. Not Isla. She’ll ask.”

“She asks a great many questions. It stays with me,” he said.

She put her head on his shoulder.

✦ ✦ ✦

He made tea she’d said she didn’t want and left it on the counter within reach of her hand. When he sat down again she was looking at a photograph on her phone, and turned the screen to him.

A man in a pilot’s shirt with the sleeves rolled, in front of the nose of a big grey freighter on a sunny apron, one hand up against the light, smiling at whoever held the camera. Ordinary. Warm. A little amused, like he knew something funny he hadn’t told anyone yet. Her smile was exactly his.

“He’s handsome,” said Ren Hao.

“He knew.”

She gave him a sideways look. “Don’t say it.”

She zoomed in until it was only her father’s face.

“He used to send me pictures of the sky out of the cockpit window, with something stupid underneath. The clouds are behaving today. Bumpy over the sea, tell your mother I’m fine. I miss him in ordinary ways. Asking him stupid questions. Him telling me my shoes were ugly. Him ringing from some airport at three in the morning his time to ask if I’d eaten.”

Her eyes were wet again.

“I miss someone who knew me before I was this. Everyone I meet now knows the investigator, the one who can tell you what happened. He knew me when I was just his daughter.”

He put his mouth to her temple. “You’re still his daughter. You don’t stop being somebody’s daughter because they’re not here any more. And you don’t have to stop missing him because you’ve learned how to live without him.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Some time after one she said, “Do you think I’m going to be hard to love? I don’t know how to do this. Let someone this close. Have someone who expects me to come home. Have someone who tells me he loves me in a restaurant, at volume.”

He laughed, low, and she smiled, and then it went.

“People say things like for ever. But nobody knows. Nobody.”

“You’re right.”

She looked surprised that he hadn’t argued.

“I can’t promise you life will always be kind. I run a firm whose whole business is that it isn’t. But I can promise I won’t make you carry anything on your own while I’m here.”

“And if I get scared and can’t say so?”

He kissed her hair. “Then sit next to me. I seem to have got quite good at sitting on floors. There’s no exam, Song-Zhu. You don’t have to pass anything.”

“You’re very annoying when you’re sensible,” she said, and put her head back on his shoulder.

✦ ✦ ✦

By three the tea on the counter was stone cold, and she’d fallen asleep against him.

He didn’t move. His back had started to hurt and one leg had gone to sleep and the tiles were cold through his trousers. He could have carried her to bed. But she’d fallen asleep with her hand wrapped round his, holding on, and he wasn’t going to wake her for anything.

He thought about her at nineteen in a meeting room in another country, listening to fifty seconds on a laptop, waiting for a voice to say something that would make the world make sense again. He wished he’d been there. Not to explain anything. Just to sit next to her on the plane home and give her somewhere to put her head. He hadn’t known her then. All he could do was be here now.

✦ ✦ ✦

She woke before six and didn’t know where she was, and then felt his arm and lifted her head and looked round at the kitchen floor and the clock and him.

“You’ve been here all night? Why didn’t you move me?”

“You looked comfortable.”

She put her hand on his shoulder, and he winced.

“Ren Hao.”

He laughed. “All right. A bit.”

She leaned forward and kissed his cheek, and rested her forehead against his, and whispered, “I want to say something.”

He went still. He could see her trying. He could see the words come right up to the edge of her and stop, the way a car stops at the edge of a drop.

“I can’t. Not yet. I’m sorry. But I’m not going anywhere. I came here last night instead of sitting on my own kitchen floor, and I’ve never done that, not once, not with anyone. That’s what I’ve got. That’s what I can say.”

He let her have the whole of what she’d just given him without trampling on it. “That’s more than enough.”

“You’re not going to make a speech? You’re thinking about one.”

“I’ll keep it.”

She kissed him, and when she pulled back she didn’t look frightened. Tired, and a little lighter.

“Not yet,” she said against his mouth.

“Not yet,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

He helped her up off the floor. Her knees cracked, and she made a face at him for choosing to sit on tiles all night.

“Thank you for staying.”

He brushed her cheek with his thumb. “Always.”

She raised an eyebrow, and he heard it, and corrected himself. “Whenever you want me there.”

“Better,” she said.

There was a message from Mabel about the morning review. She wrote back that she’d be in after lunch, and asked if she could stay a bit. At the bedroom door she stopped.

“There’s one more thing I’ve got of his. I think I’ll want to show you. Not today.”

“Whenever you’re ready.”

Later that morning, while she slept, he sat at the end of the bed in yesterday’s clothes and looked at her: her phone charging on his bedside table, her jacket over his chair, one of her socks somehow by the door.

He loved her. He’d said it in a restaurant and a car and a message, and he’d say it again on pavements and to Joyce and probably to the man about the meter. Now he understood something he hadn’t before. For her those words weren’t only an invitation to be happy. They were an invitation to risk losing something again. He couldn’t take that fear away, or give a nineteen-year-old another fifty seconds. He could love the woman who’d grown up afterwards, who laughed too loudly and forgot to eat and worked through typhoons, and sometimes sat on kitchen floors because there were things she couldn’t say anywhere else.

He bent and put his mouth to her hair. Without opening her eyes she reached across the sheet for his hand, and he took it, and stayed.

chapters.title: His Client, Her Crash
chapters.desc: A client of his owns the group behind the airline in her next investigation. Both of them declare it. He offers to drop the client; she tells him not to.
chapters.epigraph: “You know that even the appearance of influence can sink a report.”
chapters.content:
On the night of Thursday the second of October, a seventy-seat turboprop landing in heavy rain at the city airport touched down long, aquaplaned, and left the end of the runway at sixty knots into the soft ground beyond it. The nose gear folded. The fuselage broke behind the wing. The first officer and a passenger in the second row were killed, and nineteen people went to hospital.

Song-Zhu wasn’t on duty. She heard the way everyone did, from a news alert in bed, and sat up, and didn’t sleep.

On Monday morning she was put on the team.

✦ ✦ ✦

She told him that evening at his flat, over two cartons of noodles she’d brought. She’d meant to tell him in an ordinary way: complain about the paperwork, warn him he’d hear less from her for a few months.

“I’ve been put on the turboprop,” she said, and named the operator, which had been on every front page for four days.

Ren Hao put his chopsticks down. It was a small thing, a fraction of a second, but she was trained to notice things that stopped.

“The airline belongs to a holding group. The man who owns the group has been a client of mine for five years.”

Song-Zhu leaned slowly back in her chair. “That’s inconvenient.”

He gave a short laugh, though his face stayed serious. “Very.”

“How close?”

“Corporate risk and crisis work. Business continuity, executive protection, two internal investigations, reputation. Nothing on this accident. Before, yes, through the holding company and some of their senior people. There’ve been projects that touched the airline.”

“Then we’ve got a problem.”

He pushed his carton aside. “Yes. Even if neither of us does anything wrong, it matters what it looks like. If anyone asks at an inquiry in a year whether the investigator on this accident was seeing the man who advises the owner, the answer can’t be yes, but nobody thought to mention it.”

She almost smiled. “Look at us. Two adults behaving responsibly. I only got the assignment at ten this morning. I didn’t know there was anything to declare until about forty seconds ago. I’ll go to Mabel first thing.”

He held her eyes across the table. “Compliance at eight, for me. I’ll declare the relationship, the scope of the work, the people, and ask to be taken off anything that could touch this. My client can’t get anywhere near your investigation through me. I won’t ask you for anything. Not a detail, not a direction, not a feeling.”

She leaned forward. “You’re not getting the file. Or the witness list. Or anything off the recorders. And if your client asks what the investigators are doing, you don’t say I can’t say. You say nothing. You change the subject to his golf. I’m saying it out loud so it’s been said. So that if anyone ever asks me, I can tell them we said it on the sixth of October at your dining table, over noodles.”

“Fair,” said Ren Hao.

“Will he try to contact you?”

“Probably. If he’s heard about us. He’ll want advice on the response. He may want more than that.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Before eight the next morning Song-Zhu went into Mabel Wong’s office, shut the door, and declared a potential conflict of interest. Her partner had an existing professional relationship with the owner of the airline’s parent group, and his firm had in the past done work that touched the airline itself. She didn’t make the connection sound smaller than it was. She didn’t suggest that she was immune to it because she trusted him.

Mabel listened with her reading glasses on their cord, asked six questions, and wrote the answers down in a hand so small it was nearly illegible. “In writing, signed and dated. It’ll go to the review. Until then I’ll keep you away from anything that would be hard to explain. If they think it’s too close, you come off. You’d mind.”

“I’d mind. I’d do it.”

Mabel looked at her over the glasses. “You know that even the appearance of influence can sink a report.”

“Yes.”

Mabel took her glasses off. “Is he worth it?”

Song-Zhu looked at her, startled. In three years Mabel had never asked her a single personal question.

“Yes.”

“Then write it properly,” said Mabel, and put her glasses back on.

Song-Zhu: Declared. Written version by tonight. Review after that.

Hao (Three-Piece): Same here. Compliance has it. Potential conflict, not an automatic withdrawal. They’ll look at the actual work.

Song-Zhu: Sensible. I was hoping for a courtroom scene.

Hao (Three-Piece): We can arrange one after work. Bring snacks.

✦ ✦ ✦

He declared it in full. Every project that had touched the airline or its parent in five years, every executive he’d dealt with, what the firm was still contracted to do. He said plainly that his partner was on the investigation team, and asked to be taken off anything to do with the airline’s response to the accident.

His head of compliance, a precise woman of fifty who’d once made him sit an online ethics course on the afternoon of a hostage release, asked whether he’d step away from the whole account if it came to it.

“Yes. Even if the client objected.”

She made a note. “Until I come back to you, you don’t touch anything connected with the accident or the airline’s handling of it. You receive nothing from your partner about the investigation, and she receives nothing from us.”

When he got back to his office Joyce had left a note on his keyboard. The owner had rung twice and wanted Mr. Ren personally. Ren Hao looked at the note for several seconds, and rang back.

“I hear you’ve got a connection to the investigation. Your girlfriend. And you didn’t think to tell me.”

“She was assigned yesterday. I declared it this morning, as soon as I knew there was an overlap.”

The client breathed out down the line. “Come on, Ren. I’m not asking for the file. Just a sense of where they’re going. Whether it’s the crew. Whether it’s us. You could ask her what the team thinks.”

“No.”

“Two people are dead. The airline needs to understand what these people are likely to conclude.”

He heard himself say it and let it stand. “The airline needs to co-operate fully and preserve every record it has. It mustn’t try to anticipate the investigators’ conclusions or influence them through anybody. Above all not through me. I’m taking no part in any work on this accident. Compliance is reviewing the rest of the account.”

“Five years, Ren. And you’ll walk away because your girlfriend has a case?”

Ren Hao’s face didn’t change at all. “I’m going to make sure nobody can reasonably say that your company, or that investigation, got special treatment because of me. That protects you too. You’ll see it in about a year.”

The line went dead. He looked at the phone a while. Then he pulled his laptop towards him and wrote it all down: the time of the call, who’d said what, in what words. Nobody had asked him to. It was what she would have done.

✦ ✦ ✦

She came to his office after seven with two cartons of noodles in a paper bag, in a black top and jeans with her hair tied back. He was standing at the window.

“You’re saving my life.”

She kissed him and stood back. “Don’t exaggerate. It’s noodles. My review’s thinking about safeguards. I might come off. And your client?”

He told her about the call. Not the words, which were his client’s; the shape of it. When he’d finished she didn’t say anything for a while.

“You shouldn’t have to drop him because of me.”

“I’m not deciding it because of you.”

She put the bag on his desk and came closer. “You’re standing at a window thinking about dropping your biggest client because I’m on the investigation. You built this with him over five years, before you ever met me. If you can keep working with him without going near the accident, you should be allowed to. That’s your work. If the overlap’s too wide, your compliance woman decides that. Not me. And not you, standing there feeling noble about it.”

“And if it’s serious?”

She reached for his hand. “Then you step back. But because it’s right, not because I’m your girlfriend. Those aren’t the same reason, and I need to know which one you’re using. I don’t want to be the reason you lose something you built. I’d never be able to stop seeing it.”

He looked at her a long while. There was something familiar about the way she said it. Not the words, what was under them. She didn’t want him reorganising his working life round her without asking what she wanted. She wanted him to trust her judgement about her own life, and about his.

“I won’t decide anything on my own tonight. Compliance decides whether the safeguards are enough. If they’re not, I step back from what needs stepping back from, or the whole account. If they are, I keep him, and keep every inch of this accident away from me,” he said.

“That’s reasonable. I had a whole day to think about it. Some of us work, Hao.”

✦ ✦ ✦

They ate at his desk because he still hadn’t finished the note compliance had sent. She sat opposite with one leg folded under her and ate straight out of the carton. He’d put his on a plate.

She took a piece of beef off his plate. “Making a takeaway look like a state dinner. Does he know it’s me? By name?”

“He knows your name.”

She smiled a little. “Then he knows he can’t come near me. If he does, I’ll report it. And I won’t tell you I’ve reported it. That’s going to be the strangest part. Not telling you things.”

He took her free hand. “Are you worried? About him? Us?”

She thought about it properly. “A bit. But I don’t think we should pretend we haven’t got working lives just because we’ve got each other. That’s how people end up in reports. You’re allowed clients I don’t like. You’re allowed to disagree with me.”

“That happens fairly often.”

She kicked him under the desk, and he laughed and lifted her hand and kissed it.

“Thank you for not asking me to make this easier by pretending it isn’t there,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

Just after ten compliance rang. She stayed at the window looking out at the city and didn’t listen to anything she didn’t need to hear. When he put the phone down she turned round.

“There’s a conflict. They don’t think the whole relationship has to end. I’m walled off from anything to do with the accident, the airline’s response or any inquiry that comes out of it. Another partner takes all of it. I won’t see the files or sit in any of the discussions. The rest of the account gets looked at every quarter, and if keeping it separate stops being realistic, I step away completely.”

“That sounds right. How do you feel?”

“Relieved. And annoyed. At all of it.”

“That’s allowed,” said Song-Zhu.

“Whatever your review decides, I won’t ask you to change anything for me. And I won’t expect you to tell me anything.”

“Good,” said Song-Zhu, and leaned down across his desk and kissed him.

At the lift she turned round. “Do you regret it? Having a client who owns an airline?”

He touched her cheek. “I regret the overlap. I don’t regret building something before I knew you existed. And I don’t regret you. Even when you’re difficult.”

She kissed him, and he held her there with a hand at the back of her neck. “Don’t drop him for me. Don’t let him push you either. And don’t let this be something we fight about.”

“That’s three things.”

“Then that’s all I’m asking. Three things,” she said, and stepped into the lift, and stuck her hand out between the closing doors to make them open again so she could kiss him once more, and the lift alarm complained, and Raymond, coming along the corridor with a folder, turned smartly round and went back the way he had come.

✦ ✦ ✦

The following Tuesday her review came back. The disclosure was accepted with safeguards. She stayed on the team, under the same rules of access as everyone else. The conflict went on the file, and any approach to her through anyone would be logged and reported. His firm kept its wall. The client stayed. Another partner took every call about the accident. Neither of them got anything from the other, and neither of them asked.

On Friday evening she sent him a photograph of a page of her notebook. At the top, underlined, in her small fast hand:

Things I’m not telling my boyfriend
1. The investigation.
2. The witnesses.
3. The recorders.
4. What I want for dinner.

He laughed alone in his office.

Ren Hao: I see you’ve adopted a robust information policy. What do you want for dinner?

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Soup. No business. And you tell me one thing that happened at work today with nothing to do with aeroplanes.

Ren Hao: Raymond wore a bow tie to a board meeting.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): I need photographs.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): I’m glad you’re keeping him. Don’t make me responsible for your business decisions.

Ren Hao: I wouldn’t dare. I love you.

The reply took a minute.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): I know. Soup at eight. Bring the bow tie photograph.
