There were things they could share and things they couldn’t, and for the first time Ren Hao understood that keeping the line between them wasn’t a distance. It was part of how they stayed close.

chapters.title: Chaos in Three Parts
chapters.desc: A week of her life as he sees it: a training hangar, a funeral, karaoke. Friday, nowhere at all: explicit, all day in bed.
chapters.epigraph: “On Tuesday I learned that your work smells terrible.”
chapters.content:
By Monday evening Ren Hao had concluded that he didn’t understand how Song-Zhu fitted a whole week into one day.

On Monday the twentieth of October she rang after seven to ask if he wanted dinner, rang back to say she was still at work, sent a photograph of a vending-machine sandwich with the message this is a personal insult, and asked if he could come over. When he got there at nine she’d forgotten she’d asked. He found her on the floor of her living room in a ring of paper, wearing one sock, holding half a packet of crackers.

“You’re early.”

“It’s nine.”

“Exactly.”

She looked at the papers too.

“I’m not working. Not officially.”

He laughed, and stepped over a stack of books, and let her pull him down onto the floor beside her.

She heard herself ask what he’d had for dinner, and smiled. “Sorry. Your habit. It’s catching.”

“You’re allowed to ask.”

“Good. Because I’m starving.”

“Those aren’t dinner,” he said, of the crackers.

“They’re emotionally supportive,” said Song-Zhu, and he ordered food, and that was how the week began. He’d thought he’d be spending a few evenings with his girlfriend. He was about to discover that dating her was less like being invited into someone’s routine and more like being handed a pass to a production with no script, no fixed cast and a suspicious amount of instant noodles.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Tuesday it was the hangar.

He’d expected a hangar to be impressive, and it was. He hadn’t expected the smell: metal and hydraulic oil and dust and fuel and something under all of them he couldn’t name. It was the authority’s training hangar, far across the airfield from everything that mattered, and once a year the investigators gave a day there to fire crews and new recruits and anybody who might one day be first to a wreck. Under the high roof sat the fuselage of an old regional jet the authority had bought from a scrapyard for almost nothing years ago and had been taking apart on purpose ever since. Song-Zhu had put his name on the visitors’ list herself, under partner, and given him a laminated pass that said VISITOR in red, and he wore it with more pride than anything he’d ever worn to a board meeting.

She looked him up and down. “You look nearly employable. Stay behind the yellow line. Don’t touch anything. If anyone in hi-vis tells you to move, move.”

“Do you think I’m incapable of following instructions?”

“I’ve seen you with a camp bed,” said Song-Zhu.

He stood behind the line for three hours and watched her teach twenty-two firefighters and nine new investigators how to approach a wreck: where to put their feet, what not to move, why the position of one switch in a cockpit might matter more than anything else on the site, and why the most important thing to do with a flight recorder you’d just found was nothing at all until someone with a camera arrived. Her voice changed when she taught. It went exact. She wasn’t trying to sound clever. She was trying to make sure that one day, on a hillside at four in the morning, somebody in this room got it right.

In the break Dexter stood beside him at the line with a cup of tea. “She doesn’t bring people here. Never. She’s protective of the work. How are you finding it?”

“There’s much more patience in it than people think.”

Dexter nodded slowly, like a man hearing the right answer to an exam question he hadn’t known he’d set.

From across the hangar Song-Zhu shouted, “Dexter! Stop interviewing my boyfriend!” and smiled at Ren Hao over an open access panel with three firefighters crouched round her. He liked the word in her mouth. It wasn’t new any more, and she said it like it had always been true.

They ate lunch on a low concrete wall in the thin October sun, canteen rice and coffee he’d brought from the city.

“Your review of the hangar?”

“Dusty. Your colleagues are nice. And you look extremely attractive when you’re telling firefighters off.”

She nearly dropped her chopsticks. “Don’t say things like that while I’m eating. I’ll choke and you’ll have to do first aid in front of twenty-two firefighters.”

“They’d have it covered.”

She leaned her shoulder against his. “Did you actually like it?”

“I got to see something that matters to you. I think I understand a bit better why you never say I think. Why you always say we found.”

She was quiet a while. “Tomorrow’s different. A funeral. The first officer from the turboprop. His family asked if any of the team would come. Mabel and I said yes.”

He understood at once, and she watched him understand it.

She said it gently. “Not inside. It’s his family’s. And you know what you are, to that airline. But I’d like you to drive me, if you don’t mind waiting.”

“I don’t mind waiting,” said Ren Hao.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Wednesday she hardly spoke in the car. Plain black dress, dark coat, hair tied back, almost no make-up. He parked well down the road from the entrance, out of sight of it, and turned the engine off.

“Go. I’ll be here.”

She kissed his cheek and got out. At the door she stopped to speak to a woman in black who took both her hands, and Song-Zhu bent her head and listened. Ren Hao looked away. He didn’t want to watch her as if she were something breakable. He also knew there were times when even the strongest person on earth needed somewhere to put something down.

She came back almost an hour later with red eyes, and got in, and didn’t put her seat belt on, and he didn’t start the car.

“His daughter’s seven. She kept asking when her dad was coming home, and her mother kept telling her he couldn’t. She had a yellow dress on, and a toy aeroplane too big for her hand. She wouldn’t put it down.”

Song-Zhu looked straight ahead.

“Sometimes I hate that I know what comes next. I know the questions families ask, and how long they’ll wait, and what we can tell them and what we can’t. And I know that even when we answer, it won’t bring anybody back. I don’t want to become someone who thinks that’s normal.”

“You won’t.”

“How do you know?”

“Because you’re sitting here frightened that you might. You’re allowed to get used to doing your job. Nobody’s asking you to get used to people dying.”

Her eyes filled. She leaned across the console into him, awkwardly, the handbrake in the way, and he held her as well as a man could across the front of a car.

“I don’t want to go home yet.”

“Then we’ll stay here.”

They sat in the parked car a long while with her eyes shut and her hand in his. When she lifted her head she said, “Sorry.”

“Let’s retire that one,” he said, and she almost laughed.

At her flat she changed into soft trousers and one of his old shirts, which she’d stolen in August and never returned, and held the tea he made without drinking it.

“Can we talk about something stupid? Tell me something embarrassing about yourself.”

“I once fell asleep in a lecture at university. In the front row. The professor asked me a question, and I answered it, apparently correctly, in my sleep.”

She stared at him, and then laughed properly for the first time all day. “That isn’t embarrassing, that’s showing off.”

He told her stories from his life he’d never thought were interesting, all afternoon, and when she fell asleep against him with the cold tea on the table her hand was still lying over his.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Thursday the idea was hers. Naturally.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Free tonight? Karaoke. Bring your singing voice.

Ren Hao: I have one.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): We’ll see.

She opened her door in a dark green top with her hair loose, and he said, “You’re beautiful,” before he’d said hello, and she rolled her eyes and kissed him and picked up her bag.

The room was small: a big screen, two microphones, a long sofa against the wall, and a table she’d already covered with drinks and snacks. She’d booked two hours and intended to use every minute.

“What’s your favourite song?”

“I listen to music. I don’t have a favourite.”

She looked at him like he’d personally disappointed her, and chose. The third was a duet he didn’t know. She held out a microphone. “That’s the point.”

She sang with enormous enthusiasm, missed lines, laughed halfway through verses because she’d misread the words, and danced in her seat. At the bridge she turned her microphone towards him and he sang the line on his own, and she stopped dead with her mouth open.

“You can sing.”

“I sang in a choir until I was fourteen. In Vancouver. Isla will have photographs.”

“Isla is going to send me every one of them. Sing the next bit,” said Song-Zhu, and watched him with a look that made him lose his place.

By the second hour she’d got ambitious: an old love song, then another, then a ballad with a chorus so high he refused point-blank. She sang it anyway, at full volume, standing on the sofa, and he applauded and she bowed and sat down beside him and leaned into his side. The next song was a slow one, and neither of them reached for a microphone. Halfway through the first verse she kissed him.

He laughed against her mouth, put his microphone down and turned to her properly, his hand at her waist. Somewhere on the recording a man’s voice rose dramatically into the chorus and she broke away just long enough to say, “You’re missing your part,” and kissed him again, and her microphone rolled off the sofa onto the floor, and neither of them picked it up until that song had finished and another had started and finished too.

On the pavement afterwards she held his hand all the way to the car. “You’re handsome. You’re a good kisser. You’re very patient. And I like you.”

He stopped and turned her round and kissed her. “The last one’s my favourite.”

✦ ✦ ✦

On Friday his phone woke him early.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Don’t make plans today. Nothing. Absolutely nothing. Here. Now.

Ren Hao: I’ll be there in twenty minutes.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Fifteen. You’re a managing director. Manage.

He was there in twenty-one with a bag of breakfast. She opened the door in an enormous T-shirt with her hair in a loose knot, and came up behind him as he put the bag on the counter and wrapped her arms round his waist and kissed the side of his neck, then his cheek when he turned, then his mouth.

“Is this the plan?”

“This is the plan,” she said, and took his hand to the bedroom, and breakfast stayed on the counter for three hours.

There was nowhere to be. She’d put her phone on silent on the windowsill, deliberately, where they could both watch it doing nothing. His laptop was in the bag by the door. The curtains were half open and the morning lay across the bed in a long pale stripe. They talked between kisses. She told him his hair looked ridiculous in the morning and he told her it was her fault, and she said she accepted no responsibility for his appearance, and he said that was a shame because he was officially her problem now, and she kissed him to stop him talking.

He undressed her like he’d been given all day for it, which he had. She lay back in the stripe of sun and watched him look at her, and liked it. He put his mouth on her throat, her collarbone, the inside of her elbow, the curve under her breast, her hip, the back of her knee, taking his time over each like they all mattered equally, until she was laughing and impatient and then neither, only breathing. When he pushed into her she wrapped her legs round him and held him there, still and deep, and they stayed like that doing almost nothing, kissing, barely moving, until the not-moving became unbearable and she said his name in a voice that meant now, and he gave her what she wanted.

Breakfast was cold by the time they remembered it. She ate cold toast cross-legged on the bed and made a face at it, and when he reached for his phone to order something else she held out her hand. “Later. Come back.”

Joyce rang after lunch about a shipping client’s revised document. He looked down at Song-Zhu drawing idle patterns on his forearm. “Send it. I’ll look at it later.”

When he’d put the phone down she said, “You’re allowed to work, you know. I don’t want to keep you from things.”

“You’re not keeping me from anything. I chose to be here.”

In the afternoon she decided she wanted tea, and then didn’t, and then did. He stood in her kitchen in his boxers looking at the kettle while she called “Maybe” from the bedroom about sugar, and then she appeared in the doorway wrapped in a sheet and crossed the kitchen and put her arms round him.

“I want you. Is that difficult?” she said.

“Extremely,” said Ren Hao, and put the kettle down.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the evening she decided she wanted him to beg. She didn’t tell him. She’d been teasing him for the best part of an hour: a kiss, then a retreat; her hand flat on his stomach, then gone as he reached for her. He’d been patient. He was beginning to regret how patient.

“Ask nicely,” she said, propped on one elbow, watching his face with enormous interest.

“Please.”

She leaned in and kissed him, deep and slow, and let him believe she’d finished teasing, her hand sliding down his stomach and closing round him, and he groaned into her mouth. Then she let go, and lay back on her pillow with her hands folded on her chest like a woman at rest, and laughed out loud at his face.

“You’re very handsome when you’re frustrated.”

He caught her hand and kissed her palm, and there was no joke left in him at all. “Please stop making me wait. I can’t. I want you so badly I can’t think. Please, Song-Zhu.”

He wasn’t managing it, or being reasonable. He was asking, plainly, with nothing held back, and she found she loved hearing him ask more than almost anything.

She rolled onto him and took him inside her in one long slow movement, and he made a sound she’d never heard from him, low and broken and grateful, and held on to her hips. She rode him slowly, watching him, then not slowly, and he said her name over and over, and please, and yes, and she gave him every single thing he asked for until he couldn’t ask for anything, and he came with his head pressed back into her pillow and his whole body arched up into hers, and she followed with her forehead on his chest and his heart going under it like something trying to get out.

✦ ✦ ✦

Later the city lights had come on beyond the curtains. She lay with her head on his chest and one leg over his under the blanket, nearly asleep.

“Did you have a good week?”

“On Tuesday I learned that your work smells terrible.”

She lifted her head in outrage.

“On Wednesday I learned that sometimes the most useful thing I can do is wait in a car. On Thursday, that you sing very loudly with no respect at all for the key the song was written in. Friday was perfect.”

She put her cheek back down. “On Tuesday I got to show you something that matters to me. On Wednesday I didn’t have to be on my own afterwards. On Thursday I got to be ridiculous. And on Friday I had you all to myself. You’ve seen the nice parts and the hard parts this week, and you’re still here. I think I like that,” she said, low, like a confession.

Late, his phone buzzed on the bedside table. She caught his wrist without opening her eyes. “Tomorrow. Whatever it is.”

He put it down. He looked at her hair spread across his chest, and said it, because he always would. “I love you.”

She was quiet so long he thought she was asleep. Then, without opening her eyes: “Not too loud.”

He laughed under his breath. A hangar, a funeral, a karaoke booth, and a day with no destination at all. He’d seen her competence and her grief and her laughter and the particular mischief she kept only for him, and he’d learned that loving Song-Zhu didn’t mean knowing what she’d do next. It meant going with her, and now and then giving up on breakfast.

chapters.title: He Gives Up Managing
chapters.desc: He gives up managing for a week and it nearly kills him. At 3 a.m. her phone rings; he checks her location once, and tells her at breakfast. She forgives him in the doorway.
chapters.epigraph: “You can worry. Just don’t make it a project.”
chapters.content:
Ren Hao lasted six days.

Six days without asking Mr. Yau to keep an eye on anything. Six days without reminding her to eat, sleep, drink water or take a break, or checking whether her plans had changed or whether the weather might affect her journey home. No timetable. No shared calendar. He didn’t even ask what time she thought she’d finish. By every measurable standard he was behaving like a perfectly normal man in a relationship, and he hated it.

It had been his idea, which made it worse. On Sunday the ninth of November, in her bed, he’d said into the dark, “I’m going to try something this week. No arranging. Nothing. To see if I can.”

She’d said, “Oh no,” and then turned over and kissed him hard, which he took as encouragement.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Monday he woke at twenty to seven and reached for his phone. The last message was from the night before.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Going to sleep. Don’t miss me too much.

She hadn’t said whether she’d got home first. She’d been at the compound till ten. His thumb hovered over Did you get in all right? He deleted it and lay looking at the ceiling, and twenty minutes later picked the phone up again, and knew he was becoming ridiculous.

At half past eight Joyce brought in the revised proposal, and stayed where she was after he’d thanked her.

“Are you all right, Mr. Ren? You’ve looked at your phone twelve times since I came in. Are you waiting for someone?”

He went back to the document. “Apparently.”

Joyce nodded like this explained everything, and left, and through the glass he saw her bend down and say something to Momo, who looked at his door.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Alive. Busy day. Don’t wait up tonight.

Ren Hao: All right.

He didn’t ask what she was doing, or when she’d finish, or offer a car. He put the phone down and spent forty minutes wondering whether she’d eaten.

✦ ✦ ✦

Tuesday was worse. After nine at night came a photograph of a convenience-store rice ball, captioned Dinner, and then a paper cup of coffee, captioned Also dinner.

Ren Hao: That isn’t food.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): It’s brown.

Ren Hao: So is the table.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Miss you.

He nearly asked what time she’d be home.

Ren Hao: Miss you too. I hope the rest of the evening goes smoothly.

She sent back a single heart. He was beginning to suspect the exercise had been designed to show him every weakness in his character.

On Wednesday rain walked across the harbour towards the thirty-second floor, and a photograph came through of a wet road and the edge of a hangar roof with water pouring off it. Weather is disgusting. She was outside, in that. He typed Have you got an umbrella? and deleted it, typed Are you still at the hangar? and deleted that, stood up, walked to the window, and sat down again.

Ren Hao: Let me know if you need anything.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): I know. You’re doing really well, Hao.

He hadn’t realised she knew how hard it was.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Thursday, at exactly nine in the morning, his phone rang in the middle of a meeting with three partners and a man from an insurer who was explaining a clause. Song-Zhu. Nine o’clock.

He stood up. “Excuse me. Ten minutes.”

He leaned against the wall in the corridor by the window.

“Hello.”

She sounded astonished. “You picked up. I wanted to see if you’d actually do it. Are you in a meeting? And you walked out?”

“I said ten minutes.”

Her voice changed. “I haven’t got anything to tell you. I just wanted the ten minutes.”

“Then have them.”

So she had them. She told him about the rain, and Dexter falling asleep in the canteen with a spoon in his hand, and a pigeon that had got into the records room and been there a week, it turned out, eating a filing system. At the end of the ten minutes exactly she said, “Go back to your insurer,” and rang off, and he stood in the corridor with the phone against his chest before he went back in.

The insurer looked at him with deep suspicion. Raymond, who’d watched the whole thing through the glass, was looking at the ceiling.

“Where were we,” said Ren Hao.

That evening she rang again, and he picked up before the first ring had finished.

She was delighted. “Not in a meeting? Not saving a company? How are you?”

“How are you? Tired? Have you eaten?”

There was a pause. He closed his eyes.

She burst out laughing. “Four days, Hao. You lasted four days.”

“I asked a question.”

“You asked the question.”

Then her voice went softer.

“Thank you for trying. You haven’t once asked me where I am, and you walked out on an insurer. I don’t want you to stop caring. That’s not what this is. I like that you worry when I’m out late. I just don’t want you to feel you have to keep me safe every minute of the day, or think that if you stop checking, something terrible will happen.”

“I can help it.”

“Maybe. I miss you. Can I see you tomorrow? Don’t make plans,” said Song-Zhu.

✦ ✦ ✦

Friday was hard because nothing happened. She didn’t message after the morning. He knew she forgot her phone existed when a case got difficult. He opened their conversation in the afternoon and closed it again. At twenty past six:

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Free? Come over.

He left the office without his laptop. Joyce watched him go past her desk with nothing in his hands at all and said, “Have a nice weekend, Mr. Ren,” in a voice that suggested she was going to tell Momo.

Song-Zhu opened her door in a loose grey T-shirt with her hair damp from the shower, and looked at the space beside him. “No bag? No laptop? No folders? Look at you.”

He stepped in and put his hands on her waist. “It’s been an awful week. I’ve been trying very hard not to interfere with your life, and I’ve discovered I have an extremely irritating personality.”

She laughed into his chest. “I could have told you that.”

They did nothing at all. She lay on the sofa with her legs across his lap and they watched a film neither of them cared about. At one point she put her hand on his jaw.

“That bit. Where you clench it. You’re pretending not to worry.”

He breathed out, and made himself lean back.

Some time after eleven she fell asleep on his shoulder and he put the blanket over her. Her phone lay on the coffee table. He looked at it, and away. He wondered whether someone might ring, whether she might have to go somewhere. He knew none of it mattered. He looked at her sleeping face and told himself he wouldn’t check, he wouldn’t ask, he’d trust her.

✦ ✦ ✦

At seven minutes past three her phone rang.

He was awake at once. She wasn’t. Duty Officer. He put it into her hand and touched her shoulder. “Song-Zhu. Work.”

She was sitting up and answering before her eyes had opened. He watched her come all the way awake in about four seconds, the sleep going out of her face like somebody had wiped it. “Which runway? Anyone hurt? Has the operator pulled the recorder breaker? Then ring them again and tell them to do it now, before anyone powers anything up. I’ll be there in forty minutes.”

She was already on her feet.

“A freighter scraped its tail landing. Nobody’s hurt. But it’s mine. I’ll ring you when I can.” She pulled on trousers, a jumper, her lanyard, and stopped at the door with her bag.

He heard the lift, and then nothing. He knew she’d driven to a hundred call-outs before she’d met him. He knew she’d ring when she could. He also knew he wasn’t going to sleep. He lasted until twenty to four.

They’d turned on location sharing the night of the typhoon, in a small room at the end of a corridor, for tonight, because the compound was three kilometres across. Neither of them had turned it off. He’d never once looked at it since.

He told himself he only wanted to see she was moving. He opened it.

A small blue dot on the airport perimeter road, moving towards the cargo gate.

He watched it for perhaps five seconds and closed the map. He sat on the arm of her sofa in the dark, and felt better, and hated himself for it, because the relief hadn’t come from trusting her. It had come from knowing where she was.

✦ ✦ ✦

She came back after eight with two paper cups of coffee. He was in her kitchen making eggs.

“How long have you been up?”

“Since you left.”

“Poor thing,” she said, and kissed his cheek.

He put the coffee down. “I need to tell you something.”

He made himself say it in order, the way he’d have wanted a report.

“After you left, about a quarter to four, I looked at your location on the map from the typhoon. I saw you on the perimeter road. I closed it. I didn’t ring you or anyone else. I looked once, and I closed it.”

She didn’t move. “Why?”

He could have given her the easy answer: three in the morning, a sudden call, he was worried. All true. Not the whole truth.

“Because I was anxious and I wanted to know where you were. I knew you were fine to go. I knew you’d ring when you could. I wanted to see it for myself anyway. I told you I wouldn’t keep track of you, and then I did. I’m sorry.”

She put her coffee down on the counter. “Would you have looked if you hadn’t promised not to?”

He thought about it honestly. “I don’t know.”

“That’s an honest answer. Why are you telling me?”

“Because you should know. Because I don’t want you finding out in six months and wondering what else I’ve done without telling you.”

Something in her face eased. She drank some coffee and looked at him over the cup.

“I’m not happy you looked. I’m glad you told me. I know last night was hard. But I don’t want you to turn my location into the way you deal with being frightened. If something happens, I’ll tell you what I can. If I need help, I’ll ask. And if I don’t ring straight away, it doesn’t mean something terrible’s happened. It means I’m under an aeroplane.”

“You’re right.”

“I need you to trust me.”

“I’m learning to,” he said.

“Better,” said Song-Zhu, and almost smiled.

✦ ✦ ✦

They ate the eggs standing at the counter. Neither of them mentioned the map for several minutes. Then she said, “Do you want me to turn it off?”

“I’d like to take myself off it. You keep yours for anything practical. I don’t want the option there every time I’m anxious.”

“You don’t have to do it because you feel guilty.”

“I’m doing it because I know myself.”

He took out his phone and removed himself from her location and turned the screen so she could see the confirmation.

She reached across the counter and touched his hand. “You look miserable. Don’t. I don’t need you to be perfect, Hao. I need you to be honest with me, most of all when you’ve got it wrong. Also, you made too many eggs.”

“I made enough for two.”

“There’s enough for four. You’re a terrible liar,” she said, and the tension in the kitchen let go. The mistake hadn’t gone anywhere. He’d told her the truth, and she’d decided to stay in the room with it.

✦ ✦ ✦

When she was getting ready to go back for the morning review he stood by her door and handed her the jacket she’d left on the sofa. He didn’t ask where she was going or when she’d be back. He didn’t offer to drive.

“You’re very quiet,” she said, putting it on.

“I’m trying not to ask six questions.”

“You can ask one.”

“Can I see you tonight?”

“Yes. Don’t book anything. Don’t send me a reminder.”

“I genuinely wasn’t going to.”

She opened the door, and turned back with the jacket half on and her bag on her shoulder. “Hao. I forgive you. For the map. All of it. I’m not keeping it.”

He stood still. She came back the one step from the doorway and took his face in both hands and kissed him. Hard, like she was stamping something.

Her thumb moved on his cheek. “If you’re frightened, tell me. You don’t have to pretend you’re fine. And you don’t have to turn into someone who never worries about me either. You can worry. Just don’t make it a project.”

He laughed under his breath.

“Don’t make a plan,” she said.

He laughed properly, and she looked at him with her head on one side. “I love it when you laugh like that.”

She heard what else was nearly in the sentence, and so did he, and neither of them said it.

“I love you,” he said instead, because one of them could.

She stood in her doorway with her hand still on his face, and nodded, and went.

He didn’t look at the time. He didn’t open the map. He closed her door and washed up the extra eggs, and trusted that if she wanted him, she knew exactly where he was.

chapters.title: Her Recorder
chapters.desc: Her father’s pocket recorder, and the four minutes of air traffic she copied onto it at twenty and never played. She plays it with him in the room. Afterwards, explicit and very quiet: she leads.
chapters.epigraph: “I want to be close to someone who’s alive.”
chapters.content:
The first thing Ren Hao noticed was that she’d tidied her flat.

Not thoroughly. There were still books stacked by the sofa, a cardigan over a dining chair, and a mug on the windowsill he suspected had been there since Tuesday. But the kitchen counter was clear, the coffee table was empty, and the small heap of things that lived beside her television had gone somewhere else.

He stood in the doorway on Saturday the thirteenth of December holding a paper bag of dinner. “Should I be worried? I recognise your natural habitat, and this isn’t it.”

She laughed. “Come in, handsome.”

She took the bag and looked inside. Noodles, and dumplings, because she’d said noodles and dumplings. She was different tonight. Not unhappy, not far away. Quieter. Her hair was tied low at the back of her neck and she wore an old oversized white shirt with the sleeves pushed up. No television. No music. Her phone lay dark on the arm of the sofa. She’d been waiting for him.

“Don’t do that. Look at me like you’re trying to find the fault. Like I’m a suspicious document,” she said.

He put his hands on her waist and kissed her cheek, and she leaned into him and stood like that in her kitchen, and said against his shirt, “I want to show you something. Something I’ve never shown anyone. My mother knows I have it. She doesn’t know what I put on it.”

He didn’t ask what it was. He nodded.

✦ ✦ ✦

First they ate. She sat across from him at her small table and stole dumplings from his bowl, and told him a colleague had saved a whole folder of evidence photographs under the name final_final_revised_ACTUAL and she intended to resign on principle. She was almost herself. Almost.

When they’d finished she washed up and he dried without being asked. Then she went into her bedroom. He heard a drawer, and then another, and then a pause that went on a long time.

She came back holding a small black zip case, old, its corners worn smooth, one scuffed pale. She held it against her stomach with both hands and sat beside him on the sofa, her thumb going back and forth over the worn corner.

“It’s my father’s.”

He remembered the photograph on his kitchen floor, a man in a pilot’s shirt in front of a freighter with one hand up against the sun. He remembered there’s one more thing I’ve got of his. Not today. He’d never asked about it again. Now she was offering.

She unzipped the case. In a bed of grey foam lay a pocket voice recorder: silver, the size of a cigarette lighter, a small speaker grille, a scratch across its face, the kind of thing people used in offices before phones did everything.

She swallowed. “He used it for his logbook. Notes after a flight, things to write up properly. And when he was away more than three nights he made little recordings for me and posted the card home in an envelope. The clouds are behaving. Bumpy over the sea, tell your mother I’m fine. Did you finish your homework, I’m checking when I’m back. It was on his desk at home when it happened. My mother gave it to me after the funeral. I’ve never played anything he recorded on it. Not once. I can’t.”

He waited.

She looked at the little silver thing in the foam. “When the final report came out, a year after, the investigators sent the families the air traffic control recording. Not the cockpit. That’s never released. But what goes out on the radio is different. Anyone at that airport with a scanner could have heard it that night. They sent it on a disc with a letter saying we didn’t have to listen. I was twenty. I copied the last four minutes onto his recorder, on a new card, so I wouldn’t lose his. I wanted his voice in something that was his, not on a disc from an office. Then I zipped the case and put it in the drawer. I’ve never pressed play. Six years.”

He understood. She’d heard fifty seconds from inside the cockpit and would never forget a breath of it. This was a recording she’d made with her own hands and never once let herself hear.

“We can put it back,” he said.

Her eyes moved over his face. “I know. But I think I want to. Tonight. With you here. I think that’s why I tidied the flat. Don’t say anything while it’s playing. And don’t try to make me feel better afterwards. Just stay.”

He held out his hand, palm up, on the sofa between them. “I’m here.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She switched it on. The little screen lit pale green: one file, and a time. 04:00. She sat with it in her lap a long time without pressing anything.

“Can I hold your hand?”

Hers was cold. He closed his round it. She pressed play.

A hiss. The hollow crackle of a radio frequency at night. A controller’s voice, a stranger’s, calm and quick, giving someone a heading and a height. And then her father.

Ren Hao had seen him in a photograph and heard her describe his voice from memory at three in the morning. This was different. It was a living voice: a man reading back an instruction in the ordinary rhythm of an ordinary working night. Calm. A little dry. Tired, in a way you’d only have heard if you’d spent years remembering him.

The controller. Her father. A callsign, numbers, a frequency. The plain language of the air at night, the same language Ren Hao had heard on a radio in a small room in a typhoon, spoken by a man whose daughter now sat on a sofa holding his hand.

He kept his eyes on her. He watched her shoulders tighten a little at a time, and her thumb press into his knuckle, and her lean towards the speaker without knowing she was doing it.

The voices got quicker. Her father said something about an engine in exactly the tone he’d have used to say the clouds were behaving. The controller asked him to confirm. He confirmed, and asked to turn back, and was given it. There was nothing in his voice but work.

Her hand tightened until it hurt. Ren Hao didn’t move.

The last four minutes of a man’s working life went by in her small tidy living room. No music, no narrator, nobody explaining anything to the people listening. Two voices and the hiss between them. Once her father’s voice came clear, a single short transmission, and her eyes filled and she leaned closer still, like there might be something on it she’d missed at twenty when she copied it without listening.

Then the controller called his callsign. There was no answer.

The controller called it again. Patient. Level. The hiss. Again, a little quicker. Nothing. Again.

The controller’s voice changed, for the first time in four minutes, slightly, and he said something to somebody else in the room with him, away from the microphone, and called the callsign one more time, and the recording ended. The little screen went back to 00:00.

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t move. Somewhere below on the street a car went past with music playing and was gone.

Her voice was barely there. “I thought he’d sound different. He sounds exactly the same. He sounds like Dad. He was talking about an engine like it was the weather. He sounded like he was going to finish his shift and come home. And the man kept calling him, Hao, and he didn’t answer.”

One tear ran down, and another.

“I’d forgotten how he sounded when he was tired. I remembered his laugh. I remembered him ringing me in my first year at university to tell me not to stay up. But I’d forgotten that voice. The working one.”

He let go of her hand only so he could put his arm round her and draw her in. Her forehead went against his shoulder and her hands took two fistfuls of his shirt, and she cried without making much sound at all. He didn’t tell her she was strong or that her father would have wanted her to be happy. He held her, one hand at the back of her head and the other flat between her shoulder blades, and let her.

“I thought I’d be ready,” she said at last, into his shirt.

Now, he thought, he could speak. “Nobody’s ready to hear someone they miss.”

“I wanted him to say my name. I knew he wouldn’t. He was flying an aeroplane. But I wanted it. And the man kept calling him.”

He held her tighter and said nothing, because there was nothing that wouldn’t have been smaller than what she’d just heard. When he did speak it was only: “You wanted to hear your father. That’s all it was. That’s enough.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Eventually she lifted her face, red-eyed and embarrassed. “I’ve cried all over your shirt again.”

“This shirt’s seen worse. You once tipped a whole bowl of soup down it.”

“That was an experiment. A very successful one.”

She nearly smiled, and he wiped under one of her eyes with his thumb.

“Thank you for not saying anything. You listened,” she said.

She kissed him, small and unsteady, and rested her forehead on his.

“I don’t want to hear it again tonight.”

He switched the recorder off and laid it back in its foam and held the case out to her, and waited for her to tell him where it went. She carried it into the bedroom, and he heard the drawer, and when she came back her hands were empty.

She didn’t put the television on. She came and stood in front of him and held out her hands, and he took them and stood, and she reached for the top button of his shirt.

“Are you sure?”

“I want you.” Her voice was quiet and clear.

He searched her face. Not for permission: for whether she was choosing this or running from the room she’d just been in. She understood what he was looking for, and put her hand on his cheek.

“I’m here. I’m not hiding. I want to be close to someone who’s alive.”

She undid the first button, and the second. There was nothing playful in it tonight, no joke about the price of his shirt. She undressed him one button at a time and he stood still and let her, and when she pushed the shirt off his shoulders she put her palm flat on his chest over his heart and left it there, feeling it go, making sure.

She kissed him, and he kissed her back but didn’t take over. Tonight she led and he followed. At the bedroom door she stopped, and her eyes filled again, and he lifted his hand to her face. She leaned her cheek into his palm, then turned her head and kissed it, and drew him in.

✦ ✦ ✦

Only the lamp by the bed was on.

She undid his belt with all her attention on her hands and on him. He touched her cheek. She took his hand and put it on the first button of her own shirt, and he understood, and undid it, and the next, and the old white shirt slid off her shoulders to the floor. They undressed each other without a single word. No declarations, no questions about tomorrow, nothing made to mean more than it had to.

She lay down and drew him down with her and pulled the blanket over them both, and kissed his shoulder, and reached for him, and he met her halfway.

She moved at her own pace, slow, guiding his hand where she wanted it and holding it there, and he stayed with every small change in her face and her breath. When he was inside her she held his face in both hands and looked at him and didn’t look away, and he didn’t either. They moved together almost without moving: the lamp, the sheets, her breath on his mouth.

Once a tear slid from the corner of her eye into her hair. He stopped at once. She shook her head on the pillow. Not sadness, exactly; something older and more complicated. She held on and moved again, and he understood she wanted him to keep going, and kissed the wet place by her eye, and kept going, slowly.

She didn’t need to fill the silence or tell him what she felt. She wanted to be held, and to touch and be touched, and to have the plain warm breathing proof of another living person against every part of her. So he stayed close, so close there was no space between them anywhere. When she came it was without a sound, her fingers digging into his back and her mouth open against his throat and her whole body trembling under him, and he followed with his face in her hair and her name on his breath, and didn’t let go of her afterwards at all.

✦ ✦ ✦

Much later she said, “Do you think you’d know his voice now? If you heard it again?”

He thought about it carefully. “I think I’d know it because you would. Not because I knew him. Because you’ve let me hear him.”

“He was funny. He was terrible at cooking.”

“That explains your relationship with the kitchen.”

She almost laughed. “He sang when he made breakfast. Terribly.”

“Then I’d have liked him.”

“He’d have told you your shoes were too shiny. And then he’d have liked you,” she said.

He put his mouth to her hair. She settled against him and said, after a long time, “I don’t think I’ll play it again for ages. But I’m glad I did.”

For six years she’d kept those four minutes like they’d break if she touched them. They hadn’t given her an explanation. They hadn’t brought her father home. But she’d heard him again, not as a photograph or a memory she had to keep polishing so it wouldn’t fade: as a voice, reading back a heading at night, alive. And she hadn’t been on her own when it ended.

✦ ✦ ✦

He woke after two. She was asleep with one hand on his chest and a dried trace of tears under one eye. He reached for the tissues on the bedside table and carefully wiped it away.

She stirred, and didn’t open her eyes. “Don’t go.”

Something in his chest turned over. He put his mouth to her temple. “I’m not going anywhere.”

She moved closer, and he held her, and for once neither of them tried to make the silence go away.

chapters.title: Christmas With Two Professors
chapters.desc: Vancouver. Two professors, delighted. Her flight suit makes his mother cry. Her first snow, a hedge, and a kiss at minus twelve.
chapters.epigraph: “Nobody told me it squeaks.”
chapters.content:
The first thing Song-Zhu noticed about Vancouver was that the air hurt her face. The second was that Ren Hao found this extremely entertaining.

“Stop smiling. I can see it from inside my scarf.”

They stood on the kerb outside arrivals on Christmas Eve, a Wednesday, with the light already going blue and the cold coming off the car park like something with an opinion.

“I’ve flown thirteen hours to meet your parents, Hao. I didn’t agree to have my face fall off.”

He pressed his mouth to her knuckles through the wool of her glove. “Your face is still there.”

She’d spent the flight interrogating him. He’d failed statistics once, in his second year, because he disagreed with the marking scheme, and passed it the following summer with the highest mark in the year, and written to the examiner to tell him. She’d laughed so loudly the man across the aisle took his headphones off to see what he was missing.

“What if they don’t like me?”

He stopped with the case handle in his fist and turned all the way round. “My mother’s been asking about your flight suit since September. My father’s read the summary of every report your authority published in the last five years so he’d have something to ask you at dinner. They’re going to adore you. I’m worried they’ll adopt you and send me back.”

She hit him in the arm with her glove, and then put the glove into his coat pocket with his hand and kept it there.

✦ ✦ ✦

She hadn’t known there’d be snow. She saw it first on the motorway verges, grey-white under the lights, and then on the trees, every branch picked out.

“Hao. Is that real snow? I’ve never seen it. My father brought me a snow globe once, from an airport. I dropped it on the kitchen tiles two days later. That’s the closest I’ve been.”

He drove a while without saying anything. “Then you’ll see enough to make up for it.”

She watched the flakes come at the windscreen out of the dark, endlessly. He’d seen her at a crash site with fuel on her boots, on a kitchen floor at three in the morning, in a karaoke booth with a microphone. He’d never seen her look like this, like somebody had opened a door onto a room she’d had no idea was there.

✦ ✦ ✦

The house was at the end of a street of wooden houses with their porch lights on: a wreath on the door, lights wound up the stair rail, books living on the stairs. His mother had the door open before they were out of the car. She was small and quick, silver at her temples, with a voice that had spent thirty years in lecture halls and never once needed raising. Behind her a tall man in glasses and a wool cardigan held a cup of tea he’d plainly forgotten about.

His mother hugged her son on the porch, hard, and then looked at Song-Zhu with the look of someone matching a person to a great many things she’d been told.

“Good evening, Professor Ren. Thank you for having me.”

The hug was immediate and warm and smelled of oranges and cloves. “Oh, no. None of that. You’re even prettier than in the photographs.”

Song-Zhu went still inside the hug. On the step below, Ren Hao closed his eyes.

His mother spoke over Song-Zhu’s shoulder. “Don’t look at me like that. You sent them. One from a restaurant. One from your office with the harbour behind her. One from a karaoke bar, which was blurred, but we could tell she was winning. One from—”

“Mum.”

Song-Zhu turned round slowly, still in his mother’s arms, with a smile spreading across her face that he knew he’d be paying for until the new year.

His father held out his free hand. “Enough for us to know you make him very happy. Welcome to Vancouver. Come in before you freeze. Isla rang this morning. She’s staying home with her inspector this year, and says you’re to report back on everything.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Inside it was warm all the way through. A tree hung with paper things children had made a long time ago, something roasting, a fire. His mother took her coat and then her hands, and frowned at how cold they were, and sent her son upstairs with both cases to the blue room. His father brought Song-Zhu tea in a mug that said I’d rather be reading.

“You’ll want to call us something. There are two of us. It’s a practical difficulty.”

“Then I’ll say Professor and you can both answer.”

He considered this with real pleasure. “That’s very efficient.”

“I’m an investigator. I work with what I’ve got.”

Dinner wasn’t the interrogation she’d expected. It was worse. It was interest. His father taught literature and translated poetry out of three languages in the evenings. His mother taught political science and had once, Ren Hao said, reduced a visiting minister to silence with a single follow-up question. They both asked something and then actually waited, like the answer mattered more than whatever they’d been about to say next.

“When you investigate an accident, do you begin with the most likely explanation?” said his mother.

“We begin with what we can establish. The most likely explanation’s a trap if you start treating it as a conclusion. Everybody’s decided what happened before we’ve opened the hangar. I have to decide nothing for as long as I can.”

“That’s what I tell my graduate students about elections, and they never believe me.”

“Families want to know why someone didn’t come home. The airline wants to know if it’s their fault. The newspapers want it by Thursday. But the report has to be honest, even if the honest answer for a year is that we don’t know yet,” said Song-Zhu.

“That sounds like scholarship,” said his father.

“With more wreckage,” said Song-Zhu, and his mother laughed out loud.

Ren Hao said almost nothing all meal, which his mother noticed and looked at her husband about and didn’t mention. He was watching his parents listen to her. She wasn’t performing. She was being herself at his parents’ table with his mother’s good napkin on her knee, and they were leaning towards her, and something in his chest that had been braced since September let go.

✦ ✦ ✦

The flight suit had been his mother’s idea. I’ve never seen a real one. Only on the news. Song-Zhu had said it smelled of hangar and packed it anyway, washed and folded at the bottom of her case. On Christmas morning, before anyone else was down, she put it on: the working one, dark blue, the authority’s patch on the shoulder, her name over the breast pocket, a scorch near one cuff and a mend on the knee in thread that didn’t quite match. She felt ridiculous, and went down anyway.

His mother was in the kitchen in her dressing gown with the kettle. She turned round, and stopped.

“May I?”

She touched the sleeve, the stitching on the patch, the name. Her fingers found the scorch at the cuff, and the mend on the knee, and stayed on the mend. “You go to the sites in this. And climb into them. The aeroplanes. Afterwards. Does it frighten you?”

Song-Zhu thought about lying, and didn’t. “Sometimes.”

“Good. I’d worry about you if you said it didn’t.”

Her eyes filled all at once, all the way. “He told us about your father. Only that he was a pilot, and that he died. He said the rest was yours. I’ve been thinking since September how proud he’d be, standing in his daughter’s— I’m sorry. I’m sorry, it’s Christmas,” she said, laughing at herself, wiping her face with the back of her wrist.

Nobody said that to her. People said I’m sorry for your loss and is that why you do it? Nobody had stood in a kitchen on Christmas morning and said the one thing she’d never let herself think in so many words.

“Thank you,” she managed.

Ren Hao stood in the doorway in a jumper with his hair wet, looking from his mother’s face to Song-Zhu’s. He crossed the kitchen and put his hand flat on Song-Zhu’s back, low. “All right?”

“Your mother likes my flight suit.”

“I love her flight suit,” said his mother, and blew her nose on a piece of kitchen roll.

✦ ✦ ✦

Christmas Day went slowly, the way it should. Her mother rang from her aunt’s and asked to speak to Ren Hao, and Song-Zhu watched him go pink in his parents’ living room answering questions in his best and most careful Chinese.

His mother gave her lined gloves, the warmest she’d ever owned. His father gave her a slim old book of poems about flight, in translation, with his own pencil notes in the margins. “I’ve marked the ones that are honest. Most poets have never been in an aeroplane. You’ll be able to tell.”

Ren Hao gave her a small box. On a fine chain, a silver snowflake no bigger than her thumbnail.

“For the globe. The one on the tiles,” he said, so only she heard.

She couldn’t say anything. She turned and held her hair off her neck, and he fastened it, and his fingers stayed on the nape of her neck a second longer than they needed to.

Across the room his mother leaned towards her husband. “They’re very sweet. You’re not saying enough.”

He turned a page. “Would you like an essay?”

“At least a paragraph,” said his wife, and he laughed, and took her hand instead.

✦ ✦ ✦

The snow began again at three, with the light going.

“It’s minus twelve,” said Ren Hao from the chair by the fire.

“Your mother told me. She said it’s the coldest Christmas in eleven years, like it was a compliment,” said Song-Zhu, already in her coat, and his mother appeared in the kitchen door and told them to take the thick red scarves.

The cold hit her like a wall. The garden she’d seen the night before had gone. In its place was a white, rounded, silent country: the lawn smoothed over, the hedges bulked into soft walls, the old tree at the end loaded and drooping, the fence posts wearing caps. The flakes came down out of a grey-violet sky without any sound at all. It was quieter than a recorder room. She could hear her own breath.

She crouched and pressed her glove into the snow, and looked up, astonished. “It squeaks. Nobody told me it squeaks.”

Her first snowball fell apart. Her second burst on his chest and left a white star on his black coat. He looked down at it, and bent, quite slowly, and gathered a handful, packing it between his gloves and looking at her the way he looked at people across a negotiating table.

“I’m a guest in your parents’ house,” said Song-Zhu.

It got her on the shoulder and a cold spray went down the inside of her collar, and she shrieked, and went for him, and slipped on the path at once. He caught her round the waist, and they staggered together into the drift by the hedge, and he turned as they fell so he hit the snow first, on his back, and she landed on top of him.

She lay on his chest and laughed until she couldn’t breathe. “You’re supposed to be a gentleman.”

“I’m lying in a hedge. This is as off duty as I get.”

She stopped laughing. His cheeks were red with cold, there was snow on his eyelashes and a flake melting on his lower lip, and he was looking up at her through the falling snow with an expression she’d only ever seen on him in the dark.

She pulled her right glove off with her teeth and let it drop, and laid her bare palm along his jaw. He hissed at the cold of her fingers. She kept it there and felt him warm under it, and kissed him.

His mouth was cold on the outside, and then, when his lips parted, so warm inside that she made a small helpless sound against him. Their breath went up between them in one white cloud. He held her down on him with one hand wide on her back through the coat and the other under the edge of the red scarf at the back of her neck, his gloved fingers on her skin where he’d fastened the chain. She kissed him slowly and then not slowly, tasted cold and cinnamon from his mother’s biscuits and him, and his hand slid down and pressed her hips into his through two coats and held her there. Snow fell on the back of her neck. She kissed the flake off his lip, and his cold cheekbone, and came back to his mouth with her bare hand going numb on his jaw and the rest of her warm.

When she lifted her head they were both out of breath. “The coldest Christmas in eleven years, and I came outside to kiss you in a hedge.”

His voice had gone rough. He took her red fingers off his jaw and put them inside his coat against his shirt, over his heart, and held them there through the wool. “You’ll lose a finger.”

“Worth it. Everything I do is listening, and this is the first place I’ve been where there’s nothing to hear.”

He turned his head and kissed her wrist at the cuff of her coat, where the pulse was.

A sharp tapping came on glass. His mother was at the kitchen window holding up two mugs and pointing at them meaningfully. Beside her his father had lifted his book in front of his face.

✦ ✦ ✦

They came in soaked to the knees with the red scarves stiff with frost.

“He threw the second one down my neck.”

“Ren Hao, you are twenty-seven years old,” said his mother.

“Twenty-seven and three-quarters.”

“That doesn’t help.”

From the armchair his father lowered his book. “Who won?”

Song-Zhu put her hand up. Ren Hao opened his mouth, and his father said, “Do you have evidence?” and when his son shut it again, went back to his book and turned a page with deep satisfaction.

✦ ✦ ✦

The house went quiet early. His parents’ door closed at half past ten and the heating ticked in the walls. At eleven the door of the blue room opened without a sound, and Ren Hao stood in it barefoot.

“My mother is directly underneath us,” he said, low.

Song-Zhu sat up in bed in his jumper. “Then don’t step on the board by the wardrobe. It creaks. I’ve been listening to this house for two days. It’s my job.”

He stepped over the board and got in beside her, and for a while only lay against her back in the narrow bed under the slope of the ceiling, the snow light coming blue through the curtains. Then he put his mouth to the back of her neck, on the fine silver chain, and left it there, and she turned over in his arms.

“So we’ll have to be very quiet.”

“You’ve never been quiet in your life.”

“I’m a professional listener. Prove I can’t.”

She kissed him, and he kissed her back deep and slow with his hand spreading warm under the jumper on her bare back, and she made a small sound, and he stopped at once and put his thumb against her lower lip.

“That was not quiet. My mother marks essays for a living. She’ll have heard the full stop.”

She bit his thumb, gently. He breathed in through his nose. They lay in his parents’ blue room and kissed without a sound, slow and endless, her hands in his hair and his hand flat and still at the small of her back, holding her against him, both of them shaking with the effort of silence, until she was flushed all over and he was breathing like he’d run. Then the board by the wardrobe creaked on its own, the way old houses do, and they both froze, and she pushed her face into his chest and laughed without a sound until the bed shook.

“Next year I’m booking a hotel. If you’ll come,” he whispered into her hair.

She lifted her head and looked at him in the blue dark.

“Ask me next year,” she said.

✦ ✦ ✦

Sunday came too fast. She stood in the blue room folding clothes into her case with the snowflake against her shirt, and he leaned in the doorway.

“Your father gave me a book with his own notes in it. Does he do that for everybody?”

He paused. “No.”

“Your mother says I can come back whenever I want. I didn’t expect to feel at home here,” she said, and touched the pendant.

He sat down beside her. “I’ll ask you every year.”

“That’s better than promising,” said Song-Zhu, and he kissed her there on the edge of the case, with the snow still coming down past the window.

At the gate she went through the photographs on her phone: him under the loaded tree, his mother laughing at the stove, his father pretending badly not to smile. And one his mother had taken through the kitchen window without either of them knowing: the two of them in the hedge in the red scarves, her bare hand on his face, kissing.

“Send me that one,” she said. Outside the big windows snow was falling across the runway in the floodlights, and the de-icing trucks were going out to the aircraft, spraying orange.

chapters.title: The Loud Client
chapters.desc: He hires FENCE, two rooms above Auntie Au’s, to test his own firm, and pays triple. In the second week Eliana Lin finds his first hire copying client files at two in the morning. Song-Zhu sits with him till dawn.
chapters.epigraph: “But let the evidence finish talking first.”
chapters.content:
The staircase was what did it.

Ren Hao stood at the bottom of it on Monday the thirteenth of April, a little before ten, on Terrace Road, with the smell of frying garlic and steamed dough coming out of the shop beside him. It was steep and narrow and built for one person at a time, and the paint was coming off the handrail. At the top, on a door with a pane of frosted glass, somebody had stuck a yellow note that said FENCE.

He’d had a staircase exactly like it once. Seven years ago, in his last year at university, above a print shop on the other side of the harbour: two rooms, two second-hand desks, a printer that jammed if you looked at it, and a sign on the door Isla had made out of a cereal box because he couldn’t afford a real one. Six people by the end of that first year. He’d shouted up those stairs every morning so everyone had time to look busy.

He went up two at a time and announced himself to the entire building.

“HELLO! IS THIS THE SECURITY COMPANY?”

At a desk by the window a young woman with her dark hair pulled tight back looked up from a laptop. At the other desk a second young woman shut her eyes. Downstairs, Auntie Au dropped something metal.

“Ren Hao. I have an appointment. I think. Someone downstairs said come up. Is this the right place?”

“You’re two minutes early, Mr. Ren,” said the woman at the laptop.

He read the note on the glass backwards from inside. “FENCE. Good name. Short. Memorable. Slightly threatening.”

“That’s what we were going for,” said the second woman, opening her eyes.

He laughed, loudly, and shook the first one’s hand hard enough to slop her coffee. “I’ve heard about you. You’re the one who found the hole in the Calder business.”

“I did part of the assessment,” said Eliana Lin, more carefully, wiping her wrist.

He went back to the top of the stairs and leaned over the rail. “And now you’ve got your own firm. Wonderful. I love independent businesses. I love a good dumpling. WHO MAKES THE DUMPLINGS?”

From below: “ME.”

“I LOVE YOU!”

A pause. “THEN BUY SOME!”

“I think we’ve found our target market,” murmured the second woman: Yen Si-Wei, fifteen per cent of the company. She looked at him like an interesting new kind of weather.

“My firm advises private clients on risk. We have a good reputation, an expensive office and an IT department that tells me everything’s fine, which is exactly why I don’t believe it. Test us. Everything you’re legally allowed to test: systems, procedures, people, habits. If there’s a hole, tell me. If someone’s incompetent, tell me. If I’m incompetent, tell me that too.”

“It won’t be comfortable. We’ll need a written scope, signed authorisation and named contacts, and we won’t go a step outside what we agree. How many people have administrator access to your systems?”

“Six. For operational requirements.”

“Why?”

He stopped and looked at her properly. She was twenty-three, sitting in a two-room office with a dumpling shop under it, and she was looking at the head of a firm on three floors of a tower exactly the way he’d once looked at a bank manager who told him to come back when he was older.

He sat down, and stayed down. “Ask your questions.”

She asked them for forty minutes, and interrupted every time he said something that sounded like an answer and wasn’t. When he said, with some pride, that the firm had never had a significant security incident, she put her pen down.

“How do you know?”

“You’re asking whether we know we’ve never had one, or whether we just haven’t noticed.”

“Yes.”

Si-Wei, at the other desk, ate a dumpling out of a paper bowl without a sound.

Eliana told him the price. He listened to the whole figure.

“Triple it. You’re taking responsibility for my company for six weeks. I want you to have time to do it right.”

He beamed at her.

“Besides, I like your face.”

“That’s not a pricing metric,” said Si-Wei.

“It should be. Thank you. I love you already,” he told them both, at full volume and without the slightest embarrassment.

He was halfway down the stairs before he came back up and put his head round the door.

“Where are the dumplings?”

✦ ✦ ✦

Auntie Au was round-faced and floury and somewhere past sixty, and looked at him across her counter like a woman who’d heard everything he’d shouted and was reserving judgement.

“So. You’re the loud one. The ones with the pleats are the prawn.”

“Four boxes. Mixed. I’m feeding an office.”

She asked as she packed whether he had a girlfriend, and whether he fed her properly, and when he said she ate rice balls out of convenience stores standing up, Auntie Au put two extra dumplings in the top box. “You take these to her. Tell her an old woman said.”

In four minutes she’d made him feel like a nephew, so he came round the end of her counter and hugged her. She stood stiff in his arms for one second, then patted his back with a floury hand, twice, hard. “Go away, handsome. You’re too much.”

He promised to bring his whole office for lunch. On the stairs he passed Si-Wei coming down for napkins and told her she was obviously the brains of the operation, and she said “Obviously” without breaking stride. He signed the proposal on the bonnet of the car before he got in it.

“Triple,” Si-Wei said to Eliana upstairs.

From the street Ren Hao’s voice rose again as the car pulled away. “KEEP THE RECEIPT, AUNTIE. I’M CLAIMING THESE.”

✦ ✦ ✦

That evening Song-Zhu was on her floor in a ring of photographs of a bent landing-gear leg.

“Dumplings. From where? Who’s Auntie Au?”

He sat down with her inside the ring. “The woman under my new security firm. To test my own people. We’ve grown too fast. A hundred and twelve people, three floors, clients I don’t know by their first names any more. The department that runs our security is the department that tells me our security’s excellent. Eliana Lin. Twenty-three. She was terrifying.”

“Did you tell her you love her? You did, didn’t you. And the woman in the shop.”

He considered lying. “She sent you these two. With the pleats. You’re to eat them sitting down.”

Song-Zhu stared at him and then laughed so loudly her neighbour knocked on the wall. “You were in that building less than an hour and you’ve got another family. Why that one? There are big firms with lifts.”

“Because my first office had stairs like that. When I went up to banks in my one suit they told me to come back when I was older. I promised myself one day I’d walk up somebody’s stairs and pay them what they were worth. And she’s good. Everyone I asked said so. Gideon thinks I’m wasting money.”

“Gideon?”

“Gideon Chai. My first hire. He thinks anyone under thirty is a liability. I told him that includes me. He said that’s what he means.”

✦ ✦ ✦

FENCE started on the Tuesday, and by Wednesday afternoon half his staff were afraid of them. Eliana had a habit of appearing silently at someone’s elbow with a question they didn’t want to answer. Why was that cabinet open. Why had a man who’d moved from research to sales eighteen months ago still got access to the research drive. Why did the managing director have administrator rights to a system he never used.

He couldn’t stay away, though Song-Zhu had started texting Have you been up the stairs again at lunchtime. He went up the stairs anyway, never empty-handed: pineapple buns on Tuesday, coffee for both rooms on Thursday, oranges on Friday. On the Friday he found that Si-Wei had drawn a table on the whiteboard headed REN HAO, UNPLANNED VISITS, with a last column marked Likelihood of food (%). Every row said 100.

“That’s slander.”

“It’s data,” said Si-Wei.

He signed every approval they put in front of him, and the one time a director tried to steer a meeting somewhere flattering, he said “Let her finish,” and the director let her finish.

On the Wednesday of the second week he was sitting on the corner of Si-Wei’s desk at six eating a dumpling when Eliana opened the post: a cream envelope, handwriting, a pressed flower under the ribbon.

“A wedding! Whose? When’s yours?”

“Ren,” said Eliana, and he put both hands up, one still holding the dumpling, and noticed she’d gone pink to the hairline, and filed it away for Song-Zhu.

They’d gone quiet, the two of them, the last two days: longer hours, the door between their rooms kept shut. When he asked how it was going Eliana said, “It isn’t finished. We’re still verifying something. You’re not going to ask me what?”

“You said you’re still verifying.”

She studied him a moment, and nodded once.

✦ ✦ ✦

His phone rang at nineteen minutes past two on Friday morning, the twenty-fourth.

“Mr. Ren. It’s Eliana Lin. I need you at your office. We found something. I’d rather not say it on the phone.”

Her voice was flat. He’d heard that voice in his own mouth on calls to clients, when the news was the kind that changed the shape of a company.

“Is anybody hurt? Have you touched anything?”

“No one’s hurt. We’ve preserved what we can without changing it. We haven’t spoken to anyone.”

“Don’t. Twenty minutes.”

Song-Zhu was sitting up in the dark. She watched him dress in the light from the street, and then pushed the duvet off and started dressing too.

“You don’t have to come.”

“I know,” she said, and pulled her jumper over her head, and he didn’t argue.

✦ ✦ ✦

Eliana and Si-Wei sat on one side of the big table on the thirty-second floor, with the city dark and wet beyond the glass, a laptop, a sealed drive in an evidence bag and a short stack of pages squared off precisely. Song-Zhu stopped by the glass at the far end of the room with her hands in her pockets and let him go on alone.

He sat at the head of his own table and folded his hands. “Tell me.”

It took eleven minutes and he didn’t interrupt once. No break-in, no stranger. Client files opened at two in the morning by an account with no reason to be awake. Copies made on three nights, each the night before an account moved to the same rival: three clients lost in five months, whom he’d written to personally and been told, politely, that it was nothing to do with the work. Records showing information leaving by a door marked staff only.

“That’s not a mistake,” said Si-Wei, after a long minute.

“He asked us to tell him. He paid us triple to tell him,” said Eliana, to her, not to him.

“You’re sure?” Ren Hao said at the end.

“I’m sure the access broke your own policies, and files were copied and taken out by a route nobody approved. I can establish which account did it. I can’t yet tell you whose hands were on the keyboard. That’s for an investigation.”

“Good. Keep that distinction. His name’s on the wall downstairs. He was here when we had six people.”

He looked up at her.

“Send me the final report. Nobody goes near him until the lawyers have it. And you know what? I really do love you.” He said the last part because it was true, and because she was sitting at his table at three in the morning having done exactly what he’d paid her for, which was break his heart accurately.

Si-Wei looked at the ceiling. Eliana pressed her lips together. “Thank you, Ren.”

✦ ✦ ✦

When they’d gone next door to ring their lawyer, he put his right hand flat on the table. It had started to shake, slightly, and he pressed it to the wood until it stopped.

Song-Zhu came away from the glass, pulled out the chair at the corner beside his, close enough that their knees touched, and waited.

He looked at the page with the name on it. “He was the first person I chose. Gideon answered an advertisement on a university noticeboard and came up the stairs above the print shop in a borrowed tie and told me my business plan had four mistakes in it. He was right about three. He slept on that office floor with me the night we nearly lost our first big client. Seven years. Three clients, and I wrote to all three and asked what we’d done wrong. He helped me draft the letters.”

She didn’t say maybe he didn’t do it. She put her hand over his flat hand on the table and turned in her chair to face him.

“I do this. It’s my job. Somebody puts a page in front of you at three in the morning with a name on it, and every part of you wants to decide the whole story right there, because not knowing is unbearable. That’s when people make the worst mistakes of their lives. You can be angry. You can hate him, if that’s where it ends. But let the evidence finish talking first.”

He looked at her a long time, and turned his hand over under hers, and held on.

✦ ✦ ✦

She stayed with him through the night. When he had the systems locked and the access records secured without alerting anyone, she wrote the times on a notepad without being asked, because she couldn’t help herself. Before four she went down forty floors and came back with two coffees and a sandwich from the convenience store on the corner.

“Eat. I didn’t ask if you were hungry. You fed me for ten months. It’s my turn.”

He ate half. She watched him do it with deep satisfaction.

When Eliana came back to say the same account’s access went back further than the three nights, he told her to expand the scope to every partner, himself included, and when the door had shut he said, “I should have hired her years ago.”

“She’d have been sixteen,” said Song-Zhu, and he made a sound that was nearly a laugh and put his face in his hands, and she put her palm flat on his back between his shoulders and kept it there.

Towards five he told her about the night above the print shop: the two of them on flattened boxes eating cold noodles out of the carton, a client’s lawyer threatening to sue them out of existence by Monday, and Gideon saying at four in the morning, if this goes under I’ll come and work for you at the next one.

“I keep going back over the last months. Meetings. Questions he asked about accounts. I keep looking at every one of them to see if it’s a lie.”

“Stop doing that tonight. You can do it on Monday with the lawyers and a timeline. Not now. Not on your own.”

“I’m not on my own.”

“No. You’re not,” said Song-Zhu.

✦ ✦ ✦

The light came up grey over the harbour after six. Eliana brought the timeline, printed and dated, every entry referenced to a record, and stood at the end of the table while he read it.

“I know this is personal. But our job isn’t to prove Mr. Chai did it. It’s to find out what happened. If that’s uncomfortable for him, it is. If it’s uncomfortable for you, it is too.”

Later Song-Zhu found him alone in his office at the internal window, looking down at the floor below: rows of empty desks, the lights coming on by themselves one by one as the building woke for a Friday that didn’t know anything yet. She put her arms round his waist from behind and her cheek against his back.

“I thought if there was one person in this building I’d never have to question, it was him. What if all of it was a lie? Seven years.”

She turned him round and put her hand on his cheek. “Then the lie’s his. Not yours. The years you worked, the things you built, the people downstairs who come in at nine and trust you. That was real. You don’t have to turn your whole life into a mistake because one man in it might have been taking it apart.”

She kissed him, not to make anything better, only so he’d know he wasn’t standing there on his own.

“Come home. You’ve got a hundred and twelve people who can work, and a lawyer, and a twenty-three-year-old who frightens you.”

For the first time since twenty past two, he nearly smiled.

✦ ✦ ✦

At his flat she made him shower, because he’d been standing in the bathroom doorway looking at the tiles for two minutes. When he came out with wet hair she was sitting on the end of his bed holding his phone.

“Eliana’s report’s come. I haven’t opened it.”

He took the phone and opened the drawer of the bedside table and put it inside and shut the drawer. Her eyebrows went up.

He sat down beside her and put his face against her neck. “Breakfast first. Stay with me today?”

“I texted Mabel at five. I’m not going anywhere.”

“I love you,” he said into her skin.

She put her fingers into his wet hair and held his head against her, and for a while, in the grey morning, with the report shut in a drawer, he let himself be held.

chapters.title: Betrayal
chapters.desc: He dismisses Gideon Chai and sits in his car for two hours. She climbs into the back seat. Explicit, windows fogged: she makes him look at her.
chapters.epigraph: “Stay with me. All the way. Don’t go anywhere.”
chapters.content:
Gideon Chai arrived just after nine on Monday carrying two coffees: one for himself, and one for Ren Hao, black, no sugar, from the cart on the corner that Gideon had insisted for seven years was better than anything in the building, which it wasn’t. It was such an ordinary thing that Ren Hao couldn’t look at him.

“You sounded very formal on the phone. And Kong’s outside your door, which is never a good start to a Monday.”

Kong was the head of legal. He was outside the door because Ren Hao had asked him to be, and because he’d spent the weekend with Eliana Lin’s final report and the partnership agreement and had said on Sunday night, in his driest voice, Do it by the book, Hao, and do it once.

Ren Hao looked at the man across his desk and remembered him in the lobby of this tower three years ago, watching the man with the ladder put their names on the wall. Look at us. We actually did it.

He opened the folder and laid three printed records on the desk, facing the other way.

Gideon’s eyes went over the first page, the second, the third. His face hardly changed at all, and it was the not-changing that Ren Hao would remember for the rest of his life. In seven years he’d never once seen Gideon read anything without an opinion crossing his face. Now there was nothing.

“Access logs. What’s this supposed to show?”

“Confidential client files copied from our systems on three nights, at about two in the morning.”

Ren Hao turned the last page so the name at the top faced him.

“That’s my account. Could be a compromised credential.”

“We’ve examined the access records, the device each session came from, the transfers, the authentication logs and the building’s badge records for each of those nights. The device was your laptop. The badge was yours.”

Gideon gave a short laugh. “Clients move, Hao. That’s business.”

“Not usually the morning after somebody’s copied their risk assessments.”

Gideon looked at him across the desk, and then at the papers, and back. “Hao. We’ve known each other seven years. Seven years. Do you really think I’d do something like that?”

The sentence Ren Hao had been dreading since Friday morning. Not I didn’t do it, or let me help you find who did. An appeal to everything between them, laid across the desk like a coat over a hole in the floor.

“That’s what I’ve been trying to understand.”

“You’re letting a twenty-three-year-old consultant tell you how to run your company.”

Ren Hao closed the folder. “Don’t make this about her age. She didn’t copy anything. On three nights your account opened files you had no reason to open and copied them out of the firm by a route nobody approved. That breaks the access policy you signed and helped me write, and that alone is gross misconduct under the agreement. Whatever else those files were used for is for the lawyers now. Your access ended at eight this morning. Kong has the formal notice. You’re dismissed, effective today, and your partnership ends with it.”

Gideon laughed once, a small disbelieving sound, and looked round the office: the glass wall, the framed photograph on the cabinet by the door of six young people on a staircase above a print shop holding a sign made of cereal box. His eyes stopped there.

“We built this together. I was there when you had nothing. I gave you seven years.”

“We gave each other seven years. That’s what I can’t—”

Ren Hao stopped, and found his voice again, lower.

“I’m not the one who copied the files, Gideon.”

Something moved in Gideon’s face. It looked less like guilt than calculation, a man seeing that the other player had turned his own cards face up long ago. Then it was gone. He stood, buttoned his jacket, and left his coffee where it was.

“You’re going to regret this.”

“I’ve been regretting it since Friday,” said Ren Hao.

The second coffee sat on the desk between the two chairs. After a while he picked it up. It was still warm. He poured it into the small sink in the corner and rinsed the cup and put it in the bin, because it was Gideon’s cup from Gideon’s cart and he couldn’t think what else to do with it. He didn’t shout or throw anything. That, he thought distantly, would have been easier.

✦ ✦ ✦

Eliana knocked on the glass an hour later. “His credentials are disabled and the records are preserved. Legal has everything. We don’t yet know the full extent of the copying.”

She looked at him longer than a consultant looks at a client.
