“Don’t let this make you careless with the rest of your people. One person can betray you without everybody else becoming a suspect. You’ve got a hundred and eleven people out there who didn’t do anything. Don’t start looking at them the way you looked at that log.”

He was grateful, and in a way he couldn’t explain, furious with the world for making her necessary.

✦ ✦ ✦

After twelve he left the building without telling Joyce. He took his own car, which he hardly ever drove, round two corners and down into the underground car park of an office block half empty since its biggest tenant moved out, to the lowest level, where there was nobody, and parked in the far corner under a flickering light, facing a concrete wall. The silence settled round him like water.

His phone lit on the passenger seat. Song-Zhu. He watched it ring out. He didn’t know what he’d say, and was afraid of what it would sound like.

He remembered a night above the print shop in the rain: damp carpet, noodles out of cardboard, Ren Hao saying they should both get proper jobs, and Gideon saying, You won’t quit. You’re too stubborn. We’ll make this work.

Isla had rung on Saturday morning, from her flat, calm, which was how he’d known it was bad. On Friday evening, in a stairwell on Lantern Lane, Wei Long had fired his service weapon, and a man was dead, and there’d be a review, and she was telling him herself before he read it. She didn’t want a lawyer. She wanted him not to send one. He’d spent the weekend not sending one, with Eliana’s report in one hand and his sister’s voice in his head.

He remembered Gideon’s face reading the name, and how nothing had moved in it at all.

When he finally turned the phone over there were messages.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): How did it go?

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): I’m not asking you to explain over text. Just tell me you’re all right.

Ren Hao: I fired him.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Where are you? Which car park?

He sent her the location.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Stay there.

He knew that tone. She used it on operators.

✦ ✦ ✦

The rear passenger door opened and she leaned in, in a loose cream jumper with her lanyard pushed into her pocket and her hair coming out of its clip.

“Get in the back, Hao. I’m not sitting with a gearstick between us.”

He got in beside her, and she took his hand.

“Did he deny it?”

He looked at a concrete pillar with a painted number on it. “He said we’d known each other seven years. He asked if I really thought he’d do that. He never said he didn’t. And he said we built the firm together. He wasn’t wrong. I keep remembering small things, things that meant nothing at the time, and holding each one up to see whether he was already doing it then. Whether he was doing it when he helped me write those letters. I don’t know if the rest of it was real.”

She thought about that properly, the way she thought about everything that mattered. “You may never know when it started. You can miss someone who hurt you. You can be angry with him and still keep the good things. You don’t have to go back and make those years mean nothing because the end of them is ugly, and you don’t have to forgive him to admit he mattered.”

Something in his face gave way, not all at once. He leaned forward and put his face against her shoulder, and she held his head there with one hand.

“I thought I’d feel relieved. I feel embarrassed. I trusted him with clients and my people and my family. I brought him to my parents’ table. I’m supposed to be the person other people hire to see this coming,” he said into her jumper.

She put her palm against his cheek. “You trusted somebody. That isn’t something to be ashamed of. Don’t punish yourself for not expecting it from someone you loved. That’s not a failure in you. That’s the thing he used.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She leaned in and kissed him. He kissed her back, slowly, his mouth hardly moving, his eyes going past her to the window and the pillar and the number painted on it, and she felt the exact second he went away again.

She took his face in both hands. “Hao. Not at the window. Not at the phone. Not at him.”

She waited until his eyes had come all the way back to hers.

“At me.”

She kissed him again, and this time he stayed.

She kept it slow. She kissed his upper lip and then his lower one and opened his mouth with hers, and when he tried to take the kiss deeper, the way he always did, she drew back half an inch and made him wait with her breath on his mouth and her thumbs on his cheekbones, until he understood that this was hers, and let her have it.

She shifted, and her knee hit the centre armrest, hard. She looked down at it, offended. She pushed the armrest up out of the way. “This car is too expensive to be this uncomfortable. Can I?”

“You never have to ask me that.”

“I know. I’m asking.”

He put his hands on her waist, and she swung her leg across him and settled astride his lap, knees on the leather either side of his hips, her head nearly touching the roof.

She undid his tie first, the knot and then the long silk sliding out from under his collar, and dropped it somewhere behind her. Then his shirt buttons, one after another, until she could put her hand flat inside on his chest and feel his heart going hard under her palm. She kissed his jaw, his temple, the place between his eyebrows where a crease had been sitting since Friday, until it let go.

He shut his eyes.

“Look at me. Stay with me. All the way. Don’t go anywhere.”

She put his hands under her jumper on her bare back. She pulled the jumper over her head and let it fall onto the front seat, and he looked at her the way he’d looked at the snow. When he reached round for the clasp she let him, and then she was bare from the waist up in the flickering light. He kissed her breast, open-mouthed, his hand spread on her back to hold her to him, and when he turned his head to the other side she rocked against him and felt how hard he was through his trousers and hers, and they both went still.

“Look at me,” she said, and he looked up with his mouth wet and his eyes gone dark and every bit of him there in the car with her and nowhere else.

She got his belt open. He got her trousers undone and pushed them down as far as he could, and she swore at the car, and lifted herself off him and fought one leg free in the space between the seats with her elbow against the window and her hair caught on the coat hook, laughing helplessly while he held her steady so she didn’t fall into the footwell.

“This is the least dignified thing I’ve ever done.”

“You once fell out of a camp bed.”

“That was the bed’s fault,” she said, and kissed him to stop him talking, and came back down astride him in nothing but her knickers, his open shirt hanging off his shoulders and the windows starting to cloud at the edges.

She pressed down and moved once, slowly, and his head went back against the seat.

“Don’t close your eyes.”

He held her gaze while she pushed his trousers off his hips, and pulled her knickers aside, and took him in her hand and held him there against her, wet, without moving.

“Song-Zhu,” he said, and it was hardly a word.

“Watch,” she said, and sank down onto him so slowly, all the way, with her hands on his shoulders and her eyes on his, and neither of them breathed.

She stayed still and let him feel it, her forehead against his, holding him inside her and looking at him from an inch away while he trembled under her hands with how badly he wanted to move.

“Please.”

“Not yet. Stay here.”

He stayed. His hands gripped her hips and didn’t move, and she could feel him holding himself back with everything he had, which was a great deal, and she loved him for it so much it nearly frightened her.

Then she began to move: slow, the whole length of him, and his breath went out of him in a sound she’d never heard him make. She kept the pace there, deliberate, and every time his eyes started to slip shut she said Hao and they came back. The windows clouded over completely. The car rocked on its springs, and there was only their breathing and the wet sound of her moving on him and the leather creaking under her knees.

“Keep looking.”

He looked at her like she was the only thing in the world that had ever been true. His hand slid down between them and found her and touched her in time with her movements, exactly as she liked it, and her rhythm broke for the first time and she gasped against his mouth.

“There. Let me,” he said, low.

She let him. She kept moving slower than either of them could bear, and he kept touching her and kept looking, and she felt it build from far down and put her forehead on his and let him see it happen. It went through her in long helpless waves, her thighs shaking either side of him, her fingers digging into his shoulders, her mouth open on his name, and she didn’t close her eyes once, and neither did he.

He was still hard inside her when she stopped shaking, waiting, taut as wire.

“Now you,” she said against his mouth.

He took her hips and moved up into her, only a few strokes, deep and helpless, his eyes on hers the whole time as she’d asked, and came with a sound torn out of the bottom of his chest, holding her down on him with both arms, his face in her neck at the last.

Afterwards she lay against his chest with his open shirt round them both, the windows white, water running in a thin line down the glass beside her head.

“Thank you for coming. I didn’t ask you to,” he said.

“You don’t have to ask. Not every time. Not with me. I’m not fixing anything. I’m keeping you company. That’s very different.”

His phone buzzed on the front seat. She didn’t lift her head. “It can wait. Kong can wait. The whole firm can wait,” she said, and he didn’t reach for it.

✦ ✦ ✦

They stayed until the windows began to clear. She fought her trousers back on in the footwell and gave up on dignity.

“Your seatbelt buckle’s been in my knee for twenty minutes.”

“You didn’t say.”

“I was busy,” she said, and he laughed, a real laugh, tired and surprised.

Her head came out of her jumper with her hair everywhere. “You’ll find out what happened, and then you’ll decide what you think about Gideon. Not before. And tonight you come home and eat something and sleep. Tomorrow you can be as angry as you like.”

She found his tie under the passenger seat and handed it to him without a word, and he put it in his pocket, and they stood beside the car in the flickering light and he held her.

“Come home with me,” he said.

“I thought I already was.”

✦ ✦ ✦

That evening he didn’t open the report again. He didn’t read the message Gideon sent at nine, which Kong had said he mustn’t answer; he forwarded it, unread, to Kong. He rang Isla, and didn’t tell her any of it, and listened to her tell him Wei Long had eaten, and that she was fine, which she wasn’t, and he let her say it.

When she slept he stayed awake a little longer, thinking about two rooms above a print shop and a man on the floor at four in the morning saying we’ll make this work. He didn’t know which of those memories were still safe to keep. He knew one thing. He’d spent seven years building something with a man he trusted, and he wasn’t going to let that man take the part of him that had been able to trust in the first place.

Beside him her hand found his on the sheet, and held on.

chapters.title: Her Promotion
chapters.desc: Investigator-in-charge at twenty-six. He throws her a party she didn’t want; she forgives him in the kitchen. He invites himself to Yu Chen’s party and lifts the doctor off the ground.
chapters.epigraph: “Believing in me. Instead of deciding how it’ll turn out.”
chapters.content:
The call came mid-morning on Wednesday the thirteenth of May, while Song-Zhu was in the corridor outside the briefing room telling Dexter that a timeline with a forty-minute hole in it wasn’t a timeline, it was a suggestion.

Director Kwan.

“Come up to my office, please. No, nothing’s wrong. Leave the Kestrel file.”

“That sounds suspicious.”

A short laugh down the line. “Just come upstairs, Song-Zhu.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Director Kwan’s office looked east over the airport, so that every few minutes something large and white went past his window slowly and visitors lost their train of thought. Song-Zhu knew where he kept the good tea and which visitors’ chair had a loose leg, and sat in the one with the loose leg. Mabel stood by the window with her arms folded, failing at the corners to give nothing away.

“From the first of June, we’re putting you on the investigator-in-charge roster for major occurrences,” said the director.

For a second she didn’t move. “Not deputy.”

He looked at her over his glasses. “Investigator-in-charge. If something big comes in after the first of June and it’s your week, it’s yours. The site, the recorders, the team, the families, the report. Mabel recommended you. I agreed. So did the board, eventually, after a conversation I won’t repeat.”

“Don’t look at me like that. I’m sixty-one. I want a holiday,” said Mabel.

“Director, I’m twenty-six.”

“I’m aware of that. Your age isn’t why we’re having this conversation. Your work is. Your evidence handling is the best in the building. You don’t rush. You know a technical finding has to survive people who’ll do anything to make it say something else. And you can make a room of people who disagree with you work together, which is rarer here than you’d think.”

“That’s a very polite way of saying I’m difficult.”

“It is,” said Mabel.

“You won’t be alone. You’ll have experienced people under you and Mabel above you, for as long as she can be kept from that holiday. This isn’t a test of whether you can do everything yourself. It’s whether you can direct it, decide, and carry it. Do you want it?”

She thought about a twin turboprop on its back in a field. A room in another country with a laptop and fifty seconds of a voice. A little girl at a funeral in a yellow dress holding a plastic aeroplane too big for her hand.

“Yes. Very much.”

He smiled properly for the first time. “Congratulations, Investigator Xu. Don’t thank me. You’ll hate me by August. And don’t mistake being the youngest person in a room for being the least qualified.”

She laughed, bright and a little shaky, and Mabel turned to the window so nobody would see her face.

At the door Song-Zhu stopped. “Can I leave this office before you give me anything else? I’d like to tell my boyfriend.”

“Go,” said Director Kwan.

✦ ✦ ✦

Ren Hao was in a meeting on the thirty-second floor, listening to his head of operations propose a new structure for client response, and had found three problems with it in four minutes, when his phone lit.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): I have news. Good news. Guess.

Ren Hao: A promotion?

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Warmer.

Ren Hao: Song-Zhu.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Investigator-in-charge. From 1 June. The next big one is mine.

He read it twice and forgot, for several seconds, that there was a meeting. Then he laughed out loud in the middle of somebody else’s sentence, a delighted bark that stopped the head of operations dead.

“Sorry. Carry on. It’s very good. It’s got three problems. Carry on.”

Joyce’s pen didn’t move on her pad, which was how he knew she was smiling.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Don’t make a big deal of it.

He was absolutely going to make a big deal of it.

✦ ✦ ✦

By six he’d arranged flowers, a cake from the bakery she’d mentioned once in February, and a private room at the back of the noodle place behind the cargo terminal. He’d invited ten people, ordered champagne, and was on the phone to a photographer Joyce had found when his other line went.

“Why has Dexter just asked me what time he should come to my party? And why did the man at the noodle shop ring me to ask how many chairs?” said Song-Zhu.

“He wasn’t supposed to ring you.”

“How many people?”

“Eleven. Including the photographer.”

“I don’t want a party, Hao.”

There was no anger in it at all. It was clear, the way she said things that weren’t going to change, and something in him that had been running at full speed since the morning came to a stop.

“All right. I’ll cancel it.”

“Thank you. Keep one bunch of flowers. Give the rest to your floor. And promise. No party.”

He hesitated, which she heard. “I promise.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t throw a party. He cooked dinner at her flat, which was different, he reasoned, because there was no photographer, no guests and no champagne. There was one bunch of white anemones in a jug on her counter and dinner for two on her stove.

She stood in the doorway of her own kitchen looking at him: sleeves to the elbow, a tea towel over his shoulder, stirring something.

“Where’s the party? The eleven people?”

“Disappointed. Dexter, mainly. He’d bought a shirt.”

She came across the kitchen and put her arms round his waist from behind, her cheek between his shoulder blades, and stayed there. He turned the heat down and put his hand over hers.

Song-Zhu held on tighter. “Mabel cried. She says she didn’t. She went and stood at the window. I have to sign things now, things with my name on that other people do what they say. It’s frightening.”

He turned round in her arms with something so open in his face that she had to look at his collar instead. “You’ve worked for this since before I knew you. You care about doing it right more than anyone I’ve ever met. And you hate fuss. But you’ll let me be glad.”

“You’re allowed to be glad. If you call me Investigator Xu at home, I’ll throw a spoon at you.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She found the cake when she went to the fridge for water: on the bottom shelf, behind a box of vegetables, hidden by someone who hadn’t tried hard. White, plain, beautiful, and on top, in dark chocolate, neat:

INVESTIGATOR XU

She shut the fridge and turned round slowly. He was looking carefully at the pan.

“You said you’d cancelled everything.”

“I cancelled the party. It’s from that place on Tanner’s Row. The one you said in February was the only good thing about the lab moving. The lemon one.”

She tried hard to keep her face straight. It was unfair. He’d remembered one sentence from three months ago, and the street, and that it was lemon. He’d only mistaken her wanting to be celebrated for wanting to be surrounded.

“Turn that off and look at me. You don’t understand the difference between making me happy and making an event out of making me happy.”

“I got excited. I wanted everybody to know.”

“Why?”

He looked at her as if it were the most obvious question she’d ever asked. “Because you’re brilliant. Because you come home exhausted and still tell me about chains of custody over dinner. Because you keep asking questions when it’d be easier to stop. Because they’ve finally seen what I’ve been seeing for eleven months, and I wanted to stand on a table and shout about it.”

She unfolded her arms and put her hand on his cheek. “You celebrate me all the time. When you listen to me talk about a mislabelled evidence box for fifty minutes, and ask questions. When you let me come home and be tired without trying to make me feel better straight away. That’s the one I like best. I don’t need eleven people in a room to know you’re glad. You laughed in the middle of a meeting. Joyce told Dexter, and Dexter told me.”

He breathed out, and he was already bending to her, and she kissed him.

It was soft, and then it wasn’t. She kissed him slowly against her own fridge with her hand on his face, and his hands came round to the small of her back and pulled her in, and he made a low sound into her mouth. She bit his lower lip, gently, and he breathed in sharply through his nose.

“You’re forgiven. Don’t make me reconsider it,” she whispered, noses touching.

He laughed against her mouth and kissed her again, and the pan sat cooling on the stove, forgotten, for some time.

They ate at the counter. He cut the cake with enormous care so the lettering stayed whole on the first slice, and she closed her eyes at the first mouthful and held out her fork, and fed him a bite across the counter.

“You were right,” he said.

“Say that again.”

“No,” said Ren Hao.

He lifted his water glass. “To Investigator Xu.”

“To no photographers,” said Song-Zhu.

✦ ✦ ✦

Two weeks later she was on her sofa with the roster handbook and her feet in his lap when his phone went, and he looked at the screen and lit up like a lamp.

“Auntie Au.”

He listened, eyebrows climbing.

“No. No. This Saturday? And she didn’t tell me? Of course she didn’t. Thank you, Auntie. I love you. Yes, I’ll buy some.”

He rang someone else immediately, at a volume that set her neighbour’s dog barking. “ELIANA! I HEARD! YU CHEN IS GOING TO EMERGENCY MEDICINE! I’M COMING. I’LL BRING FOOD.”

A small voice said something on the other end.

“Everything.”

A pause.

“It’s a promise,” said Ren Hao, and hung up looking enormously pleased with himself.

“Did you just invite yourself to a party at somebody else’s house?”

“I expressed enthusiasm. She said what food. That’s practically an invitation. You’ll come. You’ve wanted to meet her for six weeks.”

She had. She’d heard about Eliana Lin every evening since April, and read the final report over his shoulder, and thought it the most honest piece of work she’d seen from outside her own building in years.

“All right. But you’re not making a speech. And you’re not picking anybody up.”

He looked wounded. “Why would I pick anybody up?”

“Because I know you,” said Song-Zhu.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Saturday the thirtieth he stopped at Auntie Au’s on the way because he couldn’t walk past it, and came out with three bags. They were the last to arrive. He went through the side gate first at full speed, bags swinging, and Song-Zhu followed with a bottle of wine and a strong premonition.

It was a small garden with a persimmon tree and a wall at the back, and someone had strung warm bulbs through the branches and along the wall so that the whole thing glowed in the dusk. Cards on the table said CONGRATULATIONS, DR. WANG. There was a great deal of Auntie Au’s food already, and more people than she’d expected, and by the table a quiet man with his sleeves rolled up looking slightly overwhelmed.

“WHERE IS THE DOCTOR? EMERGENCY MEDICINE! YOU’LL SAVE LIVES!”

Ren Hao crossed the grass in three strides and hugged Dr. Wang Yu Chen so hard he lifted him off his heels. At the gate Song-Zhu shut her eyes.

“That’s the plan,” said Yu Chen, winded.

“YOU DID THIS? YOU’RE A WONDERFUL WOMAN,” Ren Hao told Eliana, and hugged her too, while she stood rigid in his arms with a plate in one hand.

A young woman with a business student’s neat handwriting on the place cards and an air of having seen everything twice looked at Song-Zhu properly for the first time. “You’re Song-Zhu. You’re real. He talks about you at FENCE. We assumed you were at least partly invented.”

“He does that,” said Song-Zhu, and Yen Si-Wei laughed, once, like it surprised her.

Eliana came over when she’d been extracted from Ren Hao, with the same careful attention she seemed to give everything. “Your authority published a paper last year on recovering a damaged recorder. The one from the river. I read everything about getting data out of things that have been in water.”

Her voice changed.

“I heard about June. He told Auntie Au, and Auntie Au told Si-Wei. He also said not to make a fuss, because you don’t like fuss. So I’m not.” She handed Song-Zhu a plate.

✦ ✦ ✦

At seven Si-Wei tapped a glass and held out a microphone, and Eliana looked at it like a live wire.

“You said no speeches.”

“Three minutes.”

Eliana made a toast of exactly four sentences, about a man who’d spent a long time looking after other people and forgot he was allowed to want things for himself, and the garden went quiet for a beat. Then Ren Hao clapped like a firework and everybody followed.

Song-Zhu was watching the doctor’s face, which hadn’t moved. She saw him walk over and take the microphone out of Eliana’s hand and put it down on the table, and go down on one knee in the grass in front of everybody, and kiss the back of her hand, and then kiss it again.

Beside her Ren Hao had gone completely still, like something had struck him.

“Get up. Everyone’s watching,” Eliana said, scarlet.

“I know. Thank you,” said Yu Chen, and stood, and kept her hand, and kissed her, slow and long, with his hand at her waist and her fingers knotted in his.

Ren Hao made a noise that was probably heard at the ferry pier. “THAT’S LOVE!”

Song-Zhu put her face in her hands.

✦ ✦ ✦

She found him later in Eliana’s kitchen, helping Auntie Au put dumplings on a tray with great seriousness.

“Did you just pick up a grown man? I told you not to pick anybody up.”

“You told me on Wednesday. It’s Saturday. Things change. He got the job he wanted, and she was happy.”

Auntie Au patted his cheek and took the tray out.

“You’re laughing at me.”

“Because you greeted him like he’d come home from a war.”

“Emergency medicine. That’s not inaccurate.”

She took his hand on the counter, and they stood in somebody else’s kitchen with the noise of somebody else’s good news coming in through the window.

“She didn’t mention my promotion to anyone. You told her I don’t like fuss. You worked it out. By Saturday,” she said.

He looked a little anxious. “Was that all right?”

She kissed him quickly against the counter. “It was perfect. Don’t throw another party because of it.”

✦ ✦ ✦

In the car she went quiet. He reached across and she laced her fingers through his.

“I’m a bit frightened of June. Being responsible for your own work is different from being responsible for everyone’s. Now I’m the one who decides. If I’m wrong, it’s my name.”

“You don’t have to prove you deserve it every morning. Build a good team. Ask the stupid question first so they’re not afraid to. And when you decide something, decide it because the evidence says so, not because you think you have to be right.”

“That’s what I’m afraid of. Having to be right.”

“They didn’t choose you because you’re always right. They chose you because you don’t rush to be. You listen. You check. You ask again when something doesn’t make sense.”

At her flat she kicked her shoes off and went for water, and he leaned in the kitchen doorway looking pleased with himself.

“My girlfriend is an investigator-in-charge.”

“Your girlfriend was a very good investigator before you started telling dumpling shops.”

She pulled him in and put her arms round his waist, in the same kitchen where she’d forgiven him for the cake.

“You’ll be good at it,” he said into her hair.

She lifted her head, and before she could say it he tried again.

“No. I’ll say it differently. I believe you can.”

She could take that. She kissed him, slow, his hand at her cheek, and stayed close when she drew away.

“That’s better. Believing in me. Instead of deciding how it’ll turn out.” She put her forehead on his chest and laughed, and said she was going to read the whole roster handbook tonight, all of it, and he said he knew, and went to put the kettle on.

chapters.title: Too Much
chapters.desc: She tells him he’s too much. He agrees, and goes quiet for a day: their anniversary. She calls him back with one word.
chapters.epigraph: “I just need to be able to breathe inside it.”
chapters.content:
Ren Hao sent her seventeen messages on Thursday.

Ren Hao: Morning. Did you sleep?

Ren Hao: Rain forecast from three. Umbrella.

Ren Hao: I’ve moved your car’s service to Saturday. You said you might need it on Friday.

Ren Hao: Breakfast?

Song-Zhu read them in her bathroom with a toothbrush in her mouth and answered with one thumb.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Eating.

Ren Hao: Eating what?

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Food.

Then a photograph of a small paper bag on the counter of the authority’s front desk. Left something at your reception. Don’t skip lunch. Inside, she knew without looking, would be one of the egg tarts from the bakery by his building, because she’d said once in March that they were the only egg tarts in the city that weren’t lying about the custard. She sent a heart. He sent three back.

He rang as she walked to the lift. “To hear your voice.” He asked about her morning, whether the revised evidence schedule had come through, whether she wanted picking up after work, whether the new handheld radios for the roster team had arrived or whether he should ring someone. She answered what she could. The lift doors opened.

“I love you,” he said.

“Have a good day, Hao,” she said, smiling, and the doors closed.

It was sweet. It was always sweet. That was the problem.

She loved the attention. She loved that he remembered things she’d said once in passing, and that he worried, and that he was loud about everything, including her. But since the first of June, since her name had gone on a roster that meant the phone at four in the morning would be for her, she’d felt herself being wrapped, gently, in something soft, one layer at a time. And she couldn’t find the edge of it to unwrap.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Friday she was still in the roster office near nine at night, going through an exercise plan line by line, when her phone went.

“Have you eaten?”

She shut her eyes. “Rice. Vegetables. Do you want a photograph?”

He laughed. “Are you going to be late? I’ll come and get you.”

“No. I’ve got a lot to finish. I’ll get a taxi.”

“I can book one.”

“I can book one too.”

A pause. “Text me when you leave. Please.”

Twenty minutes later her phone lit on the desk.

Ren Hao: Booked you a car anyway. Driver’s name below. He’ll wait as long as you need.

She looked at it. Then she put the phone in her desk drawer and closed it, and finished the plan, and at twenty to twelve walked out past the waiting car to the taxi rank and got into a taxi.

✦ ✦ ✦

He was in her flat when she got home. She’d given him her key in March, on a ring with a small plastic aeroplane on it, and been delighted by how carefully he’d used it ever since. He was on her sofa with his laptop open and his sleeves rolled up, and there was a plate on her counter under a second plate.

“Don’t look at me like you’re about to give me a performance review,” he said.

She almost laughed. He came over and kissed her, and that much was all right. Then he touched her cheek.

“You didn’t take the car. He waited an hour, Song-Zhu.”

“I didn’t ask him to.”

“I know. I’m only saying—”

He stopped himself.

“Eat something. There’s chicken.”

“I’m not hungry.”

“You’ve hardly eaten all day.”

She stepped back out of his hands. It was a small moment, an ordinary one. But something in her had been collecting moments for two weeks like evidence: the umbrella, the car service, the egg tart, the calls, the man outside the building waiting, the plate under a plate. All at once there were too many of them to hold.

“I need you to stop. All of it. The messages. The checking. The arranging. Ringing to ask if I’ve eaten. The service on my car, which I didn’t ask you to move. The man outside my building, waiting, so I have to walk past him and feel guilty.”

“I thought you liked those things.”

She pressed her fingers to her forehead. “I do. Not all the time. I’m not angry that you care about me. I’m tired. Since the first of June I’m on the roster every third week. I sit in rooms all day where people wait for me to decide things. I’ve got a team watching to see if I know what I’m doing, and a man from an operator who keeps calling me young lady in meetings. And when I come home I feel like there’s somebody else waiting to make sure I’ve done everything properly. That I’ve eaten. That I took the car.”

His jaw tightened. “That isn’t what I’m doing.”

“I know it’s not what you mean. You don’t have to say I can’t look after myself, Hao. You book the car.”

The silence stretched. And then she said it. She heard it come out of her mouth before she’d decided to, the way the worst things do.

“You’re too much sometimes.”

Ren Hao didn’t move. For one second he looked like he hadn’t understood. Then his face changed into something much quieter than anger, and much worse.

“Too much.”

He nodded once, slowly, like a man agreeing with a finding.

“You’re right. I am.”

“That’s not what—”

He closed the laptop. “I’ll give you some room.”

“That’s not what I’m asking.”

“Then what are you asking?”

She opened her mouth and nothing came out. She didn’t know how to say she wanted him close without feeling watched. That she wanted all of his affection without the management. That she wanted him to love her loudly, the way he did everything, only not so loudly she couldn’t hear herself think inside it.

“I just want to breathe.”

“Understood.”

He put the laptop in his bag and his jacket on, and came across the room, and she thought he was going to argue, or hold her, or ask again. He did none of those things. He kissed her cheek lightly, the way you’d kiss somebody at a station.

He told her to eat something if she got hungry, and shut his eyes, because he’d heard himself. “Sorry. Goodnight, Song-Zhu.”

At the door he stopped and waited for her to say something. She couldn’t find a single word. He went, and closed the door so carefully behind him she didn’t hear the latch.

✦ ✦ ✦

She lay in bed looking at the ceiling. No footsteps in the next room. No voice asking if she wanted water. No arm coming across the mattress in the dark. After one she opened their messages. The last thing he’d sent was the car. She looked at it until the screen went dark by itself. She’d wanted room, and he’d given it to her, so why did it feel like something had been carried out of the flat while she wasn’t looking?

✦ ✦ ✦

Saturday was the thirteenth of June.

She woke at seven and reached for the phone out of habit. No Morning. No weather. No question about breakfast. She ran along the harbour and came back and checked it. She did her laundry and checked it between the wash and the dryer. By four she was writing messages in her head and throwing them away. Are you busy? Too casual. How’s your day? Too much like pretending. I’m sorry. Not enough.

She’d never noticed how much of her day he filled until he stopped filling it. No photograph of something he’d thought she’d like. No voice note about a supplier who’d sent the wrong thing to the wrong floor. No call for no reason except that he wanted to hear her. She missed the noise. She missed him.

At six, on her sofa with the light going gold on the wall, she worked out what the date was, and put her hand over her mouth.

A year. A year ago tonight she’d walked into a French restaurant with fuel on her boots, and a man in a three-piece suit had told her to wash her face. He’d know. He’d have known for weeks. He’d have booked something, planned to the minute, with an agenda, typed. And last night she’d stood in her own kitchen and told him he was too much, and he’d gone home and unbooked all of it, one line at a time, so she’d never have to feel guilty.

✦ ✦ ✦

Ren Hao was in his office on a Saturday night because it was the only place he could think of to go. He’d read two reports, answered every email, and cleared the week’s approvals. He hadn’t messaged her. His phone lay on the desk behind his chair, where he’d turned it at eleven that morning.

He’d heard her. He’d heard the tiredness in it, and that it was true, and the part of it that went in under the ribs. He knew what he was. When he was worried, he organised. When he loved someone, he got there first, before they’d asked. When he couldn’t fix the thing that mattered, he fixed every small thing round it instead so his hands had something to do. He’d always thought it was a kind of devotion, and sometimes it was. But he’d made himself so present in every hour of her day that he’d forgotten she needed room to move in it. What he didn’t know was how to be less without becoming someone she didn’t want.

At four he’d rung the French restaurant with the candles and cancelled the table for two at eight. Then the florist. Then he’d taken a folded page out of his inside pocket, an agenda, typed, one year to the day, Item 1: Apologise for the soup, and put it in his desk drawer. At eight his phone rang.

He turned the chair round. Song-Zhu. He let it ring twice, and answered.

She didn’t say hello, or sorry. She didn’t say anything at first. He could hear her breathing, and he could hear that she was in her kitchen, because her fridge hummed in E flat.

“Come,” said Song-Zhu, and rang off.

✦ ✦ ✦

He was at her door in twenty-three minutes. He didn’t use the key. He knocked.

He was still in his work trousers and a pale shirt with the collar open, tired in a way she’d never seen him tired, all the brightness turned down. Her hair was wet from a shower she’d had for no reason except to have something to do.

“You knocked.”

“You asked me to give you room.”

Her eyes filled all at once. “Oh, Hao.”

“Did you need something?” he said, carefully.

Song-Zhu swallowed. “You. I’m sorry. I shouldn’t have said it like that. I need room sometimes. I need to be able to say no to a car, or dinner, or a phone call, without feeling I’ve let you down. That’s all I meant.”

Her breath shook.

“I don’t want you to go quiet because I said you were too much. I didn’t know what quiet would sound like. Now I do, and I hate it. I miss you.”

“You saw me twenty hours ago.”

“Not like that. Not the station kiss. Not goodnight, Song-Zhu.”

He didn’t come in yet. “I was trying to give you what you asked for. But when you said I was too much—”

He stopped, and she waited, the way she’d learned to.

“It made me feel like the way I love you is something you have to put up with.”

Her face crumpled. She came out onto the landing and put both hands flat on his chest. “I love the way you love me. All of it. The egg tarts. The weather. The ridiculous agendas. I just need to be able to breathe inside it. And you have to tell me when something hurts. You don’t have to cancel our anniversary on your own in your office so I’ll never know. I worked it out at six. I’m an investigator. You’d booked the French one.”

He didn’t deny it. “I thought you wanted me to stop.”

“I wanted you to stop doing some things. Not to stop wanting me.”

Something in his face came loose at last. “That’s an important distinction. You should put it in a report.”

“I’m putting it in a report,” said Song-Zhu, and pulled him in by his shirt.

✦ ✦ ✦

It wasn’t graceful. She was too relieved and he was too tired and their noses bumped, and she laughed against his mouth. He put his hands up to her face and held it, carefully, and the kiss slowed, and she felt the hesitation in him, a question he wasn’t asking out loud.

“You’re allowed to touch me. Stop looking like you’re waiting for written permission.”

He laughed, low, and the sound went right through her. He walked her backwards through her own door and kicked it shut with his heel and put her against the wall of her little hallway by the coat hooks, and kissed her like he’d been starved for a year and not a day. Deep and slow, then not slow at all. His hands went into her wet hair. Hers went inside his shirt. He made a low rough sound into her mouth she’d been listening for since half past eleven the night before without knowing it. She pulled him closer by his belt, and he pressed her into the wall with the whole length of his body, his thigh between hers, his mouth on her jaw and her throat and back on her mouth, like he had to check every part of her was still where he’d left it.

“I missed you. You were right here, and that was the worst part,” he said against her lips.

She held his face and kissed him again, a long slow kiss with her eyes open so he could see it in her face: everything she couldn’t say yet. He saw it. She watched him see it, and he didn’t ask her to say anything. He put his forehead down on her shoulder and stood there breathing, holding her against the wall, and she put her arms round his neck.

✦ ✦ ✦

Later he sat on one of her kitchen stools and she stood between his knees with her hands on his shoulders.

“What would you like me to do differently?”

She thought about it properly. “Ask before you arrange things. Don’t ring three times if I don’t answer once. If I say I’m working, behave like you believe me. Sometimes ask if I want help, instead of helping. And sometimes send me something stupid without expecting an answer. A dog. A cloud that’s the wrong shape. Not a question. Not a reminder. Just you, telling me something.”

He smiled slowly. “I can do that.”

“Your turn. What do you need?”

He took a long time. “I need to know you don’t resent me for caring. That when you want room, it doesn’t mean you want less of me. And I need you to tell me when I’m getting it wrong before it gets to where everything I do is unbearable.”

“I should have told you two weeks ago,” she said, and he turned his head and kissed her palm.

He held both hands up before she could speak. “Have you eaten? Half a joke.”

“I haven’t. I’ve been waiting all day for somebody to ask me.”

He laughed, really laughed, the first time she’d heard it in twenty hours, and it filled her kitchen up to the corners.

✦ ✦ ✦

In bed she lay with her back against his chest, tracing the bones of his hand. “Are we all right?”

He kissed her shoulder. “We’re learning. I don’t think loving each other means we’ll get everything right. We’ll say things badly. Sometimes we’ll need different things on the same night. But I don’t want to be afraid of telling you when something hurts, and I don’t want you to feel guilty for asking me for room.”

“Then don’t be. And don’t make me,” she said, and turned and kissed him, and tucked herself back into him.

“Happy anniversary,” he said into her hair.

She was quiet so long he thought she’d gone to sleep. “Next year I’m booking the restaurant.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He’d got up at six for a call and gone home to change. Just after seven her phone buzzed on the bedside table. A photograph: a small, entirely round dog sitting upright in a supermarket basket, wearing an expression of grave responsibility.

Ren Hao: He looks like he runs a company. No reply needed.

She put her face in the pillow and laughed until her ribs hurt, and typed anyway.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): He’s obviously the managing partner. Better qualified than you.

Ren Hao: Unnecessary.

She sent the round dog back to him with one word under it, and put the phone on the bedside table, face up, where she could see it.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Again.

chapters.title: The Last Quiet Week
chapters.desc: The day after the seven-all hacking contest on his floor, a beach house with no phones. A week before the crash. Explicit, every day: the shower, the deck, the sand, the sea.
chapters.epigraph: “There’s nobody for a kilometre.”
chapters.content:
He came to her flat on the Saturday night still talking, with his tie in his pocket and the face of a man who’d watched the best sporting event of his life.

“Seven-all. After eleven hours. And then they both said rematch at exactly the same moment, Song-Zhu, the same syllable, and Professor Szeto took her glasses off, and I laughed until I had to hold on to a chair. And at four Eliana went and sat on the fire stairs and the doctor went after her, and she came back and found two more.”

She was on her sofa in shorts with her feet up on the bag she’d packed for the morning. “You texted me all of that. In capitals.”

He dropped onto the sofa and pulled her feet into his lap. “Two of the best security minds in the city at my boardroom table for eleven hours, legally. The most fun I’ve had in years.”

“Better than me?”

He looked at her feet in his lap, and at the bag under them. “Ask me on Saturday,” said Ren Hao.

✦ ✦ ✦

He had one rule for the week: no phones. She had three: no work, no talking about work, no waking her before nine. He agreed to all four.

The beach house was two hours along the coast road at the end of a sandy lane behind a line of pines bent all one way by the wind. One bedroom with a window onto the sea, an open kitchen, a wide wooden deck with a sagging outdoor sofa, and a path through the dune grass to a little curve of beach that belonged, for seven days, to nobody but them. He’d chosen it because in November, in the dark, she’d said she wanted once in her life to wake up somewhere without traffic.

“How much planning went into this?”

He considered lying. “I drove out three weeks ago. I checked the road, the water pressure, the lock on the deck door, where the nearest hospital was. And whether the bed creaked. It doesn’t. I tested it. I sat on it, thoroughly.”

She laughed and put a finger on his mouth. “Holiday.”

They put their phones in the drawer of the little table by the door, his and then hers, and she shut it with her hip.

“I might experience withdrawal,” he admitted.

They ate fish he grilled on the deck with a bottle of cold white wine, and afterwards he hummed something tuneless and held out his hand, and she said that was worse than no music and took it anyway, and they danced barefoot on the warm boards with no rhythm at all until the first stars came out.

In the bedroom the window was open and the room was full of the sea. He undressed her by it in the dark, her T-shirt over her head, her shorts down her legs with his hands following, and stood behind her with his hands flat on her bare stomach and kissed the side of her neck.

“There’s nobody for a kilometre. For a whole week. So I want to hear you.”

He laid her on the bed that didn’t creak and took her wrists in one hand and held them above her head on the pillow, gently, and kissed his way down her: her throat, her breasts, slow, until she arched up off the mattress into his mouth; her ribs; the soft skin below her navel. Then he let go of her wrists and pushed her thighs apart with both hands and put his mouth on her. She didn’t hold back, because she didn’t have to. She came the first time with her fingers knotted in his hair and his name going out of the window into the dark, louder than she’d ever let herself be anywhere, and he didn’t stop, and the second time she was sobbing with it. When he came up over her and pushed into her in one long stroke and held there, he said, “Again. Louder,” and took her slowly and then not slowly, and she was louder.

“Five stars,” she said afterwards, into his chest, and fell asleep halfway through his laugh.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Monday they read on the deck all morning. He lasted twenty-three minutes before asking what her book was about, and ten minutes after that his hand closed round her bare ankle.

“It was there,” he said.

She lasted one more page, then climbed into his lap in the deckchair and kissed him until both books had slid onto the boards.

The shower was small, tiled in blue, with a window high up showing the dark. He washed the salt out of her hair with his fingers working slow circles on her scalp.

She turned round with the water running between them and ran her hands down his chest and over his stomach and took him in her hand. “You’re treating me like glass. My turn.”

She pushed him back against the tiles and went down on her knees on the wet floor, and looked up once through her wet lashes before she took him into her mouth. He said her name, hoarse, and his hand went flat against the tiles. She’d learned him by now, what made his breath catch and what made him swear, and she did all of it, slowly, until his other hand was in her wet hair, only holding on, and he was shaking with the effort of staying still.

“Stop. Not like this. I want—”

He turned her round as she stood and put her against the wall where he’d been, palms on the warm tiles, his body along the whole length of her back and his mouth at her ear under the noise of the water, and told her what he was going to do, in order, while his hand slid down between her legs and did the first of it. Then he did all the rest exactly as he’d said, holding her up when her knees went, until she came with her cheek against the wet wall and his arm locked round her waist, and he followed with his teeth in her shoulder and the hot water running out on them both.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Tuesday, at ten past eight, he broke her third rule. She woke to his mouth on the inside of her knee, and then higher, the sheet pushed to the end of the bed and the morning sun across her stomach.

“It isn’t nine.”

He spoke against her thigh. “I’m not waking you up. You can stay asleep. You won’t have to do anything at all.”

“You’re a lawyer’s nightmare.”

“I’m a risk consultant. I find the loopholes.”

She shut her eyes. “Fine. I’m asleep.”

He held her hips down on the mattress with both hands and kept her at the edge of it long past the point where she’d stopped pretending, until she was saying his name over and over to the ceiling and pulling his hair and begging in a voice she didn’t recognise, and only then let her go over, and it went on and on, the sun on her and his mouth on her and the sea outside. Then she rolled on top of him and showed him what she thought of his loopholes.

They walked into the village in the afternoon: one street, a harbour wall, a shop that sold everything. She bought a ridiculous straw hat and wore it the rest of the day because he said it suited her and wasn’t lying. They bought peaches, and a small blue bowl from a potter by the harbour, and she carried the bowl herself.

That evening, with her feet in his lap on the deck, she said, “Have you heard anything? About Gideon?”

His hand stopped on her ankle, only for a second. “Nothing new. Kong has it. Not tonight. I like that you ask.”

“Then I’ll keep asking,” said Song-Zhu.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Wednesday she woke alone to a crash in the kitchen and found him barefoot beside a plate in several pieces.

“How does anybody break a plate making toast?”

“Poor coordination. Don’t laugh.”

“I am laughing,” she said, and kissed him, and took the broom off its hook.

They spent the day on the beach. She collected shells. He collected her sandals, her towel, her hat and the water bottle she kept leaving behind on the sand, and when she told him he was allowed to sit down he put it all in a heap and sat, and she sat between his knees and leaned back on him, and they watched the waves for an hour without saying anything. At sunset she stood ankle-deep in his old shirt with the light going red behind her and told him to take a picture, and he said, “No phones. I’ll remember it,” and did.

That night was the warmest of the week, no wind at all, and they didn’t go to bed. They lay on the sagging sofa on the deck with the lamps along the rail off and the sea a sound in the dark, and she was in his shirt and nothing else.

“That’s mine.”

“Take it back, then.”

He undid the buttons one at a time, the way he was slow about things he wanted to remember, and didn’t take it off her: opened it, pushed it off her shoulders, left it under her on the cushions, and looked at her in the starlight.

“We’re outside, Hao.”

“The sea won’t tell.”

He came into her easy and slow and deep, and the sofa groaned under them, and she laughed out loud and put her hand over her own mouth. He took her hand away and held it down on the cushion. “Don’t you dare. Not out here.” So she let every sound out of her into the warm dark, and he moved in her slow and relentless, telling her in a low voice how she looked and how she felt round him and what he’d do before the night was over, and then doing it. Later she turned him over on the narrow cushions and rode him with the stars behind her head and the shirt hanging off one arm, and he came with his hands tight on her hips and her name going out over the water. They fell asleep out there under the blanket he’d brought, because he always brought a blanket, and woke at three, cold, and went in.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Thursday it rained all morning. The beach went behind a grey sheet and the pines thrashed. She stood at the window in his jumper. “So what do we do?”

“Anything,” he said into her neck, and she took his hand back to the bedroom.

She pushed him onto his back and sat astride him and took him in by inches, teasing, lifting away whenever he moved his hips, until he was gripping the sheets with both fists and swearing at the ceiling.

“You’re very quiet this morning. That’s suspicious.”

“I’m not quiet. I’m begging.”

She sank down at last, and he groaned like something had been taken out of him. She rode him the way the rain came down outside, steady and endless, her hands braced on his chest, and when he was close she stopped dead and held still until he opened his eyes. “Not yet. Look at me.” She took him to the edge three times like that, and back, and on the third she went over with him, both of them shaking, her hair falling over both their faces.

In the afternoon they played cards and he let her win the last game. She knew. He knew she knew.

On the wet deck steps that evening she said, “Do you ever think about after this week?”

He turned her face to his. “We go home. You go back on the roster on Monday. I go back to the office. And then we do this again. Do you want something else?”

There was something in her face he couldn’t read, and then something he could, and she didn’t say it, and he didn’t ask her to. She kissed him instead.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Friday the sun came back. She found him on the deck early with a coffee, watching the sea.

“Tell me something you’ve never told me.”

“When I was fourteen I wanted to be a chef. Not a famous one. A small restaurant. Twelve tables. A short menu that changed every week, and no bookings after eight so the staff could go home. I drew the floor plan on graph paper and my father pinned it to the fridge.”

“What would you call it?”

He looked at her. “Song-Zhu’s. Because you’d decide the menu.”

“I’d put dumplings in everything. And you’d complain about the cost of the prawns.”

He kissed her, and she didn’t say anything for a while, because there were things in her throat she still couldn’t get out.

At about eleven that night, with the moon three-quarters full and the tide going out, she led him down the path through the dune grass, let go of his hand, walked out onto the wet sand where the moon lay like foil, turned round, and pulled her dress over her head.

“You told me on Sunday there’s nobody for a kilometre. The beach is closer to nobody than the house is.”

She undressed him at the edge of the water, button by button, and stood back and looked at him silver all over, and he let her look. Then she pulled him down. The sand was cool and gave under them. She lay back on her spread dress, and the sea came in further than either of them expected and washed over their feet, and she gasped and laughed. He pushed into her slowly, and the next wave came in round his knees and her hips, cold, and she cried out and arched into him and he held her there inside her with the sea pulling out under them and the sand shifting under her back.

“Don’t stop.”

He moved with the rhythm of the water, in and out, like the sea was setting the pace and he was only following, and every time a wave came in she clutched at him and he pushed deeper, and every time it went out she pulled him down again. There was sand in everything: her hair, his knees, her mouth when she kissed him. She’d never cared about anything less.

“When I’m old I’m going to remember exactly this,” he said, with the moon behind his head.

He slid a hand under her and lifted her hips off the sand and moved faster, and she came with the sea washing over both of them and her nails in his back and his name going up into the empty sky, and he followed with his face in her neck and held her in the shallow water until the tide had pulled back off them altogether.

“There’s sand in places sand should never be,” he said afterwards.

“You’ll be finding it for a week.”

“Good,” said Ren Hao.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Saturday she woke at six before him and went down to the sea on her own in the grey light, and walked in to her waist and stood with her arms round herself, watching the light come up. He found her ten minutes later, walked in in his shorts without a word and put his arms round her from behind, and they watched the sky turn from grey to white to gold.

“I don’t want to go back. Can we stay another night?”

“We could.”

She turned round, salt water to her waist, and shook her head. “If we stay another night I’ll never leave.”

She kissed him in the sea, her body cold and then warm against his, and he lifted her and she wrapped her legs round him, and they made love standing in the waves at dawn, almost without moving, foreheads together, the sea holding them up, and neither of them said a word. When she came she only breathed his name, once, into the cold air between their mouths, as if it were something she’d been keeping all week and had only now decided to spend.

He carried her out of the sea. He checked the house twice before they left. At the door he opened the drawer by the door and there they were, both phones, dark, exactly where they’d left them. He gave her hers without turning it on.

“Not yet,” she said.

She fell asleep in the car halfway back with the straw hat in her lap and the blue bowl wrapped in a towel at her feet and sand on her neck. At a red light on the edge of the city he looked across at her. The week had been good, and she was asleep beside him, and he loved her.

✦ ✦ ✦

At her flat she turned her phone on in the kitchen and it lit up and kept lighting: emails, missed calls, the roster. The world had gone on without them.

She held out her hand. “I’m on from Monday. Seven days. Can we have one more quiet evening first?”

They stood in her kitchen and talked about the plate and the pancakes and a restaurant with twelve tables and no bookings after eight, and when she said her legs were too tired for the hall he carried her down it.

On the bed she held on to his collar. She almost said it. He saw her almost say it.

“I love you,” he said, so she wouldn’t have to.

“Again.”

“I love you,” said Ren Hao, and she pulled him down.

chapters.title: The Crash
chapters.desc: A passenger jet goes into the sea on approach with 180 people. Her phone at 4 a.m. It’s his client’s airline. He builds the wall again before six, drives her, and stays out of the way.
chapters.epigraph: “Just don’t leave him alone with the waiting.”
chapters.content:
The phone rang at three minutes past four. Song-Zhu was awake before the second ring. Her bedroom, dark; the air conditioning humming; Ren Hao asleep beside her with one arm heavy across her waist. Then it rang again and she knew exactly where she was, what week it was, and whose name was on the roster.

Duty Officer. And underneath it, before she’d answered, a second call waiting: Director Kwan. Director Kwan didn’t ring at four in the morning.

“Song-Zhu. It’s Kwan. We have an accident. A passenger jet inbound on approach to the main runway. It went into the sea about twenty minutes ago, two kilometres short. A hundred and eighty on board. A hundred and seventy-four passengers, six crew. No confirmed survivors. Nothing confirmed at all.” His voice was perfectly level, which was how she knew.

For a second the room lost every sound in it.

“Whose is it?”

He told her the airline, and she shut her eyes.

He spoke before she could. “I know. Mabel’s on her way in. We’ll deal with your declaration this morning, properly, in writing, the way we did in October. Until then you do what the roster says. It’s your week. It’s yours. Operations centre. And don’t drive.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He woke when she switched the lamp on. She was already at the wardrobe pulling out trousers and the flight suit in its bag from the hook on the door.

“An aircraft’s gone into the sea on approach. A hundred and eighty people.”

He was awake in a second. She watched it go through him, the number and then, because he was who he was, the next question. “Whose?”

She said the airline’s name. He didn’t move. She watched him understand everything it meant all at once: the holding group, the man who’d rung him three times in October, the wall in his firm, the declaration in hers. She watched his face close over all of it deliberately, like a man putting a sheet over furniture.

“I’m leading it.”

“Then my side will be in writing by six. I’ll drive you.”

He didn’t ask whether she was frightened or tell her it would be all right. He went to find his clothes.

✦ ✦ ✦

She sat with the phone at her ear and her notebook open on her knee.

“First response group at the operations centre in an hour. One command point. We go through search and rescue, not round them. Air traffic: tower tapes, approach, radar, weather, the movement records. Originals secured. Write down who touched what and when.”

It rang again the moment she put it down.

At the long straight by the container port his own phone lit in its cradle on the dashboard. The man who owned the holding group. He let it ring out and kept driving. She saw. Neither of them said anything, and that was its own conversation.

At a red light she said, looking straight ahead, “You’ll have to ring him.”

“Raymond and compliance first. Then him. The wall from October, same terms. Raymond takes the account and everything to do with this. I don’t see a file, a briefing or a draft statement.”

“He’s your biggest client, Hao.”

“I know what he is,” said Ren Hao, and the light went green.

At the operations centre every window was lit. Beyond the barrier a television van was already raising its mast. He handed her the bag from the back seat before she reached for it.

“I’ll be near, and available. You tell me what you need. If you don’t need anything, I’ll still be near. You’re the right person for this.”

He wanted to kiss her. With the mast going up beyond the barrier and the declaration not yet written, he didn’t. He squeezed her hand once, hard. She walked into the light without looking back.

✦ ✦ ✦

At five past five he rang Raymond, who answered on the first ring and said “I know” before Ren Hao had said anything.

“Same wall as October. You lead. I’m out of it completely from now, in writing by six. Copy compliance and legal.”

“He’ll want you. It’s a hundred and eighty people, Hao.”

“I know how many it is. That’s why it can’t be me,” said Ren Hao, low.

Then he rang the owner back, listened to what he said about loyalty and five years, and said, “Raymond will be with you in an hour. He’s the best I have. Look after your families,” and rang off. He sat in his car in the grey beginning of the light and wrote down the time of each call and what had been said in it, the way she would have done.

✦ ✦ ✦

The first briefing was standing up. There weren’t enough chairs and nobody wanted one.

One screen showed the end of the flight path in white: the long curve in from the south-west over the sea, the turn onto final, the line coming down towards the threshold and stopping, two kilometres short, over water. A second showed the search area, already widening. A third showed the manifest, still marked UNVERIFIED in red.

Round the table were investigators, engineers, a search-and-rescue liaison and two men from the operator’s safety department who’d plainly dressed in the dark. Some were older than her by thirty years. She saw them look at her, and at Mabel by the wall behind her, and back. Mabel didn’t move from the wall.

“What we know. Then what we don’t.”

“Contact lost on final at three forty-two, two kilometres from the threshold, four hundred and twenty feet and decreasing. The tower reports a transmission, possibly an emergency call, about thirty seconds before.”

“Then it’s unverified. Nobody calls it a distress call until we’ve heard it. Write it as a transmission. Survivors?”

The liaison looked at the table. “None found.”

“Then we don’t say anything we don’t know. No numbers to the press. Nobody turns a guess into a fact because somebody asks the same question three times.”

She looked at them one at a time.

“Our first job is to support the search and preserve the evidence. We’re not here to find a cause this morning. We’re here to make sure that in a year we still can. We’ll ask the operator for what’s theirs and keep our own record of everything we’re given.”

The two men from the safety department straightened.

“Specialist search assets for the recorders, requested now. And families: one channel. I want somebody at the terminal now. I don’t want one family finding out from a television that their mother was on that aircraft.”

When they broke up, Mabel came off the wall and stood beside her just long enough to say, low, “Good,” and went to find a telephone.

✦ ✦ ✦

The first pictures came through after six, from a helicopter.

The sea was grey and still dark, heaving with the swell that had come in overnight. On the surface, things. Seat cushions, blue, a great many, scattered across a hundred metres. A yellow life jacket, uninflated, its tapes trailing. A child’s rucksack. A suitcase, open, its clothes floating out of it in a slow fan. A section with a row of oval windows in it, floating upright and then rolling over.

“Mark the coordinates, the time, the source of the footage. Keep the original file.”

A boat moved slowly past the window section. Somebody on its deck pointed at the water, and the camera turned.

There was a man in the water, by his shirt, floating with his face in the sea and his arms out a few metres from the wreckage, moving with the swell the way the cushions moved. The helicopter held on him for a long second and swung away.

“Every person brought out of the water gets a position, a time, a condition and a chain of custody, and the recovery record stays separate from the debris inventory. Separate. Always.”

The next picture was the boat: two people in orange leaning over the side, and between them, being lifted, something heavy in a dark shirt, streaming water, arms hanging. They laid it on the deck. One knelt and put two fingers to the neck and stayed there, and then sat back on his heels, and the other put a grey blanket over all of it, head to feet.

Song-Zhu looked away for one second, at the wall above the screen, at a clock that said seven minutes past six. Then she looked back.

“Continue,” she said.

✦ ✦ ✦

The airport had opened a family assistance area in a conference suite above arrivals, and by the time she got there it was full. People sat in rows of chairs holding phones, passports, printed booking confirmations, photographs. Some were still in what they’d had on when the phone rang: pyjama trousers under a coat, slippers, a man in a dinner jacket with the tie undone. A small boy, five or six, was asleep across two chairs with his head in a woman’s lap. She held his shoes in one hand and her phone in the other, and looked at the phone every few seconds.

A man at the back paced with his phone at his ear. “Ring her again. Ring her again.”

She’d sat in a room like this herself, at nineteen, with a notebook. Knowing the shape of it was nothing at all like standing in it.

She found the authority’s liaison officer, grey in the face already. “One point of contact for each family. I don’t want anyone telling their story four times to four people in four lanyards. Set it up faster.”

A man came straight at her across the room holding up a photograph, folded and unfolded so often it had gone soft at the crease: a young woman laughing in a graduation gown. “Are you from the investigators? Can you tell me whether she survived?”

“We’re still working to find out what’s happened and who’s been brought out of the water. I won’t tell you anything that isn’t confirmed. I’m sorry. I won’t guess.”

“She’s twenty-three. She rang me yesterday. She said the plane was early and she’d be home for breakfast.”

There was no sentence in any language that could make that smaller, so she didn’t look for one. She said she was sorry again, and asked the liaison officer to stay with him, and he did.

✦ ✦ ✦

Ren Hao was still in the car park when her message came.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Can you bring coffee? Coffee only.

She met him at the staff door at the side of the building and took the cup in both hands. She hadn’t slept and wouldn’t, there was a line between her eyebrows that hadn’t been there at four. He didn’t ask what she’d seen or how many or whether she was all right. She couldn’t hand him the morning in a sentence by a fire door, and if he made her try, it would cost her something she needed for the afternoon.

She drank half the coffee standing up, looking at the lid. “There’s a little boy in the family room. Five or six. His auntie brought him. He’s waiting for his mother. He keeps asking when she’s coming. I don’t know what to say to him.”

He didn’t hurry. “You don’t have to find a sentence that makes it better. Just don’t leave him alone with the waiting.”

She looked up at him, and nodded, and gave him the empty cup, and went back in. He stood holding it a long time after the door had shut.

✦ ✦ ✦

By mid-morning the main wreckage still hadn’t been found. The search box had been doubled and doubled again, and the recorders were somewhere under forty metres of grey water. In the technical room the specialist put up a diagram of the aircraft with two small orange boxes in its tail.

“They’re in the rear fuselage. We can’t assume the rear fuselage is in one place any more. The beacons should be transmitting. The navy’s survey vessel is two hours out.”

“When they come up, they’re photographed where they’re found before anybody touches them, and they come out in seawater from the same place. Nobody cleans them, dries them or plugs them into anything until I’m in the room.”

She looked at the two orange boxes. She knew everything they could say: height, speed, heading, the angle of every control surface, the warnings, the voices. She knew what they couldn’t do. They couldn’t make the sea give anything back.

Outside the window it was a bright, ordinary, beautiful Sunday. Somebody was flying a red kite on the grass beyond the perimeter fence, and it climbed and dipped and climbed, and past the end of the runway the boats were still working. She pressed her fingertips flat on the windowsill until they went white, and went back to the table.

✦ ✦ ✦

Mabel told her at eleven that his wall was in writing, signed, with a copy to her, and that he’d sent it before she’d finished her coffee.

✦ ✦ ✦

At the evening briefing a great deal more wreckage had been found and logged, and some of it matched to the aircraft. The main wreckage hadn’t been located. There were still no survivors. The search-and-rescue liaison stood and said, carefully, in the agreed words, that the operation was moving from rescue to recovery.

Nobody moved. One of the engineers took his glasses off and put his hand over his eyes and kept it there. Song-Zhu let the silence go on exactly as long as it needed to.

“Tomorrow we start the detailed history. Maintenance back to the last heavy check and every contractor who touched it.”

Leong, who’d been doing this since before she was born, said, “Have we got an early theory?”

“No. We’ve got an aircraft in the sea, a hundred and eighty people who didn’t come home, and two recorders on the bottom. If anybody in this room says the word pilot or the word weather to anyone outside it before we’ve got the recorders open, they’re off my team.”

Nobody argued. Leong looked at Mabel by the wall, and Mabel slightly inclined her head.

✦ ✦ ✦

He was standing by his car under the floodlights when she came out, and took her bag without a word except hello. Sunday night, people coming out of restaurants laughing: it all looked exactly the way it had yesterday, and that was what she couldn’t get past.

“I saw a person in the water this morning. And then another. They lifted them onto the boats and put blankets over them. Grey ones.”

Her voice was flat. She’d spent sixteen hours keeping what she felt under what had to be done.

“That little boy was still there at six. He asked me if his mother was in the sea. Just like that. Is my mummy in the sea. I told him I didn’t know yet, and that I’d find out, and that I’d tell his auntie the truth when I did. He said promise. So I promised.”

His hands tightened on the wheel. “Then that’s what you’ll do.”

He reached across the console, and she held his hand, and he drove one-handed until the road needed both.

✦ ✦ ✦

At her flat she stood under the shower a long time and washed her hands, and then again, and a third time between every finger, and didn’t know why, because it had all been on a screen and her hands were perfectly clean.

When she came out he was in the kitchen standing over two bowls of plain rice with egg and spring onion on top. His face changed when he saw hers. He didn’t say anything. He held his arms open a little at his sides, and she walked into them, and he held her just enough that she could feel somebody there.

“I don’t want to talk. I don’t want to explain anything.”

“You don’t have to.”

They ate at the counter, and he didn’t ask her anything.

Near eleven her work phone buzzed on the coffee table and she sat bolt upright: the survey vessel had found a larger section of wreckage on the bottom. Neither recorder recovered.

“I need you to know something. When I’m working I might not answer. I might come home and not want to talk at all. And there’ll be things I’m not allowed to tell you, above all now, with whose aircraft it is. Please don’t try to fix this for me.”

“I can’t. Nobody can. But I can drive you, and bring you home, and make rice with an egg on top, and sit with you when you don’t want to talk, and get out of your way when you need to work. So that’s what I’ll do.”

Her eyes filled for the first time all day, and she didn’t let them spill. “That’s enough.”

She leaned on him, and neither of them slept.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Monday she was up before four. Messages from the operations centre: the search would resume at first light; the number recovered was being verified; neither recorder found. He brought her coffee and watched her drink it.

“Ready?”

“No,” she said, and picked up her bag, and he picked up his keys.

At the operations centre there were three television vans now. Before she opened the door he touched her wrist.

“I’ll be here when you’re done,” he said.

She leaned across, in front of the vans and the cameras and all of it, and kissed him once on the mouth, quickly, and held his face in her hand a second afterwards. Then she got out and went in, and he watched until the door shut.

chapters.title: Thirty Days
chapters.desc: Both recorders stop eleven seconds early. She stops sleeping. He moves into her flat without asking, and won’t read one line of her draft.
chapters.epigraph: “I keep hearing the silence.”
chapters.content:
The first time Song-Zhu heard the eleven seconds, she thought the playback had failed. The second time, she thought the technician had stopped it too early. By the fifth she understood the silence was real, and by the ninth she’d begun to hate it more than anything she’d ever heard.

✦ ✦ ✦

The flight data recorder had come up on Monday afternoon from forty-one metres, still bolted into a piece of the rear fuselage the size of a garden shed. The divers had photographed it where it lay. It came out of the sea in a plastic tub of its own seawater, signed for three times between the dive boat and the laboratory, and nobody touched it until she was in the room. The voice recorder came up at dawn on Tuesday, two hundred metres away, on its own, out of a field of seat frames. Both dented. Both scorched along one edge. Both memory modules intact.

In the secured room at the back of the laboratory, blinds down, door locked, she stood behind the specialist’s chair while the first verified data came up.

“Limitations first.”

“The casing took a lot of damage. The crash-protected memory’s sound. Downloaded, verified, working copy made. The data’s good.”

He hesitated.

“Until it isn’t.”

The traces came up in a long ribbon of coloured lines: altitude, airspeed, heading, pitch, roll, engines, flaps, gear, every control surface, the radio altimeter counting down towards the sea. Two hours and nine minutes of an ordinary flight, then the turn onto final, the long steady descent, everything where it should be.

Then every line stopped. All at once, at the same instant, as if someone had drawn a ruler down through them.

“Our best estimate from radar and the tower is eleven seconds before impact. No degradation, no noise. Every parameter’s clean to the last frame, and then there’s no next frame. Radar has the aircraft for another ten seconds at least.”

“Can we say what happened in those eleven seconds?”

“Not from anything I’ve got.”

He didn’t need to tell her the rest; she’d seen his face when she came in.

“The voice recorder stops at the same second. Both of them.”

Two recorders on two pieces of wreckage two hundred metres apart on the bottom of the sea, and both had stopped listening at the same instant. She knew what that usually meant. Every investigator in the building knew. She also knew usually had killed more truth than any fire.

“Then we write it exactly like that. Both recorders end at the same time, approximately eleven seconds before the estimated impact. Cause of the termination: not determined. Nobody in this building uses the word power outside this room until we can prove it.”

She wrote it in her notebook in capitals and underlined the last two words twice.

✦ ✦ ✦

They listened to the voice recording that afternoon in sections, with the door locked: her, the specialist, two authorised investigators, four pairs of headphones. It would never be copied, never leave the room, never be described to anyone outside it in more words than the law allowed.

A cockpit. Two men at the end of a night flight, tired and professional and a little dry with each other, the way people get after thousands of hours side by side. The checklists. The tower. The captain asking for the runway lights to be turned up a step. The first officer making a joke about the coffee. No speech, no warning anyone could have put in a film. Work, and questions, and answers.

Near the end something in both their voices changed. The specialist’s hand went to the pause.

“Continue,” said Song-Zhu.

A few words, fast. A sound in the airframe she couldn’t name. Another few words. And then nothing. No scream, no crash, no sea. The recording ended mid-breath, like someone shutting a door.

“Again. From two minutes before.”

By the ninth time she knew every frame of the last thirty seconds and could have drawn the waveform with her eyes shut, and still had no idea what happened in the eleven seconds after it stopped.

“Sounds identified separately: speech, background, airframe. Every uncertain segment stays marked uncertain. Nobody labels a sound until it’s been matched.”

She stood up and the chair scraped, and her knees nearly went. She collected her notes and walked down the corridor into the women’s toilets and locked herself in a cubicle and stood with her back against the door and her hands flat against it for four minutes without making a sound. Then she washed her face and went back to work.

✦ ✦ ✦

He woke to her key in the door before three on Thursday. He’d been asleep on her side of the bed because it smelled of her, which he’d never tell anyone. Her bag went down on the floor. Her shoes came off, one, two, in the dark, without the hall light. She was in the clothes she’d left in at five the morning before.

“Bad day?”

“Same day.”

He understood the difference. He brought her a glass of water, and she drank all of it, and got into bed, and he lay down beside her and didn’t reach for her. She was still for a while.
