Then she turned onto her back, and towards the window, and towards him. She got up, and came back. He heard the bathroom tap running and running. Later she was sitting at the end of the bed in the dark with her phone lit in her hands.

“Come and lie down. You don’t have to sleep. You can lie down anyway.”

She put the phone on the floor and lay down against him, and he stroked her hair from the crown to the ends, over and over. She didn’t sleep. Neither did he.

✦ ✦ ✦

The preliminary report was due within thirty days. The date had been written on the whiteboard in the investigation room in red the morning after the crash, and nobody had wiped it off.

TUESDAY 1 SEPTEMBER.

It wouldn’t find a cause. It wasn’t meant to. It would say, a month on, what had happened as far as anyone could say for certain, and what was being done to find out the rest. But the date had got into every meeting like water into a fuselage. Every evening she went down the list of what was unknown, and every evening it was longer than the list of what wasn’t.

On Saturday a senior investigator put a draft timeline on her desk. She put her finger on a line. “This says the aircraft experienced an abnormal event eleven seconds before impact.”

“The recorders stop there. Something happened.”

“We know something happened because the aircraft’s on the bottom of the sea. We don’t know what happened in those eleven seconds. We can’t use the silence as evidence. It’s the absence of evidence. That’s all it is.”

Ren Hao waited in the car park until after eight. He handed her a paper bag when she got in: an egg and cress sandwich from the place by his building.

“You’re trying again.”

“Yes.”

She ate half of it before the flyover. It was the first thing she’d had since a biscuit at eleven. He didn’t say a word about it.

✦ ✦ ✦

By the following Tuesday he’d been sleeping at her flat for nine nights.

Nobody had said anything about moving in. There’d been no conversation, no key cut. He’d just never left. The first night was the night of the crash. The second she’d come home at three and he’d been there, so he’d stayed. Then a clean shirt, groceries, his laptop charger, and his own coffee machine from his kitchen because hers was terrible and she was drinking six cups a day. By the ninth there were four of his suits in her wardrobe, pushed along the rail so her flight suits had moved to the end. His shoes by the door. His toothbrush beside hers. His shaving things on the shelf where her hair clips used to live. A list on the fridge in his tidy capitals, bins, laundry, filter changed, ticked.

She’d noticed it a day at a time, the way you notice water coming up round your ankles.

She found him in her kitchen in a white shirt with his hair wet, making coffee with his own machine.

“Why is your charger here? And your shoes? And four suits?”

He paused, holding the jug. “Because I keep staying.”

“You’re living here, Hao. Did you ask me?”

A small silence. “No.”

“Then why are you doing it?”

“Because you’re not sleeping. Because you come in at three and go out at five. Because you forget to eat until I put something in your hand. Because on Sunday night you stood in this kitchen for ten minutes holding your phone without moving, and I don’t think you knew you were doing it.”

His voice had dropped.

“I don’t want to leave you alone like that.”

“I didn’t ask you to leave. But you didn’t ask to stay, either.”

He looked down. She looked past him at the fridge and the list. She could feel the shape of the conversation they ought to have, and how long it would take, and what it would cost, and what was left in her to pay for it with. She had a briefing at eight, a draft at noon, three families at four, and nineteen days.

“We’ll talk about it after the first of September. Properly.”

He looked up, and she saw exactly what he heard in it: not not yet, but yes. She was too tired to correct him.

“And don’t reorganise my cupboards. Your eyes have,” she said.

He laughed, slightly, the first time she’d heard it in nine days. She took the coffee he held out, his coffee from his machine in her mug, and it was the best she’d had in a month, and she hated that. She kissed his cheek on the way past. She didn’t say you can stay. She didn’t say go home. She went to work.

✦ ✦ ✦

The technical team tried everything they knew. They compared the flight data with radar, the tower recording, the airport’s surface cameras and the engines’ own maintenance computers. Everything agreed with everything else right up to the instant the recorders stopped. After that there was radar, a few blurred returns, and the tower calling the callsign, and nothing from the aircraft.

“Could they have lost power? Could it be damage, to the recorders or the wiring?”

“Either. We can’t tell the difference with what we’ve got. There was no fault message, no warning, nothing before they stopped. As far as we can tell they worked normally to the last frame. There are a few damaged sectors on the memory boards. I don’t think there’s anything on them. I can’t promise.”

“Keep trying, inside the technical limits. Document every attempt, and every failure.”

On her way out she glanced back at the screen: the ribbon of lines and the edge where they ended, perfectly straight. She’d started seeing it when she shut her eyes.

She came home that night nearly two in the morning. He was asleep on her sofa, sitting up, his head tipped against the arm at an angle that would hurt in the morning, his phone lit on the cushion with a document still open. He’d waited for her and lost. She locked the phone and put it on the table and touched his shoulder, and he sat up at once.

“How was it?”

She looked at the dark television. “Eleven seconds. Both of them stop. We don’t know why. Every family asks me what happened in the eleven seconds. Every journalist. Kwan. The board.”

She pressed her palms together hard.

“I want to know so badly that sometimes I think if I listen enough times, I’ll hear something we missed. Underneath. And I know it doesn’t change because I listen again. It’s a recording. It’s the one thing in the world that never changes.”

He took her hand. “Then don’t listen to it tonight.”

She turned her face away. After a long time she said, so low he almost didn’t hear, “I keep hearing the silence.”

He moved closer, and she leaned into him, and he held her until her shoulders stopped shaking, and a long time after that.

✦ ✦ ✦

He woke at three the next Thursday to an empty bed and found her at her dining table in his old university sweatshirt, a pencil through her knotted hair, three documents open side by side on her laptop and a notebook black with her small fast writing, a cup of tea gone stone cold with the bag still in.

He came round the table and stopped at the corner, where he couldn’t see the screen. “How long have you been up?”

“Please don’t. I’m trying to finish the sequence for the report. I’ve got eleven days. Please stop asking me to sleep like I can just decide to.”

He let the breath go. He pulled out the chair on the far side of the table, opposite her, with the laptop lid between them, and sat down.

After a while she looked at him over the screen. “Do you want to read it? You could tell me if the sentences are too long. You’re good at sentences.”

“No.”

She blinked.

He said it gently. “I can’t. You know I can’t. Not one line. Raymond’s sitting in a room tomorrow with the people who own that aircraft. If I’d read a single word of your draft at your table at three in the morning, nobody could ever be sure again what I knew and when. Not Kwan. Not the families. Not you. I’m not going to be the reason anybody doubts that report.”

Something in her face crumpled slightly, and came back. “I forgot. I’m so tired I forgot whose aircraft it is.”

He reached across, not to the laptop, to her hand beside it. “I’ll sit here. You work. I’ll read my own book. I won’t look.”

He held his book open for forty minutes without once lifting his eyes above the lid of her laptop. She muttered, deleted a paragraph and wrote it again, said no out loud to the screen, quite fiercely, and he didn’t ask. When she closed the laptop he stood, and she stayed sitting, and then reached up for his hand.

“Will you come with me?”

✦ ✦ ✦

He started a list. Not of things she had to do: of things he could do without making her decide anything. Food in the fridge. Clean towels. A spare charger in her work bag. Her car filled. Her mother rung every Sunday afternoon, because her mother had rung him on the fourth of August from her sister’s in tears and said she won’t tell me anything, Ren Hao, she never does, please.

He didn’t touch the papers on her dining table or move her bag. He didn’t close the notebooks she left open, and didn’t read them either; he laid a clean sheet of paper over each open page without looking. When she came home he asked her one question: “Company or quiet?” Sometimes she said company. Sometimes quiet. He took both without making either into anything.

But he was frightened. Her rings started turning on her fingers. She forgot the names of people she’d met the week before. She woke out of thin broken sleeps reaching for her phone before her eyes were open. She sat on the floor of the shower long after the hot water had run out, with the cold coming down on her, not moving. He wanted to take her away for a day. He wanted to ring Director Kwan and tell him she needed to be stopped. He did none of it, because in June she’d told him not to turn worry into control, and it was the hardest promise he’d ever kept.

He stuck his list on her fridge under the one that said bins, laundry, filter changed, and didn’t notice that the fridge now held three lists, that six of his suits hung in her wardrobe, and that she could no longer find her own hair clips. She noticed. She didn’t say anything yet.

chapters.title: The Families
chapters.desc: The families. His firm runs the family side for the airline, behind a four-page wall. A widow asks what the pilot said; Song-Zhu can’t tell her.
chapters.epigraph: “One more moment. With someone who isn’t here.”
chapters.content:
The first family asked her whether the aircraft had exploded. The second asked whether the passengers had known they were going to die. The third asked whether the pilots had tried to save them. By the end of the morning she’d learned there were a hundred ways to ask the same question, and it was always the same underneath: Did they suffer? And there wasn’t one answer she was allowed to give that would make the room easier to breathe in.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the fourth week the family assistance centre moved to a hotel on the airport road that the airline had taken over entirely: private rooms for meetings, a quiet room for children with beanbags and crayons, a nurse, a room where people could sit without anyone asking them anything, and on the second floor, behind a keypad, the room where the belongings were.

A man stood up from a chair by the lobby door as she came in that Monday. “Are you the investigator? My wife was on the plane. We were going to have dinner.”

He turned his phone round: a message from the morning of the second of August. Boarding now. Don’t forget to buy the fruit.

“I didn’t forget. I bought it that morning, before anybody rang. It’s still in the bowl. Can you tell me if she knew?”

“I can’t. Not yet. We don’t have enough verified to answer that. I’m sorry.”

He nodded like he’d been expecting it, and sat down again.

The first session had seven families. Song-Zhu answered the technical questions. The recorders had been recovered. Both recordings ended at the same moment, about eleven seconds before impact, and the reason hadn’t been established. The voice recording was protected by law. The team was going through the maintenance history, the crew records, the weather, the air traffic recordings. A preliminary report would come out on the first of September. It wouldn’t give a cause.

A woman at the end of the table looked at her. “Then you don’t know. Everybody keeps telling us to wait. You finish work and you go home. We go home and they’re not there.”

Song-Zhu didn’t defend herself. There was nothing to defend. She came round the table and sat in the empty chair beside the woman, and stayed there for the rest of the meeting.

✦ ✦ ✦

That afternoon the identification team confirmed four more names. One was the little boy’s mother.

It didn’t have to be Song-Zhu who told them. There were people whose job it was, trained and careful and kind. But she’d made a promise on the second of August to a boy who’d asked whether his mummy was in the sea, and to his auntie, so she stood outside a door on the third floor with the family liaison officer while he knocked. The auntie saw their faces and her own went still. The boy was on the bed watching cartoons with the sound off.

Song-Zhu sat on the carpet in front of him so she wasn’t taller than him, and let the liaison officer do the talking. When he’d finished and the auntie had pulled the boy into her lap, the boy looked at Song-Zhu over his auntie’s arm.

“You said you’d find out. Is she in the sea?”

“Not any more. They brought her out. She’s on land now, with people looking after her, until your family can be with her.”

He thought about that a long time in the silent flicker of the cartoons. “Okay,” he said, and turned his face into his auntie’s shoulder.

Song-Zhu stayed on the carpet until the auntie nodded at her, and then went out and shut the door without a sound, and stood in the corridor with her hand flat on the wall.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Tuesday Raymond came up to the thirty-second floor at eight and stood in Ren Hao’s doorway with his tie already loose.

Ren Hao didn’t look up. “You can’t talk to me about the airline. That’s the whole point of you.”

“Not the investigation. Not the statements. The families.”

Raymond shut the door.

“It’s falling apart, Hao. People rung three times in a day by three departments asking the same questions. One desk says their hotel’s paid for and another says it isn’t. A man in Room 214 asked four times for an interpreter for his mother and got a leaflet. A woman was rung about claims before anyone had asked her about her husband’s wedding ring. The airline’s people are drowning and ours are running behind them with buckets. The owner wants you. On the families, nothing else. He says you’re the only person in this city who can stand in a room of people who’ve lost everything and make the hotel work. I told him it would have to go to compliance and Kong first, and to the investigators, in writing, before you set foot in the place. And that if you said no, I’d understand.”

Ren Hao sat still a long time. He thought about the wall he’d built on the second of August, and what he’d said at her dining table at three in the morning. He thought about Room 214, and a woman rung about claims before anyone asked her about a ring.

“Get Kong.”

By two it was on paper. Four pages. He’d lead the firm’s family support and nothing else: accommodation, transport, interpreters, belongings, the hotel, one named contact for every family, the people who answered the phones. Nothing about the investigation, the cause, what the airline said in public, the lawyers or the claims. He wouldn’t be in any meeting where the investigation was discussed, wouldn’t see any document about it, and would leave any room it came up in. Raymond kept everything else. Compliance signed. Kong signed. It went to Director Kwan with a covering letter that afternoon.

Before six Kwan wrote back. Two lines. No objection, on these terms. Ms. Xu has been informed.

He read Ms. Xu has been informed three times.

Ren Hao: Kwan’s told you. I should have told you first. I’m sorry. The families only. I’ll explain tonight if you want me to. If you don’t, I won’t.

At nine she replied.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Mabel read it to me in the corridor. I read it again myself. It’s a good wall. Do the hotel properly.

Nothing else. No kiss at the end. He went to her flat anyway, because his suits were there and his toothbrush, and because he no longer knew how not to.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Wednesday she saw him first, through the glass wall of a meeting room on the ground floor: across the lobby in a dark suit with two of his people and a woman in the airline’s uniform holding a clipboard. He listened. He asked a question. One of his people wrote something down. The airline woman nodded, and nodded again, and Song-Zhu watched her shoulders come down by about two inches. He looked exactly the way he looked at work, a man who could walk into a building full of grief and broken logistics and make everyone in it believe, for the first time in three weeks, that somebody had a list.

He turned his head and saw her. He gave her a small nod: I see you, and I know where I’m standing. She gave him the same one back, and walked on.

They met later by the lifts, and he was alone.

“Are you all right?”

She looked at him. “At work?”

He understood at once.

“The man in 214’s got an interpreter. His mother told the nurse,” she said.

“She told me too. In three languages, none of them mine. I can have someone else do the lobby when you’re here—”

She looked down the corridor at the meeting-room doors, every one shut, people behind every one. “Don’t. You’ve got four pages that say exactly what your job is. I’m allowed to do mine. So let’s do them.”

He stepped aside to let her past, and neither of them touched the other.

✦ ✦ ✦

Her name was Ting Mei. She was forty-one. Her husband had been in seat 23C, on his way home from a three-day conference, and every time he flew he sent her a photograph of the departures board with their two initials typed underneath.

They met on Thursday in a small room on the ground floor: two armchairs facing each other, a box of tissues on the table between them that nobody had touched, the liaison officer a little to one side with a notebook he wasn’t writing in. Mrs. Ting had brought her own notebook, a blue school exercise book, held in both hands on her knees.

The first line had been written and crossed out and written again. “I’ve written my questions down so I won’t forget any. The first one’s about the cockpit. What did the pilot say?”

Song-Zhu felt her whole body go still in the chair.

Mrs. Ting leaned forward. “I know you’ve got the recorder. The one with their voices. It was on the news. And you’ve listened to it. Did he tell the other one something was wrong? Did he say anything to us? To the people in the back?”

Song-Zhu remembered the two tired voices, the coffee joke, the runway lights up one step, the change near the end in both their voices, and the door shutting. She remembered the law. The voice recording was protected because pilots all over the world had to be able to speak freely in their cockpits, knowing that what they said in the last minutes of their lives would be used to stop it happening to anyone else, and not played on the news or read out in a courtroom or told across a low table in a hotel to a stranger. Anything that was released would be released in the report, in the words the analysis could support, and not a syllable more. She had no right to turn protected evidence into a private answer in a hotel room, or to hand anyone an interpretation nobody had established.

And underneath all of that, far down, a nineteen-year-old in another country with a notebook on her knee, asking the same question first on her list and being told no.

“I’m sorry. I can’t tell you what’s on the cockpit recording. Not now. Anything we can release will be in the report.”

Mrs. Ting’s voice dropped to almost nothing. “But you know something. Did my husband hear the pilot tell them they were going to die?”

Song-Zhu looked down at her hands for one second, and made herself look up and meet the woman’s eyes, because it was the least she could do. “I can’t answer that.”

Mrs. Ting closed the blue book, and stood, and her voice broke straight down the middle. “Please don’t explain. Everybody has an explanation. I didn’t want what I wanted. I wanted to know what he heard. Before.”

She went out and closed the door so gently the latch didn’t click.

Song-Zhu sat on in the armchair looking at the empty one. The worst part wasn’t that Mrs. Ting hadn’t asked for the cause. It was that she’d asked for so little: a few words, one moment, something her husband might have heard that she could take home and put somewhere. And Song-Zhu had nothing she was allowed to give her.

✦ ✦ ✦

He found her outside the staff entrance at the back of the hotel, sitting on a low brick wall by the bins with her folder beside her, and sat down not quite touching her. A delivery van reversed into the bay and beeped, and somebody unloaded crates of water.

“A widow asked me what the pilot said. If he knew. If he said anything to the people in the back. I couldn’t tell her.”

He didn’t ask what the pilot had said, or whether there was anything. She noticed how carefully he didn’t, and something in her that had been clenched since Tuesday let go a little.

“She looked at me like I was choosing not to. I wanted to give her one sentence to take home. That he wasn’t frightened. That someone in that cockpit was being kind.”

“You don’t know those things. And if you did, you couldn’t tell her.”

Her eyes filled. “She thanked me. She thanked me for coming to tell her I couldn’t tell her.”

He moved along the wall and put his arm round her shoulders, and she leaned her head against him by the bins, in her lanyard, with a man unloading crates of water ten metres away, and didn’t care who saw.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Saturday they were on two floors of the same building talking about the same people. On the ground floor he was reading a complaint: a family had been told by somebody on the airline’s helpline that the investigators would soon be announcing the cause.

“Find out who by four. Then find every family that person spoke to this week and ring them back and correct it, in person, today. Nobody gives a family a convenient sentence when we haven’t got an honest one.”

Four floors up, a few minutes later, she was telling her team, “If we haven’t got an answer, we say we haven’t got one. Not we’re hopeful. Not we expect.”

They found out a long time afterwards that they’d said almost the same sentence, four floors and five minutes apart, on opposite sides of the same thing.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Sunday night he locked his tablet the moment her key turned, before she’d got the door open, as he did every night now. She leaned on her counter and looked round her kitchen: his coffee machine, his third list on her fridge, dry cleaning, Mum (Sun) ✓, her car, his tea in her cupboard, and her hair clips, she knew without looking, in a little glass bowl he’d bought for them on a shelf where she’d never have put them.

“Does it bother you? That you’re working for the airline while I investigate their accident?”

“For the families, through the airline. My job is to make sure the people in that hotel are treated like people. Yours is to find out what happened to the ones they lost. Those aren’t the same, but they’re not against each other. And I don’t need to know what you’re finding. I’ve made sure I can’t.”

“Good,” she said, and almost smiled, and didn’t.

He came round the counter and stood in front of her without touching her, and she put her forehead against his chest, and he put his arms round her.

“How do you stop thinking about the people in a room after you’ve left it?”

“You don’t always. But you don’t have to take every one of them home.”

Later, while he showered, she opened her wardrobe and looked at his suits, six of them now, on her rail, and her flight suits pushed down to the far end in the dark, and stood there a long time with the door open.

✦ ✦ ✦

The last family briefing before the report was four families, and Mrs. Ting was one of them, by the window with the blue book on her knee. Afterwards she waited until the others had gone.

She turned the book over in her hands. “I’ve been thinking about what I asked you. I still don’t understand how there can be things that belong to the last minutes of my husband’s life that I’m not allowed to hear. But I understand there are rules, and that you didn’t make them up on Thursday afternoon to get rid of me. I keep wondering if he was thinking about me. It’s a stupid question.”

“It isn’t. But there’s no way I could know.”

Mrs. Ting nodded and stood up. “Thank you for not pretending.”

Not forgiveness, or relief: a woman saying out loud that another woman hadn’t lied to her, and somehow it was heavier than the anger had been.

✦ ✦ ✦

At home she sat on the sofa with her feet under her and held the tea he brought without drinking it.

“Every family has one question they keep coming back to. Some ask if the pilots knew. Some ask if the aircraft was already broken when it took off. Some ask if it hurt. She asks what her husband heard. They all want the same thing. One more moment. With someone who isn’t here.”

He put his arm round her.

“I can’t give any of them that.”

“You can give them the truth, when you have it. All of it. And you will.”

Tomorrow the report would come out and say almost nothing. She leaned against him and held the cold tea, and didn’t sleep.

chapters.title: Equipment
chapters.desc: The preliminary report says almost nothing. He organises her life so she can work. She tells him she’s his girlfriend, not his equipment. For the first time, he asks before kissing her.
chapters.epigraph: “Not your equipment.”
chapters.content:
The preliminary report was published at nine on Tuesday the first of September. Within minutes somebody on the radio called it disappointing. Soon after, a journalist asked online whether the investigators were hiding something, the father of a passenger wrote that thirty days had gone by and he still didn’t know why his daughter was dead, and the airline’s communications team asked for a paragraph to be clarified that had already been clarified twice. By half past nine Song-Zhu had read the report four times, and it still said the same thing. Facts. No cause. Nothing to explain the eleven seconds. Nothing anybody could hold on to.

✦ ✦ ✦

The briefing room was full: cameras on a riser along the back wall, microphones taped in a bunch to the lectern, Director Kwan at it in his reading glasses, Song-Zhu beside the screen in the dark blue suit she’d bought for exactly this and hoped she’d never wear.

He took them through it: the approach, the time contact was lost, the search and recovery, the hundred and eighty, the identifications so far. Both recorders recovered, both recordings ending at the same moment about eleven seconds before the estimated impact, the cause of the termination not yet determined. The voice recording under examination. The maintenance and operational history under examination.

A man in the second row stood up before Kwan had finished. “Does the report say what caused the crash?”

“No. The investigation hasn’t reached a conclusion about the cause.”

“Isn’t it unusual for both recorders to stop eleven seconds early?” said a woman at the back.

Kwan looked at Song-Zhu, and she stepped up to the second microphone. “The technical team is examining the recordings and the circumstances in which they ended. We won’t speculate about the reason until we can support it.”

“Could the aircraft have lost electrical power?”

“That’s one of the possibilities being examined. It hasn’t been established.”

“Is there anything on the voice recorder that shows a problem?”

“The voice recording is protected by law. We won’t release anything from it outside the proper process.”

The questions came in different shapes and were all the same question. Was it the aircraft. Was it the pilots. Was the airline to blame. She’d written most of the technical sections herself. She knew every qualifier, which sentences had been rewritten nine times, which claims had been taken out because the evidence wouldn’t hold them up. The report was accurate. It was also so incomplete it hurt to stand next to it.

Her phone was full when she got back to her office.

Ren Hao: It’s out. You stood up there and didn’t guess once. I watched it in the hotel lobby with forty people. Nobody in the room breathed while you were talking.

She didn’t know why it made her want to cry. She put the phone down and didn’t.

✦ ✦ ✦

Before lunch a man in his fifties stood in front of her desk holding a printed copy of the report, folded so many times on the way there that the corners had gone soft as cloth.

“It doesn’t say why. It says eleven seconds. What happened in them?”

“We don’t know yet. We’re going through the recorders, the maintenance and crew records, the weather, air traffic, and every piece of wreckage we can bring up. We’re still bringing it up.”

He folded the report again along its soft creases. “My daughter was on that plane. Twenty-six. She was starting a new job next week, at a bank. She’d bought shoes. I thought after thirty days there’d be something.”

“There’s everything in it we can stand behind. But I know it isn’t what you came here for.”

He nodded once, and went. She opened the report on her screen again: accurate, careful, defensible, and not enough.

✦ ✦ ✦

In a room on the ground floor of the hotel, blinds half down, Ren Hao was reading a draft letter. It was his letter: it would go from the family-assistance team to every one of the hundred and eighty families that afternoon, and the family-assistance team was his, all four pages of it. Under the condolences and the practical arrangements somebody he’d never met had added a paragraph.

The airline notes that the preliminary report found no evidence of a technical defect in the aircraft.

The airline’s family-assistance manager looked unhappy. “It came down from upstairs, with a request that you approve it. It’s only one sentence.”

He took his pen out. “It’s one sentence about the cause. I’m not allowed to touch the cause. It’s written down that I’m not allowed to, and Director Kwan has a copy. And it isn’t true. The report doesn’t say there’s no evidence of a defect. It says nobody knows yet. You can’t use a gap in what’s known as if it were a finding in your favour, and you can’t use it in a letter to a woman whose husband is dead.”

He drew a line through the paragraph and wrote in the margin, in capitals: NOT IN MY REMIT. NOT TRUE. REFERRED TO RAYMOND UNDER THE WALL.

“The letter goes without it, with the full report enclosed so they can read what it actually says. And somebody rings Mrs. Ting in 306 before it arrives so she isn’t alone when she opens it. Tell upstairs it was me.”

He sent the paragraph and his note to Raymond, copied Kong, wrote down the time, and sat in the half-dark with his phone in his hand. He wanted to ring her, and didn’t.

✦ ✦ ✦

By the time she came home he’d made dinner. Rice in the cooker. Soup on the stove, turned low. Greens under a plate. Her work shirts washed and hung on the airer. A new box of her tea. A glass of water on her side of the bed. Her charger moved from the sofa to her bedside table. Her work bag, which she always dropped by the sofa, picked up and put by the front door. She’d been noticing things like that for a month. And on the counter by the kettle, a sheet of paper in his capitals:

DINNER — STOVE.
CAR — 7:00 A.M.
DRIVER — CONFIRMED (MR. YAU).
SLEEP — PLEASE!

He came out of the bedroom, tired and hopeful. “You’ve got the technical briefing at nine and you were out at five today, so I thought if Mr. Yau—”

“I can book a car. And the last one?”

“That one’s a suggestion. I was trying to make it friendly. There’s soup.”

She didn’t move, and he saw it. She looked at the stove, at the charger through the open bedroom door, at her bag by the front door where she’d never in her life have put it.

“How long have you been doing this? Arranging everything?”

He came a step towards her. “Since the report got close. Some of it before. You’re exhausted. You’ve been exhausted for a month. I thought if I took the small things—”

“You moved my bag. You moved my charger. You booked a driver. You made me a schedule.”

“A reminder.”

She put both hands flat on the counter. “Can we talk? Now. It’s the first of September.”

His face changed. “Yes.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She went to the dining table and didn’t sit, and he didn’t either.

“Every morning someone needs something from me. An answer. A decision. A signature. A man came to my desk today with a report folded till it had gone soft and asked me what happened to his daughter, and I didn’t know. And then I come home and everything’s been arranged.”

“I thought it would help.”

“Let me finish. Please.”

Her voice was quiet, which made it worse.

“I know you’re frightened. I know you love me, and I know how hard you’ve tried for a month and how much you’ve stopped yourself. But you make decisions about my life as if I’m not in it. You’ve decided what I eat, how I get to work, when I sleep, where my things go. My hair clips are in a glass bowl, Hao. I don’t own a glass bowl. You moved in, and I didn’t say yes and I didn’t say no because I was too tired to say anything, and you heard that as yes. And you watch me. All the time. To see if I’ve eaten. If I’m about to fall apart. I know you don’t mean it like this, but sometimes it feels like being monitored.”

“I don’t want you to feel like that.”

“Then stop. I’m your girlfriend, Hao. Not your equipment.”

The words landed in the room between them and didn’t move. Neither did he.

She said it more gently. “I’m not one of your clients. I’m not a crisis you’re managing. I’m not a hotel. I’m not something you can optimise until every risk’s been written on a sheet of paper by the kettle. I can be exhausted and still be capable. I can miss lunch once without anyone building a whole system round me.”

Her voice shook slightly.

“I need to be the one running my life. Most of all now. Because it’s the only thing I’ve got left that’s mine.”

He looked down at his own hands. She could see the instinct rising in him to lay out every reason, the bag and the charger and Mr. Yau and the tea, to show her how much of it had been for her. She didn’t want the list. She wanted him to hear her.

He looked up. “You’re right. I’ve been treating your life like a problem I could organise. I think I’ve been doing it because I don’t know what else to do. I can’t fix the crash. I can’t get you back the eleven seconds. I can’t give the families what they need, or make you stop hearing what you’ve heard in that room. So I’ve been fixing everything round you, because it felt better than sitting here every night knowing I couldn’t do anything at all.”

He gave a small unhappy smile.

“I crossed out a sentence today that somebody wanted to send a hundred and eighty families, and it was the best I’ve felt in a month, because it was something I could do. Then I came here and did it to you. All evening. With a list.”

She looked at him a long time. “Then sit with me. When you can’t do anything, don’t do anything. Sit with me. I want you here because you’re the person I want to come home to. Not because you’ve decided I can’t look after myself.”

“I’ll take my things home. All of it. And we’ll talk properly when this is over, and you’ll decide.”

She thought of the six suits on her rail in the dark, and the coffee machine. “Not tomorrow. I can’t do that tomorrow too. Just stop adding to it. And ask.”

“And if you say no, I’ll listen. Above all when I think I know better.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He was still holding her hand. He looked at the shadows under her eyes gone almost purple, the line between her eyebrows, her hair coming out of its tie. He wanted to pull her into his arms and kiss her and wipe out the last fifteen minutes with the plain warm weight of holding her, the way he’d done after every argument they’d ever had. He stopped.

“What?”

“Can I kiss you?”

She looked almost startled. He’d kissed her at taxi ranks and in car parks, against kitchen counters and office glass, on beaches and in hedges, in the middle of arguments to end them, and once, in July, because she’d walked past him in the kitchen eating a peach. He’d never once asked.

“Why?”

“Because I don’t want to assume anything any more. Not even this.”

The tiredness stayed in her face, but something under it went soft. She put her free hand on his cheek. “Yes.”

He bent his head slowly, giving her the whole time to change her mind. It was barely anything: his mouth on hers, light and still, no persuading, no trying to tell her through it that everything was all right. He drew back an inch and looked at her, and she nodded, and he kissed her again, and this time she came into it. Her fingers slid round to the back of his neck and her mouth opened under his, and he held her waist with both hands and didn’t pull her one centimetre closer than she came on her own. She came all the way. She kissed him slow and deep and a little desperate with her eyes shut and her hand tight in the hair at his nape, the way she hadn’t kissed him in a month, and he let her lead every second of it.

“You looked terrified,” she said against his mouth.

“I was.”

She laughed, a small real laugh, the first in days, and he shut his eyes. He’d missed that sound more than he’d known it was possible to miss anything.

✦ ✦ ✦

She picked up the sheet of paper by the kettle, found a pen, and drew a line through SLEEP — PLEASE!, and then through DRIVER — CONFIRMED (MR. YAU).

He rang Mr. Yau, who was still up, of course, and told him he could have a lie-in, and Mr. Yau said something that made Ren Hao laugh once.

“He says thank goodness. He’s been driving you for a month and you never talk to him and he was running out of radio stations.”

Song-Zhu put her hand over her eyes. “I’ll buy him biscuits. When this is over. Dinner can stay. The tea can stay. The charger can stay, you were right about the charger. Don’t move my bag. And ask me if I’ve eaten once, not every hour.”

“Unless you look like you’re about to faint. That’s a different category.”

She gave him a look. Then she folded the list in half and put it in the drawer, and came and put her arms round his waist. “I know you’re frightened. So am I. But I don’t need you to make my life smaller so nothing else can happen to it.”

They ate at the table. She went back for more soup, and he saw her go back and said nothing, and when she caught him watching her over the bowl he gave up and admitted it. He told her about a consultant of his who’d that morning, under pressure, sent a meeting invitation titled Grief Workshop (Internal) to an entire external client list, and she put her spoon down and laughed with her whole face for the first time in a month, until she had to wipe her eyes.

He watched her do it: not the woman at the second microphone, or the one who’d had to tell a man with a soft folded report that eleven seconds were missing, only Song-Zhu, stealing the best pieces off his plate. He was beginning to understand that loving her didn’t mean deciding what safe looked like. Sometimes it meant leaving the door open, and sitting by it, and waiting.

✦ ✦ ✦

In bed she lay with a novel she’d given up on in July. He came out of the bathroom and stopped. “Do you need anything?”

He heard himself, and held up a hand.

“That was a question. Not a plan.”

He turned out the light and lay facing her, not touching her, until she said, “Closer,” and put her head on his shoulder.

“I’m still a little upset. But I’m not going anywhere. I don’t want you to think every time I tell you something hurts, I’m getting ready to leave.”

He breathed out. “Sometimes I think that.”

“I know you do. You’re allowed to get it wrong.” She kissed his chin, his cheek, the corner of his mouth, and stopped there.

“May I?” he said.

“Yes.”

He kissed her slowly, and when she reached for him he went where she led and not one step further, and it was the gentlest he’d ever been with her, and afterwards she lay with her fingers spread on his heart.

“Tomorrow I might be difficult,” she said, nearly asleep.

“Tomorrow you can be whatever you are. I’ll be here.”

He didn’t set an alarm for her or plan her morning. He lay in the dark with her asleep on him and tried, for the first time in a month, to do nothing at all. The report had answered almost nothing, the families were still waiting, and six of his suits still hung in her wardrobe. He knew it, and knew she knew it, and that it wasn’t over. But he understood something he’d been slow to learn. She was a person who could stand in the middle of the worst thing he’d ever seen and still choose, every night, to come home to him, and he wanted to be someone she could come home to, not someone she had to recover from.

chapters.title: The Break
chapters.desc: She asks for a break until the investigation’s done. He takes his toothbrush and leaves the fridge full. The flat goes very quiet.
chapters.epigraph: “You already did, at the table.”
chapters.content:
The first thing Song-Zhu noticed was that he’d stopped asking whether she’d be home for dinner. The second was that she’d started to dread the sound of his key in her door. Neither of them mentioned either. In eighteen days they’d got good at not mentioning things.

He still kissed her goodbye in the mornings, and asked first, every time, with his eyes if not out loud. He asked before he brought anything new into the flat. He’d moved her hair clips out of the glass bowl back to the shelf where she’d always kept them and put the bowl away in a cupboard. She still sent him photographs of things she thought were funny: a pigeon on a fuel bowser, a sign in the canteen that said PLEASE DO NOT MICROWAVE FISH (THIS MEANS YOU, DEXTER). She still slept beside him, some nights with her back against his chest, some nights on her own side with a space between them that neither of them filled.

They were still together. They were also, a little more every day, becoming strangers in the gaps between their sentences.

The eleven seconds were still eleven seconds. She slept badly and ate when she remembered and had begun to hate the sound of her own phone. And Ren Hao, who’d once been able to make her laugh with a toothbrush in her mouth, had started watching her as if every silence might be the one that meant something. He was trying. She knew how hard. That was what made it impossible.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Saturday the nineteenth of September it was raining. She stood at her kitchen counter reading a message from Director Kwan: two sets of recovered data disagreed with each other by a fraction of a second, and the technical team needed her to look at it before Monday.

“You’re not eating that?” he said from the stove.

She ate two mouthfuls and put the spoon down. She could feel him watching her on the side of her face like heat from a lamp.

“Please don’t. Look at me like you’re waiting for me to fall over.”

“I wasn’t.”

“You were.”

He put the wooden spoon down and came a step closer and didn’t touch her. “Did something happen at work? Is it the sequence? Then tell me.”

Again, the careful voice, the attention turned all the way up, the questions meant to help that made her feel she had to produce a reason for every single thing her face did.

“I don’t know how to talk to you any more,” she said.

He went completely still.

She looked away at once. “That isn’t fair. I know you stopped every single thing I asked you to stop. You ask before you kiss me. You ask before you buy milk.”

Her voice cracked.

“But now I feel guilty every time I don’t answer you properly. When I don’t want dinner. When I come in and don’t want to talk. When you ask if I’m all right and I say no, because I can see what it does to you. You look so frightened, Hao, all the time.”

She pressed both palms flat on the counter.

“I can’t keep looking after your fear and do my job. There isn’t enough of me.”

His face tightened, and she saw it, and hated herself for it. It was still true.

✦ ✦ ✦

They sat at her dining table and the food went cold between them.

“I think I need a break,” she said.

He looked at her like he hadn’t heard the words in the right order. “From work?”

“From us.”

The silence was so complete she could hear the rain on the balcony railing, one drop at a time.

“Do you want to stop seeing me?”

She went on before she lost her nerve. “No. I want you to go home. To your own flat. Until the investigation’s done. Until I can think about something other than the aircraft and the recorders and the families and the eleven seconds. Until I can come in through that door without carrying the whole thing in with me and you watching me while I put it down.”

“Until the final report?”

It could be a year. More. She knew what she was asking. “I don’t know, Hao.”

“All right,” he said.

She blinked. She’d made herself ready for an argument: what he’d done, what he could change, what he could arrange instead, a list, a plan, a better plan. He sat there.

“You don’t have to say yes straight away.”

“Would you rather I argued?”

She pressed her lips together. “I don’t want you to think this means I don’t love you.”

The word went across the table between them. She’d never said it before, not once, not to him, not in a sentence, not even sideways. She heard it leave her mouth and couldn’t take it back and didn’t want to, and it was the wrong moment, the worst moment, and she’d said it anyway, inside a don’t, folded small, where it would hurt least.

He looked at her. “Does it?”

“No.”

“Then I believe you. How much room? No contact?”

“I don’t know that either.”

“Then we don’t have to decide all of it tonight,” said Ren Hao.

Even now, she thought. Even now he was giving her room.

✦ ✦ ✦

She heard the wardrobe door, a drawer, his overnight bag lifted down from the top of the wardrobe where it had lived since August. She’d thought about saying it, and how to get it out, and the room she’d have afterwards to breathe in. She hadn’t thought about the practical part: his toothbrush, his shirts, his slippers, the charger on his side.

She went to the bedroom door. He was taking a few things out of her wardrobe, two shirts, trousers, the grey jumper, and folding every one before it went in the bag, precisely, corners to corners. He left the six suits hanging on her rail.

“You don’t have to pack tonight.”

“I should take what I’ll need.”

He went past her without touching her into the bathroom, and took his toothbrush out of the cup on the basin. It was blue. Hers was white. They’d bought them together in a supermarket in March, the week she’d given him the key on the ring with the little plastic aeroplane, and she’d laughed in the aisle at how seriously he considered the colours. He put it in a washbag and zipped the washbag shut.

Something in her chest pulled hard, like a seat belt locking.

It was such a small thing. It mattered more than anything else he’d packed. He wasn’t going on a business trip. He wasn’t coming back tomorrow to complain she’d stolen his pillow. He was going because she’d asked him to, and doing it properly, and taking his toothbrush because that was what leaving was.

✦ ✦ ✦

He stopped by the kitchen with the bag. “There’s food in the fridge. Enough for the week. It’s labelled. The soup’s on the second shelf, the greens are separate so they won’t go soft—”

“Hao.”

“Sorry.” He opened the fridge anyway, because he couldn’t help it.

The shelves were full. Not like somebody stocking up for a typhoon: like somebody who’d spent the whole afternoon, while she was at work, making sure the person he loved would have something to eat on every evening he wasn’t there. Soup, rice, fish in a marinade, greens, the yoghurt she liked, her milk. And in a paper bag on the bottom shelf, a dozen of the little mandarins she ate one after another without thinking, the way other people ate crisps. He’d cooked all of it knowing. Not for certain. But knowing.

He shut the door and gave a small helpless smile. “I’m still doing it.”

“Thank you for the food,” she said.

✦ ✦ ✦

His shoes were on and his bag was by the door. She stood a few steps away in her hallway, beside the hooks where once in June he’d kissed her against the wall until she couldn’t stand. Neither of them knew what to do with their hands.

“Do you want me to ring you?”

“Not tonight.”

He put his hand on the latch, and stopped. “I love you. I’m not saying it so you’ll feel guilty. I’m saying it so you don’t think agreeing to this means I’ve stopped.”

She opened her mouth. He saw her try. He saw the word come up into her throat and stop there, the way it had stopped for fifteen months, on a kitchen floor and on a beach and in a doorway. He saw her fight it, and lose.

“You don’t have to. You already did, at the table. Inside a don’t. I heard it,” he said gently.

Her eyes filled all the way up. He looked like he might come back the two steps across the hall, and didn’t. He opened the door.

“Hao.”

Don’t go. Please go. I’m sorry. I need you. All four were in her at once, all true, pulling in different directions like the lines in the data, and none of them would come out.

“Take care,” she said.

His face went soft. “You too.”

He closed the door behind him so carefully she didn’t hear the latch.

✦ ✦ ✦

The flat was quiet. Not peaceful: quiet. She listened to his footsteps down the corridor, the lift, the doors, and then nothing. His slippers were by the shoe cabinet. He’d forgotten them. She picked them up and thought about putting them in the cupboard, and put them back where they’d been, beside hers, toes together.

His pillow still had the shape of him. His charger was still plugged into the wall on his side, the lead coiled on the floor. Kwan’s message lit her phone again, and she put the phone in the drawer and shut it. For the first time in seven weeks nobody was waiting for her to answer anything. She had all the quiet she’d asked for, and hated it.

She opened the fridge again. The labels were in his capitals on strips of masking tape.

SOUP — MON.
RICE — TUES.
FISH — COOK BY THURS!

His black work notebook was on the coffee table, meeting notes and actions in his neat capitals, and on the last page a shopping list: MILK. EGGS. MANDARINS. GINGER. HER TEA. SOUP THINGS. HER TEA (THE OTHER ONE). She put it back exactly where it had been, at exactly the same angle.

She typed Are you home? and looked at it, and deleted it.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Sunday she woke before the alarm and reached across the bed and found the cold empty side of it. The space in the cup where the blue toothbrush had been was much bigger than a toothbrush. She’d asked him to go, and he’d gone. Nobody had done anything wrong. He’d done exactly what she’d asked, exactly the way she’d asked it. She washed her face in cold water and went to work.

On Monday she heated SOUP — MON. It tasted of ginger and too much care, and she ate half and stopped. She wondered if he was eating. She wondered if the blue toothbrush was still in the washbag at the bottom of his wardrobe because unpacking it would make it true. The last message in their conversation was his, from Saturday afternoon, before any of it.

Ren Hao: There’s a new box of your tea behind the old one. So you don’t run out.

On Wednesday she dreamed about the sea. Not the wreckage or the grey blankets or the boats: only the sea, a long dark stretch of water under a low sky, moving, with nothing on it at all. She woke with her heart going so hard she couldn’t breathe and reached for her phone, and didn’t know what she wanted. A photograph. A round dog. No reply needed. For the first time since he’d gone, she cried, a few tears sideways into the pillow, because she’d understood that the quiet wasn’t going to end by itself. It was what she’d asked for, and he was the one person in the world she knew would give her exactly what she asked for, for as long as she asked.

✦ ✦ ✦

A week to the hour after he’d gone, Ren Hao was in his own flat on the other side of the harbour.

He’d made himself unpack on the Sunday: the shirts in his wardrobe, where they now looked like they were staying in a hotel; the running shoes by the door; the blue toothbrush in a glass by his own basin, where it looked like nothing at all. He went to work, and to the hotel on the airport road every day, and sat with the man from Room 214 while his mother told a long story in a language Ren Hao didn’t speak, nodding where the interpreter said to.

He hadn’t rung her. He’d nearly rung on Sunday, when a client sent him a video of a dog falling into a swimming pool with enormous dignity. He’d nearly rung on Tuesday when his car went past the French restaurant with the candles, and on Thursday at three in the morning when he reached across the bed and found the cold enormous side of his own mattress and lay there an hour with the phone on his chest. He didn’t ring Mabel or Dexter to ask how she was. He didn’t ring Mr. Yau to ask whether she’d taken a taxi on Wednesday. He didn’t ring Isla in Lima, who’d have known from his voice in four seconds. He didn’t want to turn her asking for distance into one more problem he could find a way round.

He sat on his own sofa with nothing in his hands and listened to his own fridge hum, and found it hummed in a different note from hers.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the seventh night she opened her fridge and it wasn’t full any more. Half a carton of milk. Two eggs. A small box of rice marked THURS that she’d have to throw away and wouldn’t. And in the paper bag on the bottom shelf, the last mandarin.

She peeled it at the counter in one long spiral, the way her father had taught her at six. She’d wanted quiet. She’d wanted to hear her own thoughts and stop being watched. She’d got every single thing she’d asked for, and the flat had gone so quiet she could hear her fridge humming in E flat.

She ate it slowly, one segment at a time, until there was nothing in her hand but the peel. Outside it started to rain again. She understood, looking at the empty chair across the table, that asking somebody to leave wasn’t the same as wanting them gone, and that he’d listened, the way he always listened, all the way to the end.

Now she’d have to work out what she wanted when she wasn’t asking out of exhaustion. She didn’t know yet. She went into the bedroom and opened the wardrobe and stood in the dark looking at six suits on her rail that nobody had come back for.

chapters.title: The Missing Eleven Seconds
chapters.desc: A cabin crew member’s phone from the seabed: the lights go out, the brace call, and the captain on the PA with his last words about his daughter. Alone in the laboratory, she finally cries.
chapters.epigraph: “Nobody calls these his last words.”
chapters.content:
On Friday the ninth of October, just after eight, a message came from the evidence laboratory. One sentence.

A personal device recovered in the latest seabed search has completed initial assessment; your presence is requested for review.

Sixty-eight days. Nine weeks of comparing every source against every other and refusing, over and over, to let anyone turn an absence of data into an explanation. Now there was something else. Not a recorder. A phone.

✦ ✦ ✦

It didn’t look like a phone any more. It lay in a clear sealed box on the bench under the lights, its case bent into a shallow curve by forty metres of water, the screen crazed into a hundred pieces, white salt crusted along every seam, part of the back lifted from the frame like a fingernail.

Device: personal mobile telephone.
Recovered: seabed sector 14, rear cabin debris field.
Found in: cabin crew uniform, inside jacket pocket.

He moved to the workstation. “One of the cabin crew. Au-Yeung Hiu-lam. Twenty-nine. Aft crew. Confirmed through the uniform and the identity card in the same pocket. Her family’s been told a device was recovered. Nothing about what’s on it. Photographed where it was found, brought up in seawater, never powered, dried under control. Full forensic image of everything that can be read. The original’s sealed. We found a video. Recorded during the flight. Three minutes and nine seconds of picture, then some sound after the picture stops. Two things before you watch. The phone’s clock isn’t the aircraft’s clock, so whatever time it says is the phone’s opinion, not a fact. And it’s the cabin. It doesn’t show you a single instrument,” said Mr. Seto, a precise grey man who’d been at the laboratory since before it had a name.

He opened the file.

✦ ✦ ✦

Black for two seconds. Then a tilted picture: the ceiling of the aft galley, a curve of grey plastic and a strip of dimmed light.

A woman’s voice, low, laughing. “Say it again. Say it for the camera.”

Two cabin crew on the rear jumpseats, strapped in for landing in their harnesses. The one on the left held a paper cup she should have handed in twenty minutes ago, tired and amused and pretending to be offended. “I said if the captain wants a better coffee he can come back here and make it himself.”

Song-Zhu had heard the captain ask for that coffee forty-one times, on the voice recording, twenty minutes before the end. Is there any chance of a coffee that isn’t burnt? The first officer had laughed and said he’d ask the back. The back had answered.

She forgot, watching it, what she was watching. There was a life in it: two women at work at four in the morning at the end of a long night, making a joke for somebody’s sister. A voice behind the camera saying it’s for Mei-mei, she says we never do anything fun. Rows of sleeping heads through the gap in the curtain, a reading light on halfway down.

Then a sound: a deep short thump through the phone’s tiny microphone, more felt than heard, from somewhere under the floor. The cup jumped in the woman’s hand. Song-Zhu knew that sound. It was the sound in the airframe she couldn’t name, on the voice recording, in the last second before it stopped.

“What was that?”

And the lights went out. The galley strip, the cabin lights beyond the curtain, the reading light halfway down, all at once. The screen was nearly black. A second later, small and low, the emergency lighting came on along the floor of the aisle in a line of dull points, like a landing strip at night.

“Stop. Go back five seconds.”

The thump. The cup. What was that. The lights.

“The cabin lights. Every one. At once. And the floor lighting a second after.”

“About a second. On the phone’s count.”

Everyone in the room had read the installation diagram for this type. Everyone knew which electrical supply the cabin lighting was on, which supply fed the two recorders, and which one the emergency floor lighting ran from instead. She wrote one line, small, and boxed it.

Cabin lights + recorders: same moment? CORRELATE. DO NOT SAY IT YET.

“Go on.”

The picture swung in the dark. A child began to cry. The woman with the phone said fast, we’ll be told, we’ll be told, and the other said put that away, Hiu-lam, and didn’t put down her own cup, like she’d forgotten she had it.

A chime. The PA. A man’s voice through the cabin speakers, the captain, calm, with something under it like a wire pulled tight. “Cabin crew, this is the captain. Brace, brace, brace.”

Both crew shouted it at once, the words they’d been trained to shout a thousand times and never once had to. Brace! Brace! Heads down! Stay down! The camera fell, pointing at the floor, at the dull line of emergency lights and the woman’s black shoes braced against it. The picture broke into blocks of grey and green, and froze, and stopped.

“That’s the end of the picture. But some audio packets survived further on in the file. Twenty-two seconds, with holes,” said Mr. Seto.

Noise first: an enormous rushing roar that wasn’t any one thing. Inside it the cabin. The crew still shouting, hoarse now, heads down, stay down. The child crying. Somebody praying in a language Song-Zhu didn’t speak. Something striking the floor again and again.

The PA chime again. The captain. “Brace. Brace. Stay down.” A breath, much closer to the microphone than before. And then, low, under the roar, a sentence that wasn’t an announcement at all, as if he’d forgotten his thumb was still on the button. Or remembered, and not taken it off.

“Tell my little girl...”

The rest went under a long rasp of distortion.

“Again,” said Song-Zhu.

Tell my little girl...

“There’s more. In the packets after. Damaged. I can try to separate it. I won’t make it clearer than the data is,” said Mr. Seto.

“I’m not asking you to. Get the audio specialist.”

✦ ✦ ✦

They went through it the proper way, with the audio specialist in the third chair and every step written down as they took it: the raw packets, then the PA channel separated as far as it would separate, then the processed version, with every filter explained, what had been taken out and what left alone.

The sentence came up out of the noise a piece at a time. A few words. A breath. A gap where the data wasn’t. Then his voice again, close, tired, gentle, the voice she’d heard asking for a coffee that wasn’t burnt.

“Tell my little girl...”

The specialist moved a slider by a millimetre.

“...Daddy tried.”

Then the roar, and the end of the file.

The specialist took his hand off the controls and put it in his lap. “That’s the best we’ll get from what’s there. The processed audio is consistent with that reading. I’ve heard it fifty times this morning and I hear the same thing each time. But the segment’s damaged. The processing gets documented and the original kept, and nobody calls what I’ve made a clean recording. It isn’t one.”

She wrote in the plainest words she had.

Recovered cabin audio contains speech over the PA, attributed to the captain. Processed audio consistent with: “Tell my little girl . . . Daddy tried.” Reading subject to further verification. Original preserved.

And underneath: Timing relative to end of recorders NOT YET ESTABLISHED.

“Do we know this is the last thing he said?”

“No. We know it’s the last thing that can be heard on this phone. We don’t know what he said on the flight deck after. We may never know. Nobody calls these his last words. Not in this room, not in a report. Not until we can prove there was nothing after.”

Her handwriting was perfectly neat and her face perfectly still. She’d spent her working life learning that an investigator couldn’t mix up what she felt with what the evidence showed. She knew exactly where the line ran. She couldn’t stop hearing it.

When she signed the review record Mr. Seto asked whether she was all right, and she said yes, and he didn’t believe her and didn’t push. In the corridor she looked down at the sentence in her own writing. It looked so much smaller than it had sounded.

✦ ✦ ✦

She answered the technical lead, and then Kwan: a short summary, and a request in plain words that no interpretation of anything on the recording go one inch beyond the authorised team until it had been documented and correlated. Then the family liaison officer, who wanted to know whether anything on the device could be shared with Au-Yeung Hiu-lam’s family.

She thought of a voice behind a camera saying it’s for Mei-mei, and a younger sister somewhere in the city who’d been waiting since August for a clip of two tired women and a paper cup.

The device contains recoverable personal material. Some of it may be returned to the family once it has been examined and separated from material relevant to the investigation. Please let them know, gently, that there is a short recording Ms. Au-Yeung made for her sister during the flight, and that when we can, we will make sure her sister receives the part of it that was meant for her.

At lunchtime Dexter put his head round her door. “It’s Friday. It’s the fish. You like the fish. Eat something, boss.”

She opened the container she’d brought from home, rice and an egg and greens she’d made herself at eleven the night before, standing up in her own kitchen the way he’d shown her in August, and the smell made her feel sick, and she closed it.

Outside the city carried on exactly as it did. Somewhere a little girl was waiting for her father to come home. Song-Zhu had the crew file. She could have found the girl’s name, her age, her school, whether he’d promised to bring her anything back. She didn’t look. She had no right to know any of it yet, and no right at all to invent it.

✦ ✦ ✦

By the afternoon she had the first correlations. The airframe sound on the phone and the airframe sound on the voice recorder were the same event; the specialist was certain, and could show why. On the voice recorder the sound came nine-tenths of a second before both recorders stopped. On the phone the cabin lights went out a little under a second after it. Within the margin of the phone’s clock, the cabin lights and the two recorders had gone at the same moment.

So for the eleven seconds after that moment she had something nobody had had for sixty-eight days. Not the flight deck, not one instrument. The inside of the aircraft: the dark, the floor lights, the crew shouting the brace, and the captain on the PA, which ran from a different supply, still talking, still doing his job, all the way down.

It didn’t give a cause. It didn’t say what had made the sound under the floor or why the power had gone. But for the first time the eleven seconds weren’t empty.

She wrote the next steps: the electrical supplies, the wiring in the area under the floor, every component from that area that had been brought up and every one that hadn’t, the maintenance history of each part back to the last heavy check, and who had signed for it.

Director Kwan (Red Pen): I’ve seen your summary. Take what time you need with it this weekend. Well done.

✦ ✦ ✦

By evening the building had mostly emptied. Mr. Seto gave her the sealed envelope with the review record and took his coat from the hook, and stopped at the door with it over his arm.

“I’ve watched you hear a great deal in this job for four years. You don’t have to take every sentence home.”

“I know,” she said, when she could.

The door sighed shut behind him on its closer, and she was alone in the laboratory.

She should have gone home. The evidence was preserved and the findings written down, every one, in the right words. She sat down instead in the specialist’s chair in front of the dark workstation, with the sealed box on the bench beside her and the crumpled phone in it under the lights, and opened her notebook to a clean page.

The captain’s last words were

She crossed it out. That wasn’t what the evidence showed. She’d told a room full of people that morning that she knew better.

The last identifiable speech on the recovered device

Her hand had started to shake. She put the pen down.

Daddy tried.

Something in her face went. She pressed her lips together and tried to breathe through it the way she’d breathed through sixty-eight days, through the helicopter footage and the grey blankets and the little boy on the bed and Mrs. Ting’s blue exercise book. It had always worked. It didn’t work.

The first sound that came out of her was so small she hardly knew it was hers. She bent forward over the bench with her hand pressed over her mouth, and her shoulders started to shake, and she couldn’t make them stop.

She wasn’t crying because she’d found the cause. She hadn’t. She was crying because after nine weeks of listening to silence she’d heard a father talk about his daughter: a man with a hundred and seventy-nine people behind him in the dark, still on the PA, still saying brace, doing everything he’d been trained to do with eleven seconds and no power and the sea coming up, and at the very end of it still somebody’s father, who’d known at four hundred feet he wasn’t going to get there, and had tried anyway, and wanted her told that he had.

And under that, much further down, a nineteen-year-old in a room in another country listening to fifty seconds of her own father’s voice on a laptop, as hard as she’d ever listened to anything, for her name, and not hearing it. He hadn’t said her name. He’d been flying an aeroplane. But maybe he’d thought it.

She cried until her throat hurt, with her face on her arm on the laboratory bench under the bright lights, for the captain and the little girl and Au-Yeung Hiu-lam’s sister who’d been promised something fun, and a hundred and eighty people, and her father, and herself, because there was nobody in the building to see her. No family waiting, no Kwan needing her composed at a lectern, no Ren Hao in a doorway trying not to ask whether she’d eaten. Only the bench and the box and the sentence.

✦ ✦ ✦

When she lifted her head the lights had gone to their night setting, half-dim. She wiped her face with a paper towel from the dispenser by the sink, and her breath kept catching.

She opened his name. Their last messages were exactly as they’d been. There’s a new box of your tea behind the old one. She wanted to ring him, not so he’d fix anything, only to hear his voice and tell him she’d cried at last, after sixty-eight days, on her own on a bench, and that it had been the first honest thing her body had done since August.

She’d asked him for room. He’d given her every inch.

I heard something today, she typed, and deleted it. There was a father on that plane, and deleted that too. She couldn’t put it in a message. She didn’t know yet whether she could put it into words at all.

Outside the rain had stopped. She stood under the canopy over the entrance and breathed the wet air. At home the flat would be quiet, the cup on the basin would still hold one toothbrush, and six suits would still hang on her rail. Tomorrow she’d go back in, Saturday or not, and chase the electrical supplies and the parts under that floor and every signature on every one of them.

Tonight she’d heard a father try to say goodbye to his little girl, and for the first time since the second of August she’d let herself cry about it. Not as the person in charge. As a woman who’d heard a father miss his child, and wished for one terrible minute in an empty laboratory that she could give him back eleven seconds, or eleven more, and who had heard, at last, what was in them.

chapters.title: The Report
chapters.desc: The interim statement names a maintenance failure. The airline’s owner asks Ren Hao to ring her; he refuses and reports it. His client turns on her in the press. Two days earlier he paid for Wei Long’s seat to Lima.
chapters.epigraph: “Then don’t help it happen by pretending the finding isn’t there.”
chapters.content:
Before seven on Monday the nineteenth of October a message came in from the man who owned the airline.

We need to speak before the statement is released. Ring me. Now.

Ren Hao had been awake since four in his own kitchen on the wrong side of the harbour, with a cold coffee. Everyone knew the authority would publish an interim statement that morning, ten weeks after the accident. He didn’t know what was in it. He’d made sure he didn’t. The operator would have had the draft over the weekend, in confidence, to check for factual errors, and it would be on Raymond’s desk and Kong’s and on three desks on the twenty-ninth floor. It wasn’t on his. He’d built the wall himself on the second of August and tightened it on the twenty-fifth, and hadn’t put a finger through it once.

He rang.

“I’ll tell you what it says, since you won’t look.”

The voice had lost every ounce of its usual ease.

“It says maintenance failure. It says a part fitted at our last heavy check wasn’t what the paperwork said it was, and that’s why the power went, and why the recorders stopped. It’ll be on every screen in the city by ten, Ren, with our name in the same sentence.”

Ren Hao hadn’t known. Now he did. He wrote down the time, and owner told me content of draft, unsolicited, on the pad by the kettle.

“It’s an interim statement. It’s what they’ve established so far.”

“Don’t give me vocabulary. Ring her. Ask her to hold it. Twenty-four hours. Ask her to look at the wording again.”

“No. I won’t ring her about the investigation, this morning or ever. I’m not going to use a person to lean on an independent report. And before nine I’m going to tell Kong and Raymond and the authority that you asked me to. That’s what the letter you signed in August says I do if anyone approaches me. Including you. Above all you.”

“Then what am I paying you for?”

“For the families. That’s all I’m on your account for. Raymond’s on it for the rest, and he’ll tell you what he told you on Saturday: acknowledge it. Don’t dispute what you can’t disprove. Look after the families first.”

“And if we’re destroyed before the final report?”

“Then don’t help it happen by pretending the finding isn’t there.”

“I hope you understand what this does to our relationship,” said the owner, precisely.

“I do,” said Ren Hao.

At eleven minutes past seven he sent a full note of the call, timed and as nearly word for word as he could make it, to Kong, Raymond, his head of compliance and, under the letter of the twenty-fifth of August, Director Kwan. Reported as required: an approach this morning from the client asking me to contact the investigator-in-charge. Declined. Full note below. Then he poured the cold coffee down the sink and stood under the shower a long time, and thought about Saturday.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Thursday afternoon, Lima time, the ground had moved under the city where his sister worked, and a city had come down. He’d found out a little after five on Friday morning, and for a day and a night nobody could tell him whether Isla was alive. At twenty past six that Friday, with the first pictures from Lima on every screen, there’d been one message from a number he hadn’t heard from in four weeks.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Isla?

Ren Hao: Nothing yet.

Early on Saturday morning Isla had rung Wei Long from a satellite phone in the embassy’s shelter, two minutes and eleven seconds, alive, and not coming home, because she was the consulate and the consulate was needed. He’d sent one line.

Ren Hao: She’s alive. She rang Wei Long.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Thank God. Tell her I said so.

That was all. It was the most they’d said to each other since September.

He’d been awake since five on Saturday, on the phone to two people at the ministry, one airline, and a man in a call centre who seemed to think the operating status of an airport was a state secret. And Wei Long was going to Lima, of course he was going, and at a quarter past one on Saturday afternoon had booked nothing at all. Ren Hao rang him and drove over in twenty-three minutes with a laptop and a coffee, and found the dining table covered in travel advisories and itineraries in small square handwriting with every connection time underlined. Three routes compared. Not one booked.

There’d been one seat. Business class, five to midnight that night, through the Pacific hub, into Lima at half past twelve the next afternoon, their time.

“It’s business class. I can go economy,” Wei Long had said.

“Then go economy next time. I’m paying.”

“I can pay for my own ticket.”

“I know you can. I’m paying.”

Wei Long had caught his wrist over the laptop keys, and neither of them said anything.

“Let me do this. Please. I need to fix something. Let it be this,” Ren Hao had said, and heard his voice go quiet in a way it never went.

Afterwards, with the booking reference on the screen and his own phone lighting up twice beside his coffee with the owner’s name, both times turned over on the table, he’d told Wei Long. He hadn’t meant to. He’d told nobody, not Isla, who was in a shelter in an earthquake and didn’t need it, not his parents. Song-Zhu and I are on a break. Since the nineteenth of September. He’d told him about the crash and the organising. She told me she was my girlfriend and not my equipment. She was right.

It sounds familiar, Wei Long had said, and Ren Hao had laughed, once, for the first time in a month.

✦ ✦ ✦

Song-Zhu was in the main conference room at the authority when the statement went out. She knew every word of it, and knew even better what it didn’t say.

It said the aircraft’s normal electrical power had been lost approximately eleven seconds before impact, and that this was why both recorders had stopped at the same instant. It said that a component of the electrical distribution system, recovered from beneath the cabin floor, had been fitted at the aircraft’s last heavy maintenance check eleven months before, that the component recovered didn’t match the record of its installation, and that it showed signs of previous service the record didn’t mention. It called that a significant finding concerning the maintenance of the aircraft, and said the investigation was continuing into the component, how it came to be fitted, and the organisation that fitted it.

It didn’t say every factor had been established. It said nothing about the voice recording beyond the fact that it existed. It didn’t mention a cabin crew member’s phone, or a paper cup, or two words at the end of a long roar. But it was the first time anyone with the authority to say so had named a failure, and she knew the word failure would travel faster and further than every careful clause round it.

Kwan spoke to the room. “This isn’t the final report. We aren’t blaming any individual. Will the airline dispute it? Almost certainly. Then they can show us through the formal process.”

Song-Zhu looked round the table. “And the cabin recording stays in the evidence inventory and nowhere else. There’s a woman’s sister who’s going to get a clip of a paper cup, and a little girl who’ll be told something by somebody kinder than a newsreader, and neither of those is going in a headline. Not while I’m in charge of it.”

The headlines came within the half hour.

CRASH INQUIRY FINDS MAINTENANCE FAILURE

180 DEAD: AIRLINE’S MAINTENANCE IN THE DOCK

She didn’t open any of them. She put her phone in her desk drawer and closed it.

Kwan appeared in her doorway. “The airline’s holding a press conference at eleven. Don’t sit through every accusation they make on the way. And I thought you ought to know before you see whatever you’ll see today: Mr. Ren reported at eleven minutes past seven, in writing. The owner rang him before seven and asked him to ring you and ask you to hold the statement. He refused. He sent me the whole call, word for word, before I’d had my breakfast.”

She sat at her desk a long time looking at the closed drawer.

✦ ✦ ✦

At the hotel on the airport road somebody turned the lobby television to the news channel before eleven, and turned it up. By the time the press conference began nobody in the lobby was doing anything else. Forty people, most of them families, stood where they were and turned to the screen. Mrs. Ting was by the window with her blue exercise book. The man with the fruit was in a chair by the door.

On screen the airline’s chief executive stood at a lectern with two directors, and at the back of the stage, half in shadow, not speaking, the owner.

The first paragraph was about safety, and it was good; Raymond’s team had written it, and Ren Hao recognised the rhythm. Then the chief executive turned a page Raymond’s team hadn’t written.

“While we respect the work of the investigating authority, we believe the public should be cautious about accepting conclusions before the full investigation is complete. We are confident our maintenance programme followed every established procedure.”

A journalist near the front asked the question Ren Hao would have spent three days making sure nobody on that stage answered. “Do you believe the investigators have been influenced by pressure from the victims’ families?”
