The chief executive frowned. “We believe any investigation must remain independent of public emotion.”

By the window Mrs. Ting closed her blue book and stood up. She didn’t say anything. She walked across the lobby, past the television and past Ren Hao, and out through the glass doors.

A woman by the lifts said, clearly, to nobody, “Public emotion.”

Ten weeks of interpreters and hotels and belongings, one named person for every family, every phone call returned, ten weeks of making that building somewhere people could bear to be, and the chief executive had taken it apart in nine words.

“Turn it off,” said Ren Hao.

He found Mrs. Ting by the low brick wall at the back, by the bins, where Song-Zhu had sat in August, holding the exercise book against her chest with both arms.

“Don’t. You work for them.”

“I work for you, in there. That’s all I’ve done for ten weeks. I didn’t write that, and I’m sorry anybody said it in a room you were standing in.”

“Is it true? What the investigators said this morning?”

“I don’t know what’s in the investigation. I’ve made sure I don’t. But I know who’s leading it. And she has never once in her life said a thing she couldn’t prove.”

Mrs. Ting looked down at the book. “No. She hasn’t.”

The owner rang before the press conference had finished. Ren Hao answered by the bins.

“That wasn’t what Raymond advised. You’ve told forty families in my hotel their grief is contaminating the evidence. One of them walked out. I’m standing next to her bin.”

“You’re protecting her. Your girlfriend. Perhaps you should have thought of that before you took our money.”

A plane went over low on the approach, and the noise filled everything and went.

“Everything was declared, in writing, on the morning of the crash. You signed it. Don’t use my relationship with her to discredit that report.”

The owner hung up. Ren Hao wrote down the time, and went back in to find forty people who needed lunch.

✦ ✦ ✦

Raymond sent it to him just after twelve: a website first, two of the papers by the evening editions.

CRASH INVESTIGATOR IN RELATIONSHIP WITH AIRLINE’S CRISIS CONSULTANT

There was no evidence in it that she’d ever shared anything with him or that he’d influenced anything. It rested on two facts: that they’d been together, and that his firm worked for the airline. There was a photograph of the two of them at the taxi rank outside the French restaurant, kissing, that somebody on that pavement had taken on a phone in June 2025 and kept. And three paragraphs down, a line he read four times. A person close to the airline said the relationship “raised obvious questions about the timing and tone of this morning’s statement.”

“Don’t deny it. It’s true,” he told Raymond.

He heard himself say we’re together and didn’t correct it, though she’d asked him to leave a month ago to the day.

“Say the relationship was declared in full on the morning of the accident and walled off on both sides from the first hour, and the record’s been with the authority since the second of August. Say I’ve had no part in anything but family support. Don’t let anyone imply she’s ever had one word of our client work through me, because she hasn’t. And nobody from this firm contacts her. Not today.”

Song-Zhu saw it in the afternoon media review. The taxi rank, her fist in his waistcoat, fuel on her boots, sixteen months ago. Her first feeling wasn’t anger. It was a tiredness so deep it felt like falling. She opened the declaration she’d written on the second of August with Mabel beside her, checked every date, and saved copies in three places. She wasn’t going to let a website make her careless.

A number she didn’t know: How much did your boyfriend tell you before you wrote it? She took a screenshot, forwarded it to the building’s security contact, and didn’t reply.

Kwan had the article printed out on his desk. “Has anything changed since the declaration?”

“We’ve been on a break since the nineteenth of September. That’s all.”

“That isn’t a change in the conflict. That’s a change in your life. Have you discussed the investigation with him?”

“Not one word since the morning it happened. He wouldn’t let me. In August at three in the morning I offered him my draft to check for typos, and he wouldn’t look at the screen. He sat on the other side of the table for forty minutes with a book. I forgot whose aircraft it was. He didn’t.”

Kwan nodded, and let her go.

✦ ✦ ✦

At a quarter to five Kong brought up a letter from the airline’s lawyers. It asked the firm to distance itself publicly from the interim finding, to say its earlier advice had been based on incomplete information, and, in the last paragraph, whether the managing director’s personal circumstances were consistent with the firm’s continued role.

“No. To all of it. We won’t say anything that suggests the finding is wrong. We don’t know if it’s wrong. Neither do they.”

“Prepare the withdrawal assessment. Every engagement in the group, what it costs us and who it costs. On my desk on Wednesday. Until then the families still get their lunch.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At home Song-Zhu put her bag down by the sofa, where she’d always put it, and heated greens and a box of rice she’d cooked herself on Saturday and labelled in her own small writing, SAT. She knew he’d seen the photograph. She knew his client had called her finding premature in front of the families. She knew he’d reported the owner’s call before seven. She wondered if he was angry, and stopped herself; she had no right to ask him to look after her feelings about something she hadn’t decided how to talk to him about.

He was still in his office, with a page in his capitals headed WHAT IT COSTS. On Sunday afternoon a message had come in from the Pacific hub, and at twenty to two that morning another from Lima.

Wei Long (Inspector, Brief): Landed. Going to her now.

And before half past eight this evening:

Wei Long (Inspector, Brief): She’s eaten. Finally. She says to tell you she doesn’t need you to send another plane.

Ren Hao smiled for the first time all day.

Ren Hao: I wasn’t planning to.

Wei Long (Inspector, Brief): She says you were. She says you have a very readable mind. Thank you for the ticket. I mean it.

He was glad that Wei Long was there and Isla was eating, and that somewhere in the world two people who loved each other weren’t separated by anything any more. He opened Song-Zhu’s name. I saw the article. I’m sorry they’ve dragged you into it. It sounded like an apology for something he’d done. My client’s statement wasn’t what my firm advised. Too much of the thing she’d asked him not to bring home. I hope you’re all right. He deleted that too. She’d asked for room. He’d promised himself in a doorway with his bag in his hand that he’d never turn her silence into something he could manage.

Late that night she sat up in bed with the interim statement on her tablet. She’d signed it because it was what the evidence supported. Not because of who his client was, or in spite of it. Because a part under a floor hadn’t been what the paperwork said it was, and the power had gone, and two recorders had stopped listening, and a man had gone on talking to his passengers in the dark until the end.

She wouldn’t take back one word because a company didn’t like what it showed. She wouldn’t soften the truth to protect a man she loved.

She heard herself think it. A man she loved. In the dark, on her own, it came out whole.

chapters.title: He Chooses Her Report
chapters.desc: He drops the airline, his biggest client, and doesn’t tell her. Ruby rings her from the coat room. She kisses him by the reception desk.
chapters.epigraph: “The coat room isn’t technically the building, Mr. Ren.”
chapters.content:
At eight on Thursday the twenty-second of October Ren Hao asked Kong to shut the door.

There were three documents on the table between them: the five-year-old agreement with the airline’s holding group, forty pages with his signature on the last; the letter asking his firm to distance itself in public from the interim finding; and a termination notice, two pages, already drafted, waiting for a date.

“Before we do this, I need to be sure you understand what it costs. They’re our biggest client. The whole crisis-response division was built round them. Fourteen people on the account. Two other engagements under the same group,” said Kong.

He named the figure.

“And the board will ask why now, straight after a public fight. It’ll look like temper. I have to ask, because someone else will. Is this about Song-Zhu?”

He put one finger on the letter. “No. It’s about the client. We told them to acknowledge the finding. We told them not to question the independence of the investigation, and not to say anything that suggested the families had tainted the evidence. They ignored every word of it in front of forty families in a hotel lobby, and then wrote to ask us to stand up and say we’d been wrong to tell them. We can’t. And then they put a photograph of me at a taxi rank in a newspaper so everybody would talk about that instead of a part under a floor. I won’t sign a statement that says an investigation is unreliable because a client doesn’t like what it found.”

Kong was quiet. “Then it’s straightforward.”

“It should have been straightforward on Monday,” said Ren Hao, and dated the notice.

✦ ✦ ✦

The owner came himself, with two of his directors, which Ren Hao had expected. They met in the big conference room on the thirty-second floor, where Ren Hao had sat at the head of the table six months ago at three in the morning and listened to Eliana Lin tell him about Gideon. He sat at the side of it now and let the owner have the end.

The owner didn’t sit. “You’re walking away. After five years.”

“After Monday. We advised you to respond responsibly to the finding. You chose not to. Then you asked us to say in public that our advice had been mistaken. It wasn’t. We won’t,” said Ren Hao.

“You’ve had my crisis plans for ten weeks. I have a right to challenge a finding.”

“Through the proper process, with evidence. Not by telling the families in that hotel that their grief is contaminating the investigation.”

“You’re doing this for her.”

“Her work has nothing to do with mine. That’s been on paper since five o’clock on the morning of the second of August, with your signature under it.”

One of the directors was looking at the table. The other looked at the window with the face of a man who’d advised exactly what Ren Hao had advised, and been overruled, and not been permitted to say so.

“A component in your aircraft didn’t match the paperwork that came with it. If the finding’s wrong, you have a process. What you can’t do, with my firm’s help, is put the investigator’s private life in a newspaper as if it were evidence against her.”

The owner leaned on the table. “You’re choosing her.”

“I’m choosing the advice we gave you.”

For a second Ren Hao watched him look for another version of the conversation, a delay, a softer word, a way to keep it. There wasn’t one.

“You’ll lose more than the account.”

“That’s possible.”

The owner walked out without offering his hand. The director who’d been looking at the window held the door, and on his way through it turned and gave Ren Hao one small, tired nod.

✦ ✦ ✦

The statement went out before eleven. Five sentences. It didn’t mention her, or a taxi rank, or anything personal at all, and didn’t criticise the airline. It said the firm had ended its engagement with the carrier’s holding group with immediate effect, following a review of its professional obligations in the light of the client’s public communications, and wouldn’t comment on the investigation, its findings, or the personal circumstances of anyone connected with it. Kong had approved every word. No adjectives. Nothing that made anyone look noble. A decision.

CRISIS FIRM DROPS AIRLINE OVER CRASH STATEMENT

He read the coverage once and closed it, and called everybody into the big room.

“We’ve ended our work with the airline. It was our largest client. Some of you have spent ten weeks on it, some of you five years. It’ll hurt this year’s numbers and change who works on what. I’m not going to pretend it won’t, and I won’t give you reassurance I can’t back up, because you’d remember it if I did. No decision’s been made about anybody’s job.”

A first-year from research asked carefully, looking like she wished she hadn’t, “Is it because of the investigator?”

“It’s a fair question and I’ll answer it properly. No. My relationship was declared on the morning of the accident and walled off on both sides from the first hour. Nobody in this building has seen a word of that investigation, including me. The client’s entitled to disagree with our advice. It isn’t entitled to make us say we don’t believe it. If you’re worried about your job, come and ask me. Don’t read the papers to find out what’s happening to you.”

His head of operations stayed behind. “The board’s going to ask whether it was worth it.”

“I’ll tell them I’d do it again on Monday.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Ruby had been on the firm’s front desk for six years and had cake on her birthday every year because he made sure of it. She’d been at the back of the big room by the door and heard every word. And the day before, through the glass of his office, she’d heard him tell Kong on the phone, low, And nobody tells her. Not from this building. She doesn’t need one more thing to carry.

Just before noon she went into the small room behind reception where the coats were, shut the door, and rang a number she’d had in her phone since July of last year, when a woman in a white blouse had stood at her desk and asked, quite seriously, what her boss was like when nobody was looking.

“Ms. Xu. It’s Ruby. From Mr. Ren’s office. He’s fine, he’s at his desk. He’ll be furious with me. He told everybody yesterday that nobody from this building was to tell you anything. So I’m not telling you from the building. I’m in the coat room.”

Ruby took a breath.

“He dropped them. The airline. All of it. This morning. They came up here and shouted and he signed it anyway. It was the biggest thing we had.”

Her voice wobbled, and she was annoyed with it.

“And he hasn’t told you, because he doesn’t want you to think you owe him anything. I’ve worked for him six years, Ms. Xu, and I know what his face looks like when something’s cost him. It looks like this morning. I’m going to hang up now before he finds me in here.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Song-Zhu hadn’t planned to go. She sat at her desk with the statement open on her screen and read the five sentences six times. She asked the press office to confirm in writing that the firm’s withdrawal had no bearing on the investigation’s independence or findings, and they did. He’d built that firm out of two rooms over a print shop, and this morning he’d let a fifth of it go, and he hadn’t told her.

Director Kwan looked up as she went past his door. “Where are you going?”

“Out. For an hour.”

“Don’t discuss the investigation,” he said, and went back to his screen, and she saw the corner of his mouth move.

In the lift up the tower she watched the numbers change. Her hands were steady. Nothing else about her was. Ruby looked up from the front desk and went pink to the ears.

“I didn’t ring you,” said Ruby.

“No. Of course you didn’t.”

The door to the inner corridor opened, and Ren Hao came through it with his jacket off and his sleeves rolled and his tie pulled loose and a folder in one hand, saying something over his shoulder, and turned and saw her by the reception desk, and stopped dead.

She’d imagined it in the lift. She’d thought she might ask why he hadn’t told her, or be angry, or tell him he had no right to make a decision like that without letting her see what it cost.

“Hello,” she said.

“Hello.”

He didn’t come towards her. She watched him not do it. He stood in the corridor doorway and left her the whole distance across the reception floor to decide what to do with.

She crossed it. She walked past Ruby’s desk and took the front of his shirt in her fist, the way she’d taken his waistcoat at a taxi rank sixteen months ago, and pulled him down, and kissed him. The folder hit the floor.

For one second he didn’t move. Then his hand came up to her face and the other went round her back, and he kissed her back without any of the restraint he’d been practising since September, like a man who’d missed her every single day for thirty-three days and spent every one of them refusing to turn his missing her into something she’d have to carry. Behind them a phone rang and rang, and Ruby picked it up without a sound and said “Please hold,” and put it down again.

From behind the reception desk came a deliberate sound of papers being shuffled.

Ren Hao didn’t look round. “Ruby. Did you ring her? From the coat room?”

There was a pause. “The coat room isn’t technically the building, Mr. Ren.”

Song-Zhu laughed against his chest with her fist still in his shirt, really laughed, for the first time in so long it hurt, and he looked down at her like he’d been waiting thirty-three days to hear it, and Ruby announced to nobody that she’d make some tea and went off to the pantry with enormous dignity.

✦ ✦ ✦

In his office she stood by the glass with her arms folded.

“Your biggest client. Why didn’t you tell me? I found out from your receptionist. In a coat room.”

“Because I didn’t want it to be something you had to answer. It was my firm’s decision. It wasn’t a message to you, and it wasn’t asking you for anything.”

She looked out at the harbour. “I spent twenty minutes after she rang thinking you’d done it because of me. Because of the newspaper. Then I read it six times. You did it because they asked you to say your own advice was wrong, and because they tried to use me to get out of a part under a floor. Are you sure you know what you’ve lost? That’s a great deal of money, Hao.”

“Kong read me the numbers twice, slowly.”

She almost laughed, and it came out as a breath.

“Are you angry?”

She thought about it honestly. “Yes. Not with you. With them. With the papers. With whoever stood on a pavement sixteen months ago and kept that photograph. With the fact that they made it about us, when it should only ever have been about the evidence. And with you for not telling me. A bit.”

“I didn’t leave that account to protect you from a newspaper. I left it because I wouldn’t stand up and defend something I knew was wrong. And because I told you at your table at three in the morning in August that I’d never be the reason anybody doubted your report. I meant it then. It cost more this morning. That’s all.”

She thought of a toothbrush going into a washbag, a full fridge, a man at her door who’d seen her try to say it and told her she already had. He hadn’t asked her to change her mind or made her responsible for his sadness. He’d done the most expensive thing he’d ever done, and hadn’t asked her to carry any of it.

Ruby brought the tea, looked at nobody, and shut the door behind her this time. Song-Zhu sat down on the sofa at last.

“How bad is it? Properly.”

He told her: the number, the fourteen people, the other engagements in the group that would follow, a board meeting at half past two. “I don’t regret saying no. I regret that it got to where it was the only honest thing left, and that the families had to watch people argue about vocabulary while they waited.”

“I didn’t come to ask you for anything. I’m not coming back because you dropped a client. I haven’t changed my mind about the break. The investigation isn’t finished, and I’m not ready to go back to how it was.”

“Then you’ll have the time.”

There were shadows under his eyes she’d never seen there, and his collar had turned in on one side and nobody had told him. He looked like a man who’d been working too long and sleeping in the wrong key, and like somebody she’d missed so badly she’d had to sit down.

“Aren’t you going to ask why I came? I saw what you’d done. And I wanted to see you. I missed you, Hao.”

His face changed slowly, all the way through. “Every day. Even the days you’d have hated me ringing.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She had a technical review at three.

“Would you like me to arrange a car?”

He held up one hand before she could answer.

“That was me asking properly.”

She took his hand. “No. I came on my own. You really are learning. I can’t promise when this will be over, or what I’ll feel when it is. And I don’t want you sleeping at my flat because we kissed by Ruby’s desk. I’m not asking you to disappear. I’m asking us to be careful. Can I see you again? Not tonight. Soon.”

He looked down at their hands. “You’re asking me?”

“I’m asking you.”

“Yes,” said Ren Hao.

At the lifts Ruby finished a call and looked up with impeccable professionalism. “Mr. Ren’s half past two has arrived early, Ms. Xu. They’re the board. They’re always early when it’s bad.”

Song-Zhu stepped into the lift and held the door with her hand. “Go and tell them you’d do it again. And don’t forget to eat lunch.”

He laughed out loud in the middle of his own reception. “That’s my line.”

“Not today,” she said, and let the doors close.

Ruby didn’t look up. “Shall I move your half past two by fifteen minutes, Mr. Ren? You look like you need to sit down. It’s in my job description. Under coat room.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Her phone buzzed in the taxi.

Ren Hao: You left your folder.

The folder was on her knee.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): No, I didn’t.

Ren Hao: I know. I wanted a reason to message you. I didn’t know if I was allowed.

Something in her face went soft.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): You’re allowed. Don’t expect an answer when I’m working. And don’t send me a driver. You were thinking about it.

Ren Hao: I was assessing the risk.

She laughed out loud in the back of the taxi, and the driver looked at her in the mirror.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Eat lunch.

Ren Hao: Yes, Investigator.

That night, at her own table with a bowl of rice she’d made herself:

Ren Hao: Home? The board was bad. I told them I’d do it again on Monday. Nobody resigned. Goodnight, Song-Zhu.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Goodnight, Hao.

Nothing was mended. The airline was still furious, his firm had lost a fifth of itself, and his slippers were still by her shoe cabinet and six of his suits on her rail. But he’d kept his word when it cost him and hadn’t asked her to reward him for it, and when she’d walked across his reception floor he’d let her decide, every metre of the way, how close she wanted to stand. She turned the light off and lay in the dark, and found she was smiling.

chapters.title: Not Yet, Still
chapters.desc: One dinner, no agenda. She still can’t say it. At the taxi rank, again, she asks before she kisses him.
chapters.epigraph: “That’s all tonight has to be.”
chapters.content:
The first time he asked her to dinner, he did it without making it sound like a question with consequences.

It was Tuesday the tenth of November, after eight at night. She was at her desk with three documents open, one a table of torque values she’d stared at so long the numbers had started to look like decoration, when her phone lit.

Ren Hao: What did you have for dinner?

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): A biscuit. A large biscuit.

Ren Hao: Then I won’t interfere with your culinary achievements. Would you like to have dinner with me one evening this week?

She looked at it. There was no I’ll pick you up in it, no I’ve booked somewhere, no you need to get out of that office. It was a question with nothing hidden behind it.

The investigation was moving, slowly. The interim finding had opened a dozen new rooms of questions: who had fitted that component, where it had come from, who had signed for it, who had signed for whoever signed for it. The families were still waiting. And she was tired, in a way she couldn’t quite admit, of deciding every evening what to do with the gap between her and him.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Thursday. Somewhere ordinary. Don’t book somewhere ridiculous. You once rang a restaurant because they’d run out of the tart I liked.

Ren Hao: That was a quality-control matter.

She put the phone face up on the desk before she could smile any more, and spent the rest of the evening looking at the clock more than she needed to.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Thursday he was there early, under the awning of a small place two streets from the authority, squeezed between a stationer’s and a chemist: wooden tables, warm light, a menu chalked on a board that changed with whatever the kitchen had been sent that morning. He’d chosen it because it was near her office, because the noodles were good, and because there was nothing memorable about it whatsoever. No private room, no view, no candles. He’d tried hard not to make dinner into something that had to be remembered.

She came along the pavement with her hair half up and a dark jumper under her long coat, tired, and he saw the line between her eyebrows before she saw him. Then she looked up, and it went, and her mouth moved a little at one corner, and he forgot for half a second what he’d been going to say.

“How long have you been standing out here?”

“Seven minutes. So you wouldn’t have to come in and look for me.”

“Hao. You could have sat down.”

He held the door. There were no flowers on the table, no wine waiting, no card with her name. Two glasses of water and a small dish of pickled radish.

“Very normal,” she said, looking round.

“That was the hope. And nobody here will look at you. And the noodles are good.”

She ordered the noodles she liked and prawn and chive dumplings. When the waiter had gone there was a silence, and it wasn’t uncomfortable: cutlery at the next table, a couple talking low by the door, a bus going past.

“How’s the review?”

“Professional answer: it’s ongoing. Complaining answer: I’d like to throw the whole thing in the sea.”

He nodded gravely. “That seems inconvenient, given where the aircraft already is.”

She stared at him, and then laughed, a short sudden burst that made her put her glass down. “That was terrible.”

“I’d prepared myself for that.”

He watched her. Not the woman in the laboratory with headphones round her neck, or at the second microphone, or the one who’d stood in his office three weeks ago and told him she still needed time. Song-Zhu, laughing at a bad joke. He’d missed her laugh more than anything, and didn’t say so.

“What else would you throw in the sea?”

“My inbox. My laptop. Director Kwan.”

“Let’s keep that one hypothetical. I’m protecting your career.”

✦ ✦ ✦

For a while they talked about ordinary things. A junior investigator had sent an internal timetable to an entire distribution list, including a deputy minister who’d been trying to book the same meeting room for a fortnight. He told her about the firm and kept it factual: two more accounts gone, the fourteen people found new work inside the building, a forecast rewritten three times, a director who’d needed it explained that a company couldn’t replace its largest client by wishing hard.

“Is the firm all right? Really.”

He put his chopsticks down. “It’s adjusting. We’ll be all right. But there are decisions coming, and some of them won’t be nice. I’m not panicking. Raymond’s been extraordinary. It’s going to be a hard winter. And yes, I’m worried.”

Just that. There was something so familiar about it: the measured careful answer with the human part sitting just behind it, where she could see it if she looked. He was frightened, and he wasn’t asking her to make him less frightened. That mattered more than she could have told him.

“You’re good at knowing when to tell me something and when to leave it,” she said.

“I’m not always good at it.”

She pushed the dumplings across the table. “No. You’re not. But you’re getting better. Eat. You’re being sentimental.”

“I didn’t know sentiment affected appetite.”

“It affects mine,” said Song-Zhu.

A while later she asked how Isla was. “Is she still in Lima?”

He turned his glass. “Till the spring, she says. At the end of October she found the last name on her missing list, alive, in a field hospital. Somebody had spelt the surname wrong on the admissions board, and she went through every board in the city until she found it. Wei Long flies home next Friday. He’s been there a month. She rings me after he’s gone to sleep and tells me he’s learned to say thank you in four languages and no, I’m a police officer in two.”

Song-Zhu laughed. “Tell her I asked.”

“I always do.”

✦ ✦ ✦

They stayed far longer than either of them meant to. They talked about a film she’d seen on a flight years ago and could never remember the end of, and a man in his office who’d spent twenty minutes arguing that the printer on the twenty-ninth floor was sabotaging him personally.

“Does the printer have previous?”

“Not that I know of.”

“Then don’t make assumptions. Investigate first.”

She’d started listening to music again on the bus home. When he asked what, she said nothing he’d know, and then picked up her phone and sent him a song. His phone buzzed on the table. He looked at the title and put it in his pocket.

“You’re not going to listen?”

“Later. I’d rather hear you talk.”

It was said low, not polished, not offered in the hope of anything back. Heat came up into her face. “You can’t say things like that.”

“I can,” he said, and smiled, and didn’t push it.

It was strange how easily it came back: his hand resting by his glass, the way he listened without cutting in, the small movement of his eyebrows when she said something absurd, the way he looked at her like there was nobody else in the room. She’d missed all of it. But missing something wasn’t the same as being ready to have it back, and she didn’t know how to say that without it sounding like wait for me.

✦ ✦ ✦

Outside the air had turned cold. He walked beside her, not too close, not so far that she had to turn her head to talk to him. At the taxi rank on the corner there was a short queue under a streetlight and a cab at the front with its light on.

He looked at the cab. “Would you like me to wait till you’re in? I know you can get into a taxi on your own. I don’t mind waiting.”

When it was her turn she didn’t reach for the door. She turned round. He was standing under the streetlight in his coat with his hands in his pockets, perfectly calm. He didn’t look like a man waiting for an answer. He looked like someone who’d learned that wanting something didn’t give him the right to ask for it before she was ready, and that was what made it so hard.

I missed you. True. I want to do this again. True. I don’t know how to come back. The truest of the three. And under all of them the one she’d said once in September, folded small inside a don’t, and hadn’t been able to say since. It was right there in her throat like a stone. It wouldn’t come.

He saw her try. “You don’t have to say anything.”

She took a step towards him, a small one. He didn’t come to meet her. He waited until she’d reached for the front of his coat and closed her fingers in the wool.

“Can I?” she said.

His eyes went down to her hand, and back up. “Yes.”

It wasn’t the way she’d kissed him by Ruby’s desk, all relief and fistfuls of shirt. This one started unsure and found its way slowly to something she knew. His hand came to rest at her waist, lightly, and didn’t pull. When she leaned in, he leaned with her. When she tipped her face, he followed. His thumb moved once against her coat. That was all. She kissed him a long time at a taxi rank under a streetlight, sixteen months after the first one, and when she stopped he stayed close enough that their foreheads nearly touched.

Behind her the cab gave a short impatient toot.

“That’s my taxi.”

“Get home safely.”

“You too.”

“That isn’t how taxis work,” he said.

“Don’t ruin it,” said Song-Zhu, and got in, and looked at him once more before she shut the door. He wasn’t waving or asking her to stay. He was watching her with that quiet, whole attention, and he stayed at the rank until the tail lights had gone.

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t text her. He’d already said thank you, and she knew he’d liked seeing her, and he’d decided a long time ago, in a doorway, not to turn caring into an obligation. He walked to the main road with the cold on his face. At the crossing his phone buzzed.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Nearly home. I liked that we didn’t talk about anything important.

Ren Hao: We discussed a criminal printer.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Don’t open an investigation. You’ll start managing it.

He laughed, alone, at a crossing. The dots came and went and came.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): I don’t know when I can do this properly. I don’t want you to wait for something I can’t promise.

Not a no, and not a promise. The truth, in the only shape she could get it into. The lights changed and he didn’t move.

Ren Hao: Then don’t promise me anything. We had dinner. It was good. You kissed me. I kissed you back. That’s all tonight has to be.

He sent it before he could make it longer.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): You’re being very reasonable.

Ren Hao: It’s a horrible experience.

✦ ✦ ✦

She stood in the middle of her flat with her coat still on. The same shelves, the same sofa, the photograph on the side table that leaned slightly and that she kept meaning to straighten. Nothing had changed, except that she knew exactly what the room sounded like with nobody else in it.

She read his message again. He hadn’t asked her to come back, or to decide, or even when they could do it again. She should have been relieved. What she felt was a small aching disappointment she couldn’t justify, because she’d wanted him to ask, and she hadn’t wanted him to ask, and both of those were true at once, like the lines in the data.

She loved him. That hadn’t changed in September or October or tonight under the streetlight. But loving him wasn’t the same as being ready. She could kiss him at a taxi rank and laugh at his terrible jokes and want his hand at her waist. She still couldn’t tell him she was ready to come home, and she still couldn’t say three words to his face.

She typed I miss you and deleted it. It was true. It just wasn’t the answer to anything yet.

✦ ✦ ✦

He stood in his own kitchen without the big light on. He’d spent years arranging his life so silence was comfortable and every evening could be accounted for. Then she’d arrived and made a mess of all of it: hair ties in places with no logical reason to contain a hair tie, cups on his desk, windows opened when the air conditioning was perfectly adequate, conversations begun while he was reading a contract and carried on on the assumption that he’d been listening, which he always had. He’d never been so happy to have his routines wrecked.

He played the song she’d sent him, twice. He thought of her hand in his coat and her asking can I?, when they’d kissed a thousand times, like it was the first one again and she wanted it to be.

One dinner. One kiss under a streetlight. For now that was enough. Not because he wanted so little, but because he wanted her to be the one who chose what came next.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Home.

Ren Hao: Good. Sleep well.

Neither of them said I love you, or come back, or wait for me. But the kiss stayed, a small warm thing between two people who still knew exactly how to find each other, and still didn’t know what to do once they had.

chapters.title: The Widow
chapters.desc: The captain’s widow and daughter, and six words in ordinary writing. He waits outside in the rain for three hours. She tells him the last thing her father ever said to her.
chapters.epigraph: “Night, Zhu-zhu. Back Thursday.”
chapters.content:
The request came through the family liaison office on Wednesday the ninth of December in a single typed line.

Mrs. Yuk Wai-ling, widow of Captain Yuk Kam-fai, asks whether the investigator-in-charge would be willing to meet her privately.

Everybody on the fourth floor knew what Mrs. Yuk wanted. Three weeks before, Director Kwan had decided that the speech recovered from the cabin crew member’s phone wasn’t the cockpit voice recording, wasn’t protected in the same way, bore nothing on the cause, and was, in his words, a message addressed to his family that has been in our evidence store for two months too long. The captain’s next of kin would be told privately before the final report, by the investigator-in-charge if the family wished it.

The family wished it.

Yes, she wrote back. Saturday. Whenever she likes.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Friday night she took the black zip case out of her bedside drawer. She hadn’t opened it since the December before, when she’d sat on her sofa with Ren Hao’s hand under hers and listened to four minutes of a controller calling her father’s callsign.

The silver recorder in its grey foam. And in the little pocket in the lid, the thing she’d never once touched in seven years: his card, the one that had been in the recorder on his desk the morning he flew. The last things he’d said into it.

Tomorrow she was going to sit across a table from a woman whose husband had said six words to his daughter in the dark at four hundred feet, and give them to her. She was going to hand a stranger her husband’s voice. She didn’t think she could do that honestly if she’d never been able to do it for herself.

She took out the card with the air traffic recording and put it in the lid, and took out his, and pushed it into the slot until it clicked. Her fingers shook so badly it took three tries. She sat with the recorder in her lap, and then she pressed play.

His voice came out of the little speaker so close and so ordinary that she put her hand over her mouth.

Tuesday, oh-four-hundred. Block time six forty. Fuel figures on the sheet. Number two pack running warm again, tell engineering, they won’t believe me, they never believe me.

A rustle of paper. Then the voice changed, the way it had always changed, the way she’d forgotten it changed.

And this is for Zhu-zhu. Hello, Zhu-zhu. Bumpy over the sea tonight, tell your mother I’m fine, I’m always fine. It’s raining on the apron and the coffee’s terrible and I’ve bought you something from the shop here, it’s ugly, you’ll love it. Did you finish that problem set? I’m checking when I’m back. Don’t stay up. You never listen. Night, Zhu-zhu. Back Thursday.

A click. That was all.

He’d said her name. Twice, in the first fifteen seconds: the name only he had ever called her, that nobody had said out loud since the funeral. At nineteen, in a room in another country, she’d listened to fifty seconds as hard as she’d ever listened to anything, waiting for him to say it, and he hadn’t, because he’d been flying an aeroplane. He’d said it here. In the last thing he ever recorded, on an ordinary Tuesday, with the coffee terrible, telling her not to stay up.

She played it again, and again. On the fourth time, at it’s ugly, you’ll love it, she began to laugh, and the laughing turned over into something else, and she curled up on top of the duvet with the little silver thing held against her chest and cried until two in the morning. Nobody was there, and for the first time that didn’t feel like the point.

At ten past two she picked up her phone.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): I’m seeing the captain’s widow tomorrow. At eleven. At the authority. I don’t know how long. You can wait nearby, if you want to. You don’t have to.

The answer came in under a minute, as if he’d been lying awake on the other side of the harbour with the phone on his chest.

Ren Hao: I’ll be there.

✦ ✦ ✦

Mrs. Yuk was standing by the window in reception when Song-Zhu came down: small and neat and about forty, in a grey coat with a thin silver chain at her throat, thinner than the woman in the photograph in her husband’s crew file. Holding her hand was a girl of about twelve with her hair in a long plait and a pale ribbon tied round her wrist.

“This is Bo-yee.”

The girl looked at Song-Zhu with a look Song-Zhu knew from the inside: ready for the worst, pretending not to be.

“Would you like Bo-yee in the room with us? Or to hear it first and then decide?” Song-Zhu asked her mother gently.

“She wants to be there. I said no. She said she was twelve and it was her father.”

“I’m twelve. And it’s my dad,” said Bo-yee.

“Then you should be there,” said Song-Zhu.

✦ ✦ ✦

The meeting room had pale walls, three chairs, and a box of tissues nobody had moved. A liaison officer sat apart by the door. Song-Zhu brought no laptop and no headphones, only a single sheet of paper, blank side up.

“I want to explain exactly what this is before I tell you anything, so you know what you’re being given and what you’re not. It isn’t from the cockpit. That recording’s separate and protected, and I can’t tell you anything about it. This is from a phone. A member of the cabin crew was recording a short video for her sister when the power went, and the phone kept recording after the picture failed. It picked up an announcement over the cabin speakers. It’s damaged and parts of it are missing. Specialists have examined it, every step is written down, and the original’s been kept exactly as it was. The voice on it has been identified as your husband’s, on the PA, to the passengers. After the brace call there’s a short piece of speech we’ve been able to make out. It isn’t an announcement. I can’t tell you what he knew at that moment, or whether it was the last thing he said, because I don’t know what he said on the flight deck afterwards. I can only tell you the words.”

Mrs. Yuk had gone still. Bo-yee held her mother’s hand in both of hers.

“Please,” said Mrs. Yuk.

Song-Zhu didn’t turn the paper over. She’d heard it more than fifty times. “He said: Tell my little girl. Daddy tried.”

For a moment nothing happened. Then Mrs. Yuk’s eyebrows drew together like she hadn’t understood, and her mouth moved, and her free hand came up and pressed flat against her lips.

It was Bo-yee who spoke, with her voice cracked down the middle. “He said little girl? I told him not to call me that. On the phone, on the Saturday, before he went. I said I’m twelve, Daddy, I’m not little, it’s embarrassing, and he laughed and said you’ll always be my little girl, it’s the law, and I hung up on him.”

She was sobbing now, the way children do, with her whole body.

“I hung up on him. That was the last time. And he said it anyway. He said it anyway.”

Her mother pulled her in, and the two of them held each other in the small pale room, and the liaison officer looked at the floor, and Song-Zhu sat absolutely still across the table and let them. She didn’t say it would be all right, or that he’d have forgiven her. The room was full of the one thing nobody in it needed her to add to.

“He always did that. Every time she told him not to. She used to pretend to be furious,” said Mrs. Yuk at last, into her daughter’s hair.

“I was a bit furious,” said Bo-yee, into her mother’s coat, and Mrs. Yuk laughed, wetly, helplessly.

“Daddy tried. He wanted her to know he tried.”

“Those are the words. That’s all I can tell you about what he meant. But I can tell you, because it’s in the report and it’ll be in the final one, that the evidence shows the crew did everything they could have done with what they had. And that he was still on the PA to his passengers after the power went. He didn’t stop. He kept talking to them all the way down.”

Bo-yee lifted a face that was blotched and wet and furious and twelve. “Did he sound scared?”

Song-Zhu had promised herself on her bed at two in the morning that she wouldn’t lie to this child by one syllable to make anything easier. “He sounded like a man doing his job. And then, for those words, he sounded like your dad.”

The girl looked at her a long time. “Okay.”

At the door Mrs. Yuk turned back, so low Song-Zhu almost didn’t catch it. “Did he sound like himself?”

She thought of the roar and the distortion and the two words coming up out of it like something surfacing. “It was his voice.”

“Thank you for not making it prettier than it was.”

“Thank you for letting me be the one to tell you,” said Song-Zhu.

Bo-yee spoke from the doorway. “Is it written down somewhere? Can I have it written down? In ordinary writing. Not report words.”

Song-Zhu turned the sheet of paper over. In the middle of the page, in her own small handwriting, there was nothing but the six words, and a date. The girl took it in both hands and folded it once, carefully, and put it inside her school coat against her chest, and the door closed behind them so gently the latch didn’t click.

✦ ✦ ✦

He’d been outside since before twelve. It started raining at half past and didn’t stop. The building had a narrow overhang over its side entrance, deep enough for one person if that person stood straight against the wall. He bought a coffee from the kiosk across the road and it was cold before he remembered he was holding it. He answered two messages from Raymond about the restructuring, and one from Ruby that said only Is she all right?, which he didn’t answer because he didn’t know.

He could have gone in, or asked at the desk, or rung. He’d learned in a doorway with a bag in his hand that waiting and being useful weren’t the same thing, and sometimes waiting was the whole of what you’d been asked to do.

After three the glass doors opened and she came out, holding her coat shut with one hand, and stopped on the step, and looked for him.

He was soaked from the knees down. The shoulders of his good coat had gone black with rain and his hair was stuck to his forehead.

“How long have you been standing here?”

He looked at his watch. “About three hours and twenty minutes.”

“Three hours? You could have gone somewhere dry!”

“I bought a coffee.”

She looked at the paper cup on the wall beside him. “That coffee’s dead, Hao. Why didn’t you go in?”

“You didn’t know how long you’d be, so I didn’t know when you’d come out. I wasn’t standing in the rain. I was standing next to it.”

She took hold of his wet sleeve and looked at it like it had personally offended her, and then her face went, all at once, and what was under the exasperation was something he’d only seen on her twice before.

“I told her. She brought her daughter. She’s twelve. Her father used to call her his little girl, and she told him not to, on the phone, the Saturday before he flew, and she hung up on him, and she’s carried that since August.”

Her voice wobbled and she let it.

“And now she’s got it written down. In ordinary writing.”

She stepped forward and put her forehead against his wet coat, and stood there.

It wasn’t something she did when she was hurting. She usually had to put herself back together first, alone, before she let anyone close. He’d learned that. His hand hung in the air by her back: ask, don’t assume, don’t make her body one more thing to solve. Then her fingers closed in his coat, and he understood, and his arms came round her. She let out a long shaking breath, and he held her under the narrow overhang, his cheek against her hair.

“Three hours. You’re an idiot.”

“You asked me to wait.”

She was quiet against him. “Yes. I did.”

✦ ✦ ✦

They found a small steamed-up café two streets away. He wrapped both hands round his cup and she watched him.

“You’re shivering. It’s December.”

“Air conditioning isn’t seasonal,” he said, and she touched the back of his hand, which was like ice, and laughed slightly for the first time that day.

She turned her cup. “I’m not going to tell you what he said. It was evidence. It wasn’t mine. Now it’s hers, and Bo-yee’s. But there’s something that is mine, and I want to tell you. Last night I played my father’s card. Not the air traffic. His. The one that was in the recorder on his desk the morning he flew. I told you I’d never played anything he recorded, and I hadn’t. Then I thought, tomorrow I’m going to hand a woman her husband’s voice, and I’ve never been brave enough to take my own father’s.”

He reached across the table slowly, and she let him take her hand.

She took a breath. “It’s mostly his logbook. Fuel. Block time. A pack running warm. Engineering never believing him. And then at the end there’s a bit for me. Hello, Zhu-zhu. Bumpy over the sea, tell your mother I’m fine. He’d bought me something ugly from an airport shop and I’d love it. Had I finished a problem set. Don’t stay up, you never listen. And then: Night, Zhu-zhu. Back Thursday.”

Her eyes had filled. She didn’t stop.

“He said my name, Hao. Twice. I spent seven years thinking the last time he spoke he didn’t think of me. And he had. Two days before. On a Tuesday. About homework. That’s his last words to me.”

He held her hand across the café table and said nothing, because there wasn’t anything he could say that would be bigger than that, and he’d learned not to try.

“Nobody calls me that. Nobody’s said it since the funeral. My mother can’t.”

“I won’t. It’s his,” he said.

She looked at him with her eyes wet and her hand in his, and something went through her face he couldn’t read and then could. He saw the word come up, the closest it had ever been, closer than at the door with his bag or at the taxi rank. He saw her reach for it, and saw it stop. It was true; she just wasn’t ready to say it into a café on a wet Saturday afternoon like it was the answer to something.

“Not today. Not here. That you want to is enough,” he said gently.

She put her other hand over his. “I still can’t come back yet. Not because you held me in the rain, or because I told you that.”

“You told me your father said your name. That’s what today is. I can be hurt without you having done anything wrong. I miss you. There are days something absurd happens at work and you’re the first person I think of, and days I want to ask whether you’ve eaten and have to remind myself you’re a grown woman with a canteen. But I don’t want you to come back because you feel responsible for how much I miss you. Ever.”

“I don’t want that either.”

“Then we agree,” said Ren Hao.

✦ ✦ ✦

The rain had eased when they left. She made him take her umbrella, and he held it over both of them as far as the taxi rank on the corner.

“Go home. Dry your shoes. Not on the radiator. And have something hot.”

“Yes, Investigator.”

She reached up and pushed his wet hair off his forehead and left her hand on his cheek. “Thank you for not asking me to promise anything.”

“I don’t need a promise. You’ve given me your father’s voice saying your name. That’s more than a promise.”

She kissed him under the umbrella with her hand still on his face. The taxi rank in November had been a question. This was something heavier and older, and she held it longer.

That night she sat at her kitchen table with her hair wet from the bath and the black case shut in front of her.

Ren Hao: Home. Shoes drying. No radiator involved.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): A historic day.

Her thumb hung over the keys. Three words. She typed the first one, looked at it, and deleted it, and typed something else.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): He’d have liked you. He’d have said your shoes were too shiny. Then he’d have liked you.

Ren Hao: You told me that last December. I’ve been trying to deserve it ever since.

They were still living apart. The final report was eight months away. But that afternoon she’d given a twelve-year-old her father’s words in ordinary writing, and the night before her own father had said her name to her, twice, after seven years. Neither had brought anybody home. Both were true, and for tonight that was what she had.

chapters.title: The Crumpled List
chapters.desc: A crumpled list in his coat: eighty-one reasons, crossed out and rewritten for a year. On his kitchen counter, explicit, she says I love you in the middle, and he stops dead, and then doesn’t.
chapters.epigraph: “Some things don’t have to be written down.”
chapters.content:
His coat was on the wrong chair. That was the first thing she noticed, on Saturday the ninth of January, standing in his flat for the first time in four months.

Ren Hao had a system for coats: work coats in the wardrobe on the left, weekend coats on the right, anything he meant to wear the next morning on the chair in the bedroom. Never, ever, a dining chair. His good dark wool coat was over the back of a dining chair, still damp at the hem from the night before, when he’d met her outside the authority and walked her to the noodle place and then to the taxi rank, the third Friday in a row.

He’d asked on Wednesday. Would you like to come over on Saturday? I’ll cook. You can leave whenever you like. She’d said yes before she’d finished it.

“Your standards are slipping,” she called towards the kitchen, and picked the coat up to put it on the right chair, because somebody had to.

Something crackled in the inside pocket: a wad of paper folded small, soft at the corners from being handled. She’d meant only to check it through the wool, the way you’d check for a phone. But it was so thick and so worn that as her fingers closed on it the outer fold came loose, and she saw his narrow capitals, cramped, in black ink and blue.

Six sheets torn from a notebook and folded together into one square. At the top of the first, underlined twice:

REASONS. (FOR S-Z, WHO SAYS I WON’T GET PAST FIVE.)

Underneath, smaller: Sun 11 Jan 2026. A year ago, nearly to the day.

She sat down on the arm of his sofa.

1. She laughs at her own jokes before she gets to the end of them.
2. She says she isn’t hungry and then eats half of what’s on my plate.
3. She has no idea how loud she is when she’s excited about a weld.
4. She can listen to the worst thing a person ever says and still remember to ask the man who brought her the tape whether he’s eaten.
5. She argues with traffic lights.

She remembered that January. His sofa, seven months in. She’d been cross after cancelling a dinner at the last minute for a call-out, and she’d made a joke that wasn’t one, about how he’d get tired of her eventually, everybody got tired of her eventually, she was a lot. He’d said he wouldn’t. She’d said how could he possibly know. He’d said he’d make a list. She’d laughed and said he wouldn’t get past five.

He’d got past five.

12. She’s kind when nobody’s watching.
15. She looks at me when she thinks I’m reading.
21. She tells me when I’m being an idiot. (Frequently. With evidence.)
22. She makes me want to be better and has never once asked me to be somebody else.

She laughed out loud at twenty-one, and turned the page, and stopped laughing.

There were eighty-one of them; the last page had the number written at the bottom and circled. Some she could date to the minute: the cake, the camp bed, the snowball. And some had been written later. She could tell from the ink and the hand. The later ones were cramped, pressed too hard into the paper, written late and alone, with dates in the margins: March. June (after “too much”). August. September. October.

And there were the crossings-out. On the fourth page one line had been struck through so many times the pen had nearly torn the paper: She lets me look after her. Underneath, in blue:

47. She lets me look after her when she wants it, and tells me when she doesn’t. I am learning the difference. Slowly. She is patient. She shouldn’t have to be.

Further on, She makes me laugh had a line through it, and under it, I miss making her laugh. And She is home, crossed out, and under it:

62. I miss being let into her home.
63. I love her when she needs me to stay away. I didn’t know that was possible until 19 September.

She stopped breathing. In the kitchen the coffee machine finished, and then there was nothing.

He’d written these while they were apart, and not as a letter or a plea. He’d written them for himself, in a coat pocket, for a year, and crossed them out when they stopped being true, and written something truer underneath. The last page was black ink again.

79. I love who she is. Not the version of her that’s easiest for me.
80. I want to be next to her. I don’t want being next to me to be one more thing she has to carry.
81. I love Xu Song-Zhu. Not because she makes my life easier. Because she makes it mine.

And beneath it, the ink still dark: Sat 9 Jan 2027. Today. He’d written the last one this morning.

✦ ✦ ✦

He stood in the doorway with two cups of coffee in a grey jumper with the sleeves pushed up, and took one look at the paper on her knee and went completely still.

He put the cups down on the nearest bookshelf carefully, like they might go off. “Ah. I thought I’d left it in my desk drawer.”

“You wrote eighty-one reasons.”

“I can count. Are you upset? You’ve got a face—”

“The face of a woman reading eighty-one reasons.”

“It was private. I wasn’t hiding it. I just didn’t write it for anyone to read, and I didn’t write it to make you do anything.”

She turned a page. “You did it because I said you wouldn’t get past five. On your sofa. After the call-out. I remember everything, Hao. It’s my job. You kept the crossed-out ones. All of them. Why?”

He thought about it properly, in the middle of his living room. “Because I don’t think they were wrong. They just weren’t finished.”

“And eighty-one. This morning.”

“I was making coffee, and I saw your mug on the draining board, the one you left three weeks ago. The ugly cat with one eye.”

“It’s a design choice.”

“You leave things here now. A mug. A hair tie. A scarf on Tuesday. Not because you live here. You come round and forget something and come back for it. And I realised I didn’t want to treat those things as a tally, as evidence that you were halfway back. I wanted them to be exactly what they were. You came round, you left your mug, and I was happy. So I wrote eighty-one. It’s the only one I’ve written in the present tense since August.”

She folded the pages along new creases and smoothed them flat. “Can I keep it?”

“It’s always been yours.”

She put it in her coat pocket and drank some cold coffee. “Seventeen’s missing. You go sixteen, eighteen. I counted.”

“I couldn’t get it right. I wrote it nine times. Everything I wrote sounded embarrassing.”

“Try.”

He said it low. “I love the way you look at me when you’re half asleep. Because you haven’t remembered to keep anything back yet.”

Her fingers closed on the paper. She looked away, out of the window. “That’s seventeen. Don’t write it down.”

✦ ✦ ✦

They made lunch. She announced she was making it and he could assist provided he didn’t touch the arrangement of anything. Noodles, greens, eggs. She kept looking at her coat on its hook. In the end she fetched the list and read him thirty-four while the water boiled.

“She talks to animals as though they’ve been fully briefed.”

“That’s slander.”

“You explained to a cat in a car park why it shouldn’t sit on a hot bonnet.”

“It was a safety matter.”

She touched sixty-two with one finger. “Do you regret writing any of them? The hard ones?”

He turned the tap off and dried his hands. “Those least of all. I used to think loving somebody meant knowing how to make them happy: seeing what you needed before you did, and arranging it, and clearing everything out of your way. I know now I can make your life harder by trying to make it easier. I don’t want to forget that. So I kept the crossings-out.”

She put the list down by the fruit bowl and came round the counter and put her hand flat on his chest. “Can I kiss you?”

His face did what it always did when she moved first: total, careful attention. “Yes.”

His hands came to her waist and stayed there and let her decide how close. She came close. She kissed him the way she hadn’t since the beach in July, slow and deep and certain, and he made a sound into her mouth that was almost nothing and almost everything, and his fingers tightened, and still he didn’t pull.

“Your noodles are going to boil over,” he said, not steadily.

“Let lunch suffer,” said Song-Zhu, and reached past him and turned the hob off without looking.

✦ ✦ ✦

He asked first, with his hands on her hips, and she said yes into his mouth, and he lifted her onto the cold stone edge of his counter in her jeans and her soft jumper, knees either side of him, the fruit bowl at her elbow and the list folded beside it.

“Are you sure?”

She knew he wasn’t asking about the counter. His face was tired and careful and so full of hope he was trying with every muscle not to show it.

“I’m not having a romantic emergency because you wrote eighty-one sentences. I’m here because I want to be. I’ve wanted to be every Friday at that taxi rank for three weeks. Stop asking questions.”

She pulled his jumper over his head and put both hands flat on his chest and ran them down, learning him again the way she’d learn a piece of wreckage she thought she knew: the same and not the same, every centimetre to be checked. He was thinner. She could feel his ribs. He’d been sleeping badly on the wrong side of the harbour for four months and she could feel every week of it under her palms, and she put her mouth on his collarbone where it stood out, and kept it there.

He undressed her slowly. Her jumper over her head, and he had to stop and look. Her bra, unhooked with one hand, landed in the fruit bowl, and she laughed helplessly with her head back against his cupboard and he laughed into her skin, and then neither of them was laughing. He took her breast in his mouth, slow and warm, and she arched off the counter into him with both hands in his hair. This was a man who’d thought for four months he might never be allowed to again, and he did it properly, every part of her in order, like he was reading her back. He drew her jeans off her and her knickers with them and dropped them on his kitchen floor, and went down on his knees in front of the counter.

“Let me. Please. I’ve missed you. Let me.”

He put his mouth on her and she made a sound she’d never made in his flat before. He held her thighs open with his hands. He was slow, then not, then slow again on purpose every time she got close, until she was gripping the edge of the counter and saying please to the ceiling, and he lifted his head with his mouth wet and his eyes nearly black.

“Not until I’m inside you. I want to be there.”

“Then get up here,” she said, and he laughed, hoarse, and stood.

She got his belt open with hands that wouldn’t work. She wrapped her legs round him and pulled him in, and he pushed into her slowly, all the way, until there was no space left between them anywhere, his arm round her back and his other hand flat on the counter by her hip, and neither of them could breathe properly.

“Four months,” he said, so low she barely heard it.

He moved slowly and deep, each stroke whole, her heels locked behind him, his face an inch from hers so she could see everything it did. The fruit bowl rattled. It built in her in a long rising tightness and she didn’t want it to end. He was looking at her the way he’d looked at her in the snow, and on the beach in the moonlight, like she was the only true thing he’d ever seen.

She held his face in both hands. “Hao. I love you.”

He stopped dead inside her, his whole body gone rigid, his breath caught halfway in. His hand on the counter closed into a fist. He stared at her from an inch away, and his face did something she’d never seen a face do, like every light in it had come on at once.

“Say it again.”

“I love you. I’ve loved you since the camp bed broke. Before. Since you sent me minutes of our date at fourteen minutes past midnight. I tried at your door with your bag in your hand, and in the café, and at the taxi rank every Friday, and I couldn’t, and I can now. I’m saying it to your face, in your kitchen, with you inside me, so you know it isn’t folded up inside anything. It’s just true.”

His eyes filled and spilled over. He didn’t wipe them. He was shaking all through, against her.

“I had things prepared for when you said it. I had them ready for a year. I can’t remember any of them.”

“Then don’t stop,” said Song-Zhu.

He didn’t. It wasn’t slow any more. Something that had been held back for sixteen months broke and she broke with it. He drove into her against his kitchen counter with his face in her neck and her name and I love you going into her skin over and over, and she said it back every time until the words weren’t words any more. She came with her nails in his shoulders and her head back against the cupboard door, crying, laughing, saying it, and he followed holding her so tight she couldn’t breathe and didn’t want to, with one long broken sound that was the closest she’d ever heard him come to silence.

He stayed inside her afterwards with his forehead on her shoulder, both of them breathing like people come up from deep water.

“I’m going to have to clean this counter,” he said into her shoulder, in a wrecked voice.

She laughed and he slipped out of her, and they both gasped, and then they were laughing helplessly, naked in his kitchen, with her bra in the fruit bowl and an orange on the floor.

✦ ✦ ✦

The afternoon went into evening. She wore one of his shirts over her jeans and read the list again on his sofa.

“There’s something missing. Not seventeen. You didn’t write she loves me back.”

He smiled slowly, the whole way across his face. “I didn’t know she did. I’ll add it.”

She folded the list. “No. Some things don’t have to be written down.”

“I want to come back. Not because everything’s finished. The investigation isn’t. There’s the contractor and the signatures and seven months of work. But I don’t want to keep pretending that loving you and being with you are two separate problems I have to solve one after the other. I want to try again. Properly. Slowly, if we have to. But not how it was.”

His face changed, his eyes first, then his mouth, then the rest of him, like a man who’d held a breath so long he’d forgotten he was allowed to let it go. “Differently.”

“You can come round to my flat. But you’re not moving your toothbrush back in without asking. No scheduling my meals. No sending a car because it looks like rain.”

He hesitated, slightly. She narrowed her eyes, and he said, “Agreed.”

“And you can still ask if I’ve eaten. Once a day.”

“Even if you say you’ve had a biscuit?”

“Then twice,” said Song-Zhu.

✦ ✦ ✦

Before nine his phone rang. Isla. It was half past seven in the morning in Lima, and his sister’s voice came through loud enough for the whole room.

“Are you busy? You’re lying. I want to hear you admit it.”

Song-Zhu laughed, and there was a silence from Lima.

“Is that Song-Zhu? Is she there?”

Song-Zhu leaned towards the phone. “Hi, Isla.”

A sound came down the line from eighteen thousand kilometres away, somewhere between a gasp and a shriek. “Are you back together?”

Song-Zhu looked at him, and smiled. “Yes.”

Isla went quiet. Then, low, from the other side of the Pacific: “Okay. I’m not going to ask anything else. I’m going to be extremely respectful. Wei Long lands on Monday for eleven days and I’m telling him the second he walks out of arrivals, and he’s going to do his face, the small one. Hao? Don’t mess it up.”

“I’ll try not to.”

“Don’t try. Do. Love you. Goodbye,” said Isla, and rang off before anyone could say anything else.

“She’ll be insufferable for a week,” said Ren Hao.

“Two.”

At his door, with her coat on and the list in the inside pocket against her heart, where he’d kept it, she held her hand out and he took it.

“Next year, make it eighty-two. You missed one. Because I love you too.”

“I’ll write it down.”

“No, you won’t. I want you to remember it.”

“I will,” he said, and this time, when they left, neither of them was leaving the other behind.

chapters.title: Back In
chapters.desc: Seven conditions on a noodle-shop napkin, and a clause about six suits. He signs, adds an eighth, and keeps every one. Signed with a kiss.
chapters.epigraph: “We remember we’re on the same side.”
chapters.content:
The napkin had come from the noodle place behind the cargo terminal, the one where they’d eaten on the nineteenth of June 2025 and she’d told him what she listened to for a living. It had the shop’s name printed in red in one corner and a grease spot in the other, and she’d brought it home in her coat pocket on Friday night without knowing why.

On Sunday the seventeenth of January, at her kitchen counter, she found out.

He was at her stove, making tea, because she’d asked him to come round for lunch and he’d asked whether he could make the tea and she’d said yes. He heard the scratch of her pen behind him. Then the scrape of the salt pot being moved out of the way.

“What are you writing?”

“Something important.”

“Should I be worried?”

“Possibly.”

He looked over his shoulder. She was sitting at her counter in his old university sweatshirt, which she’d never given back, with her hair in a clip and a napkin flat in front of her and an expression of enormous seriousness.

He turned off the kettle. “Is that a contract?”

“Not yet.”

“That sounds worse.”

She didn’t look up. “Bring the tea.”

He brought it, and put the cups down, and she slid the napkin across the counter to him. At the top, in capitals:

TERMS AND CONDITIONS FOR REN HAO MOVING BACK INTO MY FLAT

He read it. He looked at her.

“Moving back?”

“Don’t get excited. Read it first.”

“I haven’t said anything.”

“Your face has.”

He looked down at the napkin again. There were seven conditions, numbered, in her small fast hand, crammed in round the grease spot.

1. Not all at once. A few nights first. Then we see.
2. You ask before bringing anything. Clothes, toiletries, chargers, coffee machines, and any suspiciously large box you say is “just something useful”.
3. My kitchen stays my kitchen. You can cook. You can wash up. You may not rearrange anything. This includes the coffee machine.
4. You can ask if I’ve eaten. Once a day. You may not monitor, remind, or send food to my building without asking.
5. No tracking my phone. Ever.
6. If either of us is upset, we say so. No going quiet for a day. No pretending it’s fine to be considerate.
7. I get a life outside us. So do you. Not every evening has to be together.

And at the bottom, squeezed in under the grease spot:

The six suits can stay. They’ve been here since August. I’ve got used to them.

And under that, smaller still:

Breach of any of the above may result in immediate eviction and the loss of kitchen privileges.

He read the whole thing twice. Then he put the napkin down carefully on the counter, as if it were something that might break.

“Kitchen privileges,” he said.

“Yes.”

“That’s the worst penalty?”

“Don’t underestimate me.”

He looked at her. She was trying hard to look stern, and the corners of her mouth weren’t managing it.

“May I ask a question?”

“One.”

“Are you asking me to move back in?”

She looked at him across her counter. “Yes,” she said.

The smile went out of his face, and something quieter came into it.

“Properly?”

“Properly. Slowly. But properly.”

He looked down at the seven conditions and the suits.

He looked up. “I want you back in my life, Ren Hao, and more than dinner on Fridays and a kiss at a taxi rank. I want to wake up and hear you in my kitchen making coffee in my terrible machine. I want to complain about your meetings. I want you to complain that I leave cups everywhere.”

“You do leave cups everywhere.”

“There. You’ve started already.”

He laughed.

Her voice dropped. “But I don’t want what we had in August. I don’t want you to think being together means you’re responsible for everything. And I don’t want to feel managed in my own flat. Ever again.”

“I understand.”

“I need you to mean it.”

“I mean it.”

She studied his face. Then she pushed the pen across the counter to him.

“You’re supposed to sign it.”

“Where? There’s no room.”

“Write smaller.”

He laughed under his breath. He found a space along the right-hand edge, between condition five and the printed shop name, and wrote in his narrowest capitals:

I agree to all seven, and to the suits. I’ll ask when I’m not sure. I’ll listen when you say no. I’ll tell you when something’s wrong, instead of trying to manage it on my own. REN HAO.

She read it upside down. “Very formal.”

“I take contracts seriously.”

“Good. There may be penalties.”

“I assumed.”

She reached for the napkin. He held it back.

“Wait. I’d like to add something.”

“You’re not adding an eighth condition.”

“It isn’t a condition.”

He turned the napkin over. On the clean side, in the middle, he wrote one line.

8. We remember we’re on the same side.

She read it. All the teasing went out of her face.

“I’d like that one to bind both of us,” he said.

She looked at him. “Agreed.”

He wrote, underneath: Initialled by both parties. And his initials. And held out the pen.

She took it and wrote hers beside his. X.S.Z. Then she put the pen down.

“Done.”

He looked at it. Seven conditions on one side, a clause about suits, one shared promise on the other, two signatures and two sets of initials, on a greasy napkin from a noodle shop. It was worth more than any contract he’d signed in seven years.

“Now sign it properly,” she said.

“I’ve signed it.”

“Not with a pen.”

He looked up at her. She’d come round the counter. She was standing right in front of his stool, in his sweatshirt, with her hands on her hips.

“Contracts in my flat are signed with a kiss. It’s in the small print,” said Song-Zhu.

“I didn’t see any small print.”

“It’s very small.”

He stood up. She put both her hands on his face and kissed him slowly and thoroughly in her own kitchen, the way you’d put a seal on something with your whole weight so that it would never come off. He held her waist and kissed her back, and it went on so long the tea went cold on the counter, and neither of them cared.

When she drew back she kept her hands on his face.

“Signed,” she said.

“Witnessed,” said Ren Hao.

He folded the napkin into a small square and put it in his wallet, behind his cards.

“You’re keeping a napkin in your wallet?”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“So I don’t forget.”

“You’ve got a perfect memory.”

He looked at her. “I know. I don’t want to forget what it took for you to ask me back.”

She went quiet.

“Thank you for letting me try again,” he said.

She reached for his hand. “Don’t make me regret it.”

“I won’t take it lightly.”

“I know.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The first night wasn’t moving in. It was a trial. She insisted on the word.

He arrived at quarter past seven on Monday with one small overnight bag.

She opened the door and looked at it. “That’s all?”

“One change of clothes. A toothbrush. Nothing else.”

“No charger?”

“My phone’s charged.”

“No spare shoes?”

“No.”

“No suspicious boxes?”

“No suspicious boxes,” said Ren Hao.

She stepped aside. “You’re learning.”

He came in and stood in her hall and looked round. It was exactly as it had been. Shoes by the door. Books on the side table. A cardigan over the back of the sofa. The photograph that leaned. The smell of her washing powder. His slippers, still beside hers by the shoe cabinet, toes together, exactly where she’d put them on the nineteenth of September.

He looked at the slippers. He didn’t straighten the shoes. He didn’t pick up the cardigan. He put his bag down by the sofa and stood there.

She shut the door. “Well?”

“Well what?”

“How does it feel?”

He thought about it honestly. “Like being invited somewhere I missed.”

Her face went soft. “That’s a very careful answer.”

“I’m trying to be respectful.”

“You can be honest.”

“It feels very good,” said Ren Hao.

He looked at the kitchen. “May I make dinner?”

“Yes.”

“May I use your chopping board?”

“Yes.”

“May I...”

“Hao.”

He stopped.

She came over and kissed his cheek. “You can cook. You don’t need permission to breathe. Just don’t move anything.”

“I remember.”

He made noodles. She sat on the counter and talked about work and swung her feet. When she mentioned a review that had been moved to next week, he looked up.

“Do you want to talk about it?”

“Not tonight.”

“All right,” he said, and went back to the pan, and she watched him go back to it, and smiled to herself. It was such a small thing. It was so different.

Afterwards he washed and she dried, and he put each plate where she pointed even when he obviously thought another cupboard made more sense.

“You want to move that,” she said.

“I do.”

“But you won’t.”

“No.”

“Good.”

“May I say one thing?”

“Go on.”

“Your cupboard arrangement is objectively inefficient.”

She laughed out loud. “You’re welcome to leave.”

“I’ve only just got here.”

“Then behave.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At bedtime he put his bag down by her wardrobe and didn’t unpack it.

She noticed from the bed. “You’re not putting your things away?”

“You said a few nights. I thought I’d wait.”

“There’s a drawer. The bottom one.”

He looked at her. “Are you sure?”

“I’m sure.”

He opened it. It was empty. She’d cleared it on Sunday afternoon, after he’d gone home with the napkin in his wallet.

“You made room.”

“One drawer.”

“One drawer,” he said, and his voice wasn’t quite steady.

“Don’t get ambitious.”

“I wouldn’t dare.”

He put his folded things inside it, and took out his toothbrush, and stood holding it. It was the blue one.

She looked at it from the bed. He looked at her.

“There’s a cup on the shelf. Next to mine,” she said.

He went into the bathroom. She heard him put it down. She heard him stand there without moving. Then he came back, and didn’t say anything about it, and neither did she.

He got into bed and lay on his side facing her, and didn’t reach for her. She closed her book.

“What?”

“I’m looking at you being here.”

“In my bed.”

“In your bed. With my toothbrush next to yours. I’m allowing myself one minute to look,” he agreed.

She put the book down and moved across the bed into him. He put his arm round her. She could hear his heart, and it was a sound she’d known for eighteen months and hadn’t heard for four, and she lay with her ear against it and didn’t say anything a while.

“Hao?”

“Mm.”

“Don’t make this perfect.”

He looked down at her. “What?”

“Don’t try so hard that you stop being you. We’ll get things wrong. We’ll argue. I’ll leave cups everywhere. You’ll annoy me about something stupid. Some nights I’ll want to be on my own. Some days you’ll come home and not want to talk.”

“All of that’s fine.”

“We have to be allowed to be ordinary.”

“I want ordinary with you. I’ve wanted ordinary for four months more than I’ve ever wanted anything,” he said.

She lifted her face and kissed him without any hurry, the two of them in her bed with one drawer occupied and a blue toothbrush standing next to a white one on the shelf.

“Goodnight, sweetheart.”

“Goodnight,” she said, and fell asleep on his chest before he’d finished breathing out.

✦ ✦ ✦

The first week was a negotiation, an easy one, a small adjustment a day.

On the first morning he asked whether he could leave a second shirt. She said there were six suits in the wardrobe already and a shirt was hardly going to tip the balance.

On Tuesday he nearly moved her coffee machine. She caught him with his hands on it. He put it back without a word, and she kissed him for it.

On Wednesday he asked whether she wanted him to cook or order. She said she wanted to cook. He asked what she needed. She handed him a knife.

On Thursday she came home late and found him reading on the sofa.

“Long day?”

“Very.”

“Do you want food?”

She dropped her bag by the sofa, where she’d always dropped it, and he didn’t look at it. “Yes.”

“All right,” he said, and got up. He didn’t ask why she hadn’t eaten or remark on the hour. He made food.

On Friday he had a bad day. She heard it in how he shut the door. He stood in the hall with his coat on.

“Bad day?”

“Yes.”

“Do you want to talk?”

He thought about it. “Not yet.”

She patted the sofa beside her. “All right. Then sit.”
