He sat. She leaned on him. After a long while he said that one of the directors had disagreed with the restructuring, and had been partly right, which was the worst kind, and that he thought he’d made the wrong call on one of the people.

“Do you want to go through it?”

“Yes,” he said, which he had never once said to her before, about his own work, in eighteen months.

So they went through it. He explained. She asked three questions. On the third one he went quiet.

“That is actually useful,” he said.

“I know.”

“You’re very modest.”

“One of my many qualities.”

In bed he told her he’d been afraid she’d think less of him for getting it wrong.

She turned to him in the dark. “Why would I?”

“Because I usually know what I’m doing.”

“Hao. You’re allowed to be a person.”

He was quiet. “All right.”

On Saturday morning she found the napkin on his side of the bed, unfolded, flattened under his watch.

“You brought it out?”

He was in the bathroom. “I read it every night.”

“Every night?”

“Before I sleep. It takes forty seconds. It’s a good way to end the day.”

She looked at it. Two signatures. The ink had smudged a little at one corner, over the grease spot. She folded it again along his creases, and went and slid it into the inside pocket of the jacket he’d hung on the back of her bedroom door. He came out and watched her do it.

She straightened his collar, although he wasn’t wearing a shirt with a collar. “Somewhere safe. You’re officially allowed to stay another week.”

“Another week?”

“Don’t push your luck.”

He laughed. She reached up, and he bent, and she kissed him, and he held her and smiled against her mouth. She tapped the pocket with the napkin in it.

“That’s your contract.”

“I intend to keep every line.”

“Good,” she said, and kissed him again, longer.

When she drew back he looked at her the way he’d looked at her across the counter with the pen in his hand. A little disbelieving. A little overwhelmed. Very happy.

“What’s that face?”

He touched her cheek. “I used to think coming back would feel like getting back something I’d lost. It doesn’t. It feels like being invited somewhere new.”

“Maybe it is,” said Song-Zhu.

“Then I’m glad you asked me.”

✦ ✦ ✦

That evening, at the supermarket, he opened his wallet to pay, and the napkin was in it, folded small behind his cards. He unfolded it while the woman at the till scanned the eggs, and read it once, and folded it again.

Song-Zhu was by the fruit, holding up two oranges.

“Which?”

He looked. “The left one.”

“Why?”

“It’s smaller.”

“That’s not a reason.”

“It’s easier to carry.”

She stared at him. “You’re optimising oranges.”

“I’ll stop.”

She put both in the basket. “Good.”

They walked to the till together with the groceries on an ordinary Saturday, and when they got home they’d be going to the same place. Neither of them had moved into the other’s life and taken it over. They’d both made room, and this time they both knew where the edges were.

She moved the coffee machine herself on Sunday, eight centimetres to the left, and asked him what he thought. He said it was blocking the socket. She said she knew.

chapters.title: Her Terms
chapters.desc: She runs the schedule now, under a yellow duck. He loves it. Explicit in the training hangar after hours, against a wing strut, on his suit jacket.
chapters.epigraph: “My schedule’s optimistic.”
chapters.content:
Ren Hao discovered, on a Tuesday morning in February, that his girlfriend was a great deal more frightening with a calendar.

At work Song-Zhu had never been disorganised. She could rebuild a sequence of events from a field of wreckage, tell you to the second when a witness had changed one word in a statement, and spot a mismatched part number in a maintenance log while eating noodles over a sink. At home her schedule had always been a set of ambitious suggestions. She would get up at six, run, finish a report, ring her mother, and learn at last to pleat a dumpling. By nine she would have got up at half past seven, forgotten the run, found something new in a different case, eaten half a packet of crackers for breakfast, and decided dumplings were a problem for her next life.

He had once tried to help. He’d learned. Now she’d decided to help herself. He found the evidence on her fridge under a magnet shaped like a yellow duck: a sheet ruled into neat columns, some things highlighted, some crossed out hard. At the top, in her capitals:

FEBRUARY. OURS.
MON: work. Dinner together if neither of us is dead.
TUES: work. H. not to order food until S-Z has decided what she wants.
WED: walk. H. picks the route. No complaints about hills.
THURS: H. late meeting. Don’t wait up. (You can ring if you miss me.)
FRI: S-Z marking. Home by 8.30.
SAT: shopping, washing, and something. Isla on video, 9 a.m. Lima = 10 p.m. here. Both of us.
SUN: NOTHING. DO NOT MAKE PLANS. THIS MEANS YOU.

He took a photograph of it.

From the bedroom: “If you’re photographing my schedule I want royalties.”

“I’m documenting a historic event. A piece of paper that has successfully organised your life.”

She came to the bedroom door fastening her watch, hair wet from the shower, in black trousers and a white shirt, with the face of a woman who’d already done three things in her head before breakfast. “Don’t sound so impressed. It’s embarrassing.”

“Is it binding?”

“Legally?”

“Emotionally.”

“Unfortunately, yes.”

“Then I submit to your authority. Do I get a copy?”

“It’s my schedule.”

He pointed at the top of the page. “Ours.”

She looked at it, and at him, and came over and straightened the collar of his shirt, which didn’t need straightening. “Ours,” she agreed.

✦ ✦ ✦

By the end of the week he was its most devoted supporter.

She hadn’t become punctual. She still left the flat with one shoe in her hand and a piece of toast in her teeth, and lost her keys despite a bowl she’d bought specifically for keys. The difference was that now she decided before the chaos arrived: which evenings belonged to work and which to them, when she wanted company and when she wanted a book and tea and the silence she liked, where they’d eat. And she told him.

It was, Ren Hao found, an almost unbearably attractive quality.

On Thursday night she came into the kitchen and put a container on the counter in front of him. “Dinner. I acquired it. I went to the shop, chose it, paid for it, carried it. That’s practically cooking.”

It was the dish from the place by her building that he’d mentioned once, in March last year.

“You remembered.”

“I have an excellent memory.”

“You left your house keys in the freezer on Monday.”

“That was a test of the freezer.”

He put his phone face up on the counter and didn’t look at it again, and she looked pleased with herself and tried to hide it behind a glass of water. He loved that look, the small satisfaction of a plan going right. He’d spent so long trying to make her life easier that he’d nearly missed how much she liked deciding what it looked like. Now she was doing it, and he was happy to be told where to stand.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Friday the training hangar was dark after nine.

It was the one on the far side of the airfield where in October 2025 he’d worn a laminated VISITOR pass with more pride than anything he’d ever worn to a board meeting. The old regional jet from the scrapyard still sat under the high roof with half its panels off, and since the summer it had a wing beside it, a donated one, mounted on steel stands at working height with its insides labelled in yellow for trainees. Nothing in there was anybody’s evidence. It belonged to the authority and to whoever was learning.

The day’s course had finished at six. The instructors had signed out and the tools were in the cage. Song-Zhu had stayed to mark twenty-two written assessments from a class of fire crew, because she’d promised them back on Monday.

She looked up from the trestle table under the wing and saw him inside the side door with his suit jacket over his arm. “You’re not on the schedule. You were supposed to be at home watching the duck.”

“I was at home. I missed you. I signed in. The man on the gate said her again?”

“That’s a procedural reason, not an emotional one.”

He came across the concrete. “Would you prefer I’d come to learn about aviation safety?”

“Absolutely not.”

“To see my girlfriend?”

Her face changed. “That’s acceptable.”

She’d taken off her work jacket. Her sleeves were rolled up and her hair was knotted with a pencil through it, some of it coming down round her face, and there was a long smear of red marking ink on the side of her hand. He took her hand and rubbed his thumb over it, and it didn’t come off.

“Your schedule says you finished at half past eight.”

“My schedule’s optimistic. Three papers. And before you say it, that’s my fault. I know when I’m wrong.”

“I was going to say you’re beautiful.”

“That’s a completely different conversation.”

“I can have two.”

She laughed and marked the last three papers while he sat on an upturned crate and watched her, and then she took him under the wing to the main gear leg, where a strip of light from one of the high lamps fell across the floor.

“This is what I taught today. The inspection notes on that fitting don’t match the maintenance record. I put it there on purpose. Half the class didn’t see it. A woman from the airport fire station found it in four minutes.”

He asked a question when he didn’t follow, and she answered with the easy certainty of somebody who knew her work right down to the bolts.

“You’re very good at this.”

“I know. I’ve been told not to undersell myself.”

“By whom?”

“Me,” said Song-Zhu.

Far off, past the shut doors, a vehicle went along the perimeter road and was gone. The lamps lit the long curve of the wing and left the space underneath it in shadow.

“You’re staring,” she said.

“It’s turned into a habit.”

She came a step closer and reached for his tie, and he looked down at her fist round it. “Is this on the schedule?”

“No.”

“Should I be worried?”

“Very,” she said, and pulled him down.

✦ ✦ ✦

She kissed him the way she always did when she’d decided something, without asking permission of anything, including gravity. She held him by the tie and kissed him slow, then less slow, until his hand had come round the back of her waist.

When she let him go he looked like he’d been hit. “Have you finished work? You’re sure?”

“You’re allowed to ask. I’m allowed to say yes.”

He turned his head and kissed her palm, over the red ink, and kissed her again, and she walked backwards until her shoulders met one of the wing stands, a big angled leg of steel, cold through her shirt. She gasped against his mouth.

He stopped and looked round. “Are we on our own?”

“Everybody signed out at ten past six. The main doors are locked. You locked the side door behind you; I heard you, you always do. I’ve checked the cage. Nobody’s in before seven. And it’s a training airframe. We’re not touching anything we shouldn’t.”

“Did you plan this?”

“I planned to mark twenty-two papers and go home and have a bath. Then you came in with your jacket over your arm, and the schedule changed.”

“An amendment.”

“An urgent one,” said Song-Zhu, and took the jacket from him.

Dark grey, beautifully cut, made in another country by a man who’d measured him for an hour. She spread it on the clean padded mat under the wing that the trainees lay on to look at the undercarriage, and looked back at him over her shoulder.

“You’d better be careful with it.”

“You’re the one who put it there.”

He put his hands on her waist from behind and his mouth against her neck below the knot of hair, and she shut her eyes.

“Tell me what you want,” he said into her skin.

The teasing went out of her. What was under it was plain. “You. Here. Against that.”

He turned her round and put her back against the cold steel of the stand and held her there with the whole length of his body. She knew that look. She’d been missing it for months without knowing what she was missing.

“Do you know what I’m going to do?”

She shook her head, although she did.

He told her. He told her slowly against her ear while his hands did the first of it: her shirt, button by button, until it hung open, and his palm flat on her bare stomach, sliding up. He told her what he’d been thinking about since half past eight on the sofa. He told her what he was going to do to her against the stand and then on his jacket, in what order, how long he’d take over each part, what sound he wanted to hear her make. Then he began to do every one of those things exactly as he’d said.

He pushed her trousers down and she stepped out of them. He knelt on the concrete and kissed the inside of her knee, and her thigh, with the cold steel at her back and his warm mouth on her, and she put her head back against the stand with a dull clang and laughed, breathless, and then didn’t, because he’d put his mouth between her legs and she couldn’t do anything but hold the steel above her head with both hands.

“Hao...”

“Not yet. I told you the order,” he said against her.

He kept her at the edge until her legs shook and her knuckles were white and she was saying his name up into the dark under the wing. Then he stood and lifted her, and she wrapped her legs round him, and he held her up against the stand, her back to the cold and her front to him, and pushed into her in one long slow stroke, and the noise she made went up into the roof and came back.

He held still. “That’s the sound. That one.”

He moved, hard and slow, his hands under her, her arms locked round his neck and her heels in the small of his back. The steel rang slightly behind her every time and she could feel it in her spine and she’d never cared about anything less. She kissed him with her teeth. Somewhere above them the old wing creaked on its stands.

“Your jacket. You said. That’s next,” she gasped.

He carried her, still inside her, three steps to the mat, and knelt and laid her down on the silk lining and came down over her. On the jacket it was slower. Above his head the underside of the wing was grey with yellow labels on it, CONTROL CABLE RUN and DO NOT STAND, and she looked up past him and started to laugh again in the middle of everything.

“Do not stand.”

He looked up, and back down at her. “I’m very much not standing,” he said, and moved in her, deep, and her laugh broke in half.

He took his time, like he’d said he would. He watched her face and talked to her in that low voice, told her how she felt and what she looked like with her hair coming out of its pencil and red ink on the hand on his shoulder. When she got close he slowed further, and when she said please he kissed her and didn’t speed up at all, and when at last she came it went on and on, under the wing, with her fingers knotted in his shirt and his name going up into the dark. He followed with his face in her neck and a sound that was nearly hers.

Afterwards she lay on his chest and he looked up at the wing.

“You’re thinking about your jacket,” she said.

“I’m deciding whether it goes to the cleaner or gets retired with full honours.”

She laughed. When she shivered he reached for his shirt and stopped with his hand on it. “May I?”

She smiled with her eyes shut. “You may give me your shirt.”

She put her arms into the sleeves and looked down at herself.

“It’s too big.”

“That’s generally how my clothes work.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She checked the doors, and the cage, and turned off the lamps over the section they’d used, one by one. He waited by the door with his jacket over his arm, rumpled beyond saving, and didn’t hurry her once.

Outside the air was cold and clear. Mr. Yau was in the car by the gate, reading a paperback under the interior light.

“You asked him to wait?”

“I asked him to bring me. I didn’t tell him when to leave.”

Ren Hao knocked on the window. Mr. Yau wound it down, looked at the two of them, at the shirt, at the state of the jacket, and wound it up again without a word, and started the engine.

✦ ✦ ✦

At home she took the February sheet out from under the duck and wrote a new line under Friday in capitals.

FRI 9 P.M. HANGAR. (UNSCHEDULED. APPROVED RETROSPECTIVELY.)

He read it over her shoulder and had to hold on to the counter.

When he’d recovered he put his hands on her waist. “May I have a copy? So I know when I’m allowed to miss you.”

Her face went soft. “You don’t need a schedule for that. Miss me whenever you like. Tell me whenever you like. I might not answer straight away, but I’ll read it. You’re getting better at this.”

“So are you. Making room for me without making room for everything.”

She put her forehead on his chest. “I like having you here. Even when I make you live by a sheet of paper under a duck?”

“That’s the part I like best. I’m in love with you.”

“That isn’t a defence.”

“It wasn’t meant to be one,” he said, and kissed her, once, and then again.

His girlfriend was running the schedule now, and judging by the line she’d just written in capitals under a yellow duck, he suspected he was going to love February.

chapters.title: The Final Report
chapters.desc: A year on, the final report names the cause: a reused part signed off by a contractor. A hundred and eighty names read by the sea; he holds her hand in the front row. Then she times his toast at eleven minutes fourteen.
chapters.epigraph: “Eleven minutes, and fourteen seconds.”
chapters.content:
The report was published at nine o’clock on Monday the second of August 2027.

Song-Zhu had been awake since four. There’d been no phone call and no dream. She’d opened her eyes in the dark and known what day it was, the way she’d known a year before, just before the phone had rung.

She lay and listened to the flat: her fridge humming in E flat, a car below, Ren Hao asleep on his side with one arm bent under the pillow. After a while he stirred, and without saying anything reached across the bed and found her hand under the duvet.

“Is it still night?”

“Technically.”

“Then why are you awake?”

She looked at the ceiling. “Today.”

He was awake all the way at once. He didn’t say it would be fine, or that it would give the families answers, because some answers couldn’t give anybody back what they’d lost. She’d spent a year walking towards this morning, and she’d done it for a hundred and eighty people who’d never be able to ask the questions themselves.

He rubbed his thumb across her knuckles. “Do you want me to come?”

“Yes. You don’t have to stay all day. You’ve got work.”

“Raymond’s got work. I’ll stay as long as you want me there. If you need me to go, I’ll go. If you want me next to you, I’ll be next to you.”

She moved across the bed and put her face against his chest. “Next to me.”

He held her until the alarm went.

✦ ✦ ✦

The final report didn’t arrive with a fanfare. It went up on the authority’s website at nine with a summary for the public and four volumes of appendices: diagrams, metallurgy, maintenance records going back eleven years, the laboratory findings on a crumpled phone, and two hundred and twelve pages of analysis argued over sentence by sentence by people who knew one careless word could matter for twenty years.

Final Report: Loss of a passenger aircraft on approach, 2 August 2026.

Her team were in. Nobody was saying much. A printed copy lay squared off beside her keyboard. She’d read every word more times than she could count, and sat in rooms where an engineer, a lawyer and a pilot turned each sentence over, and turned it again. She knew exactly what was in it. That didn’t make it easier to open.

Ren Hao: I’m downstairs.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Don’t come up yet. I’ll come down when I’m ready.

Ren Hao: Take as long as you like.

At nine the page went live, and she opened it.

The first pages were what they always were. The aircraft, the flight, the crew. Rain, low cloud, a crosswind well inside the limits. The approach, the search, the recovery, the recorders. And then on page ninety-one, the section she’d written most of herself.

Maintenance and component history.

A component in the main electrical distribution system, under the cabin floor, had been fitted at the aircraft’s last heavy maintenance check eleven months before the accident by a contracted maintenance organisation. It had come through that organisation’s supply chain with paperwork showing it as new. It wasn’t new. It had been removed from another aircraft in another country five years before, at the end of its approved service life, refurbished by a supplier further down the chain, and given a new identifying plate. The records that came with it didn’t show where it had been. A traceability check required by the contractor’s own procedures hadn’t been carried out to the required standard. The contractor’s inspector had signed for the part. The airline’s system had accepted the signature.

At four hundred and twenty feet on final approach, at night, in rain, the part had failed. Normal electrical power went in less than a second. The recorders stopped. The cabin went dark. The crew were left over water at the lowest and slowest point of the whole flight with eleven seconds and almost nothing.

The report named the cause in plain words: a reused part, presented as new, signed off by a contractor whose checks had failed. It named the other failures too: traceability controls that relied on paperwork nobody could verify, a quality system that had been audited and passed twice, oversight that should have caught the mismatch and hadn’t. It didn’t pretend one man’s signature explained everything.

It didn’t blame the dead. On page one hundred and four, in a sentence she’d fought for in four separate meetings, it said the evidence didn’t support any finding that the flight crew had caused or contributed to the accident, and that after the loss of power their options had been extremely limited. In a footnote on the same page it said the captain had remained on the cabin address system to his passengers until the end.

She read the conclusions twice, and shut her eyes.

Dexter spoke behind her. “Boss? It’s live.”

“I know. Has the liaison team got the family packs?”

“Since eight. Translations checked against the report, not the press summary. Three times.”

“The press conference is at eleven. I want the technical people in the room for the supply chain, and nobody, nobody, is to speculate about who knew what at the supplier. That’s for the police and the regulator.”

She stood up. Her legs felt like she’d been sitting for a year. One year since four o’clock in the morning. One year since the sea had turned into a place where people waited for names.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Coming down.

✦ ✦ ✦

He was by the entrance in a dark suit with no tie, holding two coffees. He’d thought about flowers on the way, and decided they’d be an attempt to decorate a day that didn’t need it.

He looked at her face first, then at the report in her hand. “Black. No sugar.”

She looked at the lid of her coffee. “The cause is established. A part under the floor. It came off another aircraft at the end of its life, got a new plate and new paperwork, and went round again. The contractor signed it in. The airline took their word for it. And it wasn’t one signature. People should have seen it at three different points and didn’t. The report says that. They’ve waited a year. And some of them will read it and still not understand why it had to be their person on that aircraft.”

There was no professional answer to that, and he didn’t give one. “I don’t think they should have to understand it for it to be true. You haven’t handed them one word you couldn’t stand behind. That’s what you promised a little boy on a bed a year ago.”

Her mouth tightened. “I wanted it to be complete.”

“It’s as complete as an investigation can be. That doesn’t mean the loss is.”

He reached for her hand and stopped a few centimetres short. She saw him stop, and slid her fingers into his.

“There’s a briefing. And then there’s the sea,” she said.

✦ ✦ ✦

At the press conference she stood beside Director Kwan at the second microphone and answered for forty minutes. She explained the contractor’s role, the component’s history, how the metallurgy showed it worn beyond anything it should ever have been allowed to carry, how the paperwork had said otherwise.

A journalist asked whether the contractor had falsified the records on purpose.

“The report sets out that the documentation was inaccurate and that the contractor’s verification and sign-off failed. Intent, and criminal or civil responsibility, are for the police and the regulator. They have the report. Our job is to find out what went wrong so it doesn’t happen again.”

Another asked about the eleven seconds: could she say for certain the missing data hadn’t hidden a chance to prevent it?

“We can’t recover data that was never recorded. But the findings don’t depend on those eleven seconds. They rest on the physical evidence, the recorded data up to the loss of power, the cabin recording, and the wider technical analysis. And we know why the recorders stopped. That was the first thing we found.”

Her voice didn’t break once, and she didn’t let one finding be turned into a headline it couldn’t carry.

He’d sat at the very back, and hadn’t spoken to a journalist or gone near the families. He stood up when she came through the side door.

“Did I go too fast?”

“No.”

“You think everything I do is excellent.”

“You put the milk in the cupboard on Saturday.”

She laughed, small and tired and real, for the first time that day, and then looked down the corridor towards the family briefing room. “I’m not ready. But I have to go. Come with me.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The families had chosen the place for the memorial: a long grass headland two kilometres from the end of the runway, where on clear evenings you could see the approach lights come on across the bay. A hundred and eighty white chairs faced the sea. Under an awning a long table was covered with photographs, and on a wooden board at the front were a hundred and eighty names in plain black letters.

A woman in the third row held a child’s drawing against her chest. A man in the second had his hands knotted so tight the knuckles had gone white. Two old sisters sat side by side, shoulders touching, neither looking at the other. Some people had flown in from the other side of the world.

A woman from the families’ committee met them at the end of the rows. “Ms. Xu. The front row is for the investigators, and the families who asked to sit at the front.”

She looked at Ren Hao.

“And for your guest. Mrs. Ting asked. She said he was the one who rang everybody back.”

His face had gone still. They sat in the front row and she reached for his hand.

It began with a silence made of people: breathing, holding hands, trying not to make a sound. Then the names were read, one by one, each followed by a pause the length of a breath.

A year ago these names had been lines on a manifest marked UNVERIFIED in red. Then recovery records, identification forms, liaison notes. She’d learned to say every one of them properly. She’d learned which families wanted a call in the morning and which couldn’t bear the phone, which mothers wanted every technical detail and which needed it in small pieces with a long pause between. She’d been shouted at across tables, and thanked, and asked the same question a hundred ways, and she’d never once forgotten the report was about people, even when every sentence in it had to be about systems and parts.

Ting Ka-chun, seat 23C. In front of her Mrs. Ting sat upright with a blue exercise book closed on her knee.

Song-Zhu’s fingers tightened. He moved his hand so his palm lay flat against hers, and held it, just firmly enough that she couldn’t mistake it for anything else.

Two names before the end the reader said, “Captain Yuk Kam-fai,” and further along the front row a girl with a pale ribbon round her wrist put her hand inside her school blazer, flat against her chest, where she’d kept a folded piece of paper for eight months.

Song-Zhu couldn’t breathe. His thumb moved once across the back of her hand.

When the last name had been read nobody moved or clapped. A minute went by, and another, and a long way out across the bay the approach lights came on in a line on the water.

✦ ✦ ✦

Mrs. Yuk found her afterwards by the end of the awning. Bo-yee was taller than in December, her plait gone, her hair cut to the jaw.

“They let us read it last night. All of it. I didn’t understand half the engineering. But I understood the part about the component, and the footnote.”

Her voice shook.

“He checked the locks twice. He read the instructions before he built a shelf. He told Bo-yee that if you’re responsible for something you do it properly every time, even when nobody’s looking. He’d have been so angry. At least now I know it wasn’t anything he did.”

“I’m sorry this is what the answer cost,” said Song-Zhu.

Mrs. Yuk touched her arm. “You didn’t cause it. Do you know that?”

Song-Zhu didn’t answer.

“Thank you for staying with it. For a year.”

Bo-yee stepped forward. “Did you find out everything? Will you remember him, now it’s finished?”

Song-Zhu bent so their eyes were level. “We found out what caused it, and how all the failures happened. Some things the evidence couldn’t tell us, and I won’t pretend it could. And yes. Every name. For me that’s what finishing means.”

Bo-yee nodded, and her mother took her hand, and they walked away across the grass towards the sea. Then Ren Hao was beside her, and didn’t ask what had been said, and she held on to him.

Later, when she’d helped pack the programmes and checked that no photographer had come past the rope, she sat at last on a white chair in the empty front row. He put a bottle of water beside her and sat down.

“I thought there’d be a moment where I could put it down. I don’t think there is one. And now I have to remember what I did before.”

“You made a mess of my kitchen.”

She turned and looked at him, outraged. “Your kitchen was sterile.”

“It was efficient.”

“It was depressing. Perhaps I’ll make a mess of yours again.”

“I’ll take my chances,” said Ren Hao.

He didn’t tell her to go home or sleep or take a holiday. He sat beside her by the sea until the approach lights were all on across the bay, and when she was ready she stood up, and he held out his hand, and she took it.

✦ ✦ ✦

Twelve days later, on Saturday the fourteenth, he gave the toast.

He’d called it a small family dinner, and Isla, home from Lima since April, had believed him. It was the top-floor private room of a restaurant, a table for twelve with flowers down the middle and a seating plan in a silver frame by the door with eleven names on it, and he’d put himself between his sister and her inspector.

Song-Zhu sat opposite him and laughed less than anyone at the table. She ate slowly and listened, and once, when he was in the middle of a story, she reached across and straightened his collar without either of them stopping. At some point they argued about a soup he’d sent back once, and he appealed to Wei Long, who considered it and asked what his expectations had been, and when Hao said room temperature asked, “For a cold soup?”, and she heard Hao laugh like somebody had given him a present.

At a quarter past nine, with the dessert on the table and nobody brave enough to touch it, he stood up, and Isla told him to sit down, and he said, “Everyone,” and lifted his glass. Song-Zhu took out her phone and set it face up beside her plate and touched the screen.

“Are you recording this?” said Isla.

“No, I’m timing it,” said Song-Zhu.

She’d heard it twice already, in her kitchen, with him standing by the fridge and the duck holding a glass of water. On Tuesday it had been eight minutes. On Thursday, nine. He went back to Vancouver, to a four-year-old who fell off everything and got up and said she was fine, to French learned out of spite, to a stairwell on the thirty-second floor where he’d gone so nobody would see his face. Then October. He didn’t tell it well. He kept stopping. He said that for a day and a night nobody could tell him whether his sister was alive, and that the only person who’d answered every one of his calls was a police inspector he’d once tried to have investigated. Then he said the line about the plane ticket and the boat, which he hadn’t said on Thursday.

When the table had erupted and somebody at the far end had shouted about time, she looked at the screen. “Eleven minutes, and fourteen seconds.”

“Then I should go into public speaking.”

“No,” said the entire table.

Under the noise she leaned towards Isla. “He practised it on me. Twice. On Thursday it was nine minutes. He added the boat.”

Across the flowers he caught her eye, and she saw in his face that he’d seen her laugh, properly, all the way, for the first time since the morning of the report. It was the thing he’d wanted most out of the whole evening, and it hadn’t been in the speech at all.

chapters.title: His Firm, Her Rules
chapters.desc: He makes Raymond managing partner and comes home at seven. Isla gets engaged. At Eliana and Yu Chen’s wedding he takes the microphone uninvited, and lasts one minute fifty-two.
chapters.epigraph: “Go home, Hao.”
chapters.content:
The first time Ren Hao came home at seven, Song-Zhu thought something had happened to him.

It was a Monday at the start of September. She was in the kitchen deciding whether the greens in the fridge were still legally greens when the front door opened, and she looked at the clock on the oven, and at the door, and back at the clock. Seven o’clock.

He came in with his briefcase, wearing the face of a man who’d just pulled off an extremely complicated negotiation. “Hello. What’s wrong?”

“You’re home. It’s seven. Are you ill? Has the building closed? Has somebody sacked you?”

“Not today. Would you like me to go out and come in again?”

“I’d like to know why my boyfriend has appeared before I’ve had a chance to get cross with him for not appearing.”

He put his arms round her waist from behind and his chin on her shoulder. “Because I’ve decided to run my firm, instead of letting it run me.”

She was quiet, and then she smiled. “Good.”

“That’s all? I was hoping for a little admiration.”

When he reached for the chopping board she took it away and pointed at a stool. “You’re getting dinner. Sit. I want to look at you being home.”

✦ ✦ ✦

It hadn’t been decided in an afternoon. It had taken nine months, a long hard look at how the firm worked, and more than one conversation in which he’d had to admit out loud, to people who’d been waiting years to hear it, that being good at something didn’t mean doing every part of it himself.

The firm had grown up round his habit of taking responsibility. When a client was in trouble, he took the call. When a negotiation went bad, he walked into the room. When a decision would be unpopular, he made it himself so nobody else had to carry it. It had made him successful. It had also made him necessary in ways that had stopped being any use to anybody. Losing the airline had shown him that, more than the money had, and more than the winter: how much of the firm hung on a handful of relationships, most of them his, and how little authority had ever been allowed to reach the floors below him.

He spent the spring and summer rebuilding the shape of it, and the hardest part was the first: he stopped being where every problem went.

He made Raymond managing partner, with equity, a real share, and authority over the client portfolio and the operating decisions without waiting for anybody’s signature. Raymond, who’d taken the airline account at five past five on the morning of the second of August without being asked twice, and run it behind a wall for ten weeks, and never let a page of it cross onto Ren Hao’s desk. Raymond, who’d been right on the Saturday before the interim statement and been overruled and said nothing, and who argued with Ren Hao in meetings in a way that made junior staff go pale.

Raymond looked at the papers for nearly a full minute. “You’ve looked at what it costs you? The partnership deed?”

“Three times. Kong read it to me slowly. I’m not asking you to marry me. I’m asking you to run this place with me. As my partner, not my deputy.”

Raymond laughed at last. “That’s more complicated. Why now?”

“Because you’ve been doing the job for a year and a half, and the title ought to catch up.”

Raymond pushed the papers back across the desk, signed. “And because you want to go home at seven. Can you, though? Then you’ll have to stop answering email at eleven. Just a suggestion. Partner.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At the staff meeting the following Monday Ren Hao explained the new structure, who decided what, where problems went now, and made it plain that Raymond’s role wasn’t ornamental.

“From this month I’ll generally be leaving this building at half past six. We work in a business where some things can’t wait till morning. But there’s a difference between an emergency and a client who’s discovered that emailing at five to seven gets an answer at six minutes past. We’ve got very good people in this building. I intend to let them do their jobs.”

Raymond, beside him, folded his arms. “That would be a welcome development,” and the room laughed.

The first month wasn’t perfect. Clients rang just before seven and insisted it couldn’t wait. One Thursday he got as far as the lifts and turned back because he’d remembered something he hadn’t told Raymond, and Raymond, in his office with the door open, didn’t look up.

“No.”

“I haven’t said anything.”

“Email me. Go home, Hao.”

He went home, and the next evening he didn’t go back to the office after dinner, or the evening after that. He still took the hard calls and went to the meetings that mattered. But he’d stopped treating every delay as a failure of his own, and stopped believing the only safe hands in the building were his, and slowly the firm got better for it.

✦ ✦ ✦

Dinner at seven became a habit they both wanted. Sometimes she cooked and sometimes he did, and sometimes they ate noodles at the counter because neither of them could be bothered to lay the table. For the first fortnight he looked at the clock while they ate, a little astonished to be allowed to be there.

On the third Monday she found him in the kitchen with his phone, a client wanting an update.

“Does it need an answer tonight?”

“No. I thought I’d reply.”

She took it out of his hand and put it on top of the fridge beside the yellow duck, where he’d have to reach. “Dinner. Wash your hands.”

They ate. She told him about a colleague who’d written obviously defective in a draft report without one reference to support it.

“I asked him to define obviously. He said the defect was apparent. So I asked him to define apparent.”

He put his chopsticks down. “You’re terrifying.”

“I’m thorough. There are several differences,” said Song-Zhu, and took the best piece off his plate while he was laughing.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Monday the fourth of October, at half past eight, he got his phone down from beside the duck to ring his sister about nothing in particular, and she answered on speaker with the sound of a car round her.

“Hello.”

“Where are you?”

“In the car. Hao, I’ve got news.”

He went still. Song-Zhu, at the sink, turned round.

“What news?”

“I’m engaged.”

Silence. Then, with great care: “To whom?”

“Hao.”

“I know to whom. I want to hear you say it.”

“To Wei Long. He asked me at the airport. At the custody desk. Where we met.”

Ren Hao sat down on the stool slowly. Song-Zhu put her hand over her mouth. The silence went on so long that the car noise was the only thing in the kitchen.

“Put him on.”

“You’re on speaker.”

“Inspector. You proposed. Did you have a ring? Did you say anything? Or did you just hold it out like an exhibit?”

“I read her a statement.”

“A statement?”

“Three pages. Seventeen paragraphs,” said Wei Long.

The noise Ren Hao made was half a laugh and half something else, and it went on for some time, and Song-Zhu watched every guard on his face come down at once so that he looked about nineteen. When he spoke again his voice had dropped all the way.

“Good. I’m happy for you. Both of you. And don’t tell Mum and Dad, I want to tell them.”

“Hao, it’s six in the morning in Vancouver.”

“Then I’ll wait till seven,” he said, and hung up, and stood in the middle of the kitchen holding the phone with his eyes wet.

“She’s engaged. To the glacier. I tried to have him investigated.”

“I know you did.”

“I’m so happy I don’t know what to do with my hands.”

“Put them here,” said Song-Zhu, and took them, and put them round her.

He rang Vancouver at half past nine. She heard him through the bedroom door telling his mother about the seventeen paragraphs, and then telling his father, and then telling his mother again because she’d asked him to.

✦ ✦ ✦

Three weeks later, on Saturday the twenty-third of October, Eliana Lin married Dr. Wang Yu Chen across two back gardens in the Walled City.

The waist-high wall between the gardens had a gate in it now, framed in dark timber, with the old persimmon leaning over both. There were lights strung through its branches and along the wall, a little crooked, chairs in rows on the grass, three triplets in a row like exclamation marks, and an old woman in dark blue in the front row who used her walking stick, before anyone could stop her, to rearrange the chairs. Isla sat beside Wei Long in the second row with her ring turned inward so it wouldn’t take attention from the bride.

“You’re not taking the microphone,” said Song-Zhu at the side gate.

“Of course not.”

“You said of course not at Yu Chen’s party in May last year, and you picked him up off the ground.”

“Only a little way.”

The ceremony was short. When the celebrant got to and so by the authority, Yu Chen leaned in, and Eliana said “Wait—” laughing, and he kissed her before the celebrant got to the end of the sentence. The gardens erupted, and the old woman banged her stick on the grass, and Ren Hao made a noise they probably heard at the ferry pier.

“I was going to say you may now kiss,” said the celebrant.

Song-Zhu looked at the man beside her. His eyes were wet. “There isn’t any wind,” she said, before he could say it.

✦ ✦ ✦

After the meal, when the music hadn’t started yet, she found his chair empty, and shut her eyes, and opened them to see him at the little table by the gate saying something charming to the man with the microphone.

“Ren Hao,” said Eliana across the whole garden.

Ren Hao bowed to her and spoke into the microphone. “Good evening. First, I’d like to apologise to the bride. She asked me to behave. I’ve failed.”

Song-Zhu took out her phone and pressed start on the stopwatch, and he saw her do it across the grass and smiled. “I’ll be very quick. I’ve been timed before.”

The garden laughed.

“Three things. One: Yu Chen is the luckiest man in this city. I’ve met most of the men in this city, so I’m confident about this. Two: Eliana is terrifying, in the best possible way. She’s the only person I’ve ever hired who told me my coffee machine was a security risk and was right. And three: I personally have no idea how anybody survives six years in love with a woman who can take apart a bank’s security in an afternoon and still lose her phone in her own kitchen.”

Eliana balled her napkin and threw it at him across the grass. He caught it with one hand.

“See? Terrifying. To Eliana and Yu Chen. And to the gate.”

“To the gate,” said everybody.

He came back with Eliana’s napkin and sat down looking extremely pleased with himself, and Song-Zhu turned the phone round. 1:52.

“That’s the shortest I’ve ever been.”

“It’s the shortest anyone’s ever been. It’s a medical event. And it was perfect. It was all theirs. You didn’t mention your sister once.”

His face changed. “That one was hard.”

He made up for it later at the drinks table under the lights, with the triplets and the old woman and two of the Lin sisters round him: seventeen paragraphs, numbered, at a custody desk, and paragraph two had a statistic in it. Across the first dance Eliana spotted Isla’s ring and stopped dead in Yu Chen’s arms and mouthed WHAT, and Isla mouthed later.

Eliana came to their table twenty minutes after that, with Yu Chen behind her, and pointed at him.

“You took the microphone. At my wedding. After I specifically asked you not to.”

“Correct.”

“I can hate you and like the toast.”

“That’s fair.”

She turned to Song-Zhu. “Did you know he was going to?”

“I told him if he did I’d leave him there. Then I timed him.”

Eliana read the stopwatch and looked at Ren Hao with real respect for the first time all evening. “One fifty-two. You can come to the next one,” she said, and pulled her husband off towards the music.

✦ ✦ ✦

They got home before midnight. He hung his jacket on the right hook. She kicked her shoes off in the middle of the hall, and he looked down at them and stepped over them.

“You’re learning,” she said.

On the sofa, with a glass of water each, she asked him whether he missed it: being the one who had to be in every room.

He turned his glass. “Sometimes. I liked being needed. I liked knowing that if something went wrong I could walk in and take it on my back. Now I know the firm doesn’t fall down if I’m not in it, and it turns out I don’t either. I think I mixed up being indispensable with being good at my job.”

“You built something, and now you’re letting other people help you keep it. Raymond. Seven o’clock. That took more nerve than anything you did when you were in every room.”

She said it plainly, without teasing, and he looked at her like nobody had said anything of the kind to him in a long time.

“You helped.”

“I’m not running your firm.”

“No. You’re running dinner.”

She stood and held out her hand. “Somebody has to. Bed. And before you ask, it isn’t on the schedule. Not everything has to be.”

On top of the fridge beside the yellow duck his phone lit up once with an email, and then again, and neither of them looked.

chapters.title: Vancouver Again
chapters.desc: Vancouver again, with Isla and Wei Long. In the little study she asks the professors how to propose to their son. His mother cries again.
chapters.epigraph: “Make it a question.”
chapters.content:
He asked her on the eleventh of November, at the kitchen counter, with the yellow duck watching.

“Will you come to Vancouver for Christmas?”

She looked up from her noodles. “You asked me that two years ago, in the blue room, in the dark. You said you’d ask me every year. You didn’t ask me last year.”

“Last year, I wasn’t allowed to ask you anything,” said Ren Hao.

She put her chopsticks down and looked at him across the counter. “Yes. And ask me again next year.”

✦ ✦ ✦

A month later, on the eleventh of December, his sister’s engagement party took the whole top floor of a restaurant on the waterfront. He’d told everyone it was a few drinks. There were sixty people and a band of three in the corner by the window.

Song-Zhu spent the first hour by the drinks table with retired Superintendent Pun, seventy-five and upright, with a medal ribbon on his dark suit and a voice that had once cleared a riot without a loudhailer. Two of Hao’s colleagues had come up to him and retreated. She’d stayed, because he’d asked her what the approach lights at the airport were actually for, and nobody at a party had asked her a real question about runway lighting in her life. She’d got as far as the difference between approach lights and the edge lights when Ren Hao arrived, and a minute later he had an arm round Pun’s shoulders and both of them were laughing, and she never found out how it happened.

Then Isla got Wei Long onto the floor. He danced like a man following a procedure he’d been issued that afternoon, and the first person to film it was Ren Hao, and the second was Yu Chen, and the third was Pun, who said he was checking his camera worked. Song-Zhu didn’t film it. She watched Isla, under the fairy lights, telling him not to look at his feet, and saw the moment he stopped looking at them, and later she watched Ren Hao delete his video in front of his sister without being asked twice, because Isla had asked once.

✦ ✦ ✦

They landed on Christmas Eve in the dark of the afternoon. He hired a car and drove and talked the whole way: about the traffic, his father’s latest letter to a newspaper, Isla and Wei Long, who’d flown out the day before, and what Wei Long’s face had done at his first proper snow, which Isla had described on the phone in such detail that Ren Hao was furious he’d missed it.

“You’re going to be unbearable,” said Song-Zhu.

“I’m going to be delighted. Those are different.”

He was up the steps with two bags and a bottle of wine before she’d undone her seat belt, and in the hall before anybody had said anything.

“I’m here. I missed you,” he shouted, and hugged his sister, and lifted her off the floor.

“You saw me a week ago.”

“I missed you since then.”

Wei Long took the bag off the bottom stair before Ren Hao fell over it.

“Still carrying everyone’s things, Inspector? Good. You’re useful,” said Ren Hao, and went to find his father.

Song-Zhu came up the steps with snow on her shoulders and kissed Isla’s cheek. “He’s been like this since the airport. I nearly left him at a petrol station.”

Within an hour he was in the kitchen arguing with his father about a novel neither of them had finished. Wei Long had been given a box of decorations to carry upstairs. His mother found Song-Zhu in the hall taking her boots off, and hugged her, and smelled of oranges and cloves and the same soap as two years ago.

“Your face is cold. When did you last have something hot?”

“On the plane.”

“That doesn’t count,” said his mother, and held her at arm’s length and looked at her properly, at whatever was in her face that hadn’t been there two Christmases ago.

Song-Zhu didn’t know what it was. She suspected his mother did.

“You look better than the photographs. He still sends them every week. He thinks we don’t know he’s doing it on purpose.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She waited until the kitchen was loud, and went up the narrow stairs.

The little study at the end of the upstairs hall had its door half open, and his parents were both in it, his father at the desk with a pencil, his mother on the arm of the sofa with a cup of tea. They looked up.

“Professor? Both of you? Can I ask you something? It’s private.”

There was a pause. Then his mother, with great interest: “Oh?”

She came in and didn’t shut the door. The house was old and the hall narrow and she didn’t think about it. She stood in the small room with its books up to the ceiling, where two years ago his father had told her she’d made a life that asked a great deal of her and kept giving it.

“I want to propose to Hao.”

“Oh, that’s lovely,” said his mother, and her voice had gone thick.

“I didn’t know if you’d think it was strange.”

“Why would it be strange?” said his father.

She made herself look up. “Because we stopped. Last year. For four months. I couldn’t say it to him, and he couldn’t stop trying to fix it, and we stopped. We’re better now than we’ve ever been. I know I want my whole life with him. But I don’t want him to think I’m asking to make up for that. I don’t want it to be an apology. I want it to be the start of something.” Her voice went lower as she said it.

His mother said, “Then don’t make it an apology. Make it a question.”

“I thought that’s what a proposal was.”

“You’d be amazed how many people turn it into a lecture on their own history,” said his father, dryly.

His mother put her tea down and took both Song-Zhu’s hands. “Ask him, because you want to begin something. Not because you want to prove you’d have chosen differently. He’ll hear the difference. He’s always heard everything.”

Then she began to cry, the way she’d cried in the kitchen two years ago with her hand on the mend in Song-Zhu’s knee, and his father said something gentle to her, and Song-Zhu laughed, wetly, in the middle of the study with both her hands held, because she’d said it out loud to someone and nobody had told her it was strange.

Out on the landing a box of Christmas decorations had been put down on the table at the top of the stairs. Nobody noticed it. Later it was gone, carried to the end of the landing by a man who’d heard every word through a half-open door, and who never told anybody.

✦ ✦ ✦

When his mother had found her a tissue and herself three, Song-Zhu said, “How? That’s the bit I don’t know.”

“Start with him, not the ring.”

“Nothing big. He thinks he wants big. He doesn’t. He likes things with a reason. And he remembers everything.”

His mother nodded. “Above all the things people say when they think he isn’t listening. He was like that at four. Give him somewhere that belongs to the two of you. He’s loud, and he thinks everybody should know everything, but the things that matter most to him he’s always kept very close. And he’ll want to have asked first. He’ll get over it.”

His father looked up from the desk. “What does he love most about you? If you had to guess.”

She thought about a list in a coat pocket, eighty-one lines and one missing. About a man on a beach in the dark saying I’ll remember it instead of taking a picture. About him at her door with his bag, and her mouth not able to make the shape.

“My voice. When I finally use it.”

His father nodded once, like she’d answered an exam question correctly. “Then use it. And you’re both terrible at secrets. I’d do it before Easter.”

✦ ✦ ✦

In the morning there were pancakes, and his father reading the paper, and Ren Hao stealing from her plate, which she allowed, watching his mother over her coffee and turning the advice over in her hands.

A moose biscuit had been placed, without comment, on Wei Long’s plate.

“Your friend,” said Isla.

“It’s not my friend.”

“You ate its brother.”

He broke off an antler.

His father looked over the top of the paper. “I hope you’re enjoying the biscuits, Inspector. Your future mother-in-law has made eighty.”

Isla choked on her coffee. Ren Hao looked up with his mouth full. His mother didn’t look up at all.

“It’s only a matter of time,” she said serenely, and passed Wei Long the syrup.

Wei Long ate the moose in three exact pieces, antlers first, and said it was good, which made his future mother-in-law go pink with pleasure and bring him two more from a tin nobody had seen her open. Song-Zhu looked round the table at all of them: his father pretending to read, Isla with crumbs on her jumper, Wei Long on whom something like a smile was slowly happening, Ren Hao wiping his eyes. Two years ago she’d sat here for the first time with his mother’s good napkin on her knee and been asked about the structure of accident investigations. Now she was part of the noise.

✦ ✦ ✦

After breakfast he took Wei Long out into the garden. The snow had come down all night, deep and dry, the hedges bulked into walls and the old tree at the end bowed under it. She watched from the kitchen window with Isla.

Ren Hao bent down, slowly, and gathered a handful of snow. Wei Long watched him do it with the expression of a man who’d interviewed a great many suspects and recognised the look.

“Oh no,” said Isla.

The snowball hit Wei Long in the middle of the chest. He looked down at the white star on his coat, and up at Ren Hao, and didn’t move for three full seconds. Then he bent without any hurry, gathered a great deal more snow than Ren Hao had, packed it, and threw it with such precision that it took Ren Hao in the side of the head and knocked him into the hedge.

Isla shrieked. Song-Zhu put her coffee down.

“That’s the hedge. He did that to me. I won.”

“Do you have evidence?”

“Your father ruled on it,” said Song-Zhu, and went to get her coat.

✦ ✦ ✦

That night they were in the blue room across the landing from Isla’s, which his mother had given them both without discussion this year. He came up behind her at the window where she was watching the snow come down past the glass.

“You’ve been thinking.”

“About Christmas. The first one I was a guest.”

He kissed the side of her neck where the chain was, the silver snowflake she’d worn every day for two years. “And this one?”

She turned round in his arms. “This one I’m family.”

He looked at her for so long she almost said it. She felt it come all the way up, will you marry me, there in the blue room with the snow behind her, and it would have been easy. She didn’t, because she wanted to ask him properly, in her own voice, somewhere that was theirs, and as a question, not because a window and the snow made it easy.

She smiled instead. “Take me to bed.”

“The board by the wardrobe still creaks.”

“I know. I’m not going to be quiet this year,” said Song-Zhu.

She wasn’t. Across the landing, in a bed too small for one, his sister and her inspector had spent an hour being so silent that the springs were the only thing that had spoken, and they lay in the dark and listened to the board by the wardrobe creak, twice, and Isla put her face in Wei Long’s shoulder. Downstairs a literature professor and a political scientist looked at the ceiling, and then at each other, and his mother put her hand over her mouth and laughed until the bed shook without making a single sound.

✦ ✦ ✦

On their last morning she walked with his mother along the snowy path at the end of the street, in gloves, this time.

“Look at you. He’ll be relieved.”

“He’ll find something else.”

The snow squeaked under their boots.

Song-Zhu watched her breath go white. “I haven’t decided when, or where, but I think I know how. Are you happy? That it’s me who’ll ask, and not him?”

His mother stopped in the middle of the path. She took Song-Zhu’s gloved hand. “My son spent his whole life thinking love meant being responsible for everything. If he got there first and arranged it all, nothing bad would ever happen to anybody he loved. He was a very serious little boy. Even happy, he was worrying about what came next. He worries still. Of course he does, he’s mine. But he laughs at the table now. He comes home at seven. He lets other people help him. You didn’t turn him into somebody else. You showed him he doesn’t have to carry it all on his own.”

“He showed me the same thing.”

“I’ve watched you both do it for two years. So yes, I’m happy, and happiest of all that it’s you who’ll ask. He’s spent his life asking everybody else whether they’re all right. Somebody ought to ask him something, for once.”

At the gate she let go of Song-Zhu’s hand. “Don’t make it perfect. Make it yours.”

chapters.title: She Proposes
chapters.desc: A week after Isla’s registry, she proposes at the flying club fence, in her own voice, out of her father’s recorder. He says yes at volume. The next morning he buys her a ring anyway.
chapters.epigraph: “I want to listen to you asking me.”
chapters.content:
On Saturday the twenty-fifth of March, a week before, his sister married her inspector at the registry.

It was a small room with blond wood and a window onto a courtyard tree, and Wei Long had checked every box on every form twice. There were two witnesses, Yu Chen and Song-Zhu, and Isla carried a bunch of ranunculus she’d bought herself on the way because she’d wanted to choose them. Ren Hao stood at the back in his good suit and didn’t say a word through the whole of it, which Song-Zhu later described to his mother as the most moving thing she’d ever seen him do.

Afterwards there was dinner for twenty at a long table in a back room above a noodle shop by the harbour that did the best fish in the city, because Isla had refused anywhere with a seating plan. Her parents had flown in. Her father read a poem in the northern language that he’d translated himself, and got two lines wrong, and nobody minded. Her brother gave a toast that went on long enough for Song-Zhu to check her watch twice.

The second time, he caught her doing it, across the table, and grinned at her, and carried on. She didn’t tell him what she’d been thinking about. She’d been thinking about a little silver recorder in her bag, and a new card in it, and a field.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the following Wednesday she asked him not to make plans for Saturday morning, and added, casually, don’t ask why. On Friday night she told him to wear something comfortable. On Saturday the first of April he opened his eyes at eighteen minutes to seven and found her sitting on the end of the bed, fully dressed, looking at her phone with the concentration of a woman defusing something.

She jumped. “Go back to sleep.”

“You’re up. You’re dressed. You told me not to make plans and to wear something comfortable. You’re doing something.”

“I’m allowed to do things without reporting them to you.”

“Absolutely. Should I bring a jacket?”

“Yes.”

“Passport?”

“No.”

“Phone?”

She kissed him and got up. “Unfortunately. We’re leaving in an hour.”

He lay looking at the ceiling after she’d gone. From the way she’d kissed him, he suspected he was going to like it.

✦ ✦ ✦

She drove, and agreed to answer three questions. He spent the first on whether she’d had breakfast, and the second on whether they were going anywhere that needed security clearance, and she told him to stop watching films. He spent the third on whether he ought to be nervous.

She looked at him at a red light. “A little.”

He spent the next ten minutes trying to work out whether she was joking. Then she turned off the coast road onto a lane he knew, and he sat up.

He knew the hedge, and the windsock, and the low brown clubhouse with its corrugated roof and faded sign, and the long hangar at the end with its doors rolled half open, and the wire fence round the apron. The flying club airfield. Where on the fourteenth of June 2025 a twin turboprop had come down in the field and she’d pulled its recorder out of the tail cone, and the next afternoon he’d turned up at that fence in a three-piece suit with lunch for twelve.

She parked by the fence, in the same spot.

“Song-Zhu. Why are we here?”

“Come with me. Please.”

That did it. She put her hand on his on the gearstick. “Happy April Fool’s Day, by the way.”

“You’ve brought me to an airfield on the first of April. Should I be concerned I’m about to be sold?”

She laughed, and got out.

✦ ✦ ✦

It was a bright, cool morning. Two people were pushing a small high-winged aircraft out of the hangar by hand, and a man in a club jacket was making tea in the clubhouse doorway, the same man, Ren Hao was nearly sure, who’d made tea for everybody three years ago like it was his sacred duty. At the far end, by the fuel bowser, a little two-seater was running its engine up. The man with the tea nodded to her as if he’d been expecting them.

She walked across the apron like she owned it. This was where she was most herself: the smell of fuel, the low mechanical hum, the flat open concrete and the sky.

“Am I going to have to sign something?” he said.

“Possibly.”

She stopped by the wire. On the other side the grass had grown back long ago, but if you knew where to look there was still a faint line of slightly different green where the turf had been relaid. He knew where to look.

She took something out of her coat pocket and held it up between them: small and silver, the size of a cigarette lighter, with a speaker grille and a scratch across its face.

He went completely still. “That’s your father’s.”

“There’s a new card in it. I put it in on Tuesday. His are in the case at home. This one’s mine. I wanted you to hear my voice come out of it, because that’s where I keep the voices that matter most to me.”

She pressed play.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Ren Hao. If you’re hearing this, I’ve managed to get you somewhere without telling you why. Well done me.”

It was her voice, and it was different: recorded on purpose, alone at her kitchen table at night, without any of the interruptions and teasing and small changes of face he was used to watching while she talked.

“I thought about a restaurant. But you’d spend the whole evening watching to see if I’d eaten enough. I thought about home, but you’d start the washing-up halfway through. So I’ve brought you to the fence. Where you turned up in a three-piece suit the day after you met me, with lunch for twelve people you’d never heard of, because I’d said in a voice note that I hadn’t eaten. And where I looked at you over the wire and thought: oh no.”

He laughed once under his breath. His eyes had gone bright.

“I know what we’ve been through. I know there were months when loving each other wasn’t easy. We had to learn to stop mistaking looking after for managing, and how to stay when it was hard without making the other one feel trapped. I couldn’t say it for a year and a half, and you waited, and didn’t make me.”

A breath on the recording.

“I’m not asking because we survived something, or to apologise for last year, or to promise that nothing hard will ever happen again. Your mother told me not to make it any of those things, and your father told me not to make it a lecture on our history, so I’m going to stop that part now.”

He laughed out loud and wiped his eyes with the heel of his hand.

“I’m asking because I love the man you are. The one who comes home at seven. The one who remembers everything, and can make a room go quiet without raising his voice, and still argues with me about whether oranges go in the fridge. The one who learned he doesn’t have to carry everything. Who lets me be inconvenient, and seems to like it best when I am. I want the ordinary days and the hard ones. I want to travel with you and argue with you and come home to you and keep finding out who we turn into. I don’t need you to always know what to do. I want you to keep choosing me, and I want to keep choosing you, in my own voice, out loud. So, Ren Hao...”

The recording clicked off. She lowered the little silver recorder and said the rest herself.

“Will you marry me?”

✦ ✦ ✦

For a moment he didn’t move. He looked at the recorder, at the fence, at the faint line in the grass, back at her. She’d imagined this a great many times. In some versions he laughed at once. In one he asked whether she’d checked the weather. She hadn’t imagined his mouth opening and nothing coming out.

“Hao?”

“You’re asking me?”

“No. I’m asking the man with the tea,” said Song-Zhu.

He laughed all the way down, and his face broke open into a smile so wide that her own eyes filled.

“YES!”

It went right across the apron. The man with the tea turned round. The two people pushing the high-wing stopped pushing. Somebody by the bowser looked up from the two-seater.

He reached her and took both her hands, recorder and all. “Yes. Song-Zhu. Of course. Yes.”

“You’re shouting. The tower heard you. It’s four kilometres away.”

“Good,” said Ren Hao, and pulled her into his arms and held her so tight her feet came off the concrete.

When he put her down a tear went down his face, and she wiped it off with her thumb.

“You’re the one who brought a recording. In his recorder. Did you make it on your own? How many evenings?”

“That’s classified. Three. Four if you count the one where I deleted everything and cried and ate a whole tin of your biscuits.”

“I wondered where those went.”

Then he looked alarmed. “Wait. Did I just say yes without a ring?”

She took a small box from her other pocket. Inside was a plain band, white gold, with nothing on it but a fine line round the middle. She’d chosen it in January in a shop on Tanner’s Row, after Vancouver, and gone back for it three times before she let herself buy it. She held out her hand for his, and slid it on, and it fitted.

“Hello, fiancé.”

He made a sound between a laugh and a breath. “Hello. Fiancée.”

He kissed her hand, and stopped.

“You don’t have one.”

“I didn’t need one. I was the one asking.”

His face did something determined. “Tomorrow is Sunday. I’m noting it.”

“Don’t start.”

“I’m not starting. I’m noting.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He was quiet a while. “I’d thought about asking you. Very frequently. One idea involved a booking. One involved a trip. One involved a carefully planned evening at home with an agenda.”

“Typed?”

He looked at the ring on his hand. “Laminated. But I’m glad you asked. You chose where, and the words, and his recorder. You made it yours. And I got to say yes.”

The two-seater had finished running up. Its engine note changed, and it came trundling down the taxiway towards them, a small bright plane with two people in it going out to the end of the grass strip on an ordinary Saturday morning. She heard it first, and smiled against his mouth, because he was kissing her again.

“Your audience.”

“I don’t care,” he said, and kissed her on the apron with the plane going past, not carefully, not one bit carefully, with relief and laughter and the astonishing knowledge that the person he loved had just asked him to spend the rest of his life with her, out loud, out of her father’s recorder. She held the front of his jacket in her fist. He held her face in both hands. The pilot raised one hand from the cockpit in a cheerful salute and neither of them saw it.

When they stopped he kept his forehead on hers. “Can I tell everybody? Now? My mother? Isla? Raymond?”

“Not Raymond before your sister.”

He took his phone out, and stopped, and put it back. “One minute first.”

“I love you. I’m going to say it so often you’ll get sick of it,” said Song-Zhu.

“I’ve waited for it for eighteen months. I’m owed,” said Ren Hao, and hugged her so hard she told him she needed her ribs.

✦ ✦ ✦

His mother answered on the second ring. It was Friday evening in Vancouver.

He held his left hand up to the camera. His mother looked at it, and at his face, and at his hand.

“Oh. Oh, my goodness.”

Song-Zhu leaned into the picture. “Hello, Professor. I asked him.”

“She asked. I said yes. Very loudly. The tower heard,” said Ren Hao.

His mother began to cry, and his father’s face came over her shoulder and went soft. “You did it before Easter,” he said to Song-Zhu.

“I did it on April Fool’s Day.”

“Even better. Nobody will ever believe him.”

His mother took the phone back. “Thank you, sweetheart. For asking him. Somebody finally asked him.”

Isla answered on the move, with wind in the phone, looked at his hand, and screamed.

“SHE ASKED YOU? I’ve been married a week, and you’ve—Wei Long. Wei Long. Look at his hand.”

Wei Long’s face appeared beside hers. He looked at the screen, and then at Song-Zhu, a second longer than he needed to, and something moved at the very corner of his mouth.

“Congratulations. It was a good question,” he said.

Song-Zhu didn’t know why he’d said it like that. She’d think about it for years.

“Did he cry?” said Isla.

“No,” said Ren Hao, at the same moment Song-Zhu said yes, and Isla shrieked, and he told his fiancée she was supposed to be on his side.

“I am. I’m on the side of the evidence.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The man with the tea came across from the clubhouse with two cups and put them on the bonnet of her car without a word, and went back. Ren Hao tried three times to photograph her with the hangar behind her and cut off half her face, then blurred it, then put his thumb over the lens.

“You run a firm on three floors.”

“I’m emotionally compromised.”

She took his phone and took one picture: their two hands on the wire of the fence, his ring catching the light, the field behind, blurred, with its faint different line of green.

“Why here?” he said later, at the car.

“Because it’s where you first came to my work. You stood at that fence with twelve lunches and didn’t ask me one question about what I was doing. You just wanted me to eat. And because it was the first time I thought it. Oh no. Right there.”

“And his recorder?”

“Because that’s where I keep the voices I can’t lose. Now mine’s on it, next to his.”

He couldn’t say anything for a while. “Can I have the recording? Not today. I want to listen to it when I’m not standing here trying to understand that I’m engaged.”

“You want to listen to yourself being proposed to?”

Ren Hao looked at the field. “I want to listen to you asking me.”

✦ ✦ ✦

On Sunday morning he was gone when she woke. There was a note on the pillow in his capitals.

GONE OUT. BACK BY TEN. NOTED, NOT STARTED.

Before ten he came into the bedroom with two coffees and a small box, sat down on the edge of the mattress, and held it out on his palm without opening it.

“You said you didn’t need one because you were the one asking, and that’s true. So this isn’t an answer. You’ve had my answer. The tower had it. This is so I can look at your hand and know.”

One clear stone, small and perfectly plain, the kind of thing you wouldn’t notice across a room and couldn’t stop looking at from close to.

“I went back to the shop on Tanner’s Row. The man remembered you. He said you’d been in three times about a man’s band in January and cried in his shop once, and he’d been hoping someone would come in for the other one.”

She put it on. It fitted. “You couldn’t wait one day.”

“I waited eighteen months for three words. I wasn’t waiting a day for this,” said Ren Hao.

chapters.title: Loud Wedding
chapters.desc: The loudest wedding of the year. Isla’s toast in three languages. The wedding night, quiet, explicit: forty-two buttons, and then every button of the three-piece suit.
chapters.epigraph: “Ask what?”
chapters.content:
By nine o’clock on the morning of Saturday the twenty-first of October 2028, Ren Hao had been told to calm down six times.

The first was Wei Long, his best man, by text, one word: Breathe. The second was his mother, in the hotel corridor, holding his face in both hands. The third was Isla, who rang specifically to say: “If you start managing this wedding, I will have you removed from it. I’m a consular officer. I know people. Wei Long’s got handcuffs.”

The fourth was Raymond, who found him in the ballroom counting chairs. The fifth was his father, who looked at his son over his glasses and said only, “Son. Sit.” And he sat.

The sixth was Song-Zhu. He wasn’t supposed to see her, and four separate people had told him so. But just before nine she’d sent one line, Come to the door of the bridal room. Don’t come in. Knock twice, and he’d gone, and knocked twice, and the door had opened four inches and her hand had come out through the gap, palm up.

“Phone. Isla says you’re on the seating plan again,” said her voice.

“My aunt’s been moved twice and nobody’s told her.”

“Hao.”

He put his phone in her hand. The hand and the phone disappeared. He heard her put it in a drawer and shut the drawer.

Her hand came back out through the gap, empty this time. “Hold it.”

He held it. Through four inches of door, with his best man’s text in his head telling him to breathe, he held her hand and she held his, and neither of them could see the other.

“Are you nervous?”

“No.”

Silence from the other side.

“Yes.”

“Good. I’d be worried if you weren’t.”

“Are you?”

Her fingers tightened. “I’m marrying the loudest man in the city at three o’clock in front of three hundred people, including your entire firm and half of mine and a dumpling woman who’s insisted on doing the food for the evening. Of course I’m nervous. Go away. Go and sit somewhere your father can see you.”

“I love you.”

A pause, through four inches of door. “I love you. Out loud, in a hotel corridor. Now go away before Isla finds you,” said Song-Zhu.

He let go, and went, and sat in the ballroom where his father could see him, and didn’t count a single chair.

✦ ✦ ✦

It was the loudest wedding of the year. Even people who’d been to louder ones agreed.

The hall was on the top floor of a hotel above the harbour, glass on one side, the water and the ferries laid out behind them and the airport lights coming on in the distance as the afternoon went. There were three hundred chairs. They were all full before three, because people kept arriving who’d been told it was half past.

On the groom’s side, his parents in the front row, his mother already with a handkerchief. Isla in dark green, married since March, with Wei Long standing at the front beside Ren Hao with the expression of a man guarding a doorway. Raymond, and Kong, and Ruby, who’d been given a seat in the third row and a corsage and had cried since the lift. Joyce, with Momo on her knee in a small bow tie. Mr. Yau, in a suit nobody had ever seen. Eliana and Yu Chen. Auntie Au, who refused to sit down because she had to keep checking on the kitchen, which wasn’t hers.

On the bride’s side: her mother in pale blue, holding a framed photograph of a man in a pilot’s shirt squinting in the sun. Her aunt. Her cousins. Mabel, out of retirement for exactly one afternoon. Dexter, in the shirt he’d bought in May 2026 for a party that never happened. Director Kwan and half of the fourth floor. And, at the end of the second row, a woman in grey with a silver chain at her throat, and beside her a girl of fourteen with her hair cut to the jaw and a pale ribbon round her wrist, who had written to Song-Zhu in August to ask if she could come, if that isn’t strange, and to whom Song-Zhu had written back, it isn’t strange at all.

At three o’clock the doors at the back opened. Song-Zhu walked in with her mother.

She’d said she didn’t want anyone to give her away, because nobody owned her to give. And then, in July, her mother had said, low, at her kitchen table, Then may I just walk with you? Your father would have wanted to. Let me do the half he’d have done. And so they walked together, arm in arm, down the long aisle between three hundred people. Her mother carried the photograph in her other hand against her chest.

Ren Hao, at the front, saw her, and stopped breathing.

She was in plain heavy white silk that moved when she did, high at the neck, long sleeves, a long line of tiny covered buttons all the way down her back that she knew he’d seen in the fitting photograph Isla had shown him by mistake and that he’d been thinking about for three weeks. At her throat, on its fine chain, the silver snowflake. On her left hand, the one clear stone.

Wei Long, beside him, put one hand flat between his shoulder blades for a second.

“Breathe,” said Wei Long, low.

Ren Hao breathed.

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t make it through his vows. He’d written them himself, in three drafts, and torn up the typed copy, because Song-Zhu had told him in August that if he brought a laminated card to his own wedding she’d marry Dexter.

He got as far as “I promise to ask,” and stopped, and couldn’t go on, and three hundred people waited, and his sister put her hand over her mouth in the front row.

Song-Zhu, opposite him, took both his hands.

“Ask what?” she said, gently. In front of everybody.

“Everything. Before I decide it for you. For the rest of my life. And I promise to keep saying it. Out loud. Every day. Even when you’re tired of hearing it,” said Ren Hao.

“I won’t get tired of hearing it. I waited a year and a half to be able to say it back. I’m not getting tired of anything,” said Song-Zhu.

Then she said hers. She had no paper. She said that for her whole working life she’d listened to the last minutes of strangers, and that it had taught her one thing above everything else: that people never say the most important thing at the end. They say it in the ordinary minutes before, about coffee, about homework, about coming home on Thursday. She said that she wasn’t going to wait for the end to say anything to him, ever. She said she’d say it in the ordinary minutes, every day, in her own voice.

“I love you. That’s the first one. There’ll be a lot more,” she said.

The celebrant pronounced them married.

He didn’t wait to be told he could kiss her. Neither did she.
