They met in the middle, and three hundred people stood up, and the sound that went up in that glass room was enormous, applause and shouting and somebody whistling through her fingers, which Eliana had apparently learned to do, and above all of it, cutting through, unmistakable, a single voice from the front row shouting THAT’S LOVE!, which turned out to be Ren Hao’s own mother, who had heard about it from Isla and had been waiting two years to use it.

Ren Hao, mid-kiss, started laughing so much he had to stop kissing his wife, and put his face in her neck, and shake.

✦ ✦ ✦

The speeches went on into the evening.

Wei Long gave the best man’s speech. It was four minutes long and dry. A sentence about Ren Hao trying to have him investigated made the fourth floor applaud. It ended with him looking at Song-Zhu with something at the corner of his mouth, and saying, “She asked a good question. He gave a good answer. That’s all a marriage is,” and sitting down, and Song-Zhu still not knowing why he’d said it quite like that.

Her mother didn’t give a speech. She stood up with the photograph and held it up, so that everyone could see the man in it squinting in the sun, and said, in Chinese, “He’d have said your shoes were too shiny,” to her son-in-law, and sat down again, and Ren Hao had to leave the room for three minutes.

His father read a poem he’d translated himself out of the northern language over the summer, about a bird that flies a long way and lands somewhere it doesn’t know, and finds it’s home. He didn’t look up from the page once, and when he’d finished his wife was crying so much that Isla had to give her own handkerchief. And then Isla stood up.

She gave the toast in three languages. In English first, about a brother who’d organised her entire childhood and once tried, at fifteen, to timetable her friendships. Then in French, which nobody could follow but Song-Zhu’s cousin, who’d studied in Lyon and laughed so loudly by herself that everybody laughed at her laughing. And then, at the end, in Chinese, for Song-Zhu’s mother, about a woman who’d walked her daughter halfway up an aisle so that a man who couldn’t be there could do the other half. And two hundred people cried.

Song-Zhu, at the top table, didn’t time it. She’d left her phone in the drawer with his.

✦ ✦ ✦

Later Eliana took the microphone without asking anyone. Everyone had known she would.

“Two and a half years ago this man walked up my stairs, announced himself to the entire building, told the woman downstairs he loved her, and tripled my fee. Last year he took the microphone at my wedding uninvited and was quite good.” She held the microphone up at him across the room.

“One minute fifty-two, Ren. Beat it.”

“I’m not making a speech at my own wedding. I’m the groom.”

“Coward,” shouted three hundred people, and he stood up, laughing, and took it from her.

He looked at his wife across the room. “I spent two years trying to keep her safe. I organised and booked and watched everything. And she told me she was my girlfriend, not my equipment. She was right. So I stopped. And she came back. And then she asked me. Out of her father’s recorder. On an airfield. On April Fool’s Day, which nobody here believes, and I don’t blame you. I’ll never organise anything again. That’s a lie. But I’ll ask first. I love you, Song-Zhu. Thank you for asking.”

He handed the microphone back to Eliana.

Eliana read it off the screen. “Forty-one. Disgusting. Best client I ever had, Ren,” and the whole room heard Ren Hao laugh until he had to hold the back of a chair.

✦ ✦ ✦

It was nearly one in the morning when they got to the room. It was the top floor of the same hotel, a corner, with glass on two sides and the harbour and the airport laid out below in the dark like a map of their whole life: the cargo terminal, the authority’s low building on the perimeter road, the far side of the field where the training hangar was, and further out, past the end of the runway, the dark headland, and the sea.

The door closed, and the noise of the wedding stopped like somebody had shut it in a drawer with their phones.

She stood by the window in the white silk with her back to him, looking out. He stood by the door in his three-piece suit, the charcoal one, the one he’d worn to a French restaurant with candles on the thirteenth of June 2025, which he’d had let out by a centimetre at the waist in September and taken back in by a centimetre in October.

Without turning round she said, “The buttons.”

“I know.”

“There are forty-two.”

“I know. Isla showed me the photograph by accident.”

“Isla doesn’t do anything by accident.”

He crossed the room. He stood behind her. He put his hands on her shoulders, on the silk, and then he began.

He undid them one at a time, every single one, forty-two of them from the nape of her neck to the base of her spine, and his hands weren’t steady, and he didn’t hurry, and with each one the silk opened a little further and more of her back came bare under his hands in the light from the harbour. She stood absolutely still and let him. Halfway down he stopped, and put his mouth against her skin between her shoulder blades, and left it there, and she shut her eyes.

When the last one was undone the dress slid off her shoulders by itself and went down onto the carpet round her feet with a sound like a long breath out. She stepped out of it. She turned round.

“My turn,” she said.

She’d undone this suit before. On the floor of his office, on the thirty-second floor, against the glass, when she’d been angry and wanted him and had sent a waistcoat button skittering under his desk. That had been fast, and this wasn’t.

She took his jacket off and laid it over the chair as carefully as he’d ever laid anything. She undid his tie and slid it out from under his collar. Then the waistcoat. The buttons on the waistcoat she undid one at a time, from the top, the way he’d undone hers, and she didn’t look at the buttons once. She looked at his face. When it was open she put both her hands inside it on his shirt, flat on his chest, and felt his heart going under them like something trying to get out.

Then the shirt, and the cuffs. She took the cufflinks out, the silver ones his father had worn at his own wedding in 1996, and put them on the windowsill side by side. She pushed the shirt off his shoulders and it fell and she stood and looked at him in the light from the window, and he let her look.

“Every button,” he said. His voice had gone.

“I’ve wanted to do that since the soup,” said Song-Zhu.

He laughed, low, and she kissed the laugh, and then neither of them laughed.

It was quiet. After three hundred people and three languages and a dumpling woman shouting at a hotel kitchen, it was the quietest thing either of them had ever done. He laid her down on the bed by the window and came down over her, and neither of them said anything after that. They’d said all of it in front of everybody.

He kissed her slowly all the way down: her throat above the snowflake, her breasts, her ribs, the soft skin inside both wrists where the pulse was, the way he’d kissed one wrist in a snowy garden at minus twelve, her stomach, the inside of her knee. She held his head in her hands and breathed his name, once, and he came back up her body and looked down at her.

“Mrs. Ren,” he said, hardly a sound.

“I’m keeping mine.”

“I know you are. I’m just saying it once. In here. Where nobody can hear.”

“Then once,” she said, and smiled, and pulled him down.

He came into her slowly and stayed there without moving, looking at her.

The harbour lights moved on the ceiling. A ferry went across the water far below, small, lit up. Out past the end of the runway, the approach lights were on in a line on the sea.

He began to move so slowly it was almost stillness, deep and long, his forehead against hers, their breath mixed. She wrapped her legs round him and held his face and looked at him the whole time, and he looked at her, and the wedding rings on both their hands touched every time he moved, a tiny sound, metal on metal, again and again, the only sound in the room.

She came without a sound, with her eyes open, holding his face, trembling under him, saying I love you into his mouth with no voice at all. He followed her a moment later, without a sound, holding her so tight that she couldn’t tell any more where she stopped, his face in her hair, his whole body shaking.

They lay afterwards tangled in the dark, with the harbour moving on the ceiling.

“Mrs. Ren,” he said again, eventually, into her hair.

She made a small sound. “That was twice.”

“Then thank you for marrying me.”

She lifted her head. “You said yes. Very loudly. You frightened a man with a cup of tea.”

“I regret nothing. Today was perfect,” said Ren Hao.

“It was loud. Your sister cried four times. Your father read a poem about a bird. Your mother shouted that’s love at our wedding.”

“That, I didn’t see coming. And you were there.”

She lifted her head again. “Of course I was there.”

“I know. I just wanted to say it. Out loud. In the ordinary minutes. You said that was where the important things go.”

She looked at him in the dark. “Goodnight, husband.”

He smiled into her hair. “Goodnight, wife.”

Outside the city went on. Inside there was only his breathing, and her hand flat over his heart, and two rings that touched each other every time either of them moved. For once in his life Ren Hao had nothing left to organise, and Song-Zhu had nowhere else she needed to be.

chapters.title: The Recorder on the Shelf
chapters.desc: Epilogue. Her father’s recorder on a shelf, and a new one beside it with their wedding on it. She plays it; he kisses her through it. A fourth card.
chapters.epigraph: “You’ll find out in twenty years.”
chapters.content:
The shelf had been her idea. He’d suggested a cabinet. A proper one, with a glass door, and a seal, and a small sachet of silica gel in the corner to keep the damp off, and possibly a lock. He’d sent her a link to one in May, at eleven at night, from the sofa, while she was sitting on the other end of the same sofa.

She’d looked at the link. Then at him.

“It’s a recorder. Not the crown jewels,” she’d said.

“It’s your father’s recorder.”

She’d gone quiet. And he’d heard it himself, at once, the thing she’d heard: one more careful, loving, expensive way of organising something that didn’t need organising. He’d closed the link.

So they’d bought a shelf. One plank of plain oak, on two brackets, which he’d put up himself on a Sunday in June in the small study at the back of the flat they’d bought together in the spring, with a spirit level, three times, until she’d taken the spirit level away from him and hidden it in the washing machine.

It hung between her bookcase of work and the window. There were two things on it.

The first was small and silver, the size of a cigarette lighter, with a speaker grille and a scratch across its face. Her father’s. Its corners were worn pale. Inside its little black zip case, which lay open beside it, were three cards in a row in the grey foam. His last one, from a Tuesday in 2019, with the coffee terrible and her name on it twice. The one she’d made at twenty with the air traffic recording, which she hadn’t played since December 2025 and didn’t need to. And hers. The one with a proposal on it, made at a kitchen table over four evenings, and a tin of biscuits.

The second was newer. Black, flat, with a small screen. The authority’s own make, one of the field recorders they gave to new investigators, which Dexter had borrowed from stores without a form and set on a stand at the front of a glass room on the top floor of a hotel above the harbour, on the twenty-first of October 2028, and pressed record, and forgotten about for five hours.

It had their wedding on it. All of it. Everything from please take your seats to Auntie Au shouting at the kitchen at eleven at night.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Sunday the twenty-first of October 2029, a year to the day, he stood in the study doorway and looked at it.

“You’re staring,” said Song-Zhu, from the desk.

She was in one of his old shirts with the sleeves rolled up and her hair knotted with a pencil, going through photographs on her laptop. The first year. She’d been meaning to sort them since February.

“I was looking.”

“At the shelf?”

“Yes.”

“What’s wrong with it?”

“Nothing.”

She went back to the screen.

He came and stood behind her chair. “Do you think it wants a little light? Over it? Just a small one.”

She shut her eyes. “Hao.”

“I’m asking.”

“Why?”

“So you can see them.”

“I can see them perfectly well.”

“At night?”

“At night I’m generally asleep.”

He bent and put his mouth on her hair. “Fair.”

She reached up and caught his hand on her shoulder and held it. Then she turned the laptop off.

“Do you want to hear something?”

He looked at the shelf. “Which one?”

She smiled. “The wedding.”

✦ ✦ ✦

It had taken them most of the year to get through it, because they kept stopping.

They’d stop at the moment the doors opened and three hundred people stood up, and there was a sound on the recording like a wave going over. They’d stop at Wei Long saying breathe, which neither of them had known the recorder had caught. They’d stop every single time at his mother shouting THAT’S LOVE! and laugh until one of them had to leave the room. In March they’d got as far as Isla’s French and then stopped for six weeks, because work had eaten everything. In June they’d got as far as the poem about the bird, and she’d cried, and he’d had to turn it off.

She took the black recorder down off the shelf now and sat on the little sofa under the window with it in her lap. He sat beside her.

“Where did we get to?”

“The bird. In June,” he said.

“Not the bird. I can’t do the bird today. Something else.”

She scrolled back. All the way back, to the start of the afternoon, before the speeches. To the vows. She pressed play.

The room came out of the little speaker. Three hundred people, settling. A chair scraping. A cough. Somebody’s child saying is it now? and being shushed. Momo, somewhere near the third row, sneezing. And then his voice.

“I promise to ask.”

On the recording, a silence. A long one. It went on, and on, in the study, the way it had gone on in that glass room in front of three hundred people while he stood and couldn’t.

Beside her, on the sofa, a year later, he shut his eyes.

And then, out of the speaker, her voice, gentle, close to the microphone, because she’d been standing right in front of it and he hadn’t known:

“Ask what?”

“Everything. Before I decide it for you. For the rest of my life. And I promise to keep saying it. Out loud. Every day. Even when you’re tired of hearing it.”

“I won’t get tired of hearing it. I waited a year and a half to be able to say it back. I’m not getting tired of anything.”

She stopped it there.

She sat with the black recorder in her lap. “I’d forgotten I said that. The year and a half.”

“I hadn’t.”

“You wouldn’t have. You don’t forget anything.”

“I forget where I put my spirit level,” said Ren Hao.

She laughed, wetly, and looked at him, and then she pressed play again, and her own voice came out of the speaker into the little study, saying her vows to him, about listening to the last minutes of strangers, and how people never say the most important thing at the end, they say it in the ordinary minutes before. He didn’t wait for the end of it.

He turned on the sofa and took her face in his hands and kissed her, while her voice was still going on the recording, while she was still promising him, out loud, a year ago, in a glass room above the harbour, that she’d say it every day in the ordinary minutes. He kissed her through every word of it. Slow, and deep, and not carefully, with her own voice going on in her lap between them, until the recording had got to I love you, that’s the first one, there’ll be a lot more, and three hundred people roared, and his mother shouted, and she was laughing into his mouth so much she couldn’t kiss him back.

“You’re supposed to listen,” she said, when she could.

“I was listening.”

“You were kissing me.”

“I can do both. I heard every word. I’ve heard every word every time.”

“You’ve heard this eleven times.”

“Twelve. I listened in the car on Thursday.”

She stared at him. “On your own?”

“In the car park. Under the building. Where Ruby can’t see me.”

She put her forehead against his and laughed until she had to wipe her eyes.

✦ ✦ ✦

Afterwards she got up and went to the shelf and stood looking at it with the black recorder in her hand.

“There’s room,” she said.

“For what?”

She turned round. “For one more card. In my father’s. There are four slots in the foam. There are three cards.”

He looked at the little zip case lying open on the shelf. She was right. Four slots. One empty.

“What would go in it?”

She thought about it. “This year. Us. No wedding or proposal or anything. Just what’s ordinary. What we’d want to hear in twenty years, when we’ve forgotten.”

“You never forget anything either.”

“I’ll forget what this felt like. Everybody does. That’s the only thing I’ve ever learned from the recorders, Hao. It isn’t the words people lose. It’s what the ordinary minutes felt like. What their voice was like on a Tuesday, about homework.”

He was quiet.

She took a new card out of the drawer of her desk, where she’d bought a packet of them in March and never said. She took her father’s recorder down off the shelf and put the new card in the fourth slot of the foam, and then into the recorder, and pushed until it clicked. She came back and sat down beside him, and held it between them.

“You first,” she said.

“Me?”

“You’re the one who talks.”

“I don’t know what to say.”

“That’s a first,” said Song-Zhu, and pressed record.

The little red light came on. He looked at it.

He cleared his throat. “This is Ren Hao. It’s the twenty-first of October 2029. It’s a Sunday. It’s raining a bit. I’m sitting in the study with my wife. I put a shelf up in June. She hid the spirit level in the washing machine. I found it in August.”

She covered her mouth.

He looked at the red light again. “I’m married to Xu Song-Zhu. She kept her name. I’m glad. I’d have liked to keep mine too, but nobody gave me the choice.”

He looked at her.

“I love her. Even though she leaves her shoes in the hall and says they’re resting. I love the way she listens. I love that she listens to the worst minutes of other people’s lives and still comes home and asks me about my day. I love that she taught me to ask. I still don’t ask enough. I’m working on it.”

He paused.

“I hope that when we listen to this again, we’re still doing the same things. Dinner at seven. Arguing about soup. Finding each other at the end of the day, in whatever room. That’s all.”

He gave it back to her. She held it.

She held it close. “This is Xu Song-Zhu. Same day. Same rain. I’m married to Ren Hao. He thinks everything needs a system.”

“Most things do.”

She ignored him. “I love the way he comes home. I love the way he laughs when he forgets to be serious. I love that he learned to ask before fixing things, and that he still tries to fix them anyway, and then stops halfway, and looks at me, and asks. I love that he puts his phone on top of the fridge next to the duck without being told now.”

She looked at him, and her voice went down.

“And I hope that when we listen to this again, we’ve still got each other, and that we kept changing together and kept choosing it.”

She stopped. Then she leaned closer to the microphone.

“Also. He still owes me an apology for the kitchen drawer.”

He stared at her. “What kitchen drawer?”

She pressed stop.

“Exactly,” said Song-Zhu.

“What kitchen drawer?”

“You’ll find out in twenty years.”

He laughed and pulled her into his arms on the little sofa, and she let herself be pulled, still holding her father’s recorder in her hand, with the fourth card in it.

She put it back on the shelf, carefully, in its case, beside the black one.

The old one. The wedding one. Four cards in the foam now. Her father’s voice on a Tuesday. A controller calling a callsign. Her voice asking a question out of a dead man’s recorder on an airfield. And this. Two people on a sofa, on an ordinary Sunday, in the rain.

Behind them the shelf stood in the grey light from the window, keeping what they’d chosen to keep: the minutes that would matter in twenty years, when the rest had gone soft.

✦ ✦ ✦

At seven they ate at the kitchen counter, because neither of them could be bothered to lay the table on their own anniversary, and argued about whether the rain counted as weather or just Sunday. He did the washing-up. She dried, and put each plate where she wanted it, and he didn’t say a word about the cupboards, although she could see him wanting to. When she put the big bowl in the cupboard by the fridge, which was objectively the wrong one, he closed his eyes for a second and then opened them and said, “Good choice,” and she laughed out loud and nearly dropped the colander. A year married, and he still did that: caught himself halfway, and looked at her, and let it go.

Afterwards he went into the bedroom and shut the door, which he never did, and she heard the wardrobe open and close twice, and the zip of a bag. She stood in the hall with a tea towel over her shoulder and narrowed her eyes at the door.

At quarter past eight she was in the bathroom taking her earrings out when her phone buzzed on the edge of the basin.

Ren Hao: Wear something comfortable.

She looked at it in the mirror, and then she laughed out loud, alone, in the bathroom, with one earring in her hand. She knew that line. She’d written it herself, on a Friday night the spring before last, to a man who’d lain awake trying to work out what she was planning.

Song-Zhu: Define comfortable.

Ren Hao: Something you can move in.

Song-Zhu: Am I being kidnapped?

Ren Hao: No.

Song-Zhu: That’s exactly what a kidnapper would say. You’re in the next room.

Ren Hao: Happy anniversary, sweetheart.

She put the earring down beside the other one, and went to find out.

chapters.title: Quiet
chapters.desc: A whole evening when he doesn’t say anything, and she loves it.
chapters.epigraph: “Don’t get too used to this.”
chapters.content:
It was raining, a steady drizzle on the windows so even that it had stopped being a sound and become part of the room.

It was a Friday in November 2029. Song-Zhu had got home first, at six, and found a parcel on the mat addressed to both of them in his mother’s handwriting, with a customs label that said BAKED GOODS (HOMEMADE) and, underneath, in smaller letters, please be careful with the antlers. She’d put it on the kitchen counter unopened, because it had both their names on it, and gone to the sofa with the novel she’d begun three days ago and had been carrying round the flat ever since, from the kitchen to the bath to the bed and back, like a cat with a toy.

He came in at seven, wet, because he’d walked from the station without an umbrella. He’d been given one in December 2026 by a woman outside a building, and had never quite forgiven umbrellas for being necessary. He saw the parcel, and read the label, and laughed once under his breath, and left it where it was.

Then he was in the kitchen. She could hear him: a cupboard, a drawer, the kettle going on, a spoon on the side of a mug, twice, the way he always did it, like the mug might not have heard the first time.

Usually by now he’d have said something. About the rain, or her book, or whether the parcel was a bomb or a biscuit. He’d have come to the kitchen doorway with something he’d just remembered, or a thing he’d been saving for her since lunchtime, or a story about Raymond and a client and a printer.

Ren Hao was a man who shared things. Observations, plans, complaints, small funny details, information nobody had asked for, at length, with his hands. He loved out loud. He always had. He’d said I love you to a dumpling woman on a staircase and to Joyce’s dog and to a security consultant across a boardroom table at three in the morning, and he’d said it to her at volume in a restaurant in September 2025 until half the room applauded.

There’d been a time when she’d thought the silence of a flat without him in it would be the hardest thing she’d ever have to get used to. The kitchen went quiet. She turned a page.

He came in, in a dark T-shirt and soft trousers, with his hair still damp, and put a mug down on the low table by her elbow. Tea, exactly how she liked it. She looked up. He smiled. She smiled back.

Then he sat down beside her on the sofa and didn’t say anything.

✦ ✦ ✦

At first she thought he was tired. Raymond had been in Singapore all week and a client had been on fire, figuratively, and he’d spent most of Thursday in a room he’d described in a text as full of men who think volume is a strategy, which she’d found funny, given the source. He’d been home late on Thursday, and had texted to say so, and had apologised for it twice.

She watched him out of the corner of her eye. He leaned back into the sofa, drank some tea, put the mug down, and looked out of the window at the rain. He didn’t ask anything or tell her about Thursday. She went back to her book.

His phone buzzed once on the table. She saw Raymond’s name come up on it. He looked at it, and turned it over, and didn’t tell her what it said, and she found she didn’t need to know.

A few minutes went by, then ten, then twenty. She read the same paragraph twice, because she’d become aware of him: there beside her, warm and familiar, his knee against hers now and then when he shifted, his hand lying open on the sofa between them, palm up, not asking for anything.

She waited for him to start talking. He didn’t. She turned a page she hadn’t read.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the end she put the book down open on her knee and looked at him properly.

He was looking at the rain. His face was perfectly calm, and there was nothing in it that needed anything from her. It wasn’t tiredness, quite, or sadness, or a problem waiting to be noticed. He looked like a man on a sofa on a Friday night with his wife, watching the rain, with nowhere on earth he’d sooner be and nothing he needed to say about it.

She’d spent her whole working life listening to silences. On recorders. In rooms full of families. In the gap at the end of a callsign. She knew every kind there was: the silence before something terrible, and after it, the silence of people holding something back, and of people who’d run out. She’d never in her life heard this one.

He turned his head and found her looking, and raised his eyebrows slightly. What? She shook her head. Nothing. He smiled, and went back to the rain.

She closed the book and put it on the table and moved along the sofa into him. He lifted his arm without being asked and she went under it and put her head on his chest, and he put his hand on her back and left it there.

She could hear his heart, slow, and the rain, and their fridge, the old one from her flat, humming in E flat in the kitchen. A car went by below with its tyres hissing on the wet road. The kettle ticked as it cooled. His thumb moved once on her back, and stopped. That was all, for an hour.

✦ ✦ ✦

At some point she realised she was going to fall asleep there, on him, and didn’t mind.

She spoke into his T-shirt, hardly louder than the rain. “Hao. You haven’t said anything for an hour.”

His chest moved under her cheek: a laugh with no sound in it.

“I’m not asking. I’m telling you I noticed. I used to think that if somebody went quiet it meant something was wrong. That they were angry, or there was something I was supposed to say and hadn’t, or that something had gone and they were waiting for me to notice. This is the first time I’ve ever heard it mean nothing at all. Just: here,” she breathed in rain and soap and him.

His fingers moved slowly in her hair.

She lifted her head. “Do you know what I mean?”

He looked down at her and nodded, once.

“Good.”

She put her head back down. A moment later she lifted it again.

“You can talk tomorrow, though. Don’t get too used to this.”

His whole chest shook under her with silent laughter.

✦ ✦ ✦

When they went to bed he still hadn’t said anything. He turned out the lamps one by one. He checked the door twice, because he always would. He brought her water. He lay on his back and she lay against his side, and he took her hand and laid it flat on his chest, over his heart, and held it there under his own.

She felt his wedding ring under her fingers, cold for a second and then warm.

He wasn’t holding anything back from her. He wasn’t disappearing into himself, the way he had for one terrible day in June 2026, or waiting for her to guess what he needed. He was tired, and happy, and there, and for once in his loud life there was nothing in him that needed saying, because it was all already known.

Just before sleep took her she heard him whisper, so low it was nearly not a sound, “Love you.”

She smiled without opening her eyes. “Love you too.”

He didn’t say anything else, and she fell asleep smiling, in the quiet they’d spent four years learning to trust.

✦ ✦ ✦

He started talking at eight minutes past seven the next morning, before she’d opened her eyes.

“The thing about Thursday is that there were eleven of them, and they’d all been told by somebody that if you say a number loudly enough it becomes true,” said Ren Hao, to the ceiling, at full volume.

She put the pillow over her face and laughed into it.

He told her all of it. He told her in bed, and then in the kitchen while the coffee machine did its noise, with his hands, walking up and down between the counter and the window in his bare feet. He did the man at the end of the table who said with respect before everything that wasn’t. He did Raymond on the phone from Singapore at two in the morning, saying Hao, I’m in a hotel bathroom, I’m not your conscience. He did the moment on Thursday afternoon when he’d stopped talking in the middle of the room, and waited, and let the silence go on until the loudest of them had heard his own number back in the quiet and gone pink.

He pointed his coffee at her. “I learned that from you. You leave the gap. People fill it with the truth.”

“Sometimes they fill it with nonsense.”

“Then you’ve learned something too. It’s very efficient.”

She sat on the counter with her feet swinging and her mug in both hands and listened to forty minutes of it, every word, and loved every word, the way she’d known the night before that she would. The flat was full of him again. It was full the way it ought to be. Halfway through he stopped and made her toast and put it in front of her without asking, then caught himself, and asked, and she said yes, and he carried on exactly where he’d left off, mid-sentence, as if the toast had been a comma.

At the end of it he looked at the parcel. “Shall we?”

They opened it together. Inside, in layers of greaseproof paper, were twenty-four moose-shaped biscuits, every one with its antlers intact, and a card in his father’s square hand.

Your mother made eighty. The Inspector has been sent forty. These are yours. She asked me to tell you that she’s listening for the quiet, and is told it’s good this year.

Song-Zhu read it twice. “How does your mother know about the quiet?”

He looked at her, and said it plainly, the way he said true things now. “I rang her on Tuesday. I told her that some evenings I come home and don’t want to say anything, and it frightens me, because I’ve never not wanted to say anything. And she said: then don’t. See what she does. You put your head on my chest and fell asleep.”

She stood across the kitchen with the card in her hand and looked at him, and let the quiet stay.

Then she took a moose out of the box, and broke off one antler, and gave it to him, and ate the rest herself, and he laughed until he had to hold on to the counter.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the afternoon she rang Vancouver herself, which she’d never done without him in the room. He was in the shower. His mother answered on the third ring in a dressing gown, with her reading glasses pushed up into her hair and a pencil behind one ear, and his father somewhere behind her saying who is it? in the voice of a man who already knew.

“The biscuits came. With their antlers,” said Song-Zhu.

“All of them? The Inspector’s lost two in the post. Isla sent a photograph. She says he’s taken it personally.”

His mother looked at her through the screen, the long careful look she’d given her in a hall in 2025 with snow on the mat. “And?”

Song-Zhu knew exactly what she was being asked. “He didn’t say a word for an hour. And then he talked for forty minutes this morning about a man who says with respect.”

His mother put her hand over her mouth, and her eyes did what they always did, and behind her his father said, “I told you,” with deep satisfaction, and came into the picture holding a cup of tea.

His father settled into the chair beside her. He looked at Song-Zhu over his glasses. “He was a very quiet small boy. Nobody believes it. His whole first year at school he said almost nothing, and sat at the window and watched, and his teacher sent a letter home about it. Then one day in the second year he put his hand up, and he hasn’t put it down since. It seems he’s found somewhere to put that first year back.”

She didn’t trust herself to answer that, so she held up a moose instead, and his mother laughed until her glasses fell out of her hair.

When he came out of the shower she was still on the sofa with the phone in her lap.

“Who was that?”

“Your parents. Your father says you were a quiet little boy.”

He stood in the doorway with a towel round his neck and looked genuinely betrayed. “I was thinking. There’s a difference. I was gathering material.”

“For thirty years?”

“It was a great deal of material,” said Ren Hao, and came and sat down beside her, and took the phone out of her lap and put it on the table, and for a while, with the rain still going, neither of them said anything at all.

She’d loved, from the first night, the way he filled every room he walked into with his voice. She loved it this morning, every loud minute of it. And she’d found out last night that she loved, just as much, the evenings he didn’t need to fill one, and that she didn’t either.

chapters.title: The Sister Who Set Them Up
chapters.desc: Isla’s pink file, ten candidates and an eleventh who handed her the bigger half of a cereal bar in a hospital stairwell. He says no; she books a French restaurant anyway.
chapters.epigraph: “Then you need the bigger half.”
chapters.content:
Isla Ren had a file, a real one, made of card, and it was pink.

Her brother would later argue that the colour alone should have disqualified it from being taken seriously. Isla would argue that his opinion was irrelevant, since he wasn’t the one doing the work. On the front, in her round hand, it said PROJECT: GET MY BROTHER A LIFE, and underneath, smaller, Confidential. Don’t let Hao see this.

Unfortunately Hao had a key to her flat, and she’d left it on her dining table.

✦ ✦ ✦

The project began in April 2025, at lunch, when she noticed that her brother had spent an entire meal on a restructuring plan, answered two calls, checked his calendar three times, and not once mentioned a single person he might want to see on a Saturday night.

“Are you seeing anyone?”

“No.”

“Do you want to?”

“I’m busy.”

“Are you planning to stay single for ever?”

“That seems unnecessarily dramatic,” said Ren Hao, which in Isla’s professional opinion was a yes.

She looked at him over her iced tea. “You’re twenty-seven. You run a firm on three floors. You’re reasonably attractive. You own a decent flat and eleven ties. And you have no romantic life whatsoever.”

He put his fork down. “Are we discussing my personal life or conducting an annual review?”

“Both.”

He sighed. She smiled. And that was how the file began.

✦ ✦ ✦

By May she had ten candidates, printed out with notes in the margins. A corporate lawyer: Smart. Independent. Probably also never leaves the office. Two of them in one flat would be a hostage situation. A lecturer: Calm. Likes travel. Would let him plan the travel, which is the problem. A friend’s cousin: Lovely. Very polite. They would both wait for the other one to say something until they died. An architect, a doctor, a financial analyst (would turn the relationship into a quarterly review, and he’d enjoy it), a journalist (slightly frightening; I like her), a pilot, a museum curator.

And then there was number eleven, who wasn’t printed at all, because Isla had never needed to look her up.

She’d met Xu Song-Zhu on a cold night in November 2024, in the stairwell of a hospital, at two in the morning. Isla had been there for a citizen’s family, a tourist who’d come off a motorbike, and Song-Zhu had been there for a pilot, a private one, who’d put a light aircraft into a hillside and walked away from it with a fractured wrist and a great many questions only the investigator could answer. They’d both ended up on the same landing with the same vending machine, which had taken Isla’s last coin and given her nothing.

The stranger beside her in a dark blue flight suit had hit the machine once, precisely, in the corner, and a cereal bar had dropped. She’d broken it in half and handed one half over without a word.

“Thank you. What do you do?”

“I listen to aircraft. And you?”

“I sit with families on the worst night of their lives.”

The woman had swapped them. “Then you need the bigger half.”

They’d talked on the stairs for forty minutes. About work, the kind nobody at a dinner party wanted to hear about. About families. About the strange things people did when they were frightened. Song-Zhu had laughed and said, “Some people start organising things. Sometimes they organise the whole room. I had a man re-sort a hospital’s leaflet stand while his brother was in surgery.”

Isla had nearly choked on her half of the cereal bar, because she knew someone exactly like that.

“Siblings?” Song-Zhu had asked.

“One older brother.”

“Close?”

“Unfortunately,” said Isla, and Song-Zhu had laughed again, and it was the laugh that did it. It was loud, and it arrived before the end of her own sentence, and it didn’t care who heard it in a hospital stairwell at two in the morning.

They’d had dumplings in March, and Isla had sent her brother a photograph of the two of them at the dumpling place, without comment, which he’d ignored. They’d had wine in April. By May Isla knew that Song-Zhu argued with traffic lights, owned no indoor voice, had grown up on the other side of the harbour, and had lost her father when she was nineteen; and that she was funny and intelligent and impossible to impress with money, and kind in a way she didn’t make any fuss about at all.

On the evening she wrote it down, Isla sat with the pink file for an unreasonable length of time.

CANDIDATE 11. XU SONG-ZHU.
Air accident investigator. Twenty-five.
First impression: cereal bar.
Conversation: excellent. Temperament: warm, not accommodating.
Will not be managed. This is the point.
Could make him laugh. Could also tell him to shut up.

She circled the name in red and drew a small star beside it. At the bottom she wrote FIRST CHOICE, and underlined it twice, because she was her brother’s sister after all.

✦ ✦ ✦

The problem was Hao.

“I know someone,” she said, over dinner.

“No.”

“I haven’t told you who.”

“Your opening suggests an agenda.”

“She’s clever. She’s funny. She’s an investigator.”

He looked up at that, and then down again. “No, Isla. Thank you. I don’t need introducing to anyone.”

“You don’t need to work fourteen hours a day either, and here we are.”

“Goodnight, Isla,” said her brother, who’d already paid, and that was that.

So she rang Song-Zhu instead.

“He said no,” she said.

There was a pause on the line, and then the laugh. “Then I’m not coming.”

“You are. He doesn’t have to know it’s anything. It’s dinner. Me and a friend. He’ll come because I’ll tell him he’s paying. And if you hate him, you’ve had a free dinner in a French restaurant and you can go home and tell me I’m a terrible judge of character.”

“And if I don’t hate him?”

“Then I’ll leave early.”

“Isla. That’s a terrible plan.”

“It’s a beautiful plan.”

“Is he nice? Actually nice, or family nice?”

Isla looked at the ceiling. “Both. He’s loud. He’ll try to organise you inside ten minutes. He’ll bring a list. He’ll order your water. And he’s the kindest person I know, and nobody ever lets him stop being in charge long enough to notice.”

Song-Zhu was quiet a moment. “All right. I’ll find out for myself.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The dinner was on Friday the thirteenth of June. Isla chose the restaurant and booked it in his name, and told him the time and nothing else.

She wore green. She watched him take his hand away from his inside pocket, where she knew perfectly well there was a typed list. At ten past seven she rang Song-Zhu’s duty phone, and at twenty past her mobile, and when Song-Zhu said she was in the car park of the crash site, Isla put her phone away and didn’t let one muscle of her face move.

At twenty to eight a woman in a flight suit with aviation fuel on her boots and mud on her cheekbone stopped beside their table, and her brother stood up.

Isla watched it happen for exactly twenty-five minutes. She watched Hao order Song-Zhu’s water, and tell the kitchen she didn’t eat coriander, and send back the soup, and tell her to wash her face. She watched Song-Zhu look at him across the candle like a component she’d found in the wrong place and wanted to take apart.

At five past eight Isla’s phone buzzed with nothing at all. She read the nothing, and sighed beautifully, and stood up.

“Work. The consulate. I’m so sorry. Hao, you’ll look after her.”

“Isla.”

“Be nice,” she said, and kissed his cheek, and left them there, and walked out into the warm street and stood by the river for ten minutes with her hand over her mouth, laughing.

✦ ✦ ✦

At eleven o’clock her phone rang. She’d been waiting by it in her pyjamas with the pink file on her knee.

“WHY DO YOU THINK I NEED HELP FINDING SOMEONE?” said her brother, at full volume.

“Because you do. Did you tell her to wash her face?”

He said nothing, which she would treasure for the rest of her life.

“Oh, Hao.”

“It was a reasonable observation.”

“Good night, Hao. Be nice to her,” said Isla, and rang off laughing, and lay down on the floor with the file on her chest.

Just before midnight she texted the other half of the operation, the way you’d radio a team still in the field.

Isla (Matchmaker): ALIVE??

Song-Zhu: Unfortunately.

Isla (Matchmaker): He rang me at eleven. At full volume. What did you DO

Song-Zhu: He told me to wash my face.

Isla (Matchmaker): HAHAHAHAHA I KNEW HE WOULD

Isla (Matchmaker): And?

The dots came and went, and came again.

Song-Zhu: I kissed him.

Isla (Matchmaker): YOU WHAT

Song-Zhu: Taxi rank. Good night, Isla.

Isla read it four times, and put the phone face up on her knee, and pressed both hands over her mouth.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the morning, in a bed that wasn’t hers, she told the inspector.

He’d been asleep with his head on her stomach after a night search for a missing boy, and at a few minutes past eight his phone had told him the boy was home, and he’d put it down, and she’d stroked his hair and said, “I have news too. Hao has a date.”

He lifted his head. “With whom?”

“Xu Song-Zhu. She’s a crash investigator. I introduced them last night at dinner and left early.”

“Without telling him?”

“He knows now. He rang me at eleven, at full volume.”

She told him the rest: that Song-Zhu was clever and patient and funny, which Hao would need, and that she’d warned her he said I love you the way other people said hello, talked too much when he was nervous, and thought he was always right. Wei Long said that was accurate. She said maybe they’d get married. He said that was a large conclusion to draw from one dinner.

“Let me dream,” said Isla, and he put his head back down and let her, and she lay looking at his ceiling, which she was beginning to know by heart, and thought about a pink file in a drawer across the harbour, and about how she’d never once in her life put anyone of her own in a file.

✦ ✦ ✦

That night, at home, she opened it again and added a page.

PROJECT UPDATE. 13 JUNE 2025.
Subject brought a list. (Predicted.)
Subject ordered her water. (Predicted.)
Subject sent back the soup. (Predicted.)
Subject told candidate to wash her face. (NOT predicted.)
Candidate kissed subject at taxi rank.
Subject rang sister at full volume. Subject is gone.

Beside each of the other ten candidates, in black biro, she wrote NOT PURSUED. She didn’t throw them away. It was a good file, a thorough file. She closed it, and then, because she was Isla, she wrote on the cover: PROJECT STATUS: SUCCESSFUL. DO NOT TELL HIM.

✦ ✦ ✦

Three months later he let himself into her flat with a box of egg tarts from the bakery by the ferry pier.

“Song-Zhu said you liked these.”

“She remembered?”

He walked into the kitchen like he owned it, which he didn’t, and put the box down. “She remembers everything. It’s her job. Where’s your pink folder?”

Isla went still. “What pink folder?”

“The one on your dining table. In April.”

“You weren’t supposed to see that.”

“I know. I only read the cover.”

He considered.

“And the first page. Project: get my brother a life.”

She put her face in her hands. He laughed, and then, when she looked up, he’d stopped laughing.

“Thank you. Really,” said her brother.

She couldn’t say anything for a second. “You’re welcome. So?”

“So what?”

“Candidate Eleven.”

He smiled, and it was a smile she’d never once seen on him in twenty-five years, and it came easily.

“She’s wonderful.”

“You’re in love.”

“Isla. It’s been three months.”

“Exactly. Does she know?” said Isla.

“That I like her?”

“That you’re hopeless.”

He picked up his coat. “She knows. She says thank you for introducing us.”

When he’d gone she took the pink file out of the drawer and opened it to the page with the red circle. She printed a photograph she’d taken a fortnight before, outside a restaurant: her brother looking down at a woman who was laughing at something he’d said, and neither of them looking at the camera. She put it in the file behind the circle and wrote underneath, Selected, and then, after a moment, He’s forgotten to look at his watch.

The other ten had been perfectly good people. But matchmaking, Isla had found, wasn’t about finding the eleven best people on paper. It was about knowing the one who’d hand you the bigger half of a cereal bar in a stairwell at two in the morning, and who would never, under any circumstances, let her brother order her life for her.

chapters.title: The Agenda for the Second Date
chapters.desc: The agenda for the second date, found by his sister at a quarter past six. Item seven: kiss, if appropriate. She already knows. He asks anyway.
chapters.epigraph: “Is that on your agenda?”
chapters.content:
Ren Hao had prepared an agenda. A real one, printed on a single sheet, with numbered items, estimated durations, and a narrow column on the right headed Notes. He’d reviewed it twice before leaving the office and put it inside a card folder, because a loose piece of paper seemed unprofessional.

It was Friday the twenty-seventh of June 2025, and it was the first evening with Xu Song-Zhu that he’d been allowed to plan himself. The first had been his sister’s ambush in a French restaurant. The second had been a photograph of a plastic tray at a hangar and a noodle place behind the cargo terminal with sticky tables, chosen by her. This one was his. He’d booked it on Monday, and she’d said yes in four letters, fine, followed eleven minutes later by it’s a date, Hao, you can say it, which he hadn’t.

At a quarter past six his sister let herself into his flat to return a laptop charger he’d lent her in 2019, and found the folder on the hall table.

“What’s this?”

“Nothing.”

Isla had already opened it. She read the heading, and read it again, and began to laugh.

“THE AGENDA FOR THE SECOND DATE.”

“Give it back. It’s the third, technically. I’m not counting your dinner.”

She held the page above her head and backed down the hall. “You took a list to my dinner, too. Four items. I watched you touch your pocket. Item one: establish a comfortable conversational environment.”

“That’s a reasonable objective.”

She stopped. Her eyebrows rose. “Item two: ask about her work properly, this time without ordering her water. Item three: listen. Item four: avoid discussing my work excessively. Item five: offer to pay without making it a negotiation. Item six: walk her to her transport and do not arrange a car. Item seven.”

Ren Hao went still.

“Kiss, if appropriate.”

A rare, satisfying silence came down over the hall.

Isla stared at him. “She’s kissed you twice. At a taxi rank to shut you up and against your own car in a cargo terminal car park. I know, because she told me. And you’ve put it on an agenda. As an if.”

“The first two weren’t my decision. I’d like the third to be a question,” said Ren Hao, with dignity.

His sister lowered the paper and looked at him with an expression he didn’t recognise on her at all.

“Oh, Hao.”

He took the folder back. “Go home, Isla. And keep the charger. Clearly it’s yours now.”

She laughed all the way down the stairs.

✦ ✦ ✦

He’d chosen the restaurant carefully: a small place on the hill above the old harbour with eight tables, no candles, and a view of the ferries going across. It was quiet without being formal, with good food and enough room between the tables to talk without the evening turning into an interview. He arrived twelve minutes early, naturally, and checked his watch, and the booking, and his phone, and put the phone away.

Then she walked in.

She wasn’t in a flight suit. She was in a dark green dress and flat sandals, with her hair down and a small bag on a long strap, and for the first time since he’d known her there was nothing on her face but her face. She looked round the room like she was trying to remember whether she’d been there before, and found him, and smiled. He stood up.

She sat down before he could pull her chair out, which he noted. “No mud. Both sides. I checked in the taxi.”

“I wasn’t going to say anything.”

“You were looking at my cheekbone.”

“Out of habit,” said Ren Hao, and she laughed, and item one became unnecessary.

✦ ✦ ✦

She told him about her week. A runway incursion review, which was a man on a tug who’d crossed where he shouldn’t have, and a three-day argument with an airline about whether one timestamp in a log was wrong. He asked about the timestamp. She looked at him for a second like she was checking whether he meant it, and then told him, properly, for twenty minutes, with salt cellars for aircraft.

“People always think it’s like television. That somebody stands up in a room full of people and announces the answer,” she said.

“Doesn’t anybody?”

She moved a salt cellar an inch. “No. Sometimes you spend three days establishing why one number’s wrong. And then you write it down, and somebody changes a procedure, and nobody ever knows that a man on a tug in June is the reason. I like it. The truth doesn’t get less important because it’s hard to find.”

He looked at her across the table, and something in his chest rearranged itself without asking his permission.

Item two, completed. Item three, he found, didn’t need to be on the list.

When she asked about his work he told her about the firm: three floors, risk and crisis, a great deal of time spent persuading frightened people not to make bad situations worse.

“So you’re paid to tell people they’re making bad decisions.”

“Among other things.”

“Do they listen?”

“Less often than they should.”

She pointed her fork at him. “Sounds like my job. Except you’ve got better clothes. Do you always dress like you’re about to acquire a company?”

He looked down at his shirt, which was the most casual thing he owned that had a collar. “Would you prefer something less corporate?”

“No. I think it’s sweet,” said Song-Zhu.

He sat with that. She carried on eating like she hadn’t said anything significant at all, and he revised his expectations for the evening, comprehensively.

✦ ✦ ✦

By dessert the agenda was in trouble. They both liked quiet restaurants, terrible puns, and travelling without an itinerary, although he admitted he preferred somewhere with reliable accommodation at the end of it, and she called him an old man. She liked the sea. So did he, from a balcony.

“Do you organise everything?”

“Most things.”

“Your weekends? Your meals? Your socks?”

He looked at her. She was grinning.

“Do you organise your socks?”

“No.”

“Good. I was beginning to worry.”

He laughed, and it was becoming a problem: he’d stopped thinking about the next question or whether he’d asked her enough about herself. He was enjoying himself so much he’d forgotten there was a folder in his jacket.

She rested her chin on her hand. “Can I ask you something? Are you nervous?”

He considered a diplomatic answer and decided against it. “Yes.”

“Why?”

“Because I wanted this one to go well. The other two happened to me. This one I chose.”

Her face changed. “It is going well. Isla said you were very serious. She also said you once sent back a coffee because they’d given you the wrong milk.”

He closed his eyes. “That was one time. It was a matter of principle.”

She laughed so loudly that a man at the next table turned round, and Ren Hao watched her do it, and there was no item on his agenda for that, no duration and no measurable outcome. He only knew he wanted to hear it again.

✦ ✦ ✦

He walked her out at half past nine. The evening was warm and the pavement still held the heat of the day.

“Would you like me to arrange a car?”

He heard item six in his own head, and stopped.

“No. Sorry. You’ll get one yourself.”

She looked at him sideways. “You were going to.”

“I was. I’m not.”

“You’re very polite.”

“I try.”

“Is this what you do on all your second dates?”

He put one hand in his pocket. “I haven’t had many second dates. Or firsts. Work, mostly. And I hadn’t met anyone I wanted to make time for.”

She looked at him for a second, and her smile got smaller and warmer. “Oh.”

“Would you like to do this again?”

“Yes.”

It came so easily he nearly forgot to answer it. “Yes?”

“Yes, Ren Hao.”

Her taxi was four minutes away on the app. Neither of them moved. And he remembered item seven, and considered the evidence: two and a half hours; laughing; it’s a date, Hao, you can say it; her standing close enough that he could see the smile she was trying not to show. None of that was permission.

“Can I ask you something?”

“Mm?”

“Would it be all right if I kissed you?”

She blinked. Then a slow smile came. “Is that on your agenda?”

He stared at her. For one terrible second he wondered whether his sister had sent her a photograph of it.

“Oh, your face. Isla texted me at twenty past six. He has an agenda. There’s an item seven. Be kind,” said Song-Zhu.

“Of course she did.”

“Did you really write kiss, if appropriate?”

“I was trying to be considerate.”

“I know you were.”

Her teasing went soft. She took a step closer.

“You’ve asked. That’s the first time anybody’s asked. Yes, Ren Hao. You can kiss me.”

After all the preparation, the restaurant, the folder, he found himself entirely unprepared. He touched her cheek, the clean one, both sides. She tipped her face up. The kiss was warm and careful at first, a question being answered, until she smiled against his mouth and put her hand flat on his chest and he kissed her again, properly, on a pavement on a hill above the harbour, with the ferries going across below and her taxi turning into the street.

When they’d stopped she stayed close. “Well? Was it appropriate?”

“Very.”

She got into the taxi and turned once with the door open. “Tell your sister thank you.”

“For what?”

“Item seven,” said Song-Zhu, and shut the door.

✦ ✦ ✦

He stood on the pavement and watched the taxi go, and took out his phone.

Isla: So?

Hao (Loud): It went well.

Isla: Define well.

Hao (Loud): We’re seeing each other again.

Isla: AND?

He looked at the screen a long while, and typed.

Hao (Loud): Item seven completed. With permission.

Isla: I KNEW IT

At home he took the agenda out of its folder and looked at the printed page. Items one to six, completed, more or less. Item seven, completed with permission. He picked up a pen to add an eighth, Arrange next one, and stopped, and for the first time that evening decided not to schedule something. He’d ask her tomorrow.

Under item seven he wrote, small, Better than expected. Then he folded the page carefully and put it in the drawer of his bedside table, where it stayed, behind a passport and a spare watch, for the next three years: the only agenda he ever kept because it hadn’t gone to plan.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Saturday morning he didn’t put anything in his diary. He rang her instead, at ten, which he’d decided was late enough not to wake a woman who’d been on nights and early enough not to look as if he’d been waiting since seven, which he had.

She answered on the second ring with wind in the phone and an engine running up somewhere behind her. “If this is about item eight, there isn’t one. I checked with Isla.”

“There isn’t an item eight. I nearly wrote one. I didn’t,” said Ren Hao.

“What would it have said?”

“Arrange the next one.”

“And instead?”

“Instead I’m ringing to ask you when you’d like the next one. And where. And whether you’d like to choose, this time, or for me to, or for neither of us to, and we just see.”

There was a pause on the line, long enough that he heard someone behind her shout about a torque wrench.

“You’re asking,” she said.

“I’m asking.”

“Ring me on Tuesday. I’ll have decided by then. And Hao? You were very good at item seven,” said Song-Zhu.

She rang off before he could answer, and he stood in his kitchen holding the phone and grinning at the kettle like a man who’d won something, and on Tuesday, when he rang, she said, you’ve seen where I work, now I want to see yours, and he said Friday so fast that she laughed at him for a full minute before she said yes.

chapters.title: The Receptionist
chapters.desc: Ruby on the front desk, and a florist who never fixes the address. Every Monday from June to Christmas the flowers go to the wrong desk first, and he never corrects it.
chapters.epigraph: “I like that they go through you.”
chapters.content:
Ruby had been on the firm’s front desk in the lobby for five years before her managing director fell in love.

She knew his coffee, the names of his regular clients and their regular crises, and exactly how long a document could sit in his tray before he came out and asked where it was. She knew that he hugged people. He hugged clients who’d just been released by men with guns, and the cleaners at New Year, and her, every year on the fourth of July, lifting her an inch off the floor so her reading glasses swung on their chain, and there was cake in the fourth-floor kitchen whether she liked it or not, because he made sure of it. She knew he was loud in the corridors and quiet in meetings, and that the quiet was the dangerous one.

She also knew that Mr. Ren didn’t send flowers. Not to clients, or colleagues, or his own mother, unless Ruby reminded him in writing in March that there was a day for it.

So when the first bouquet arrived on Monday the sixteenth of June 2025, she assumed it was a mistake.

It was white tulips and small green branches in pale paper. The card said, in the florist’s printed hand, For Xu Song-Zhu. The delivery address was Ren Hao, thirty-second floor.

“There’s no Xu Song-Zhu here,” said Ruby.

The courier checked his phone. “Thirty-second floor. Ren Hao’s office.”

“That’s correct. The recipient isn’t.”

She looked at the flowers. Her employer was a private man about the things that mattered and a loud one about everything else, and she had no intention of investigating which this was. But tulips were perishable.

“Leave them with me,” said Ruby.

At twelve minutes past nine he came out of the lift, stopped dead in front of her desk, and looked at the flowers, and then at her.

“Who sent those?”

“I was hoping you’d tell me, Mr. Ren.”

He read the card. And he went pink, which she’d never in five years seen him do, from the collar up.

“Those are mine. I mean, I sent them. To her. To the authority. The aviation one. On the perimeter road.”

He stopped.

“The florist has my address on the account.”

“Would you like me to have them sent on?”

“Please. Carefully.”

He went back towards the lifts, and turned round. “Thank you, Ruby.”

She watched the lift doors close on him. Then she looked at the tulips again. Interesting, thought Ruby.

✦ ✦ ✦

The second bouquet came the following Monday, pale pink roses, For Xu Song-Zhu, thirty-second floor. She didn’t bother asking the courier whether he was sure. She rang through.

“Mr. Ren, the flowers have come.”

“Thank you.”

“Here.”

A silence. “Again?”

“Yes. Shall I send them on?”

“Please. Same address.”

Another silence.

“Ruby. Do you think roses are too much?”

She could hear him over the line, not reading whatever was in front of him.

“That depends on the recipient, Mr. Ren.”

“Right. Thank you.”

She arranged the courier, and didn’t smile until she’d turned away from the desk.

✦ ✦ ✦

By the fourth of July there’d been three. On the fourth of July there was also a cake in the fourth-floor kitchen, lemon, because she’d mentioned lemon in 2022, and in the middle of the day a woman she’d never seen walked into the lobby in a white shirt with a work bag over her shoulder, looking up at the building like it was a wreck she’d been asked to assess.

“Hello. I’m here to see Ren Hao. Xu Song-Zhu.”

Ruby had typed that name onto three courier forms in three weeks. She could have written it in her sleep. She typed it now, slowly, while delight came up through her like a fizz and she held it down with every year of professionalism she possessed.

“Miss Xu. Please do take a seat.”

He came across the lobby from the lifts before she’d sat down, in about four strides, said something to her that made her roll her eyes, and then remembered himself and turned to the desk.

“Ruby. Happy birthday.”

He came round the end of the desk and hugged her, the way he did every year, an inch off the floor. Over his shoulder Ruby saw Miss Xu watching it with an expression of enormous interest, and filing it away.

“Thank you, Mr. Ren,” said Ruby, pink to the hairline.

Late that evening, when the lobby had emptied, she put a slice of the lemon cake on a plate under a napkin at the corner of her desk, for nobody in particular, and went home. She’d heard the lifts. She knew who’d be crossing the atrium last.

✦ ✦ ✦

By September Ruby had learned three things. The first was that Mr. Ren could be distracted. Never in a meeting, or a negotiation, or while a client was talking. But if his phone lit up with a name she’d seen on a great many flower cards, his face changed before he’d even opened it.

The second was that he’d become impossibly particular about flowers. He asked whether the florist could get a certain kind of narrow white tulip, because she’d mentioned once that she liked them. He sent one bouquet back because it was too big.

“She doesn’t like things that are hard to carry. She carries a lot of things already,” he said.

“Something smaller, then.”

“Something she can put on her desk without moving a binder.”

Ruby made a note. The third was that the florist never, once, changed the address. Every Monday, for three months, the flowers came to the thirty-second floor, and every Monday Ruby rang for a courier and sent them out to the perimeter road. In August she’d suggested, gently, that the account could be corrected. He’d said he’d see to it. He didn’t. She’d begun to suspect he didn’t want to.

✦ ✦ ✦

The flowers in the second week of October were white lilies, and the courier looked at her apologetically, and Ruby rang through.

“Mr. Ren. Miss Xu’s flowers.”

He came down and looked at them. “Again. I thought I’d corrected the address.”

“You did say you would, Mr. Ren.”

He rubbed his forehead. “I’ll ring them.”

Ruby lifted the lilies carefully. And then, because she’d spent four months watching a man who could talk a gunman down a telephone line become steadily less composed over a woman, she said, “Mr. Ren. May I ask something?”

“Go on.”

“Are you aware that you’ve sent flowers to the wrong desk almost every Monday since June?”

He looked at her. She held his gaze with perfect professional calm. For a second she thought he might argue. Then his mouth went, and he looked down at his shoes, and then back at her, like a man caught.

“I am aware,” said Ren Hao.

“Of course, Mr. Ren.”

Then, unexpectedly: “I like that they go through you.” He went back to the lifts before she could answer, and she stood holding the lilies with her face warm.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the Monday after, her desk phone rang with an outside number she didn’t know.

“Ren Hao’s office. Ruby speaking.”

“Hi, Ruby. It’s Song-Zhu. Xu Song-Zhu. The flowers.”

“Hello, Miss Xu. How can I help?”

A small pause on the line. “Can I ask you something? You can say no. Does he send flowers to everybody?”

Ruby thought of the thirty-second floor, where he’d be on the phone with his feet on a chair, which he only did when nobody important could see.

“No, Miss Xu. He doesn’t send flowers to anybody. I remind his mother’s florist in March.”

Another pause, and a little laugh that sounded like it had surprised its owner. “Right. Good.”

“Is there anything else?”

“No. Thank you, Ruby. And Ruby? Thank you for sending them on. Every week. He told me.”

“You’re very welcome, Miss Xu,” said Ruby, and put the phone down, and sat with her hand on it a while.

✦ ✦ ✦

The one that came on Thursday that week wasn’t from the florist at all. It was a small bunch of narrow white tulips in brown paper, and a card in his own narrow capitals, delivered by a courier he’d sent out himself at lunchtime and told to bring back to the desk first.

FOR THE WOMAN WHO MAKES ORDINARY THURSDAYS BETTER.

Ruby looked at it a long time. Then she rang the courier herself, and asked him to read back the delivery point at the authority, and wrote it down, and read it back to him again. This one wasn’t going anywhere near a wrong desk.

At twenty to seven he came out with his coat over his arm. “The flowers?”

“Delivered, Mr. Ren. To her desk. In person.”

He looked so relieved that she nearly laughed. He went to the lift, and she said, before she could think better of it, “Mr. Ren?”

“Yes?”

“Are you happy?”

It caught him. She watched it catch him, in the middle of her reception floor, with his coat over his arm and his hand already out for the lift button.

“Yes. Very,” he said.

“Good evening, Mr. Ren.”

“Good evening, Ruby.”

✦ ✦ ✦

In December Miss Xu came up on a Thursday afternoon with no appointment and a paper bag from the bakery by the ferry pier, and put it on the corner of Ruby’s desk.

“Is he free?”

“He’s finishing a call. Would you like to wait?”

Miss Xu leaned on the counter. “Can I ask you something? How many times did the flowers come here first?”

“Do you want the official answer or the honest one?”

“The honest one.”

“Every single Monday since June. I knew your name before I knew your face.”

Miss Xu put her hand over her mouth. “Oh, no.”

“He was very particular that they got to you.”

Something went soft in her face, and she looked down at the bag. “He’s ridiculous.”

“Yes, he is,” said Ruby, and they smiled at each other across the desk like two people who’d been on the same long project and only just been introduced.

The lift opened and he came out, and saw her, and the paper bag. “What’s that?”

“Egg tarts. For you. And one for Ruby, she’s in the bag on the left.”

“Why?”

“Because it’s Thursday,” said Song-Zhu.

In the last week of December, Ruby saw something that made her smile more than any bouquet. Miss Xu was leaving, and he walked her to the lift. She said something and he laughed, loud, the way he laughed in corridors. Then she reached up and straightened his tie, and he stood completely still under her hands, looking at her like the rest of the building had stopped existing. She kissed his cheek. He caught her hand before she could take it back and kissed her knuckles. The lift doors opened and she stepped in, and he stayed where he was until the doors had shut.

He came back past the desk with his hands in his pockets and the look of a man who’d forgotten where he was going, and remembered, and decided it didn’t matter. He saw Ruby watching, and didn’t pretend he hadn’t been seen.

“Good evening, Ruby.”

“Good evening, Mr. Ren.”

He stopped. “Ruby. Could you cancel next Monday’s flowers?”

She looked up. “Certainly. May I ask why?”

He was grinning. “She’s coming home with me for Christmas. Vancouver. My mother’s already cried twice on the phone. There’ll be nobody at the authority to send them on to.”

“Of course, Mr. Ren.”

He went back up. Ruby looked at her calendar, and then at the empty corner of her desk. For the first time since June there’d be no flowers arriving at the wrong desk on Monday.

She found she was going to miss them. They’d been beautiful, but that wasn’t it. For half a year they’d been the most reliable evidence on the thirty-second floor that a man who was certain about almost everything had found one thing he was frightened of getting wrong, and was getting it right anyway, one Monday at a time.

chapters.title: Voice Notes
chapters.desc: Forty-one voice notes, kept in a folder with her name on it: a field, a printer, a pigeon, a bath. They stop in August 2026. Years later she adds the forty-second.
chapters.epigraph: “That’s how saving works.”
chapters.content:
The first voice note was a minute and fifty seconds long, and Ren Hao listened to it four times before he went home.

It arrived just after eight on Saturday the fourteenth of June 2025, from a number he didn’t have, while he was alone in his office at the top of his three floors with an exposure report on a shipping client. He’d sent the woman from his sister’s dinner a set of minutes at fourteen minutes past midnight, with numbered items, because he hadn’t known what else to do with the evening. Nobody else he knew would have answered minutes with a voice note.

“Good morning, Mr. Ren. Before you start: yes, I’ve eaten breakfast. Yes, I’ve washed my face. Both sides.”

He could hear her smiling. Then wind, and an engine running up somewhere, and her voice going smaller, the way a voice does when someone steps into a narrower room, to tell him about a twin in a field and two people who hadn’t made it.

He saved it. He didn’t know yet that he was beginning a collection.

✦ ✦ ✦

By the end of June there were six. The second was three minutes long, because she’d forgotten she was recording. He heard her ask somebody for a document, and complain about a printer that refused to cooperate on principle, and then, a long way off, remember the phone.

“Oh. You’re still there. Well, obviously. It’s a voice note.”

A door.

“I was going to tell you something. What was it? Oh. The team ordered too much lunch. I sent you a picture and you said it looked like a crime scene. It did. I’ve saved you some cake. It’s in my fridge at work. Don’t eat it before I get there, that’s not how saving works.”

He was smiling at his desk like a fool when Joyce knocked and came in with the revised figures. She looked at his face, and at the phone, and at his face again.

“Is everything all right, Mr. Ren?”

“Very.”

He was, in fact, having an excellent day.

✦ ✦ ✦

They became a habit. Not a scheduled one; she’d never have tolerated that. They came at strange hours from strange places, with no pattern at all. Sometimes she had something to tell him. Sometimes she was bored, or waiting for a photographer, or standing in the dark beside something broken that wasn’t allowed to be touched yet. And sometimes, he suspected, she only wanted him to know where she was in the world.

There was one from a hangar a little after two in the morning.

“Hao, are you asleep? Don’t wake up. I just—”

Wind across the microphone.

“I can see the moon through the hangar doors. It’s enormous. I thought you’d like it. Actually, you’d tell me it’s exactly the same size as usual and I’m being dramatic. Anyway. Good night.”

He’d been asleep. He sat up in bed and listened to it and laughed into his pillow.

Ren Hao: It’s the same size as usual.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): I KNEW IT

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Good night, boring man.

He saved that too.

✦ ✦ ✦

There were ones in which she sounded worn through.

He learned the particular tiredness in her voice after a day of interviews: how she slowed towards the ends of sentences, the small pauses where she was looking for a word and finding the wrong one. In September there was one that was only thirty-two seconds long.

“Today was difficult.”

That was all. He listened to it in his office with the door shut and rang her.

She answered on the fourth ring. “Did you get my voice note?”

“I did.”

“I’m not asking you to fix anything. I just wanted to tell you.”

“I know, sweetheart.”

A breath on the line. “Can you talk to me for a bit? About anything. Your day. A client. The ferry timetable.”

He pushed the papers on his desk aside and talked to her about the ferry timetable for twenty minutes, in detail, with opinions, until he heard her laugh.

He never told her he’d kept that one. He wasn’t hiding it. He didn’t want her to feel that every hard thing she said to him was being filed. Some things belonged to the minute they’d been said in. He could remember them without a recording. But he couldn’t bring himself to delete it, either.

✦ ✦ ✦

There were ridiculous ones. Ninety seconds on a vending machine at the authority that had taken her money and given her nothing, delivered with the full gravity of a preliminary report. One she’d whispered because she was standing beside a sleeping colleague on a night shift, only to knock something metal off a bench and wake him, followed by her voice at normal volume saying sorry, Dexter and then don’t tell anyone. One where she’d tried to explain a hydraulic fault, given up halfway, and concluded: “I think the aircraft’s having a worse day than I am.”

He’d listened to that one in the lift and laughed so loudly that a man from the twenty-ninth floor got out early. On a wet afternoon in October:

“There’s a bird.”

A pause.

“On the wing. Not the actual wing. Near the hangar. He keeps walking about like he owns the place. I think it’s a pigeon. Anyway, I thought you should know.”

Ren Hao: Thank you for the update. I hope the pigeon is well.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): He’s promoted himself to supervisor.

Ren Hao: Has he got the qualifications?

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): More than some people on my floor.

✦ ✦ ✦

By the winter he had a private ritual. When he travelled, he listened to one before he slept. When work was ugly, he picked one where she was laughing. When he missed her, he chose at random. He never made a playlist, or sorted them by date or length. He kept them, in a folder on his phone that he’d named, after some thought, Song-Zhu, because he couldn’t think of anything she wouldn’t have made fun of.

In December they changed. There were fewer hangars and more ordinary places. Sometimes one came from her car on the way home, or from the next room. Once, from her own bath, while he was in her kitchen eight metres away:

“Hao? Are you making tea?”

“Yes,” he said aloud, to the phone, in her kitchen, which she couldn’t hear.

“Bring me some. And bring yourself.”

He kept that one too.

✦ ✦ ✦

One Sunday in March 2026 she was on his sofa when he went to get water, and his phone was lying unlocked on the coffee table, and she wasn’t looking for anything. Then she saw the folder with her name on it. She opened it. There were thirty-eight.

When he came back with two glasses she was sitting upright with his phone in both hands.

“What’s this?”

He followed her eyes. “Oh.”

“Thirty-eight? You kept my voice notes?”

“Yes.”

“All of them? Why?”

He looked at her like the answer was obvious. “Because I like them.”

She scrolled. “This one’s from June. This one’s four minutes and twelve seconds.”

“You were explaining something.”

“I was complaining about a printer!”

“It was a very detailed complaint.”

“You didn’t delete the one where I forgot what I was saying? Or the vending machine? Or where I called the pigeon your colleague?”

He sat down beside her. “That one’s the best.”

She put her face in her hands. “Some of them are completely pointless.”

“Are they?” He took the phone gently, and opened the second one, and pressed play.

Her own voice came out, younger by nine months, with a printer behind it and somebody asking her for a document. “I’ve saved you some cake. Don’t eat it before I get there, that’s not how saving works.”

Her face changed. She remembered the morning: the bad coffee, the printer, the fact that she’d been standing in a corridor at work wanting to hear him, and had made up a reason.

“You kept that,” she said.

He put the phone down. “You saved me some cake. In June. Three weeks after you met me. I liked knowing that, even when I couldn’t be there.”

She looked away with a small helpless smile. “You could have just rung me.”

“I did ring you. I also kept the cake.”

She leaned against him and laughed into his shoulder, and kept her face hidden there while he played the next one. Then she said, low, She touched the phone on the table. “I don’t know how to say things the way you do. Out loud. To people’s faces. It comes out of you like weather. Maybe that’s what these are. The bits I could say into a phone with nobody watching.”

He went still, and then put his arm round her, and didn’t push.

✦ ✦ ✦

The last one came in July 2026, the week before the beach.

It was twenty-one seconds long. He was in a meeting when it arrived and didn’t listen until he got to her flat, late.

There was no wind in it, no machinery, nobody in the background. Just her voice, close to the phone, at her own kitchen table.

“Hi. I’m home. I know you’re working late, so don’t rush. I’ve left the light on in the hall. Come round when you can. There’s food. I ate some of it first. That’s how saving works.”

He stood in her hall with the light on and his key in his hand and listened to it twice. There was a bowl on the counter under a plate, and half of it was gone. Down the corridor she was asleep with her book open on her chest.

He took the book off her and turned out the lamp, and stood in the doorway a while.

After August there were no more. After August she didn’t send voice notes from anywhere. She wrote reports, and signed statements, and on the nineteenth of September she asked him to leave, and he took his toothbrush and left the fridge full. The folder on his phone stayed at forty-one. He didn’t open it once for four months. He couldn’t have said whether he was frightened of what was in it or of what wasn’t.

When they came back to each other, she rang instead, or she was in the next room, or she said it to his face, which she’d finally learned to do, in a kitchen, in January, over and over.

✦ ✦ ✦

Years later, married, on a rainy evening in their own flat, she borrowed his phone to find a photograph and found the folder instead. Song-Zhu. Forty-one.
