She opened one at random, and her own voice filled the room, a little younger, a little breathless.

“Hao, I have a question. If a person were to accidentally bring home three different kinds of cake, would you consider that a problem? Because I think I may have done that.”

She heard herself laugh.

“Actually, never mind. It’s not a problem. It’s cake.”

He came to the doorway. “What are you listening to?”

She turned the phone round. “Your collection. You kept it for years.”

“Yes.”

“Forty-one little pieces of me talking nonsense.”

He sat down beside her. “Not all of them.”

“Most.”

“Some are very important.”

“The pigeon?”

“The pigeon too,” said Ren Hao.

She leaned her head on his shoulder and they listened to the rain on the window for a while. Then she opened the recorder on his phone and pressed the red button.

“Hello, Ren Hao. I’m sitting next to you.”

“I can see that.”

“Just documenting.”

She held the phone between them.

“It’s a rainy evening. My husband’s sitting beside me. He’s being very quiet, which is unusual, but I’m not complaining. I love him. He’s a bit ridiculous. He keeps recordings of me saying absolutely nothing important.”

Her voice went down.

“And he’s always, always been good at listening, even when what I was saying was mostly a printer.”

She stopped it and saved it into the folder. 42. Rainy evening.

“Forty-two,” he said.

She put the phone down. “You’re allowed to keep mine now. I’m keeping yours too. I’ve got a folder. It’s called Hao. I couldn’t think of anything you wouldn’t have made fun of.”

He kissed her, one hand at her cheek, and the old recordings sat on the phone between them, hangars and printers and pigeons and bad coffee and one bowl of food with half of it gone: the small ordinary sentences of a woman who’d never once thought she was saying anything worth keeping, and had been saying it all along.

chapters.title: Karaoke Rules
chapters.desc: Karaoke has rules now, because in October he turned out to be able to sing. Every one of them is broken by eleven, and none of the choruses get finished.
chapters.epigraph: “Especially during the songs.”
chapters.content:
Xu Song-Zhu had rules for karaoke. Ren Hao discovered this about twelve minutes after the door of the private room shut behind them, on the last Friday in November 2025, in the same small room as in October, with the big screen and the long sofa against the wall. In October she’d found out he could sing. Since then she’d been preparing.

“Rule one. No songs longer than five minutes,” she announced, standing in front of the screen with the microphone.

He was on the sofa with his sleeves rolled to the elbow. “Why?”

“Because some people think karaoke is a concert.”

“Some people might have prepared.”

She pointed the microphone at him. “That’s exactly the problem. Rule two: no skipping my songs. Rule three: no recording me. Rule four: no making fun of my singing.”

“Of course.”

“You’re agreeing too quickly. You look like a man planning to break all four.”

“I’m sitting here.”

She turned back to the screen. “Suspiciously. Good. Then we can begin.”

“Can I ask where the rules came from?”

She held up one finger. “October. In October you sang one line at the bridge on your own and I lost my place for the rest of the song, which isn’t fair, so now there are limits. And in October you told me you sang in a choir until you were fourteen, in Vancouver, and that Isla has photographs. Isla has now sent me the photographs. There’s one with a bow tie. So rule three is for your protection as much as mine.”

“Isla sent you the bow tie?”

“Isla sent me the bow tie on the same evening. Within the hour. With a caption.”

“What did the caption say?”

“That’s classified,” said Song-Zhu.

✦ ✦ ✦

For twenty minutes he behaved. He sang when told to. He didn’t complain about her choices. He didn’t laugh when she missed a note by a clear tone and carried on with total confidence, as if the melody had been wrong. He clapped at the end.

“Very good.”

“You’re being sarcastic. You’ve got a very sarcastic face.”

“I’ll work on it.”

She handed him the microphone. He chose a song, and she looked at the screen and then at him.

“Really? That’s a heartbreak song. Are you heartbroken?”

“No.”

“Then why are you singing it?”

“Perhaps I like the tune.”

She sat down, smiling. “Fine. Sing, Mr. Ren.”

He did. And, annoyingly, he was even better than in October: a warm steady voice that a choir in Vancouver had taught where every note was meant to go, used the way he spoke in meetings when he meant it, without any fuss at all. She watched him through the first verse with her arms folded. By the chorus she’d stopped pretending not to be impressed.

“That was unexpectedly good. Don’t let it go to your head.”

“I’ll try.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The first rule fell at a quarter past ten. Song-Zhu chose a song that was six minutes and forty seconds long and sat down beside him to wait for it to start.

“That’s over five minutes.”

“I’m making an exception.”

“On what grounds?”

“I’m holding the remote.”

It was an old favourite, one she didn’t need the words for. She stood up for the first verse with the microphone in one hand and the other conducting an audience of one. She wasn’t a good singer. She went too high, laughed through a line, drifted towards the screen whenever she forgot the words. She was having the time of her life, and he loved watching her have it more than he’d ever loved watching anyone do anything well.

At the chorus she turned on him. “Sing!”

He shook his head, and she pointed the microphone at him like a weapon until he laughed and joined in. She got a line wrong. He sang the right one. She glared at him without stopping, and sang the next one louder than him on purpose. By the second chorus they were both laughing too much to sing properly, and somewhere between the bridge and the last chorus she climbed onto the sofa, the way she had in October.

“Careful.”

“I’ve got excellent balance.”

“That isn’t reassuring.”

She held the microphone out to him, and he took it, and she leaned down with one hand on his shoulder while he sang the next line. She watched his mouth. Then, instead of singing her part, she kissed him, right there, in the middle of the chorus.

He stopped singing. The music went on without them. She drew back just far enough to smile.

“You’re missing your line.”

“You interrupted me.”

“Do you want to carry on?”

He looked at the lyrics going by on the screen, and back at her. “No.”

He put the microphone down and kissed her again, and the song ended, and neither of them noticed. The machine moved on to the next track, an instrumental introduction playing into the room, and she was still leaning over him on the sofa with her hand on his cheek and his hand at her waist.

“Rule four,” she said against his mouth.

“I haven’t made fun of your singing.”

“You were supposed to finish the chorus with me.”

“While kissing you?”

“You run a firm. I thought you could do two things at once.”

He stood up, with his hands at her waist to steady her as she stepped down off the sofa, and didn’t let go. “Show me.”

“Show you what?”

“How you expect me to do two things at once.”

She reached for the microphone. He caught her hand.

“Later.”

“That’s rule five. No making me forget the rules,” said Song-Zhu.

“I don’t remember that one.”

“It’s new.”

“Noted,” he said, and kissed her until she did forget it, against the padded wall beside the screen, with the coloured lights from the lyrics going over both of them, red and blue and gold. She got her hands inside his collar. He made a sound into her mouth she’d only heard before at three in the morning. Somebody in the corridor walked past the little window in the door and kept walking, fast.

✦ ✦ ✦

They did sing another one eventually: a duet, chosen by her. She gave him the low part and then complained that he was making her sound worse by singing it too well. He said that wasn’t his intention. She said it was clearly his intention. He kissed her cheek between verses and she lost her place and threatened to revoke his microphone privileges, and he pointed out that she’d already broken three of her own rules and invented a fourth.

“The rules are subject to revision.”

“By whom?”

“The remote.”

Just after eleven she chose a slow one, and sat down beside him for it, and sang it low, without any of the waving. He sat with his arm along the back of the sofa and listened. Halfway through she turned her head and found him watching her and not the screen, and she smiled a little shyly, which she almost never did, and carried on.

When it ended he brushed his thumb over her cheek. “Beautiful.”

“That wasn’t the singing.”

“It was both.”

“You’re biased.”

“Very.”

She put the microphone down and climbed into his lap and sat facing him with her knees either side of his hips.

“One more.”

“Song?”

“Kiss,” said Song-Zhu, and that one went on and on. The booth was warm and the sofa was cheap and the music had moved on to something with a saxophone that neither of them had chosen, and she rocked forward against him slowly without meaning to, and then meaning to, and felt exactly what it was doing to him, and laughed into his mouth. His hands slid up under the back of her jumper, flat on her bare skin, and stayed there, still, asking.

“Not in a karaoke booth. There’s a window in the door,” she whispered.

“I know there’s a window in the door.”

“Then stop looking at me like that.”

“I can’t. You’re on my lap.”

She kissed him once more, hard, and climbed off, and pulled her jumper straight, and pointed at him with the remote. “We’re going home. Now. You’re carrying the bag.”

“Is that a rule?”

“It’s an order,” said Song-Zhu.

✦ ✦ ✦

Before they left he scrolled through the list while she put her coat on.

“What are you doing?”

“Choosing one more.”

“You’re not choosing another heartbreak song.”

He turned the screen towards her. It was the one she’d played in the car four times the week before, loudly, with the windows down, on the coast road.

She looked at it, and at him. “You remembered.”

“You sang it at a red light. A man in a lorry applauded.”

They sang it standing up, with their coats on, both microphones. At the chorus he turned towards her at the same moment she turned towards him, and neither of them remembered the words, and they kissed instead, again, in the middle of the chorus, with the music politely ignoring them.

“You’re terrible at karaoke,” she said against his mouth.

“I thought I was doing well.”

“You haven’t finished a single chorus.”

“Somebody keeps interrupting me.”

✦ ✦ ✦

In the car, at the first red light on the harbour road, she turned in the passenger seat and pointed at him.

“Finish it.”

“Finish what?”

“One chorus. The last one. Nobody’s going to interrupt you. I’m sitting on my hands.” She sat on her hands to prove it.

He looked at her, and at the light, which was still red, and then he sang it: the whole chorus, start to finish, in the warm steady voice a choir in Vancouver had given him, with both hands on the wheel and his eyes on the road and the window down an inch. He didn’t miss a word. When he got to the end the light went green, and the man in the van in the next lane, who’d heard every note, leaned out of his window and applauded, and drove off.

Song-Zhu didn’t say anything for a whole street. Then she took one hand out from under her and put it on his knee and left it there.

“Well?” he said.

“I’m revising rule one. Songs over five minutes are permitted if you’re singing them,” said Song-Zhu.

✦ ✦ ✦

The next morning, from her bed, with him asleep beside her:

Song-Zhu: Your brother is terrible at karaoke.

Isla (Matchmaker): He’s terrible at most fun things

Song-Zhu: He keeps interrupting the songs.

Isla (Matchmaker): With what?

Song-Zhu: I’ll let you work that out.

Isla’s call came through on his phone thirty seconds later, and he answered it without opening his eyes.

“Did you teach Song-Zhu to complain about me to you?”

“What did you do?”

“Nothing. She keeps blaming me for not finishing the songs.”

“Well, did you?”

He thought about it, with his eyes still shut and Song-Zhu’s hand flat on his chest. “No. I had better things to do.”

The noise his sister made was somewhere between a scream and a laugh, and he rang off, and Song-Zhu laughed into his shoulder until the bed shook.

✦ ✦ ✦

Three days later:

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): I have revised the karaoke rules.

Ren Hao: I’m listening.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): One: songs under five minutes. Two: no skipping. Three: no recording. Four: no making fun of my singing. Five: kissing is allowed.

Ren Hao: During the songs?

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Especially during the songs.

Ren Hao: I believe that rule was already being observed.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Then you’re learning. Friday?

Ren Hao: I’ll book the room.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): And this time try to finish one chorus.

He looked at the message, and typed, I’ll do my best, and knew perfectly well he wouldn’t. A few seconds later another one arrived.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Actually, never mind. I like the current arrangement.

That Friday, in the same booth, with the same two microphones and a song queue nobody looked at, Ren Hao forgot the words again. The chorus played on. She kissed him. And neither of them got up to stop it.

chapters.title: The Suit
chapters.desc: One charcoal three-piece suit, from a French restaurant to a petrol station, a doorway in the rain, her sofa in the worst month of her life, and the end of an aisle.
chapters.epigraph: “You were the first person who ever undid it to help me breathe.”
chapters.content:
The suit had been bought on a Tuesday in the spring of 2025. Ren Hao remembered the day because he’d been late for a meeting, the tailor had been unusually particular about the measurements, and his sister had sent him three messages asking whether he intended to spend the rest of his life in the same two colours.

It was charcoal grey, three pieces, jacket, waistcoat and trousers, with a texture you only saw close to. The tailor asked whether it was for business or an occasion.

“Business,” said Ren Hao.

He had no idea that it was going to be present for the beginning of his marriage. For the first weeks of its life it mostly saw spreadsheets.

✦ ✦ ✦

The first time Xu Song-Zhu saw it, she was standing beside a table in a French restaurant with fuel on her boots, and he stood up in it.

She looked at the waistcoat, and the tie, and the watch, and the list he’d just taken his hand away from in the inside pocket, and he saw her decide something about him in about a second and a half. Later he found out what. When she put his number into her phone that night, at the taxi rank, after she’d kissed him to shut him up, she typed Hao (Three-Piece) and never changed it.

The next afternoon he wore it again, to a wire fence at an airfield, with lunch for twelve. She looked at him over the wire in it, with his polished shoes on wet grass, and thought: oh no.

The suit didn’t know any of that. It went to the cleaner on Monday with a little grass on the cuffs.

✦ ✦ ✦

One night in August 2025 she was on a low concrete ledge beside the vending machines at a petrol station near midnight with a packet of crackers in her lap when he arrived in it, straight from the office, tie loosened just enough to show he’d been working since seven.

“You’re overdressed. Three pieces. At a petrol station,” she said.

“You said you were hungry.”

“I said I was hungry. That’s not the same as saying I hadn’t eaten.”

“It is in your case.” He held up a paper bag. A sandwich, a bottle of water, the yoghurt drink she liked.

She looked inside, and her face went soft, and then she looked him up and down. “Your waistcoat’s very handsome. Does it have a practical purpose?”

“It keeps the shirt from creasing.”

“Romantic,” said Song-Zhu, and moved along the ledge to make room.

He looked at the concrete, and at his trousers. She followed his eyes.

“Oh, don’t tell me. You’re worried about the suit.”

“I’m assessing the surface.”

“Mr. Ren. It’s a petrol station, not a boardroom. Sit.”

He sat, carefully. She leaned on his shoulder and ate her sandwich, and a lorry pulled in at the far pump, and somewhere behind the glass a fridge hummed. When she’d eaten half she reached up and straightened his tie, and kissed his cheek, and a little grease from the sandwich paper went onto the edge of his lapel. Neither of them noticed. The cleaner did. The cleaner said nothing.

✦ ✦ ✦

In November the rain started after dinner, the kind that turned the pavement silver and made every car sound like it was driving through a river. He stood under the restaurant awning looking at it. She stood beside him holding her bag over her head.

“Your driver?”

“Twenty minutes.”

“That’s too long. We could run.”

“You’re in heels.”

“I can run in heels.”

“I know,” said Ren Hao, and she turned and found him smiling, and rolled her eyes, and stepped out into it.

They made it halfway down the block before she grabbed his hand and pulled him under the shallow doorway of a closed shop. Her hair was soaked. His jacket was dark with rain across one shoulder. She was laughing so much she couldn’t speak.

“You’re trying very hard to look dignified.”

“I’m trying very hard not to catch cold.”

She touched his lapel, the charcoal gone nearly black. “Your suit.”

“Would complaining make it stop?”

“No.”

“Then there’s no point.”

She kissed him in the doorway, and a car went past and threw water at the kerb and she laughed into it, and he caught her hand before she could step back out.

“Stay here. You’ll get wetter.”

“That’s a strange reason to keep me close.”

He bent his head. “Would you like another one?”

“Much better,” she said against his mouth.

They stayed in the doorway till the rain eased. The suit was ruined for the evening. Her hair was a disaster. It went to the cleaner again, and the cleaner, by now, had begun to keep a file.

✦ ✦ ✦

The suit wasn’t designed for sleeping in. This became obvious at a quarter past two on a Thursday morning in her flat, in the third week after the aircraft went into the sea.

He’d moved in without asking. He’d built a wall at his firm on the morning of the second of August and he hadn’t put a finger through it once. He didn’t read her drafts. He didn’t ask about the recorders. What he did was be there: at her flat, every night, with food she didn’t eat and a kettle that was always nearly hot. That night he’d come straight from the office, and sat down on her sofa at midnight to wait, and woken at two with the waistcoat still buttoned and his jacket over the arm and his trousers creased at the knee.

Her key was in the door. She stood in the doorway of the living room with her work bag still on her shoulder and looked at him.

“You’re sleeping. In a three-piece suit.”

He sat up. “I was resting. I didn’t want to crease it further.”

She stared at him, and laughed once, a small cracked sound, the first in days. “You’re unbelievable.”

“How was it?”

“Still going.”

“Do you want me to—”

“No.”

He stopped. Her face changed.

“I just want to sit.”

He moved along the sofa. She put her bag down and sat on the edge of the cushion beside him, and for a while neither of them said anything. Then she reached over and began to undo his waistcoat.

“What are you doing?”

“Helping you breathe.”

“I can breathe.”

“Debatable.”

She undid every button and opened it, and took his watch off his wrist and put it on the table, and then, carefully, she lay down against him on the sofa, which was too narrow for two, with her head on his chest over the open waistcoat. His arm came round her, and didn’t pull, until she moved into him herself.

After a while her breathing changed. She’d fallen asleep in her work clothes, with her shoes still on.

He stayed awake a long time, looking at her ceiling, with his hand flat on her back. The suit had never been comfortable for this. He didn’t move.

✦ ✦ ✦

By the autumn of 2028 it had been let out by a centimetre at the waist in September, and taken back in by a centimetre in October, because the woman he was about to marry had developed a passion for early-morning walks along the harbour wall and had made him come. The tailor asked whether he wanted a new suit for the occasion.

“No. This one,” said Ren Hao.

On the morning of the wedding, in a room in the hotel above the harbour, with his phone confiscated and locked in a drawer in another room, he stood in front of the mirror in it, adjusting a cuff. A small white flower was pinned to the lapel. She’d chosen it.

His sister came in, and for once said nothing at all.

“What?”

She came and straightened the flower, which didn’t need it. “You look good. Do you remember when you bought this? You said it was for business,” said Isla.

“It was.”

“Look at it now.”

He looked at the mirror: the waistcoat, the flower, the place on his left hand where in seven hours there’d be a ring. “Plans change.”

Her eyes went bright. “Don’t. You’ll make me cry before the ceremony, and I’ve got a toast in three languages.”

He laughed, and she hugged him, and then she stood back and looked the suit over. “You should have bought a new one. This one’s been through too much.”

He thought about the little mark near the inside pocket that the cleaner had never quite got out. A petrol station. A doorway in the rain. A sofa in the worst month of her life, and her fingers on these buttons, undoing them one by one so he could breathe.

“It’s earned the day,” said Ren Hao.

He didn’t see her until three o’clock, at the end of an aisle, walking towards him with her mother. In the evening, under the lights in the glass room with the harbour going dark behind them, she danced with him for the first time as his wife, and he stepped on the hem of her dress once, and she told him he’d pay for that, and he said he’d accept the consequences. Halfway through the second song she put her hand flat on the front of his waistcoat, over his heart.

“I’ve seen this suit in some terrible conditions,” she said.

“Several of them were your fault. You made me sit on a concrete ledge.”

“You survived.”

He looked down at her hand. “Barely. You were the first person who ever undid it to help me breathe.”

Her face did something he’d remember all his life. “I’m glad you kept it,” she said.

By midnight the jacket was off and over the back of a chair, and his tie had gone somewhere, and someone had spilt champagne near his shoes. The waistcoat stayed on. She’d said she wanted it to. And in a corner room at the top of the hotel, with the harbour and the airport laid out below them in the dark, she undid every button of it, one at a time, from the top, the way he’d just undone forty-two of hers, and didn’t look at the buttons once.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the morning after the wedding the suit was hanging in the hotel wardrobe, and he was standing in front of it in a dressing gown, looking at it.

She came up behind him in his shirt from the night before, with the sleeves rolled twice, and put her arms round his waist. “What are you doing?”

“Thinking. I was going to have it cleaned. And stored properly.”

She reached past him and touched the sleeve. “Both sensible. Do you know what I think? It deserves to retire. No more boardrooms. No more petrol stations.”

“That’s a limited future.”

“It’s earned a rest.”

He considered it, and nodded. “All right.”

She took his hand. “Breakfast.”

He stopped. She gave him a look over her shoulder. He started again. “Have you— Would you like breakfast, Mrs. Ren?”

“That’s three times. I’m keeping my name and you know it.”

“I know. Would you like breakfast, Xu Song-Zhu, who married me yesterday?”

“Much better,” said his wife.

They left the wardrobe door open. The suit hung inside it, charcoal grey and only slightly worse for the night: a little worn, a little altered, still recognisably itself. It had been bought for business. It had sat on a concrete ledge with dinner in a paper bag, and stood in the rain in a doorway while he kissed her, and lain awake on a sofa beside her through the worst month of her life. And yesterday it had stood beside her at the end of an aisle.

“Hao. You’re still staring at it,” she called from the other room.

He shut the wardrobe. “I was saying goodbye to its working life.”

“To a suit?”

“To a very good colleague,” said Ren Hao, and went to find her.

chapters.title: The Night Before the Report
chapters.desc: The night before the interim statement, alone on the fourth floor, she writes him the letter she’ll never send. Wei Long lands in Lima at twenty to two.
chapters.epigraph: “But I love you.”
chapters.content:
At a quarter to midnight on Sunday the eighteenth of October 2026, Xu Song-Zhu finished the interim statement.

She read it once, and again, and a third time, because there were sentences in it that must not be allowed to mean more than the evidence supported. A maintenance failure had been identified as a significant factor in the sequence of events. The evidence supported that. It didn’t settle every question. It didn’t explain the eleven seconds missing from both recorders, or establish the whole chain that had ended with an aircraft in the sea two kilometres short of the runway. The investigation was continuing.

Further findings will be communicated when the available evidence permits.

She looked at the sentence until the screen dimmed, and touched the trackpad to wake it.

A hundred and eighty people. A hundred and eighty families who’d waited eleven weeks for somebody to tell them something that made sense. In the morning they’d get a document that explained one important part of what had happened, and nothing that would make any of it feel less impossible.

She put both hands flat on the desk. The fourth floor was empty. A cleaning trolley went by somewhere down the corridor. The lights hummed. Her coffee had been cold since about nine.

She hadn’t looked at her phone since the afternoon. There were messages from her team, two missed calls from the recorder laboratory, and one from him, sent at a quarter past eight.

Ren Hao: I’m thinking of you tonight. No need to reply. Wei Long’s at the hub. He boards for Lima at ten.

She’d read it, and not answered. Not because she hadn’t wanted to. She’d spent four weeks learning the difference between wanting someone and being ready to let them close again, and the difference had worn her out.

She turned the phone over and opened a new document, and left it blank.

✦ ✦ ✦

For a long time she didn’t type anything. The first word came just after midnight.

Hao,

She deleted it. She typed it again.

I don’t know how to tell you I miss you without it sounding like I’m asking you to come back.

She left that there. Her fingers moved more slowly after it.

I miss the noise you make in the kitchen. I miss opening the fridge and finding things I don’t remember buying. I miss your shoes by the door, even though I used to tell you they were in the wrong place. I miss coming home and having someone to tell about the day who doesn’t need me to explain why some things are hard.

She sat back. The room had got too small.

In the morning there’d be a briefing, and cameras, and questions from the airline and the families and the press. Some people would say the investigation had gone too far, and some that it hadn’t gone far enough. Some would want certainty from a document that could only offer what the evidence allowed. She’d stand in front of all of them and explain the difference, the way she always did.

She went back to the page.

I know you’d say I don’t have to be strong all the time. I know you’d say I can ring you. I know you’d come if I asked.

She looked at the last sentence until it blurred. He’d read a message like that carefully, more than once. He wouldn’t ring straight away if he thought she hadn’t asked him to. He’d learned that. He might send something small. I’m here. And she might answer, or she might not. That was the whole of the problem. She wanted him there, and she was still frightened of what happened to her when she let herself need him.

✦ ✦ ✦

Just before one she wrote about the report.

Tomorrow people will read that a maintenance failure was a significant factor. Some of them will be angry that it took this long. Some will be angry that it doesn’t tell them everything. Some will be looking for someone to blame, and some will be looking for someone to tell them that the person they loved didn’t die for nothing.

Her throat closed.

I don’t know how to give them that.

It wouldn’t have survived one meeting on the fourth floor, and she kept going.

I know what we’ve established, and what we haven’t, and why we can’t turn not knowing into an answer just because people are suffering. But sometimes I wish I could.

She thought of Mrs. Ting, in the summer, with a blue school exercise book held in both hands on her knees, asking whether her husband had heard the pilot tell them they were going to die, and closing the book, and saying that everybody had an explanation. She thought of the laboratory on a Friday nine days ago, and a crumpled phone from the seabed, and the lights going out on it, and a man’s voice on the cabin speakers in the dark after the brace call, saying six words to somebody who wasn’t there. She’d written on the record that nobody was to call them his last words. Then, alone in that room, she’d cried with her face on her arm on the laboratory bench until her throat hurt.

She typed:

There are things I hear that I can’t bring home. I don’t mean I’m not allowed to talk about them. I mean I don’t know how to hear a voice say the last thing it ever said and then walk back into a room where the coffee machine still works and somebody’s asking if I want lunch. I don’t want you to carry those things for me.

She stopped, and then:

But I wish I didn’t have to carry all of them by myself.

The cursor blinked at the end. She let it.

✦ ✦ ✦

At eighteen minutes past one a thin line of light came on round the edges of the phone on the desk. She turned it over.

Ren Hao: Still awake? You don’t have to answer. I woke up and wondered if you were still at the office.

She almost laughed. He’d always been terrible at pretending he wasn’t worried. But there was no call after it. No car outside the authority. No food at the front desk with her name on it. He’d asked, and left the choice with her, and that was all.

She typed I’m nearly done, and deleted it. She typed It’s finished, and deleted that too. She put the phone down. She wasn’t ready, and that was allowed.

✦ ✦ ✦

The last paragraph took her until nearly two.

I don’t know when I’ll be ready to come home. I don’t know if tomorrow will make anything easier. I don’t know how much longer this will take, or how many more things we’ll find that make the world feel less safe. I don’t know how to be the woman you love when most of me is still sitting in a room with no windows, listening to things that happened to people I never met.

Her hands were shaking. She looked at the place where the next sentence would go, and typed it without thinking at all, because it was the only thing on the page she’d never needed to think about.

But I love you.

She stared at it. She’d never once said it to him out loud: not at a restaurant with half the room applauding, or on a kitchen floor at three in the morning, or in a beach house with nobody for a kilometre. Here it was, in a document with no title, on a work computer, at two in the morning, to a man who was asleep or not asleep on the wrong side of the harbour.

She added one more line.

I’m sorry I don’t know what to do with it yet.

She read the whole letter twice. She could imagine sending it. She could imagine him reading it at his kitchen table with one hand flat beside his phone, still, and understanding it. And then she’d have to let him understand. She’d have to let him see how much she missed him, how much she still wanted him, how frightened she was of needing him.

She saved it. She called it Untitled. She closed it.

✦ ✦ ✦

At two she stood up. She washed her cup. She put the statement into the secure folder. She checked that the evidence store was locked, and checked the lights, and the door, and did every ordinary thing with the same care she’d given the report. There was one more message.

Ren Hao: Wei Long’s landed. Going to her now. Good night, Song-Zhu. I hope tomorrow goes as well as it can.

She read it twice, and stood still in the empty office, because Isla was alive in a city that had come down on the other side of the Pacific and a man had just walked out of an airport towards her, and Ren Hao had sent the news to Song-Zhu before he’d slept.

She typed: Good night. I’m glad. Tell Isla. She thought about adding something else, and her thumb stayed over the keys long enough for the screen to dim twice. Then she sent it as it was, and put the phone in her bag, and didn’t take it out again until she was home.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the other side of the harbour, Ren Hao was awake on his own sofa with a book open on his knee. He hadn’t turned a page in an hour.

When his phone buzzed he looked down at once.

Song-Zhu (Fuel on Her Boots): Good night. I’m glad. Tell Isla.

He read it, and replied Good night. Get some sleep if you can, and put the phone face up on the arm of the sofa, and didn’t send anything else.

He didn’t know that she’d written his name at the top of a blank page. He didn’t know she’d written about the kitchen, and the fridge, and his shoes by the door. He didn’t know that she’d typed three words she’d never said to him and left them there. He only knew that she’d answered, and for tonight that was enough. He’d be awake again at four.

✦ ✦ ✦

She got home at half past two. She took her shoes off and left her bag by the door. The flat was quiet in the way she’d once thought she wanted.

Nobody asked whether she’d eaten. Nobody had left a glass of water on the bedside table.

She opened the freezer. At the back, behind the ice tray, there were four containers he’d left on the nineteenth of September, labelled in his narrow capitals with the contents and the date. She took out the one that said SOUP (THE GOOD ONE) and heated it, and ate half, and put the rest back in the fridge, and stood in her kitchen in the middle of the night wishing he’d been there to complain that she hadn’t finished it, and wishing just as hard that he wasn’t, and not knowing how to want both without hurting either of them.

The letter stayed on her work computer, unsent and unread. In the morning she stood in front of the cameras and spoke carefully, and explained what the investigation had established and what it hadn’t, and promised nothing the evidence couldn’t give. Across the harbour he read every word of the statement, and understood every sentence, and noticed what it didn’t say.

Neither of them knew, that morning, that the night before she’d written him the only letter she’d ever write that had no evidence number and no distribution list, and no conclusion. Only a woman alone at a desk, trying to find a way back to the person she loved without losing the part of herself she’d fought so hard to keep.

She never sent it. In January, in a kitchen, she said the middle of it to his face instead, three words at a time, until he believed her.

chapters.title: The Widow's Letter
chapters.desc: Nine days after the memorial, a letter from Mrs. Yuk and a photograph of a furious girl in a plait. She asks him to read it aloud.
chapters.epigraph: “For not looking away.”
chapters.content:
The letter came on Wednesday the eleventh of August 2027, nine days after the memorial on the headland.

It came through the authority’s correspondence channel, addressed to Ms. Xu Song-Zhu, Investigator-in-Charge, in careful handwriting on a plain white envelope, with no markings and no classification. She knew whose it was before she’d turned it over.

She sat at her desk with it unopened while the fourth floor went to lunch round her.

A year since the aircraft had gone into the sea. Eight months since a small pale room on the ground floor and a sheet of paper with six words on it. Nine days since a woman in grey had stood at the end of an awning and told her he’d have been so angry. The final report was out. The cause was named. There were answers now, though not all of them. Never all of them.

She opened it. Inside was a folded letter, two sheets, and a photograph.

The photograph was of a girl of about eleven standing beside a man in a pilot’s uniform, with her arms folded and her long plait over one shoulder and an expression of deliberate, theatrical boredom. The man had one arm round her shoulders and was grinning at whoever held the camera. On the back, in the same handwriting:

Before her school concert. She told him he was embarrassing. He wore his uniform on purpose.

She unfolded the letter.

Dear Ms. Xu,
I hope you remember me. We met last December, in a small room, with my daughter. I was the woman who asked you whether he sounded like himself.
You told me it was his voice. You didn’t tell me anything you couldn’t know. At the time part of me hated that. I wanted you to tell me he wasn’t frightened. I wanted something that would let me sleep. You didn’t give me that, and I understand why now.
I have read the final report. Many times. Bo-yee says I read it like a textbook before an exam. I wanted to know everything it could tell us, and where it stopped. I don’t think I will ever be at peace with the fact that it ends where the evidence ends. But I am grateful that you didn’t invent an ending for us. Thank you for telling us the truth, even when the truth wasn’t finished.

Song-Zhu put the page down, and picked it up again.

I want to tell you something about the six words.
Bo-yee still complains when I call her my little girl. She is twelve, and thirteen in October, and therefore, she says, legally not little. Her father called her that when she was taller than his shoulder in her school shoes. She pretends she hates it. I think she misses it more than anything.
She keeps your sheet of paper inside her school blazer. She has moved it from blazer to blazer since December. When it got soft at the folds she asked me to buy a plastic sleeve, and now it lives in that. She has never let me read it again. She says she doesn’t need to, she knows it, and that it’s hers.
I don’t know what he knew at that moment. I don’t know what he was thinking, or whether he was frightened. But I know he tried to say goodbye to his daughter, and I know she has it in ordinary writing. I’m grateful the words survived. I’m more grateful that you wrote them down for a twelve-year-old the way she asked, and not the way a report would.

Song-Zhu pressed her fingertips into her eyes.

She was back, for a second, in the laboratory on a Friday in October: the crumpled phone, the damaged audio, the specialist in the third chair, the silence after the recording ended. She remembered sitting at her desk afterwards wondering how a voice could stay in a room after the person who’d made it had gone. She remembered a night after that, alone at that same desk, writing a letter she’d never sent.

She wondered how many things people carried because they didn’t know where else to put them.

Bo-yee has the photograph I’ve enclosed, the original. This is a copy. She says her father looks ridiculous in it. I told her he spent twenty minutes getting the uniform right because he knew she would complain. She says he should have worn a different tie. I told her he would have argued about that. We still argue about him. About what he’d have said, whether he’d have laughed at something. I think that’s how we keep him in the house now.
I don’t want you to think we are only grateful because of the words. We are grateful because you treated him as a person and not a case. You treated the families as people who had to go on living after the report was finished. I know you went back to work the next morning, and that there were other aircraft and other families. I don’t know how you do that. I hope you have found a way to rest.
Thank you, Ms. Xu. For your honesty, and your patience, and for not looking away.
Yuk Wai-ling

She read the signature twice, and folded the letter along its own creases, and didn’t cry. Not then. It happened a few minutes later, when she picked up the photograph again and looked at the girl’s face and her arms folded so hard across her chest.

Mrs. Yuk was right. It was a ridiculous tie.

✦ ✦ ✦

Ren Hao came home at seven with dinner in a bag and found her on the sofa with the letter and the photograph side by side on the low table. He looked at her first, and then at the table, and didn’t take the food out of the bag.

“Something’s happened.”

She looked up. “Not exactly. I got a letter. From the captain’s widow.”

He took his watch off and put it on the side table and sat down beside her. She handed him the photograph. He looked at it a long time, the grinning man and the furious child, and turned it over and read the back, and then turned it face up again and put it down carefully.

“She loves him very much,” he said.

“She does.”

“Would you like to tell me what the letter says?”

She nodded, and then didn’t, and he waited. “Would you read it to me? Out loud. I’ve read it once. I can’t hold it by myself again,” she said.

He looked at her. She couldn’t have explained it properly. Perhaps because she’d spent a year being the one who read things out, to rooms and families and microphones. Perhaps because, for once, she wanted to be the person who listened.

“Of course,” said Ren Hao.

He read slowly. It wasn’t the voice he used in meetings, or the one for difficult decisions. He read it like a man who understood the words belonged to someone who’d spent a long time finding the courage to write them. When he got to the part about a twelve-year-old being legally not little, Song-Zhu laughed, small and wet and unexpected. He glanced at her.

“She’s exactly like him, I think,” she said.

He smiled a little, and went on. At the paragraph about the six words his voice went lower. He didn’t skip anything, or soften anything. He read I know he tried to say goodbye to his daughter, and the page shook slightly between his fingers, and he stopped, and then he read the rest.

When he’d finished he folded it back into the envelope and held it on his knee.

“She thanked me. I don’t know what to do with that,” said Song-Zhu.

“You don’t have to do anything with it.”

“I keep thinking about the day I found it. In the laboratory. I knew what it meant for the investigation, and all I could think about was that girl, and that she was going to grow up without anybody calling her that again, and I couldn’t do anything about it.”

He took her hand. “You gave her something that survived.”

“It isn’t enough.”

“No. It isn’t enough,” he said gently.

He didn’t tell her everything happened for a reason. He didn’t say the letter meant she’d done enough, or make a family’s grief into a comfort for her. He held her hand, and after a while she leaned into him, and he put his arms round her, and she cried properly against his shoulder, not the tears she’d let out in laboratories and empty offices and between meetings, but the other kind, the kind that took as long as they took. He didn’t ask how long. He didn’t look at the clock.

When she pulled back at last she looked embarrassed. “Sorry. Your shirt.”

There was a dark patch on his shoulder. He looked at it, and at her. “Song-Zhu. It’s a shirt.”

She laughed wetly, and he took the dinner out of the bag at last, and they ate it late.

✦ ✦ ✦

He was washing up when she spoke from the sofa, with the photograph in her hand again.

“Do you think she knows? That he was saying goodbye?”

He turned the tap off and dried his hands. “I think she knows what the words gave her. She says she knows he tried. Perhaps that’s what she’s chosen to keep.”

He came and sat beside her and looked at the photograph over her shoulder.

“What’s the girl’s name?”

“Bo-yee.”

He said it once, under his breath, the way he did with names he meant to keep. “Will you write back?”

“I don’t know what I’d say.”

“You don’t have to know tonight.”

Later, when he’d gone to bed, she sat in the living room on her own and read the last line again. For not looking away. She thought about everybody who’d worked on it: the divers, the engineers, the metallurgists, the liaison officers who’d sat with families and answered the same question for the hundredth time, the people on her team who’d rebuilt a sequence of events out of pieces. She’d once believed that doing the work properly meant keeping everything she felt outside it. She knew now it had never asked her to stop caring. It had asked her to care without letting it bend the truth.

She took out her phone.

Song-Zhu: I think I’ll write back to her.

Hao (Three-Piece): I think she’d like that.

Song-Zhu: I don’t know what to say.

Hao (Three-Piece): You don’t have to make it perfect. You can just say thank you too.

She went to bed, and lay down against his side, and spoke into the dark. “Thank you. For reading it.”

“Any time,” said Ren Hao, and found her hand under the covers, and held it.

✦ ✦ ✦

She wrote back three days later. It was short. She thanked Mrs. Yuk for trusting her with it. She said she’d read it carefully, and that she was glad of the photograph. She didn’t pretend to understand the shape of what the family was living with. She didn’t repeat the six words, or offer any reading of them, or promise that time would make it easier. At the end she wrote:

Thank you for reminding me that behind every investigation there are people who go on living with what we find. I will remember your family. Please tell Bo-yee that I think the tie was a deliberate choice, and that he’d have argued about it for a week.

She signed it and sent it through the proper channel.

That evening she found him in the kitchen cutting fruit, and stood behind him with her arms round his waist.

“You sent it?”

“This afternoon.”

“How do you feel?”

She thought about it, with her cheek on his back. “Sad. And grateful. I think that’s all.”

He put the knife down and turned round in her arms and held her a moment. “Then come and eat.”

The copy of the photograph went on the bookshelf in her flat, beside the final report. Not as evidence, and not as a reminder of what had gone wrong. It was there for the people who were still there after the investigation ended: for a girl who would be thirteen in October and still complained about being called little, and who’d probably spend the rest of her life pretending not to miss it. Somewhere, a father had called her that one last time in the dark. A year later her mother had written to say thank you for a voice that had survived, for a truth that hadn’t been invented, for someone who’d listened. And for someone who’d read the letter aloud, when the words had got too heavy to hold alone.

chapters.title: The Dog
chapters.desc: Joyce goes to a wedding in Penang and they keep Momo for the weekend. Momo prefers his wife, his pillow and the space between them.
chapters.epigraph: “Are you having an affair with a dog?”
chapters.content:
Ren Hao had a problem: his assistant’s dog liked him too much. Or, more accurately, he liked his assistant’s dog too much, and the dog had worked it out years ago and had been exploiting it ever since.

Her name was Momo. She was white, roughly the size and shape of a loaf of bread, and she belonged to Joyce, who’d made the mistake in 2024 of bringing her to the office once when the dog-sitter cancelled, and had been bringing her ever since, because Ren Hao had asked her to. Momo had a small tartan cushion beside Joyce’s desk on the floor above his, from which she’d supervised five years of crises and attended one wedding in a bow tie. When he came up in the lift she stood up and her tail went so fast her whole back half moved.

“How is Momo?”

Joyce didn’t look up from her tablet. “Fine, thank you, Mr. Ren.”

“Her stomach?”

“Fine.”

“Is she still frightened of the vacuum cleaner?”

Joyce looked up. “Would you like me to put a meeting with Momo in your diary?”

He considered it. “Does she have availability?”

✦ ✦ ✦

Song-Zhu found the evidence on a Thursday in June 2029, waiting in his office for him to finish a call before dinner. On his desk, in a small silver frame that hadn’t been there in January, there was a photograph of Momo in a blue bandana.

She picked it up. “Who’s this?”

“Momo.”

“I know it’s Momo. Why is Momo in a frame on your desk?”

“Joyce sent it.”

She put it down, and saw the second one, tucked under the edge of his monitor: Momo asleep on a sofa with her paws in the air. And a third, on the bookshelf behind him: Momo beside a birthday cake with a single candle in it.

Song-Zhu turned round slowly. “How many photographs of Momo do you have?”

“Those are the recent ones.”

“Recent?”

He finished his call. “Yes, sweetheart?”

“Are you having an affair with a dog?”

He laughed so loudly that Joyce, on the floor above, sent him a message asking if he was all right.

✦ ✦ ✦

Her revenge arrived the following week, when Joyce’s sister got married in Penang and Joyce needed someone to have Momo for the weekend. She mentioned it while handing him a folder, with Song-Zhu sitting on the sofa in his office at the time, eating his biscuits.

“I’ve got someone for Saturday. I’m still trying to sort out Sunday.”

Song-Zhu looked up. “We’ll take her.”

Joyce blinked. “Really?”

“Of course.”

Ren Hao put his pen down. “You’re taking Momo? To our flat?”

“That’s generally where dog-sitting happens.”

“Do you know how to look after her? She’s very particular. About her food. About her walks. She doesn’t like being left on her own for long.”

“Hao. Is there anything else I should know? Does she need a board meeting before breakfast?”

Joyce made a small choking sound and left the room.

“She’s very affectionate,” said Ren Hao, with dignity.

“I’ll manage,” said Song-Zhu.

✦ ✦ ✦

Momo arrived at their flat on Saturday morning with a bed, a bag of food, two toys, a brush, a bottle of dog shampoo, a packet of treats, and two pages of instructions in Joyce’s handwriting, with headings.

Song-Zhu read them. “She’s left us her child.”

Momo sat between them on the hall floor, looking up. Song-Zhu crouched.

“Hello, Momo. Do you remember me?”

Momo put her nose into Song-Zhu’s palm, and her tail began to go, and then she rolled straight onto her back on the hall tiles with all four paws in the air.

“Oh, you’re friendly,” said Song-Zhu, and scratched her stomach, and one back leg kicked with joy.

Ren Hao looked down. “She doesn’t usually do that straight away.”

“Perhaps she’s got good taste.”

He crouched down beside them. “Momo. Here, girl.”

Momo turned her head and looked at him. Then she turned it back to Song-Zhu.

He went still. Song-Zhu saw it, and her smile became dangerous.

“Oh,” she said.

“She’s excited. It’s a new flat.”

“Of course.”

“She knows me. I’ve known her for five years.”

“Naturally,” said Song-Zhu, and Momo sneezed.

“Traitor,” said Ren Hao to the dog.

✦ ✦ ✦

By lunch Momo had inspected the living room and the kitchen and the little study at the back with the shelf over the desk, decided that the rug by the sofa was hers, and discovered that Song-Zhu would give her carrot. Song-Zhu sat on the floor snapping a carrot into pieces.

“She doesn’t eat carrots,” said Ren Hao from the kitchen doorway.

“Page two. Under treats. She loves them.”

He watched Momo take a piece delicately from his wife’s fingers. “You’re spoiling her.”

“She’s a guest.”

“She’s got a bed. And three toys. And her own food.”

Song-Zhu smiled up at him. “Are you jealous?”

“No.”

“She’s very beautiful, isn’t she? Look at her little face.”

“She’s a dog.”

“An exceptionally beautiful dog,” said Song-Zhu.

“You’re enjoying this.”

“Immensely.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The real trouble began at bedtime. Momo had decided that Ren Hao’s pillow was the most comfortable place in the flat. Song-Zhu came out of the bathroom and found him standing beside the bed looking at it, and Momo lying on it, perfectly content, and her husband looking personally betrayed.

“What’s happened?”

“She’s taken my place.”

“Perhaps she likes your pillow.”

“It’s my pillow.”

“Perhaps she likes you.”

“She’s got a bed. A perfectly good bed. Joyce packed it.”

“Hao. She’s the size of a loaf.”

“That doesn’t make it her bed.”

Song-Zhu sat down on the mattress, and Momo lifted her head at once and climbed into her lap. He watched her settle there, and looked at the empty space beside his wife.

“Interesting,” he said.

She reached out and took his hand. “Sit with us.”

He sat. She leaned against his shoulder. Momo moved, with great purpose, into the exact space between them, and lay down.

He looked at the dog, and at the ceiling, and said evenly, “This is becoming unreasonable,” and Song-Zhu laughed so much she had to put her face in the duvet.

✦ ✦ ✦

She woke at ten past one and found him awake beside her, staring at the ceiling, with Momo asleep across his ankles.

“Can’t sleep?”

“She’s occupying a strategic amount of the bed.”

“She’s the size of a cushion.”

“A very strategic cushion.”

She laughed into his shoulder. “You’re ridiculous.”

“You’re supposed to be on my side.”

“I am. I’m laughing. Those aren’t mutually exclusive.”

She reached over him and kissed his cheek, and then his mouth, and he turned towards her in the dark, and his hand came up under the hem of the shirt she’d gone to bed in and rested warm on her back, and the kiss went slower and deeper and stopped being about the dog altogether. She moved closer. He made the small sound he made when she pressed against him, and his hand slid lower—

At the foot of the bed Momo let out a single sleepy wuff. They both froze.

“She’s watching us,” whispered Song-Zhu.

“She’s asleep.”

“She’s judging us. Look at her ears.”

Ren Hao closed his eyes. “I cannot believe this. I’m forty minutes from my own wife and there’s a loaf on my feet.”

“You’re four centimetres from your own wife.”

“Emotionally, forty minutes.”

She laughed until the bed shook, and Momo sighed the deep sigh of a creature whose patience was being tried, and turned round twice, and lay down again on his ankles.

✦ ✦ ✦

Sunday morning was worse. Momo had learned that he was where the treats came from. She followed him into the kitchen, sat beside his chair, watched him make coffee with total devotion, and when he opened the fridge she stood up on her back legs and put both front paws on his trouser leg.

“No,” he said.

She tipped her head to one side.

“No.”

A small whine.

Song-Zhu came in behind him. “What are you doing?”

“Negotiating.”

“Is she asking for something?”

“Everything.”

He picked up a piece of carrot. Momo sat at once, perfectly, like a dog in a manual. He gave it to her.

“You gave in,” said Song-Zhu.

“I rewarded good behaviour.”

“She’s manipulating you.”

“She’s a dog.”

“Exactly. And she’s winning.”

He looked down at Momo. “Don’t listen to her.”

“You’re talking to her like she understands.”

“She understands tone.”

“Then tell her you’re jealous,” said Song-Zhu, and he looked at her, and the dog looked at him, and there was a long silence in the kitchen.

“I’m not jealous,” said Ren Hao.

She laughed until she had to put her coffee down.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the afternoon she found him on the living-room floor with his laptop open beside him, typing a memo with one hand and rubbing Momo’s stomach with the other, while Momo lay on her back with her paws curled up, in bliss. She took a photograph.

“Don’t,” he said.

“Too slow.”

She sat down beside him on the rug. “You’re very affectionate with her.”

“She likes it.”

“So do I,” said Song-Zhu.

His hand stopped. He looked at her. She looked back, perfectly innocent.

He shut the laptop. He reached for her, and she laughed as he pulled her down onto the rug beside him with one arm round her waist, and he kissed her the way he hadn’t been allowed to at one in the morning, and she put her hand in his hair—

Momo climbed over her legs and pushed her nose firmly between their faces.

Ren Hao lifted his head. His expression was one of profound disbelief. Song-Zhu collapsed against him, helpless.

✦ ✦ ✦

Joyce came for her at a quarter past nine on Monday, still brown from Penang.

“Thank you so much. I’m sorry about the trouble.”

“No trouble. She was lovely,” said Song-Zhu.

Momo heard Joyce’s voice and shot down the hall like a small white comet, and Joyce crouched and gathered her up. “Hello, baby. Did you have a good weekend?”

Ren Hao appeared behind his wife with the food container. “Her breakfast was at eight. She had carrot yesterday afternoon. She seemed to enjoy it. She slept well, though she moved about a good deal. She prefers the rug by the sofa to her bed. And she doesn’t like our vacuum cleaner either.”

Joyce looked at him. Song-Zhu looked at the ceiling.

Joyce took the container. “Thank you, Mr. Ren. Did you both enjoy having her?”

“Very much,” said Song-Zhu.

“Yes,” said Ren Hao, at once.

Joyce smiled. “Would you like me to ask you next time I need someone?”

“Yes,” said Ren Hao.

When the door had shut, Song-Zhu leaned on it and looked at him. “You miss her already.”

“She’s gone home.”

“That’s not what I asked.”

He looked at the door. “She was good company.”

“Better than me?”

“Don’t be ridiculous. You can use a washing machine.”

She laughed, and reached up and straightened his collar, and kissed him, and kept her forehead against his. “Don’t worry. I’ll still love you even though you’re second favourite.”

“Second?”

“Momo comes first.”

He looked at her. “I’ll remember that.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Three weeks later Joyce put a new photograph on his desk: Momo after her first proper haircut, sitting on a cushion in the blue bandana, looking freshly offended.

“Very beautiful. Does she still sleep on your pillow?” said Ren Hao.

“Sometimes.”

“All right,” he said, and Joyce went out, and a minute later his phone went.

Song-Zhu: Did you get the new photo of Momo?

Hao (Three-Piece): Yes. She’s very beautiful.

Song-Zhu: Prettier than your husband?

Hao (Three-Piece): I am your husband.

Song-Zhu: I know. Answer the question.

Hao (Three-Piece): No.

Song-Zhu: Good answer. I miss her.

He looked at the photograph, and opened his diary, and made an entry for the next weekend Joyce had said she might be away: MOMO. DOG-SITTING. He looked at it, and added underneath: Buy carrots. Second pillow.

He never admitted he’d been jealous. He did buy Momo a new bed for their flat: an extremely good one, with a raised edge and a washable cover, which lived permanently beside the sofa from then on. When his wife asked him why, he said she was a guest.

“Of course, darling,” said Song-Zhu, who knew better. So did Momo.

chapters.title: Anniversary Hangar
chapters.desc: Their first wedding anniversary, a borrowed hangar at the flying club, a kettle with a ribbon on it, and the lights turned off on purpose.
chapters.epigraph: “I’ve found out a year isn’t enough.”
chapters.content:
She found him in the hall with his car keys in his hand and a bag over his shoulder, and a face of perfect innocence that wouldn’t have fooled a first-year trainee.

She’d changed into soft trousers and a jumper and her old canvas shoes. “Something you can move in. Is this acceptable?” she said.

“Entirely.”

“Am I allowed a question?”

“Three. That’s the rule. I learned it from a professional,” said Ren Hao.

✦ ✦ ✦

The drive took forty minutes. She spent the first question on whether she’d need identification, and he said no. She spent the second on whether there’d be other people, and he said no. She spent the third on food.

“Yes,” he said.

“What kind?”

“The kind you like.”

“That’s suspiciously vague, for a man who once laminated an agenda.”

He smiled at the road and said nothing, and she settled back in her seat and watched the coast go by in the dark, and then the hedge, and then a windsock she knew, lit from below by the light over the clubhouse door, and she sat up.

“Hao.”

“Yes?”

“This is the flying club.”

“It is.”

“You’re proposing to me again.”

“No. I’m taking you to dinner. In a hangar. On our anniversary. There’s a difference,” said Ren Hao.

✦ ✦ ✦

The man with the tea was waiting by the gate in his club jacket, with a torch and a bunch of keys. He’d been making tea at that clubhouse for longer than either of them had known it existed, and he’d stood in that doorway on the first of April last year and watched a woman propose to a man by the wire, and heard the man’s answer go four kilometres to the tower.

“Mr. Ren. Ms. Xu.”

He handed Ren Hao the keys.

“Lights are on the left inside the door. The kettle’s in the back if you want it. The Cessna’s been put to bed and chocked, so don’t go moving her, she’s had a long week. I’ve locked the clubhouse. Leave the keys in the box.”

He looked at Song-Zhu a second longer.

“Happy anniversary.”

“How did you—”

“He asked me in August,” said the man with the tea, and walked away into the dark towards the car park with his torch going in front of him.

She stared at her husband. “August?”

“Someone owed me a favour. In a manner of speaking. I paid for a new kettle.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The long hangar at the end of the field was dark except for a row of low lights along one wall. They lit the concrete floor, and the club’s high-winged four-seater standing in the middle of it with its wheels chocked and a cover over the engine, and, at the far end, a small table that hadn’t been there in April, laid for two, with a cloth and two covered plates and a bottle of wine and a small cake with a single candle on it.

She stood in the doorway and looked at all of it.

“Is that ours?” she said, of the aircraft.

“No.”

“Disappointing.”

He laughed, and she walked down the hangar with her hands in her pockets, the way she walked across every apron she’d ever been on, looking at everything.

Beside the cake there was a photograph in a frame: the two of them at the wedding, a year ago, in the glass room above the harbour, her hand flat on the front of his waistcoat and his head bent towards hers.

“You brought our wedding photograph to a hangar.”

“It seemed appropriate.”

She put it down carefully, and turned round. “One year.”

“One year.”

“How does it feel?”

He thought about it properly, the way he did now with questions she asked him. “Like I should have married you sooner.”

“That’s not how time works.”

He tucked a piece of her hair back behind her ear. “I know. But I would have. If I’d known on the thirteenth of June what I know now, I’d have married you at the taxi rank.”

“I’d have said no. I’d only known you three hours.”

“Then I’d have asked again the next morning. At the fence.”

“With twelve lunches.”

He kissed her, not quickly, standing beside a borrowed table at the end of a dark hangar. “Happy anniversary.”

“Happy anniversary, husband.”

✦ ✦ ✦

It was the food she liked, from the place by their old building, the dish he’d mentioned once in March 2026 and she’d brought home to him in a container a year later. It was still warm. He poured the wine. She stole a piece off his plate, and he pretended not to see, and she did it again.

“That’s mine.”

“Marriage means sharing.”

“Does it? Then I’ll have some of yours.”

She moved her plate out of his reach, and he laughed, and she gave him a mouthful off her own fork anyway.

The cake was from the bakery by the ferry pier. Across the top, in white icing, in capitals he’d clearly dictated over the phone:

ONE YEAR. STILL CHOOSING YOU.

“That’s terribly sweet,” said Song-Zhu.

“I considered something longer.”

“Thank God you didn’t.”

They ate it standing up by the table, feeding each other bites off the same fork, and at one point she leaned back against the table edge with her plate and looked at him.

“You’re staring,” he said.

“I’m allowed. Do you remember the first time we were in a hangar together?”

“The training hangar. October 2025. You put my name on the visitors’ list under partner and gave me a laminated pass.”

“You wore it like a medal.”

He put his plate down. “It was the most important thing anyone had ever pinned on me. And then February 2027. The same hangar. Your marking. My jacket.”

“Do not stand,” said Song-Zhu, and they both laughed, and the laugh went up into the roof of the hangar and came back.

“I’ve never told you that the jacket’s still in the wardrobe. I never sent it to the cleaner. I retired it with full honours,” he said.

She stopped laughing and looked at him, and then she put her plate down and reached for his hand. “Come on.”

“Where?”

She tipped her head at the four-seater standing dark in the middle of the floor. “Under the wing.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He’d planned for this, of course. He’d planned for everything, and then, these days, he waited to be asked. He went to the bag and took out a folded blanket, thick and soft, and two pillows from their own bed, and she watched him lay them out on the clean concrete under the high wing, just clear of the strut, and square the corners.

“You brought our pillows.”

“I brought a second blanket as well, in case you were cold. And your jacket.”

She looked at the folded jacket on the equipment case. “Of course you did. I don’t want it.”

He went to the wall and turned off the long row of lights one at a time, until there was only the faint green of the emergency sign over the side door and the light over the clubhouse coming in through the gap at the bottom of the big doors, a long thin bar of gold across the floor. The aircraft went to a dark shape above them. The wing was a roof.

He came back to her in the near dark and stood behind her, and put his arms round her waist, and his mouth against the side of her neck where the chain was.

“Nobody’s going to come in?”

He kissed under her ear. “He’s locked the gate behind him. I asked him in August. I didn’t tell him why.”

“He knows why.”

“He’s a man who makes tea for a living. He knows everything,” said Ren Hao.

She turned round in his arms and kissed him, and it was meant to be a small kiss and wasn’t. His hand went to the small of her back. Her fingers caught in the front of his shirt. He kissed her with the whole of a year of knowing exactly how she liked to be kissed, and the slow deliberate pleasure of not having to hurry at all, and when she pulled back he followed her for another.

“You’re eager.”

He spoke against her mouth. “I’ve been married to you for a year. I’ve found out a year isn’t enough.”

It was Song-Zhu who started undressing him. She took his jumper over his head and dropped it on the equipment case on top of her jacket. She undid his shirt, every button, the way she always did now, slowly, looking at his face and not the buttons, and pushed it off his shoulders, and put both hands flat on his chest in the dark and felt his heart going under them.

“Can I?” she said, with her fingers at his belt, because they asked each other things now, even after a year, even when the answer was obvious, and it had turned out that asking was its own kind of heat.

“Always,” said Ren Hao.

He undressed her in his turn, her jumper and the soft trousers and her shoes, and knelt to take off her socks one at a time, which made her laugh, and kissed the inside of her ankle, and the inside of her knee, and stood up with his hands sliding up the backs of her thighs. Then he laid her down on the blanket under the wing, on their own pillows, and came down beside her, and looked at her in the thin gold light.

“I can’t see your face properly,” she complained.

“Then you’ll have to go by other evidence,” said Ren Hao, and put his mouth on her throat.

He took his time. He always took his time with her, but tonight there was nowhere at all to be in the morning that either of them needed to be ready for, no report on her desk, no call waiting for him, and he used all of it. He kissed her collarbone and her breasts, one and then the other, slow and warm, until she was arching up off the blanket into his mouth with her hands in his hair. He kissed down her ribs and her stomach, and settled between her thighs, and held her open with his hands, and put his mouth on her, and she said his name to the underside of an aircraft wing in the dark, which nobody, she was fairly sure, had ever done in that hangar before.

He didn’t hurry. He brought her up slowly and let her down, and brought her up again, listening to her the way he’d learned to listen, every catch of breath, every change, until she was gripping the blanket in both fists and saying please and Hao and please, and then he didn’t let her down. She came with her back arched and her heels pressed into the blanket and the sound going up into the roof, and he stayed with her through all of it, and only lifted his head when she’d gone soft and shaking under his hands.

Her voice was barely a voice. “Up here. Now. I want your face.”

He came up her body and she pulled him down and wrapped her legs round him, and he pushed into her slowly, all the way, and they both went still, his forehead on hers, breathing.

“One year,” he said.

“Don’t you dare make a speech.”

He laughed, inside her, and she felt it, and gasped, and laughed too, and then neither of them was laughing. He moved slow and deep, and she moved with him, and found the light on his face at last, a thin gold line along his cheekbone and the edge of his mouth, and watched him. His ring touched hers every time their hands met on the blanket, a tiny sound in the dark. She held his face. She said I love you, out loud, into the ordinary dark, the way she’d promised in front of three hundred people that she’d say it, and he said it back into her mouth, and then he wasn’t slow any more, and she didn’t want him to be. She came again with her nails in his back and his name in the roof. He followed her a moment after, with his face in her neck and one long breath that shook all the way through him, and held her so tight that she couldn’t tell where the blanket ended or he began.

✦ ✦ ✦

Afterwards she lay on his chest under the wing with her hair everywhere and his shirt, which she’d retrieved from the equipment case, round her shoulders.

“Your anniversary surprise was successful,” she said into his skin.

“Only successful?”

“Very successful. I have one complaint.”

“What?”

“You turned all the lights off. I couldn’t see your face.”

He reached up to the equipment case without moving her, found his phone, and turned the torch on at its lowest, and laid it face up on the concrete a metre away, so that the light went up into the underside of the wing and came back soft and white on both of them.

“Better?”

She lifted her head and looked at him in it: his hair wrecked, his eyes half shut, the very particular face he only had after, which nobody else on earth had seen.

“Much,” said Song-Zhu.

They stayed until nearly midnight. At some point she was half asleep, and said, “Do you remember our first anniversary?”

“This is our first anniversary.”

She smiled into his chest. “I know. I meant the other one. The thirteenth of June. Every year.”

“The one where you kissed me to shut me up.”

“I’d like to do this next year. Come back here. And the year after. And when we’re old,” she said.

“Especially then,” said Ren Hao.

✦ ✦ ✦

At three minutes past midnight they finally dressed. He put his shirt back on, and gave up on buttoning it properly. She found one of her canvas shoes under the blanket and the other a metre away under the strut, which she checked, from habit, for anything she might have knocked, and found nothing, and patted once like a horse.

He watched her do it. “You just checked the aircraft for damage.”

“Of course I did. It’s been a long week for her. He said.”

They folded the blanket. They put the pillows back in the bag, and the photograph, and what was left of the cake. He turned the long lights back on one at a time, and the hangar came back round them, ordinary, with the four-seater standing on its chocks in the middle with its engine covered, as if it had never been anything but an aeroplane.

At the door she reached up and fixed his collar, which was crooked.

“You’re a married man. You should look respectable.”

“You’re wearing my shirt under your jumper.”

“That’s different.”

“How?”

“Because I’m your wife,” said Song-Zhu, and kissed him in the doorway of the hangar, and he locked it behind them, and put the keys in the box by the clubhouse door, beside a small new kettle with a ribbon still round its handle.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the morning she woke first, with his arm heavy across her waist, and reached for her phone. There was one photograph from the night before, taken before the lights went out: the dark hangar, the four-seater under the high roof, the little table at the end with half a cake on it, and a folded jacket on an equipment case. It was nothing anybody else would have looked at twice.

She put it in their shared album and wrote under it, 21 October 2029. First anniversary. Under the wing.

He stirred. “What are you doing?”

“Saving a memory.”

He opened one eye. “Of the hangar?”

“Of you, turning the lights off on purpose,” said Song-Zhu, and put the phone down, and turned into his arms, and outside the morning started without them.
